The charges in the present case read as follows: Alfred YEKATOM, a national of the CAR, born on 23 January 1975 in Bimbo, the CAR, also known as 'Alfred SARAGBA', 'ROMBHOT', 'RAMBO', 'RAMBOT', 'ROMBOT', 'RHOMBOT', 'ROMBO' or 'ROMBOHT', is criminally responsible for the war crimes of: (i) directing attacks against the civilian population, pursuant to and prohibited by article 8(2)(e)(i) of the Statute, in Bangui, including Cattin and the Boeing market, starting on 5 December 2013, on the basis of the conduct pertaining to Counts 2 to 6 and 8 (Count 1); (ii) murder, pursuant to and prohibited by article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, for: a.  the killing of between five and 13 persons, including Hassan Mahamat, at the Boeing market, four Muslim persons in Cattin, and Nina Pascal at the Boeing market, in the context of the attack on Bangui, including Cattin and Boeing, on 5 December 2013 (Count 3); b.  the killing of Lapo N'Gomat at the Yamwara School Base on or about 24 December 2013 (Count 16); c.  the killing of Deputy Mayor Saleh on or about 28 February 2014 in Mbaïki, in the context of the Anti-Balaka's advance through and takeover of villages along the PK9-Mbaïki Axis (including Sekia, Ndangala, Bimon, Kapou, Bossongo, Pissa, Mbaïki) (Count 27); (iii) displacement, pursuant to and prohibited by article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute, for: a.  the dislocation of nearly all Muslim persons residing in Cattin and Boeing to PK5, a predominantly Muslim neighbourhood in Bangui, other parts of the CAR or neighbouring countries, starting from 5 December 2013 in the context of the attack on Bangui, including Cattin and Boeing, on 5 December 2013 (Count 5); b.  the dislocation of the majority of the Muslim population from their towns and villages between on or about 10 January 2014 and on or about 6 February 2014, in the context of the Anti-Balaka's advance through and takeover of villages along the PK9-Mbaïki Axis (including Sekia, Ndangala, Bimon, Kapou, Bossongo, Pissa, Mbaïki) (Count 25); FINDINGS OF FACT

In this section, the Chamber sets out the material facts and circumstances of this case as they have been established to the requisite threshold upon its assessment of the evidence submitted and discussed before it at trial. They are the facts and circumstances which form the basis for the Chamber's decision under Article 74 of the Statute. The reasoning for the Chamber's determination in this regard is provided below, in Section IV ('Factual findings and evidentiary analysis'). In that section, the Chamber discusses, also in light of the arguments made at trial, the evidence which, directly or by way of inference (thus, through additional facts of a subsidiary nature), supports each of these findings on the facts and circumstances described in the charges.
The legal characterisation of these facts and circumstances, in light of the charges brought against the accused, is made in Section V.B ('Legal characterisation of facts').

The Chamber clarifies that, pursuant to Article 74(2) of the Statute, it has ensured that its findings of fact do not exceed the facts and circumstances described in the charges as confirmed by the Pre-Trial Chamber. The conflict in the Central African Republic between 2012 and 2014 The formation of the Seleka, its advance to and takeover of Bangui, and ensuing violence

Around August 2012, a coalition of armed groups opposing then-President François Bozizé emerged in the Central African Republic (CAR) under the name of the 'Seleka', led by CAR citizens and including elements from Chad and Sudan. Michel Djotodia became the leader of the Seleka.

Starting in late 2012, the Seleka advanced towards Bangui. The Libreville agreement, concluded in January 2013, presented an attempt to end the crisis, leading to a government including representatives of various factions, with François Bozizé remaining president and Nicolas Tiangaye as prime minister, Michel Djotodia as deputy prime minister and minister of defence, and Mr Ngaïssona as minister of youth, sports, arts and culture.

At the same time, the widely reported advance of the Seleka, and violent acts and abuses committed in this context, including against civilians, sparked reactions within the civilian and political sphere: 'Coalition citoyenne d'opposition aux rébellions armées' (COCORA) and 'Comité d'organisation des actions citoyennes' (COAC) were two organisations which were active in mobilising support for François Bozizé in light of the Seleka advance. They erected checkpoints or roadblocks at which passers-by and vehicles were checked, with the objective of identifying Seleka infiltrators and people deemed to be associated with or in support of them, including Muslims. The individuals manning these checkpoints were armed with bladed weapons and, in some cases, with AK-47s.
On 24 March 2013, the Seleka took control of Bangui. Michel Djotodia proclaimed himself President of the CAR.

After the Seleka took control of Bangui on 24 March 2013, they committed violence and abuses in various localities across the CAR, in particular against individuals considered to be associated with François Bozizé, his Gbaya ethnic group, his government's security forces, and non-Muslims. Mr Ngaïssona's properties in Bangui were looted. However, the Muslim civilian population was not entirely spared from this violence.

The Seleka included fighters in particular from Chad and Sudan. It was led by Central African Muslims. Due to the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and in light of its perceived composition, tensions in particular between Muslim and non-Muslim communities increased.

The number of Seleka elements varied greatly in the course of 2013. While counting several thousand elements at the time of the take-over in March 2013, their numbers grew significantly until the end of that year. Individuals and their activities in Cameroon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo

Following the Seleka taking over Bangui and control in the CAR, François Bozizé, Mr Ngaïssona, Bernard Mokom and others fled to Cameroon. Maxime Mokom, Mr Yekatom and others fled to Zongo, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Through meetings in Cameroon and communications with individuals in Zongo, in particular Maxime Mokom, who in turn liaised with persons and groups in Bangui and in the provinces, François Bozizé, Mr Ngaïssona, Bernard Mokom and others planned steps to respond to the Seleka violence in the CAR as well as to ensure François Bozizé's return to power, by all means possible, including through armed violence.

During his time outside of the CAR in 2013, Mr Ngaïssona was actively involved in planning steps to respond to the Seleka violence in the CAR and to ensure François Bozizé's return to power by meeting and liaising with François Bozizé, Bernard Mokom and others to discuss strategies and plans, reaching out to individuals within and outside of the CAR with a view to gathering support for their cause, and providing financial assistance to those willing to assist in their activities. In this context, Mr Ngaïssona travelled to the border between Cameroon and the CAR with a view to liaising with groups meant to assist their efforts. Mr Ngaïssona continued providing financial assistance also after the coordinated attacks of 5 December 2013.

At the same time, Mr Yekatom briefly went to Zongo in 2013 and then started forming a group, over which he assumed control, with Freddy Ouandjio, also known as Cœur de Lion, and Habib Beina, with a view to planning a response to the Seleka violence and removing Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power.

Maxime Mokom liaised with individuals and groups in Cameroon, Zongo and within the CAR, including his father Bernard Mokom, Mr Yekatom, and groups forming in the provinces, with a view to coordinating the activities and eventual advance onto Bangui.

Mr Ngaïssona provided financial contributions and engaged in activities pertaining to the organisation and coordination of groups for the purpose of facilitating the commission of criminal acts targeting the Muslim population, including the crimes found below. Front pour le retour à l'ordre constitutionnel en Centrafrique (FROCCA)

As part of the efforts to counter the Seleka offensive and to ensure François Bozizé's return to power, in August 2013, François Bozizé, Mr Ngaïssona and others met in Paris to create the 'Front pour le retour à l'ordre constitutionnel en Centrafrique' (FROCCA). Lin Banoukepa was the executive director of FROCCA, while Mr Ngaïssona was one of its members. The group's objective was to advocate for the return to 'the constitutional order', which signified the return of François Bozizé to power. As such, FROCCA was one of the initiatives to achieve this stated goal on a political level, which co-existed with other efforts in this regard, specifically the galvanisation of groups eventually known collectively as the Anti-Balaka. Formation of groups in different localities and emergence of the Anti-Balaka

Against the backdrop of the violence committed by the Seleka, and in parallel to the activities in Cameroon and Zongo, self-defence groups in various localities across the CAR formed or re-activated from previous existence very quickly following the take-over of power by the Seleka. Individuals within those groups also obtained amulets or gris-gris. Some of these individuals and local groups converged onto and joined together in Gobere, north-east of Bossangoa.

In Gobere, civilians and former members of the Central African armed forces (FACA) and Presidential Guard gathered, and (i) organised into various sub-groups with a leader each; (ii) set up or maintained contacts with groups and individuals in other locations, including Maxime Mokom in Zongo, who was considered to be a coordinator of operations; (iii) organised trainings in weapon handling and combat by FACA members; and (iv) made further plans with a view to descending onto Bangui and removing the Seleka and Michel Djotodia from power.

At the same time, former members of the FACA and Presidential Guard also in other localities created new or joined pre-existing self-defence groups, organising themselves into military-like structures and assuming or sharing command over them.

Initially having formed separately, these groups started out with a common enemy and increasingly coordinated their activities, thereby essentially forming one movement. This movement came to be known as 'Anti-Balaka'.

The armed groups forming at the time were armed mainly with makeshift and bladed weapons, hunting rifles, service weapons retained by members of the FACA, and weapons they seized from the members of the Seleka after engaging them in hostilities. Objectives and policies of the Anti-Balaka

The self-defence groups initially forming in the provinces aimed at defending against the abuses and violence committed by the Seleka, within which framework some considered necessary to remove Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power. Due to the religious and ethnic commonalities between the Muslims in the CAR and the Seleka, the Anti-Balaka perceived the former as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka. On this basis, as the Anti-Balaka emerged and coalesced in pursuit of its core objective, its elements targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, killing and dislocating them.

The implementation and execution of the Anti-Balaka's core objective was primed by anti-foreign sentiments and inflammatory rhetoric openly expressed by François Bozizé and others, which incited vigilance against those perceived to support the Seleka, in particular Muslim civilians.

Such rhetoric was reflected in meetings of François Bozizé, Mr Ngaïssona and others in Cameroon and repeated in a radio statement issued by FROCCA on 5 December 2013 in relation to the attack on Bangui, which referred to the attack as '\[l\]e rétablissement de l'ordre fonctionnel' and further stated that the Anti-Balaka 'sont des Centrafricains pour aller libérer leur pays des jougs des djihadistes venus du D\[arfour\], du T\[chad\], du S\[oudan\]'.

Mr Yekatom knew that the Anti-Balaka perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis.

Mr Ngaïssona knew that the Anti-Balaka perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis. Mr Ngaïssona made his contributions fully aware that the Anti-Balaka would violently target the Muslim civilian population in the west of the CAR, committing the widespread attack that ultimately took place from September 2013 through February 2014, including the seminal coordinated Anti-Balaka attacks of Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013. Hostilities during the advance towards Bangui

The Anti-Balaka groups, which had formed in the provinces and in part gathered together at Gobere, started their advance towards Bangui, with the ultimate objective to attack the capital in order to remove Michel Djotodia from power and oust the Seleka from the CAR. In this advance, various Anti-Balaka groups started engaging in attacks against the Seleka from September 2013 onwards. Such attacks were not limited to Seleka forces, but included attacking localities with Muslim civilians.
These groups going into different localities communicated with each other and individuals abroad, including Maxime Mokom, with a view to coordinating such attacks.

Attacks were launched around Bossangoa and in Bouca (Ouham prefecture), in Ndjo, Bossembélé, Boali and Gaga (Ombella-M'Poko prefecture), as well as in Bouar (Nana-Mambéré prefecture). As part of these attacks, Anti-Balaka elements attacked Bossangoa on 17 September 2013.
Throughout the advance and during these attacks, Anti-Balaka groups targeted Muslim civilians. This information was widely known across the CAR and abroad, including in Cameroon.
The advance of the Anti-Balaka groups and hostilities on the way culminated in coordinated attacks in Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013.

From his involvement in coordinating his own group's advance through the provinces towards Bangui for purposes of the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, Mr Yekatom knew of the advance of the Anti-Balaka groups through the provinces towards Bangui, including the hostilities, as well as killings and dislocation of Muslim civilians, taking place in this context.

Mr Ngaïssona knew and was informed of the advance of the groups towards Bangui as well as of the hostilities during this advance, including the killings and dislocation of Muslim civilians from the locations mentioned above. Anti-Balaka in the aftermath of the attacks on 5 December 2013

Between the coordinated attacks on Bangui and Bossangoa of 5 December 2013 and his return to Bangui on 14 January 2014, Mr Ngaïssona remained informed of the continued activities related to the Anti-Balaka, and continued liaising with various individuals in this regard.

On 10 January 2014, Michel Djotodia resigned, leading to the end of his government, following which the Seleka forces started to withdraw from Bangui, in particular towards the north and north-east of the CAR.

On 20 January 2014, Catherine Samba-Panza was elected as new transitional head of state of the CAR. André Nzapayéké was chosen as prime minister, Léopold Narcisse Bara was appointed minister for youth, sports, arts and culture, and Jean-Jacques Demafouth, Charles Ngremangou and Joachim Kokaté also received position within this new government.
Immediately following his return to Bangui on 14 January 2014, Mr Ngaïssona was installed as general coordinator of the Anti-Balaka.
As such, Mr Ngaïssona represented the entirety of the Anti-Balaka towards the CAR transition government and international authorities.

With a view to engaging with the transition government and international authorities, the Anti-Balaka structure started being further formalised with the return of Mr Ngaïssona and his appointment as general coordinator. Other individuals within this formalised structure included Maxime Mokom as operations coordinator and zone commanders, or 'ComZones' as group leaders. Mr Ngaïssona continued to provide financial assistance to the Anti-Balaka and actively engaged in formalising the structure of the Anti-Balaka.

Throughout the period relevant to the charges, Mr Yekatom retained and exercised control over an active group of elements which was seen as and understood to be part of the Anti-Balaka. Mr Yekatom was the uncontested leader of this group which first set up at Yamwara in Boeing after 5 December 2013, and moved down the PK9-Mbaïki axis following Michel Djotodia's resignation.

The structure of the Anti-Balaka evolved during the period relevant to the charges, and was subject to various leadership tussles. However, it always remained represented towards the national and international authorities as one entity through Mr Ngaïssona.

Anti-Balaka groups set up bases in different neighbourhoods across Bangui. Meetings were held at variable intervals at Mr Ngaïssona's concessions or at the Azimut hotel. In February 2014, the Anti-Balaka itself estimated counting about 50,000 elements in Bangui and the provinces. The Anti-Balaka coordination also issued identity cards or badges to some of the Anti-Balaka elements. The continuation of hostilities

Notwithstanding the retreat of the Seleka following the resignation of Michel Djotodia and the setting up of a new transition government in January 2014, the main hostilities between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka which had started in earnest in September 2013 continued largely unabated until the end of February 2014. Hostilities thereafter did continue, but subsided considerably.

The UN Security Council recurrently dedicated attention to the security situation in the CAR in 2013 and 2014. Several attempts to bring about the cessation of hostilities failed, including the 16 June 2014 PARETO mediation agreement, the 23 July 2014 peace agreement signed by the Seleka and the Anti-Balaka in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, and the agreement signed in Nairobi in April 2015. The number of internally displaced persons and refugees outside of the CAR decreased in the course of 2014, but overall remained in the hundreds of thousands throughout the year.

As part of the Anti-Balaka's pursuit of its core objective, in the context of which its elements targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, due to the Anti-Balaka perceiving the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka, the Anti-Balaka continued to target the Muslim civilian population in 2014 across the western CAR prefectures, including in the second half of January and early February 2014 in Ombella-M'Poko (Gaga, Zawa, Yaloké), Ouham-Pendé (Bossemptélé), Nana-Mambéré (Baoro), Mambéré-Kadéï (Guen, Carnot, Berbérati) and Lobaye (Boda). The attacks followed a pattern with Anti-Balaka groups killing and injuring Muslim civilians, looting and destroying their belongings, and often placing them in enclaved positions under difficult circumstances, eventually leading to many Muslims having to leave the respective areas. The attack on Bangui, including Boeing and Cattin, on 5 December 2013 Coordination of the attack

In the early morning hours of 5 December 2013, the Anti-Balaka mounted a coordinated attack on Bangui, including in Boeing and Cattin. The plan to mount an attack on Bangui existed at least as of 30 November 2013. Anti-Balaka elements and groups travelled from the provinces to arrive close to Bangui before 5 December 2013.

During their move from the provinces to Bangui, Anti-Balaka chiefs communicated across their groups, kept and maintained records or lists of elements, armed themselves, and waited at common locations and prepared for an attack on Bangui. Mr Ngaïssona provided funds to Anti-Balaka elements that participated in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. By the beginning of December 2013, several thousand Anti-Balaka elements had arrived at the outskirts of Bangui to participate in an attack. News about an impending attack on Bangui circulated in various circles within the Anti-Balaka leadership. Mr Ngaïssona knew that an attack would take place on Bangui.

The Anti-Balaka participating in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 shared the same goal, which was to target Seleka positions in Bangui with a view to 'getting rid of Djotodia' and 'chasing out the Seleka', which included systematic targeting of Muslim civilians. Various Anti-Balaka groups that participated in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 had common leaders, who coordinated their actions and instructed them. Anti-Balaka groups that reassembled close to Bangui prior to the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 were each assigned a specific target within Bangui and instructed to begin the attack on the respective targets at 05:00 on 5 December 2013. The attack was carried out as planned, resulting in clashes between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka in several locations in Bangui, including Boeing, with the Anti-Balaka beginning to retreat around 10:00 the same day. Later that day, FROCCA issued a radio statement in relation to the attack on Bangui, referring to it as '\[l\]e rétablissement de l'ordre fonctionnel' and stating that the Anti-Balaka 'sont des Centrafricains pour aller libérer leur pays des jougs des djihadistes venus du D\[arfour\], du T\[chad\], du S\[oudan\]'.
The attacks on Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 were coordinated with each other. Involvement of Mr Yekatom

Mr Yekatom's group coordinated with other Anti-Balaka groups to participate in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. In the months leading up to this attack, Mr Yekatom and his group armed and trained in the bush. The movement of Mr Yekatom's group in the bush, when superimposed onto those from other groups who proceeded towards Bangui along the same time frame, shows that this coordination had begun well before November 2013.

In the afternoon of 4 December 2013, Mr Yekatom chose some of his elements and instructed them to move towards Bangui. The same day, the group arrived in Projet, situated near the M'Poko airport in Bangui. Mr Yekatom's instructions to his elements concerning the attack on 5 December 2013 were to fight the Seleka and included targeting sectors where 'Muslims' were to be found. Mr Yekatom's instructions were understood by the elements to accept that Muslim civilians would be killed as a result of the fighting based on his elements not having been trained or instructed to apply the principle of distinction during combat and bearing strong anti-Muslim sentiment and feelings of vengeance against the Seleka. Attack on Boeing

On the night of 4 December 2013, Mr Yekatom and some of his elements visited the market in Boeing to assess its precise geographical location and conduct reconnaissance. The same night, Mr Yekatom instructed his elements to target Seleka positions along the Boeing-Cattin-PK5 direction. These instructions encompassed attacking the Muslim traders at the market in Boeing before moving along the route to PK5.

In the early morning of 5 December 2013, Mr Yekatom launched the attack on Boeing by firing an automatic pistol in the air when his group reached the market in Boeing. The armed elements in the front continued and advanced together and fired at the Muslim traders who were present there. During this time, Mr Yekatom's elements shot in all directions. Those that were inside the shops fled. Mr Yekatom's group attacked the market in Boeing during their advance towards PK5 following Mr Yekatom's orders.

Elements in Mr Yekatom's group killed Hassan Mahamat in the morning of 5 December 2013 during the attack on the market in Boeing. Hassan personally interacted with certain Seleka officials prior to 5 December 2013 in his role as delegate of the male Muslim traders at the market in Boeing. Hassan had at least one weapon in his shop with which he fired in self-defence during the attack of 5 December 2013 carried out by Mr Yekatom's elements. Further, Mr Yekatom's elements killed two unnamed Muslim traders at the market in Boeing during this attack. Traders at the market in Boeing and the Seleka personally interacted with each other at the market and were seen by others as associating with each other. There is no indication that any of the two unnamed Muslim traders were armed during the attack or otherwise engaged in combat at that time.

On 5 December 2013, and following Mr Yekatom's instructions, Mr Yekatom's elements attacked the mosque in Boeing, which was the main mosque serving the communities of both Boeing and Cattin, by firing a 'rocket' at it. Mr Yekatom's elements also torched the mosque in Boeing with gasoline. On the same day and in the days that followed, the local population took it apart. Attack on Cattin

Following the attack on the market and the mosque in Boeing, elements of Mr Yekatom's group moved on to attack Cattin, where they clashed with the Seleka. During the attack on Cattin, elements of Mr Yekatom's group killed at least one Muslim man, who was not armed, nor engaged in combat, at the time of his death. The elements targeted this Muslim man on the basis that he was an 'Arab' and the victim eventually succumbed to the injuries inflicted on him. Dislocation of Muslims from Boeing and Cattin

From 5 December 2013 onwards, the majority of Muslims of Boeing and Cattin, including Salehou Ndiaye and P-2682, fled to PK5 in Bangui, while some others fled to other parts of the CAR, in the context of the attack by Mr Yekatom's group on Boeing and Cattin. Muslim persons who fled to PK5 continued to fear for their security because of the presence of the Anti-Balaka around PK5 and Bangui generally. With the influx of Muslims fleeing the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, PK5 became overcrowded, practically uninhabitable, and unsafe. As a result, some Muslims, including Salehou Ndiaye and P-2682, then fled to neighbouring countries fearing for their safety. The attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 Unfolding of the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013

On 5 December 2013, in coordination with the Anti-Balaka attack on Bangui on the same day, Anti-Balaka elements, divided into two groups led by Florent Kema and Théophile Ndangba, respectively, carried out an attack on the town of Bossangoa. The attack started at approximately 13:00 and lasted until the late afternoon or early evening.

During the attack, the Anti-Balaka targeted residential areas, including the Boro neighbourhood, generally known as the Muslim neighbourhood in Bossangoa, with the intention of showing that the Anti-Balaka were attacking not only Bangui but also in the provinces, and to 'free' the town from Seleka and all Muslims, thereby targeting Muslim civilians and drawing no distinction between them and the Seleka. During the attack, the Anti-Balaka was well armed, with some AK-47s and RPGs, as well as hunting weapons.

During the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, Batoul Naffi and several other individuals were injured. An Anti-Balaka element forced P-2462 into sexual intercourse, having blindfolded and undressed her, and after the group of five Anti-Balaka he was in had threatened her with their weapons.

In the course of the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, the Anti-Balaka killed at least the following 18 persons who were not armed or taking part in hostilities: Khadidja Adjaro; Koursi Abdelrahim; Abdel, also known as Adaye, Abakar; Atahir Abou; 'C-17', a taxi driver; Atahir Djime (or Djimet); Halima Hisseini; Hamadou Bouba; Ousman Abacar; Ousman Abacar's mother; Abdallah Mahamat; Abdelkhadir; Mariam Yamwha; Amadou Oumarou; Abakar; Ismael; Salamatou, a Peuhl; Sale Adim. Events during and in the aftermath of the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013

At some point between 5 and 8 December 2013, the Anti-Balaka burned and destroyed residential structures, lived in by Muslims at the time of the attack, in the immediate vicinity of the imam's residence.

During the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, the Muslim civilian population of Bossangoa fled the attacked neighbourhoods to seek shelter at the École de la Liberté, where their numbers rose into several thousands.

The Muslim civilians that had sought refuge at the École de la Liberté remained confined to the school premises for fear of threats by the Anti-Balaka, staying there in cramped and generally dire conditions. The Muslim civilians at the École de la Liberté were dependent on the protection of international forces for their safety and could not leave the school premises venturing into Bossangoa without risk to their person.

Eventually, in light of the prevailing insecurity as well as the dire and cramped living conditions at the École de la Liberté, all Muslims staying at the school were transported away from Bossangoa to Chad in two separate convoys, leaving in February and April 2014, respectively, following which Bossangoa was emptied of its Muslim population. The events at Yamwara on and around 24 December 2013 Elements and structure at Yamwara

Mr Yekatom's group established a base at Yamwara at one point in December 2013 following the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. Elements who had not participated in this attack joined Mr Yekatom's group at Yamwara after 5 December 2013. Considerable number of elements received accommodation in the school buildings or in provisory shelters around the premises of Yamwara, including Cœur de Lion.
Mr Yekatom did not live at Yamwara and slept elsewhere close to the airport. Mr Yekatom did regularly visit Yamwara and maintained a constant presence there through his elements.

When the base at Yamwara was established, Mr Yekatom's group set up checkpoints along its perimeter to monitor passage of vehicles and people, including, at least, one set up by Alkanto close to Yamwara.

Mr Yekatom was in charge of Yamwara with Cœur de Lion as his deputy. All witnesses who were at Yamwara during the relevant time considered Mr Yekatom to be the 'chief' of all activities at Yamwara. Mr Yekatom was also the overall chief on matters of punishment and enforcing discipline at Yamwara, and his section chiefs also had a responsibility to discipline elements. Mr Yekatom maintained overall control over the activities at Yamwara at all times, including through Cœur de Lion. Mr Yekatom had undisputed authority over Cœur de Lion, Alkanto and Bojos, among others.

At some point in mid-December 2013, Mr Yekatom's group at Yamwara was joined by elements from Bossangoa, referred to as the 'Gobere group'. Elements within the Gobere group at Yamwara followed the orders from their own chiefs, who would, in turn, wait for the orders of Mr Yekatom. Training at Yamwara

Starting on 10 January 2014, Mr Yekatom and elements under his control left Yamwara and advanced from Bangui on the road towards Mbaïki, taking over a number of villages in the Lobaye prefecture, located in the south-west part of the country, including Sekia, Ndangala, Bimon, Kapou, Bossongo and Pissa. They did not meet with resistance as they passed from PK9 to Sekia and Pissa, since the Seleka had fled these areas after learning that the Anti-Balaka were approaching.

At the time of the group's presence on the Mbaïki road, Mr Yekatom, Cœur de Lion and Alkanto instructed the elements to kill all the Muslims in their area. Elements under Mr Yekatom's control present along the axis
Mr Yekatom was the undisputed leader of the Anti-Balaka group along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, which comprised at least 1,000 elements at the time. Locations of checkpoints and bases on the axis
Mr Yekatom's group took over checkpoints at PK9, Sekia, Bimon, Bossongo and Pissa in their advance towards Mbaïki. Mr Yekatom and his elements also set up new bases at PK9 and Sekia.

By taking over these checkpoints, Mr Yekatom and his group aimed at searching and identifying Muslims in the area and raising money to finance the group and its needs. Mr Yekatom's group was armed. The flight of Muslims from locations along the PK9-Mbaïki axis
A significant proportion of the Muslim civilian population fled their towns and villages along the PK9-Mbaïki axis due to and in fear of the advance of Mr Yekatom's group along the axis.

At least 1,000 Muslim civilians who fled from locations along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and in the Lobaye prefecture went to Mbaïki, substantially increasing the Muslim population of the town. Muslims in Mbaïki at the time were living in difficulty, under conditions of overcrowding, hunger and fear of death from the Anti-Balaka. Arrival of Mr Yekatom's group to Mbaïki

Mr Yekatom and elements under his control entered Mbaïki on 30 January 2014. That day, a meeting was held at the St Jeanne d'Arc Church in Mbaïki, with Mr Yekatom and members of his group, representatives of the Mbaïki civilian and religious authorities, international organisations and NGOs, as well as the Sangaris. At the meeting, the removal of the Muslim civilian population from Mbaïki, which was a foregone conclusion at that point, was decided. After the meeting finished, Mr Yekatom addressed the crowds outside of the meeting location and subsequently at Mbaïki's bus station, where he delivered 'peace messages' similar to those he had expressed at the meeting. The presence of the Sangaris and other international actors in Mbaïki at that time compelled Mr Yekatom to bring this 'peace message' to Mbaïki and prevented attacks of his group against the Muslim civilian population. After the meeting, the prefect and other individuals contacted the authorities to arrange the convoy that would transport the Muslim civilian population out of Mbaïki.

Mr Yekatom's group settled in at least one base in Mbaïki. During this time, elements of Mr Yekatom's group threatened and harassed Muslim civilians in Mbaïki, telling them to leave the area. Both Mr Yekatom and Cœur de Lion knew that elements of the group committed acts of violence in Mbaïki. Efforts and measures to prevent these acts were taken only after the removal of the Muslim civilian population from Mbaïki had been decided and/or carried out. The Anti-Balaka also attacked a gendarme patrol in Mbaïki which was there to protect the population, taking the patrol's weapons and the service car that they were using. Dislocation of Muslims from Mbaïki

On 6 February 2014, Chadian forces transported a first group of Muslim civilians from Mbaïki to Chad and other locations in the CAR. These Muslim civilians had to leave their belongings behind. They left Mbaïki in fear of the Anti-Balaka and, in particular, due to the arrival of Mr Yekatom's group to Mbaïki. The total number of Muslims removed from Mbaïki at the time amounted to at least 3,000. As a result of this dislocation, very few Muslim civilians remained in Mbaïki. The living conditions in the refugee camps in Chad were extremely difficult.
Thereafter, the Congolese MISCA transported a second group of Muslims out of Mbaïki to Bangui and other locations. The killing of Djido Saleh

Following the removal of Muslim civilians out of Mbaïki, Djido Saleh, the second deputy mayor of Mbaïki, and his family, were among the very few remaining Muslims in Mbaïki. Prior to his killing, elements of Mr Yekatom's group threatened Djido Saleh. There is no indication that Anti-Balaka elements demanded money from Djido Saleh.

On 28 February 2014, a group of individuals attacked Djido Saleh's house while he and his family were inside. Djido Saleh's family fled. As Djido Saleh tried to flee, the group of individuals pursued him and threw stones at him. Djido Saleh tried to defend himself with a bow and at least one arrow. The group of individuals, which included at least three elements of Mr Yekatom's group, one of them being Honorine Gbafalo, killed him as he tried to reach the gendarmerie. Honorine Gbafalo cut off his genitals. Other individuals beat him and cut parts of his body, including one of his ears and his neck, partly severing his head. These individuals targeted Djido Saleh on the basis that he was a Muslim. Following the death of Djido Saleh, Mr Yekatom told Raymond Mongbandi that the killing was 'an accident' and that he would pay for the burial, which he never did. As a direct consequence of the killing, MISCA ordered Mr Yekatom and his elements to leave Mbaïki, which they immediately did. In doing so, it has only relied 'on evidence submitted and discussed before it at the trial'. As determined by the Appeals Chamber, 'evidence is properly before a trial chamber when it has been "submitted" in accordance with the procedure adopted by the trial chamber and discussed at trial, unless it is ruled as irrelevant or inadmissible'. Furthermore, the Chamber recalls that what is required is that there has been the opportunity at trial to make arguments on the evidence concerned, irrespective of whether any such arguments are actually made. The Chamber duly considered the arguments raised by the parties and participants throughout the proceedings. Of particular importance in this regard are the arguments made in the context of the submission of individual items of evidence as well as in the parties and participants' closing briefs and statements. Nonetheless, the Chamber recalls that 'to fulfil its obligation to provide a reasoned opinion' under Article 74(5) of the Statute, it 'is not required to address all the arguments raised by the parties \[and participants\], or every item of evidence relevant to a particular factual finding, provided that it indicates with sufficient clarity the basis for its decision'. As confirmed by the Appeals Chamber, trial chambers have a degree of discretion as to what to address explicitly in their reasoning as long as there are sufficient reasons provided for their determinations.

Nonetheless, the Chamber recalls that 'to fulfil its obligation to provide a reasoned opinion' under Article 74(5) of the Statute, it 'is not required to address all the arguments raised by the parties \[and participants\], or every item of evidence relevant to a particular factual finding, provided that it indicates with sufficient clarity the basis for its decision'. As confirmed by the Appeals Chamber, trial chambers have a degree of discretion as to what to address explicitly in their reasoning as long as there are sufficient reasons provided for their determinations.

paragraph_text_preview: Moreover, the Chamber recalls that there is no procedural bar to the introduction or reliance on hearsay evidence in the Court's legal framework. The fact that evidence is hearsay does not necessarily deprive it of probative value. While the weight or probative value afforded to it may be lower, this ultimately 'depend\[s\] upon the infinitely variable circumstances which surround hearsay evidence', including for instance whether the hearsay evidence is anonymous.

footnote_content: *See* [*Al Hassan* Trial Judgment](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/o613gxre/), ICC-01/12-01/18-2594-Red, para. 21, *and the references cited therein*.
paragraph_text_preview: Similarly, nothing in the statutory framework prevents a trial chamber from drawing inferences based on circumstantial evidence, nor does the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt or the principle in dubio pro reo require that such evidence be excluded. In making findings based on circumstantial evidence, the Chamber has reached a conclusion beyond reasonable doubt when it was convinced that was the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the relevant facts. The Chamber further recalls that it is not required to articulate every step of its reasoning that led to its final conclusion. However, when the Chamber has made an essential finding based on an inference, it has explained in detail how it reached the factual conclusion in question.

The Chamber also takes note of the Ngaïssona Defence's submissions that the Prosecution has 'excessively relied on circumstantial evidence', as well as 'vast amounts of indirect and hearsay evidence'. The Chamber recalls that it will assess all of the evidence before it holistically and in light of the jurisprudence of the Court as set out above.

paragraph_text_preview: Furthermore, in accordance with Rule 63(4) of the Rules, the Chamber has imposed no legal requirement of corroboration. As held by the Appeals Chamber, '\[d\]epending on the circumstances, a single piece of evidence \[...\] may suffice to establish a specific fact. However, \[...\] this does not mean that any piece of evidence provides a sufficient evidentiary basis for a factual finding'. The Appeals Chamber also found that 'while corroboration is "an element that a reasonable trier of fact may consider in assessing the evidence", the question of whether or not to consider it forms part of the Trial Chamber's discretion'.

paragraph_text_preview: As to the Ngaïssona Defence's submissions that the Prosecution 'excessively relied on uncorroborated insider evidence, prior recorded statements and impugned witnesses', and that it relied on 'contaminated testimonies of key witnesses', the Chamber notes that these allegations essentially refer to the probative value and weight that the Chamber should attribute to said evidence, on the basis that the evidence is allegedly uncorroborated, unreliable or not credible. Therefore, the Chamber considers it more appropriate to address these issues in the context of the credibility assessments of the witnesses as well as in its evidentiary analysis for findings of facts, as necessary.

Moreover, the Chamber notes that the Ngaïssona Defence argues that the Prosecution 'abused its process regarding Article 70 of the Statute' (the 'Article 70 Investigation'), which would require the Chamber to dismiss any reference by the Prosecution to any allegations concerning witness interference by the Ngaïssona Defence when assessing the evidence, in order to safeguard Mr Ngaïssona's rights in this case. The Chamber recalls its findings that, under the Court's legal framework, it does not have the power to find an abuse of process by the Prosecution in the context of an Article 70 investigation, and, as this Chamber is not seized with the Article 70 Investigation, it has no power to order the latter to cease it. It follows that the Chamber does not find it appropriate to dismiss per se any reference to allegations made by the Prosecution on any alleged witness interference on the part of the Ngaïssona Defence.

Lastly, the Chamber takes note of the Ngaïssona Defence's submission that the Prosecution applied 'double standards' to evidence because it 'wrongly labelled' evidence as incriminating Mr Ngaïssona but later that same evidence was disclosed as exculpatory in the case of The Prosecutor v Maxime Jeoffroy Eli Mokom Gawaka (the 'Mokom Case'). The Chamber considers that the Ngaïssona Defence's contention is inapposite. Even though there might have been a substantial factual overlap between the two cases, the charges against the accused are different, and simply because an item of evidence is categorised in one way in the Mokom case does not mean that it should have been regarded as such in the present case. The Ngaïssona Defence argues that the Prosecution Facebook Material lacks authentication, more specifically, that the Prosecution did not submit any evidence that could authenticate its material, let alone assist the Chamber in understanding what was received in response to the RFAs sent by the Prosecution to the competent Irish authorities (the 'Authorities'), and that no Facebook employee or representative testified or explained the material generated by Facebook.

The Chamber notes that, in response to the Prosecution's RFAs, the Authorities secured the evidence in question and thereafter transmitted it to the Prosecution. The Chamber has no reason to doubt that the Facebook Material requested by the Prosecution through its RFAs is none other than what was obtained by the Authorities from Facebook according to the applicable domestic procedure, and ultimately conveyed to the Court. The Chamber is also not persuaded that the lack of information 'concerning the domestic court processes and whether the materials were altered in any way' in this instance raises doubts on the authenticity of the Prosecution Facebook Material to such an extent as to render it inadmissible per se, and considers that mere submissions on any alleged alteration of such material are speculative.

The Chamber considers that in the absence of a statement or testimony from an individual who participated in a Facebook exchange or authored a post, or otherwise has information about the contents, the related Facebook Material has little probative value. That being said, the Chamber does not consider it appropriate to adopt a presumption that 'all messages are misinformation unless proven otherwise, given that individuals will often present unreliable information as fact'. The Chamber recognised as formally submitted approximately 104 items related to call data records (the 'CDR'), comprising call data, cell site items, and call sequence tables (the 'CST') (together, the 'CDR Material'). The Chamber will briefly define each of these terms.

CDR provide information about telecommunications, such as the sending and receiving number, the type of communication (voice call or text message), the date, time and duration of the communication, the identification number ascribed to a particular mobile phone (the 'handset') and/or SIM card -- respectively known as international mobile equipment identification number (the 'IMEI') and international mobile subscriber identity --, and the cell towers to which the handset connected. Furthermore, CDR usually contain information as to which cell or cell site was used at the start and/or end of a connection.

Cell site items contain information on the site name, cell name and the direction of the antennas that were capturing the telecommunication signal between the concerned devices. A cell site (or base transceiver station) contains a piece of equipment that receives and emits radio frequencies used by telephones to communicate with each other. The cell is the basic unit of network coverage produced by the antenna of a single sector. This information is significant to the extent that CDR generally do not contain the details of the antenna configuration or the cell site details such as the location or address.

The Chamber notes that telecommunications companies generate CDR with data that is automatically collected in the ordinary course of business. The CDR from Moov register any communication, either phone calls or text messages, that is initiated by a particular number on the network. The type of data that is collected includes the receiver of the communication, whether it consists of a call or text message, the date and time, the duration of the call, and any other information that is useful for the business reports of the company. In its raw form, the data consists of a set of alphanumeric characters which then needs to be decoded by a programme in order to be readable by humans and used in a CDR.

paragraph_text_preview: In a CDR produced by Moov, the registration of a call begins when the receiver answers the call -- that is to say, it excludes the ringing time -- and stops in the event that the subscriber loses the signal from the network and thus cannot continue the communication. Furthermore, since CDR are used to record data for billing purposes, the operator does not register a communication that did not actually take place. The Chamber also takes note of Duncan Brown's testimony that, in the event that a phone call is diverted, some networks would indicate this in some ways in their CDR, but others would not include any information of that kind, so that it would not be possible to tell whether the number has possibly been diverted. The expert witness also indicated that it is possible that few connections may not be recorded by an operator due to technical errors, although that possibility seems rare.

Ghislain N'Douba indicated that Moov has a protocol for archiving data in digital archives, and that all other operators in the CAR are also required by regulatory requirements to store the data for a certain time, beyond which there is no further obligation. At Moov, the transfer of the data to the archives is done automatically to ensure that it is carried out properly and completely. The control mechanisms put in place to ensure that the production of CDR is well executed are also automated, and specialised staff ensure that CDR are properly collected and that the decoding process is executed correctly. The Chamber also notes Duncan Brown's testimony that networks record slightly different information into their databases, and that each operator tends to have CDR that look different.

As regards the generation of CDR, they can be produced for billing and tax purposes, as well as for legal purposes, which is the reason why they need to be as accurate and reliable as possible. Ghislain N'Douba further indicated that the generation of such data is common to all telephone companies in the CAR, since their business model is always based on this data. Importantly, he also explained that the collection of data for billing purposes is different from litigation or legal purposes. The CDR produced for invoicing purposes contain information that is limited to what is necessary for the client, omitting certain details such as the location of the call.

As regards their electronic format, CDR can be transmitted to the requesting party in an Excel, text or readable format, or in their raw or binary form. This raw form cannot be altered by either the network or the requesting party, and guarantees the authenticity of the information after the decoding process, since Excel formats can be modified. A PDF version can also be provided to ensure that the Excel format contains the same data, but in order to facilitate the analysis, Excel or 'comma separated values' (the 'CSV') formats are most commonly requested. The Chamber also notes Duncan Brown's testimony that in order to prevent a CDR file being corrupted during the analysis, best practices recommend that a copy be made before an investigator works on it. However, he also indicated that re-saving a CDR file by someone who did not produce it would not necessarily corrupt the data. In this regard, the Chamber notes the Prosecution's submission that its CDR were obtained through a series of RFAs in text, CSV and Excel formats.

Ghislain N'Douba further testified on the location of the Moov cell towers, explaining that, in Bangui, in 2013 and 2014, the range of relay of the antennas was generally set at 1 to 2 kilometres in order to avoid interference between them. Outside of Bangui, the range can reach up to 20 kilometres but may still vary based on geographical and meteorological conditions. Each cell site may be divided into sectors, each of which has an antenna that transmits its signal over a certain area and direction in an attempt to provide the best server coverage. The angle or degree at which the antenna on the cell tower is pointed is known as an azimuth. All companies have information on the areas covered by each antenna, for both technical and commercial reasons. Even when not being used, a handset communicates regularly with the network so that it knows at all times where the telephone is located. As to cell site items, the Chamber notes Duncan Brown's evidence that networks typically maintain a separate cell site information database that will be used for cell site planning and should be updated with any changes to the cells or cell sites.

The Chamber further notes that handsets normally connect to the strongest signal that is best for establishing communications, and that CDR from all telecommunications companies always reflect the cell site or sector that was actually used to make or receive a call. It is also possible that, in certain conditions, there exists an overlap in coverage so that a CDR can show that a telephone was connected to a different cell while remaining on the same spot. The Chamber notes Ghislain N'Douba's testimony that this is not necessarily a deviation that would call into question the reliability of the data contained in the CDR. The serving cell for a particular call is actually not always the closest one geographically to that handset. Depending on the technology used by a telecommunications company, the size of the area covered by a cell may vary, but the Chamber notes that, normally, in urban centres, deviations are considerably smaller as opposed to rural areas, where there are not that many antennas.

The Chamber will now address the Ngaïssona Defence's submissions concerning the authenticity and reliability of the Prosecution CDR Material.

The Chamber is not convinced by the Ngaïssona Defence's arguments that the Prosecution CDR Material is not authentic. The Chamber has no reason to doubt that the CDR and cell site items obtained from the respective networks correspond to what was requested by the Prosecution in its RFAs, nor the validity of the respective chains of custody as reflected in the metadata. Furthermore, the Chamber notes that the Ngaïssona Defence questions the authenticity of the Prosecution CDR Material by referring to the lack of factual or expert testimony on the nature, authorship and process by which the CDR were generated. However, the Chamber is of the view that these submissions appear to concern rather whether the Prosecution CDR Material can be deemed sufficiently reliable or accurate, as well as the manner in which the Chamber may or should interpret them. In addition, the Chamber considers in this instance that the potential disparities in formats of the CDR or the fact that some may have been generated for billing, tax or litigation purposes do not have an impact overall on the authenticity of the CDR. In this regard, the Chamber is of the view that these differences do not necessarily mean that some CDR 'are more genuine' or more authentic than others.

paragraph_text_preview: Based on the testimonies of Ghislain N'Douba and Duncan Brown, the Chamber considers that CDR alone are insufficient to conclusively attribute a phone number to an individual. Rather, additional extrinsic evidence is necessary to demonstrate attribution. In this regard, the Chamber notes that sometimes witnesses provided phone numbers in statements or during testimony, or that phone numbers were discovered as being saved or registered as contacts in a specific handset belonging to an individual. Unless the witnesses themselves gave or recognised a phone number, further information may be needed to determine attribution.

Relatedly, the Chamber also considers that the CDR alone are not conclusive as to whether a communication occurred between specific individuals. In certain instances, witnesses admitted or refuted having placed a phone call when confronted with a CDR. The Chamber also understands from the evidence before it that it may have been possible that a handset was shared by more than one person, that a call was made through another phone number or received by someone else who also had access to that particular handset.

Furthermore, the Chamber considers that in the event a CDR shows that a call was placed between individuals, that evidence alone cannot definitively prove that said individuals effectively engaged in a conversation. Conversely, an absence of CDR evidence does not exclude the possibility that a communication actually took place by other means or devices. Consequently, CDR alone also cannot depict with accuracy the frequency of communications between individuals. Similarly, the length of a call alone is not necessarily reflective of a conversation taking place.

As to the content of phone calls, CDR themselves do not offer information thereon, but must be read together with the witness's testimony about said phone call. If no witness provided evidence about the existence of a phone call, no conclusion can be drawn on the content by solely relying on the CDR.

Lastly, having regard to the limitations mentioned by Ghislain N'Douba and Duncan Brown discussed above, the CDR and cell site items alone cannot conclusively show a person's exact geographic location.

In light of the above, the Chamber will assess the CDR and cell site items, if at all, on a case-by-case basis, depending on the inference sought by the parties, having regard to the totality of the evidence before it, as referenced in the following sections of this judgment. For the purposes of its assessment of the reliability of any witness's testimony, the Chamber considered a number of different factors, including the richness of details and coherence of the narrative provided by the witness, as well as the coherence of the testimony with other evidence before the Chamber.

The Chamber has also considered the coherence between in-court testimony and their prior accounts in relation to the same facts. In particular, the Chamber notes that throughout the trial, witnesses who testified fully live before the Chamber have often been asked questions in relation to prior accounts they gave in other contexts. Prior accounts were typically put to witnesses in two distinct situations: (i) when a witness declared themselves unable to respond to a question, in which case a prior account was used to refresh their memory; and (ii) in case of an alleged discrepancy between in-court testimony and a prior account.

paragraph_text_preview: Having assessed P-0306's testimony about the notes he provided to the Prosecution, the Chamber considers that these notes did not render his evidence wholly unreliable. At most, his testimony regarding these notes reflected a lack of understanding of legal procedure. The Chamber notes that P-0306 appeared to have drawn some of these notes as a memory aid 'to jog \[his\] memory' and, being illiterate, prepared with the assistance of someone else, thinking that they could 'serve as evidence whenever necessary'. It was clear to the Chamber that, in making these notes, P-0306 did not fully understand the need to keep track of dates and sequence of events adequately for proper legal scrutiny. This did not reflect negatively on the credibility of the rest of his claims; however, they do render these notes unreliable for the purposes of drawing any factual conclusions. Accordingly, the Chamber has not relied on the contents of these notes in its evidentiary analysis below.

In the Chamber's view, Brice Emotion Namsio had first-hand knowledge about several events of interest to the Chamber and was forthcoming when providing details. He was in Zongo for some time in 2013 following the Seleka coup and crossed over to participate in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. In 2014, he assumed the role of the deputy spokesperson of the Anti-Balaka and spoke about the political organisation of the Anti-Balaka during this period, including the setting up of the military police. On occasion, he appeared to diminish his own role and attempted to dismiss the evidence concerning the Anti-Balaka's attitude towards Muslims. However, this did not diminish the fact that the Chamber found him internally consistent and coherent.

Having regard to the above, the Chamber concludes that Brice Emotion Namsio's testimony was generally credible. As regards the issues raised by the Yekatom Defence relating to certain other specific aspects of his evidence, as noted above, the Chamber has assessed them holistically, in light of the other evidence before it, in its evidentiary analysis below. paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber emphasises that these findings by a different chamber do not, as such and by themselves, pre-determine the assessment of the witness's testimony before it. Especially, the Chamber is of the view that it must evaluate the witness's evidence as provided under oath in the circumstances of the current case, and in conjunction with and compared to other evidence provided to the Chamber.
Having assessed Joachim Kokaté's testimony overall in this case, in light of the Ngaïssona Defence arguments, the Chamber concludes that the witness's testimony is, nonetheless, generally credible.

The Chamber notes that Joachim Kokaté was himself present in key meetings in 2013 and personally interacted with individuals of relevance to the present case and therefore was in a position to provide firsthand information about them. The witness also distinguished the sources of his knowledge.

paragraph_text_preview: Having reviewed his evidence, the Chamber finds Alfred Legrand Ngaya's evidence generally credible. He was knowledgeable about the context and political events in the CAR during the relevant period. He directly interacted with Mr Ngaïssona and was generally forthcoming about his exchanges with him. The witness appeared to be generally able to distinguish between the sources of his knowledge. For example, he considered that he was not 'the authorised person' to talk about Mr Yekatom because all that he could say about him were 'things that I learned from rumours'.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that Alfred Legrand Ngaya appeared to present a favourable and passive view of Mr Ngaïssona's role in 2014, which often led him to contradict himself. For example, he stated not being aware that anyone provided money to the Anti-Balaka. At the same time, according to him, Mr Ngaïssona supported the Anti-Balaka on his return with his 'own money' to dissuade them. He did not recall if Mr Ngaïssona provided financial resources as requested, but indicated that at some point, Mr Ngaïssona sent money to him to help the Anti-Balaka in their neighbourhood and dissuade them from bothering the population. He also thought that Mr Ngaïssona was designated as coordinator because the Anti-Balaka did not have resources to take care of themselves and Mr Ngaïssona had a reputation for being generous with money. He also said that Mr Ngaïssona 'had an influence on the movement because of his generosity, of doing good' and that they 'always needed him'.

Having reviewed his testimony, the Chamber finds P-0876's evidence generally credible.

The Chamber notes that P-0876 was knowledgeable and forthcoming about his participation in meetings with various Anti-Balaka leaders in December 2013 to February 2014, including those that took place at Yamwara, the National Assembly and Catherine Samba-Panza's house. During the relevant time, P-0876 personally interacted with both accused and had firsthand information about a number of meetings with the various Anti-Balaka groups from end 2013 to early 2014. P-0876 was well-placed to provide informed opinions about the in-group dynamics within the Anti-Balaka during the relevant time.

The Chamber found that P-0876's evidence was largely consistent and coherent. The Chamber has considered that, at times, P-0876's answers were long-winding, and tending to emphasise his own role as a mediator and being the one striving for peace among the Anti-Balaka.

Jean-Jacques Demafouth, a former government official in the CAR, testified fully live without in-court protective measures.

While not a direct insider within the Anti-Balaka, due to his various positions before, during and after the time relevant to the charges, Jean-Jacques Demafouth was well connected and proved to have vast knowledge on a variety of topics coming from various sources. He not only provided extensive information on the background to the conflict in the CAR, including the Seleka origins and objectives, but also on his observations regarding the Anti-Balaka structure, including Mr Ngaïssona's role therein, his meetings with the latter, Mr Yekatom and the Anti-Balaka elements under his control, crimes attributed to the Anti-Balaka, and the flight of Muslims in the CAR.
The Prosecution cites to parts of Jean-Jacques Demafouth's evidence in support of some of its allegations.

The Yekatom Defence argues that Jean-Jacques Demafouth's account is 'wholly unreliable' due to 'his propensity to lead serious allegations against Mr Yekatom, which 'appears to stem from personal animosity' towards him and 'a deliberate attempt to deceive the Chamber in order to exaggerate his own importance'; as a consequence of which his testimony should be disregarded.

In particular, it disputes Jean-Jacques Demafouth's 'multiple baseless, untested and inconsistent claims', including that (i) during Catherine Samba-Panza's visit to Mbaïki on 12 February 2014, '"anti-balaka" reportedly part of RFACPP and "under Mr. Yekatom's orders" brutally murdered one of the last Muslim civilians in Mbaïki'; (ii) Mr Yekatom controlled Boda, Boganangone and various secondary roads within those localities, and members of his group surrounded the enclave in Boda and attacked Muslims venturing out; (iii) 'the RFACPP was responsible for the 5^th^ December Operation'; as well as his claims concerning (iv) the structure of the Anti-Balaka and of 'the RFACPP'. The Yekatom Defence also argues that Jean-Jacques Demafouth lied when confronted in the courtroom with accusations against him involving him in fraudulent and criminal activities. Further, it argues that motivated by power and to place himself at the centre of attention, Jean-Jacques Demafouth 'wilfully fabricat\[ed\] baseless, exaggerated, and entirely unsubstantiated claims, all aimed at incriminating Mr. Yekatom to the greatest extent possible'.

In particular, allegations against the witness concerning (i) embezzlement in the context of his supervision of a demobilisation programme after the 2003 crisis; (ii) being involved in an attack on a church during which civilians died; (iii) planning an alleged coup against the transitional government of Catherine Samba-Panza; or (iv) in fact steering the transitional government headed by Catherine Samba-Panza through his influence on her; with witnesses at times referring to him as a 'manipulator' were generally either unspecific or based on rumours.

Having assessed Jean-Jacques Demafouth's testimony overall, in light of the Defence's arguments, the Chamber concludes that the witness's testimony is, nonetheless, generally credible. The Chamber is of the view that Jean-Jacques Demafouth was generally clearly capable of differentiating in his answers between the sources of information and his own interpretation. The Chamber did not find that he was necessarily biased against either of the accused or the Anti-Balaka in general. Jean-Jacques Demafouth was respectful to both accused when testifying about them and did not express any negative feelings. The witness was forthcoming and provided a significant number of details concerning events and interactions he was personally involved in.

Regarding the three purported inconsistencies pointed out by the Yekatom Defence, concerning the witness's testimony that (i) a Muslim was killed on the day of Catherine Samba-Panza's visit to Mbaïki; (ii) Mr Yekatom controlled neighbourhoods in Bangui, the Mbaïki road and suburbs and that Anti-Balaka under his command encircled the Boda enclave; and (iii) Mr Yekatom controlled the area of Boeing and PK9 and was 'the one controlling the attack from that zone', the Chamber has considered them in the context of the witness's entire testimony and did not find them such as to render his entire evidence unreliable.

During the relevant time, Adrien Poussou held various positions in the CAR government, including special advisor to the prime minister Nicolas Tiangaye, in charge of communication, national reconciliation and civic and democratic culture, as well as spokesperson for the prime minister's office; and also held a position within Catherine Samba-Panza's government. Having assessed Adrien Poussou's testimony overall, in light of the Ngaïssona Defence's arguments, the Chamber concludes that the witness's testimony is, nonetheless, generally credible. In light of his involvement in the early stages of FROCCA and within the governments of Michel Djotodia and then of Catherine Samba-Panza, Adrien Poussou had direct information about many events of relevance to the Chamber. He clearly had access to a wide variety of sources on different sides of the conflict and provided a significant amount of information. The Chamber is of the view that Adrien Poussou clearly distinguished between what he witnessed himself and what he heard about and was able to specify the source of his knowledge with sufficient detail.

The Chamber first turns to the Ngaïssona Defence's allegations that Adrien Poussou attempted to incriminate Mr Ngaïssona 'at all costs', and 'demonstrated a hostile, obstructive and aggressive demeanour' during his examination, often refusing to answer questions, making 'inappropriate and disparaging remarks' and using 'violent language'. Having reviewed his testimony in light of these arguments, the Chamber did not consider that Adrien Poussou was biased against Mr Ngaïssona or the Ngaïssona Defence. He indicated that he had no specific interest in Mr Ngaïssona nor in making things up about him or harming him. Also, when confronted with the fact that during his interview with the Prosecution he had not mentioned that Mr Ngaïssona led COAC together with Yambeté, signed COAC statements and participated at the PK0 rally, Adrien Poussou provided consistent and reasonable explanations which did not denote, in the Chamber's view, any hostility towards Mr Ngaïssona nor his defence counsel.

In the view of the Chamber, P-0954 did not have a lot of firsthand information about the charged incidents in 2013, particularly, having not participated in the preparation or the execution of the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. The Chamber notes that it is not contested, and his testimony leaves no doubt, that P-0965 was a member of the Anti-Balaka within Andjilo's group. P-0965 provides a firsthand account of his experiences and a significant number of details regarding the preparation and his participation in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. P-0965 appeared generally knowledgeable about the groups and individuals who had been in Gobere, even though he himself was not present there. P-0965's evidence concerning the advance of the Anti-Balaka groups to Bangui before 5 December 2013 and how the attack unfolded is largely coherent and consistent with other evidence received before it.
At the same time, as set out below, the Chamber noted inconsistencies in his testimony that, in its view, were not such that rendered his testimony wholly unreliable.

First, as regards the question and the timeline of P-0965's role as Andjilo's 'secretary', the Chamber notes that while P-0965 used this term to describe his role, his functions more closely resembled that of an attendant and informal scribe than a secretary in its traditional sense. In any event, the Chamber considered that the reliability of P-0965's entire account did not rest on his formal role or appointment as Andjilo's secretary.

At the outset, the Chamber notes that Chrysostome Yapélé testified about his experience in the Anti-Balaka during the relevant time, the situation in Carnot and Berbérati, including the attack in Berbérati in February 2014, and the Brazzaville talks. His testimony about Carnot and Berbérati does not directly relate to any of the charged incidents in this case.

As set out below, the Chamber concludes that his evidence concerning a key aspect relevant for this case -- whether Anti-Balaka elements made a distinction between the Seleka and Muslims -- was not forthcoming and therefore, not reliable. In the view of the Chamber, Chrysostome Yapélé distanced himself from the statements he made to the Prosecution investigators and did not offer any meaningful clarity in court about how the Anti-Balaka elements understood the terms 'Muslims' or 'Seleka'. Notably, in court, when asked about his previous statement that 'when I find a Muslim I'm going to kill him', Chrysostome Yapélé explained that 'they' did not want to kill Muslims but the Seleka because 'there was a difference' and 'some' Anti-Balaka were not educated and thought that Seleka were Muslims and did not distinguish between them.

paragraph_text_preview: With regard to his notebook, the Chamber notes the Yekatom Defence's allegation that contrary to P-1339's initial explanation, he could not have written it in 2013 because the photographs on its cover were of events that occurred in 2014. paragraph_text_preview: P-1521 P-1521, a former FACA member and Anti-Balaka, testified fully live with in-court protective measures.

P-1521 joined the Anti-Balaka after August 2013, participated in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 and was later the Anti-Balaka coordinator for operations in the context of the DDR process and national reconciliation.
All parties rely on parts of his evidence in support of their arguments.

Having reviewed his testimony, the Chamber notes that parts of P-1521's evidence stood in contrast with other evidence before it. For example, P-1521, as someone who participated in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 and continued to remain part of the Anti-Balaka during 2014, testified that he was unaware of an attack on Bossangoa on the same day.

Further, in the view of the Chamber, although P-1521 said that '\[he\] explained what \[he\] experienced in the Anti-Balaka movement' and did not 'exonerate \[himself\] or to protect Ngaïssona or the Anti-Balaka', he appeared to present a one-sided, favourable and passive view of Mr Ngaïssona's role in 2014.

On the one hand, P-1521 confirmed the suggestion that Mr Ngaïssona did not have the power to chase the ComZones from their positions and said that Mr Ngaïssona was 'even attacked by some ComZone commanders several times' and 'didn't have the power to decide on a ComZone leader' or 'exert pressure' on the ComZones ('Il n'a pas de pression en tant que telle sur les commandants de zone'). P-1521 also confirmed the suggestion that Mr Ngaïssona signed some mission orders but 'others' could have signed them as well. P-1521 also confirmed the suggestion that Mr Ngaïssona's signatures were forged at some point, but did not provide any further details as regards the basis of this information. Further, P-1521 confirmed that Maxime Mokom wanted to be the head of the Anti-Balaka movement and acted without the order or authority of Mr Ngaïssona;  and added that there were 'misunderstandings' between them and that sometimes Mokom carried out visits in the hinterland without Mr Ngaïssona's orders. On the other hand, P-1521 suggested that Mr Ngaïssona had sufficient authority to demand the Anti-Balaka to take down the roadblocks. For example, P-1521, when asked in relation to evidence concerning Mr Ngaïssona asking the ComZones to erect roadblocks or provoke disorder, testified that it was 'Ngaïssona himself who called us and asked us to tell those people to dismantle the roadblocks that they had set up'.

As regards other aspects of his evidence, P-1521 appeared generally forthcoming about his involvement in the preparation and participation in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 and how the attack unfolded. As a resident of Boy-Rabe, P-1521 was able to explain the routes taken for the attack and answer questions about locations on an annotated map. P-1521 was knowledgeable and forthcoming about several individuals of interest to the case, including Andjilo, Yvon Konaté, Thierry Lebene, Richard Bejouane, Sebastien Wenezoui and Ngremangou, among others. The Ngaïssona Defence argues that the witness is not credible because he is 'volatile', 'easy to manipulate and to corrupt', and participated in an alleged scheme to falsely accuse Mr Ngaïssona. The Ngaïssona Defence also argues that the witness's demeanour was 'revealing' in that when responding to questions he 'repeatedly chose not to elaborate on his answers, limiting himself to referring to his statement' while also providing 'crucial information' during his testimony which is absent from his prior statement, without a convincing explanation.

The Chamber notes that the Ngaïssona Defence's submissions in support of these arguments rely mostly on D30-4914's evidence. Having reviewed the information provided by the latter, the Chamber observes that D30-4914 appeared to have had some contact with P-1719 and was able to provide evidence about P-1719's role and activities in Douala and in the CAR, including in Bangui, as well as his work at the African Union in 2015. However, the Chamber is of the view that D30-4914's impressions that P-1719's was 'volatile' and 'easy to corrupt' appeared to be based on his own reading of P-1719's behaviour as he did not point to any objective information in support, and more importantly, that could affect P-1719's reliability.

As to P-1719's demeanour in court, it did not appear to the Chamber that he was attempting to withhold information. Rather, in the specific examples cited by the Ngaïssona Defence, the Chamber finds that the witness was forthcoming, provided detailed information and answered when additional clarification was needed. For example, when asked to specify the identity of an individual with whom he was in contact through Facebook, the witness provided a long answer, at the end of which he said, 'I'm going to stop here', adding that '\[p\]erhaps there may be further questions which you are going to put me as regards what I've just told you'. After a follow-up question, the witness again provided a long answer and ended with, 'I think I'll stop here on this particular point. If there are any questions, I will do my best to answer them'. In the Chamber's view, this demeanour does not show any unwillingness to respond to questions.

Furthermore, in relation to the alleged omission of 'crucial information' from his prior statement, the Chamber considers that this does not render P-1719's testimony unreliable, as such. The Chamber notes that this concerns instructions coming from Yaoundé, which he mentioned during his testimony. In the Chamber's view, P-1719 adequately explained why he only mentioned this in court. Indeed, P-1719 said that what prompted him to mention it was that the 'personalities', who were 'part of the general staff' and who are mentioned in his prior statement, 'were in permanent coordination with Yaoundé', although he clarified that he did not receive any instructions directly 'from the authority'. The Chamber is of the view that the witness was simply providing a further clarification to his prior statement and that the fact that he only mentioned Yaoundé in court does not affect the credibility of this account.
