paragraph_text_preview: P-1839P-1839, a former Anti-Balaka element in Mr Yekatom's group, testified fully live with in-court protective measures, and received Rule 74 assurances.

P-1839, a civilian, joined Mr Yekatom's group at Yamwara after 5 December 2013 and followed the group on their advance along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, carrying out various roles, including bodyguard for Alkanto, treasurer for Mr Yekatom and later his bodyguard as she gained Mr Yekatom's trust. As such, she testified about, inter alia, her experience at Yamwara, including training the elements received there; the advance of Mr Yekatom's group along the axis, including instructions on the targeting of Muslims; weapons and ammunition of the group along the axis; Mr Yekatom's relationship with Mr Ngaïssona; meetings the witness attended, including a 'mediation' meeting and one at Catherine Samba-Panza's residence; as well as the meeting at the Mbaïki church and Mr Yekatom's 'peace messages' after this meeting. Importantly, the witness also testified about several incidents involving the mistreatment and/or killing of individuals at Yamwara and along the axis by Mr Yekatom and/or elements of his group. P-1839, who at some point also worked for Léopold Bara as part of his security, left the Anti-Balaka after Mr Yekatom reportedly killed two of his bodyguards.

P-1839's testimony was comprehensive, offering evidence with a level of depth that spoke to her first-hand knowledge and personal experiences in Mr Yekatom's group. For example, she testified in detail about the command structure and hierarchy within the group and the personal interactions and power dynamics between Mr Yekatom and other Anti-Balaka such as Cœur de Lion, Alkanto or Mr Ngaïssona. In this regard, the Chamber considers entirely without merit the Yekatom Defence's submissions that P-1839 lacked military understanding and would not have been privy to these details. The Chamber notes that her evidence in this regard is extensively discussed further below.

paragraph_text_preview: P-1847P-1847, a former advisor of François Bozizé when he was president of the CAR, testified fully live with in-court protective measures. The Chamber introduced P-1847's prior recorded testimony (the 'Statements') into evidence pursuant to Rule 68(2)(d) of the Rules, as it found that the witness had been subjected to interference.

P-1847 joined François Bozizé at the Hilton hotel in Yaoundé following the Seleka coup, and stayed at this hotel for three months with him. In his Statements, P-1847 discusses, inter alia, his relations with François Bozizé and the latter's activities in Cameroon; interacting with individuals in Yaoundé; meetings or activities of groups such as COCORA and FROCCA; the objectives, organisation, hierarchy and financing of the Anti-Balaka, the roles of both accused within the movement, as well as attacks it executed, including the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013.

The Prosecution cites to parts of P-1847's evidence in support of some of its allegations. The Ngaïssona Defence submits that the Chamber should attribute minimal weight to P-1847's Statements, especially where his statements and live testimony are 'completely inconsistent with respect to Mr N\[gaïssona\]'s alleged acts and conduct'. In particular, it argues that it is impossible to reconcile the Statements with his live testimony; that the Chamber made no findings on 'P-1847 changing his testimony at the behest of Mr N\[gaïssona\] or someone close to him'; that there is evidence of this witness's prior involvement in a scheme to incriminate Mr Ngaïssona; and that given the lack of evidence on P-1847's reasons for recanting his Statements, it cannot be inferred beyond reasonable doubt that his Statements are true whereas his live testimony is false. The Ngaïssona Defence also argues that P-1847's Statements are (i) internally inconsistent, (ii) hearsay, (iii) largely uncorroborated, and (iv) contradicted by other, direct, evidence.

At the outset, the Chamber recalls that it introduced P-1847's Statements into evidence pursuant to Rule 68(2)(d) of the Rules after finding that the witness had failed to testify on material aspects included in the Statements and that such failure was due to him having been materially influenced by improper interference. Noting that the Statements made extensive references to the acts and conduct of both accused, the Chamber decided not to rely on the paragraphs of the Statements mentioning Mr Yekatom's acts and conduct to the extent that they would be unduly prejudicial to him. As for the references to Mr Ngaïssona, the Chamber found that this situation could be distinguished in that despite the Prosecution's attempts to elicit incriminating evidence contained in the Statements, P-1847 'plainly failed to give evidence on material aspects', with the Ngaïssona Defence being put 'in a position to fully and meaningfully question the Witness'. Importantly, the Chamber notes that this decision was upheld by the Appeals Chamber.

paragraph_text_preview: Turning to the Ngaïssona Defence's arguments, the Chamber first notes its submission that it is 'likely' that P-1847's evidence was contaminated in the context of the scheme or plot against Mr Ngaïssona and that his account of Mr Ngaïssona's contribution to the Anti-Balaka movement, 'riddled with inconsistencies', should be examined in light of the witness's close relationship to Touadéra and Ngrebada and the latter's involvement in the abovementioned plot. The Chamber considers that these allegations, based on P-1847's relationship with other individuals and the likelihood of his evidence being contaminated, are entirely speculative. The Chamber further considers them to be implausible, in that any involvement in a scheme or plot 'against' Mr Ngaïssona would be expected to lead to an in-court testimony less favourable to Mr Ngaïssona, rather than the opposite. Further, the Chamber recalls its findings about the witness being 'materially influenced by improper interference' and notes that this relates to his live testimony, but not to his Statements.

Regarding the Ngaïssona Defence's argument that the Chamber made no findings on 'P-1847 changing his testimony at the behest of Mr N\[gaïssona\] or someone close to him', the Chamber recalls its finding that interference under Rule 68(2)(d) of the Rules need not be attributable to the accused. Significantly, this was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber when finding that the Chamber 'reasonably concluded that the witness had been improperly interfered with in relation to his testimony, and it was not required to make any further findings on the exact nature of such interference'. For the same reasons, the Chamber equally dismisses the argument that '\[g\]iven this lack of evidence on P-1847's motives for recanting, it cannot be inferred beyond a reasonable doubt that P-1847's prior recorded statements are true whereas his live testimony is false'.

As for the Ngaïssona Defence's challenges to the substance of P-1847's evidence, the Chamber notes that it specifically disputes the witness's account on, inter alia, (i) meetings at the Golf residence (arguing that the Statements contain hearsay and uncorroborated evidence in this regard); (ii) Joachim Kokaté gathering officers on behalf of FROCCA (arguing that P-1847's source of knowledge is unclear and contradicted by more reliable evidence); (iii) François Bozizé being in touch with the Anti-Balaka in the CAR through Florent Kema (which it qualifies as a speculative and uncorroborated claim); (iv) ammunition being provided to the Gobere group by a woman; (v) Mr Ngaïssona 'regularly' visiting François Bozizé at the Hilton hotel or Golf residence (arguing that it is uncorroborated, based on hearsay and discredited by Didier Ouebio's testimony, further noting that P-1847 subsequently refuted in court having seen Mr Ngaïssona at the Golf residence during François Bozizé's stay); (vi) meetings at the Hilton hotel taking place with François Bozizé; (vii) Mr Ngaïssona 'crossing over' to Bouar (arguing that P-1847's sources of information on this aspect are unreliable) and, more generally, his evidence in relation to the border area; (viii) Mr Ngaïssona and Bernard Mokom liaising with Anti-Balaka elements at the border from the Golf residence (evidence which it argues is contradicted by other direct evidence); (ix) Mr Ngaïssona's role in providing financial assistance to the Anti-Balaka; and (x) Mr Ngaïssona giving instructions to Anti-Balaka elements, including in relation to the attack in Bangui on 5 December 2013.

paragraph_text_preview: In the view of the Chamber, the arguments raised by the Ngaïssona Defence are not such that they rendered the Statements and his in-court testimony unreliable. In this regard, the Chamber notes that P-1847 provided first-hand and detailed information about François Bozizé's activities in Cameroon -- an information which P-1847 obtained in his unique position accompanying him around Yaoundé and other places. In the view of the Chamber, the witness appeared to be honest and forthcoming when responding to the investigators' questions, also when he did not have the information he was asked about. For example, P-1847 specified that he went with François Bozizé to meetings in Cameroon but he himself did not attend, and also indicated that he did not know the names of all the people who participated in those meetings. P-1847 also explained the sources of his information, which included Anti-Balaka elements such as Levy Yakété, Dedane, Joachim Kokaté and Achille Godonam.

Overall, the Chamber noted various discrepancies between the witness's statement and the information he provided in court. However, they did not go to such extent as to render his evidence fully unreliable.

For instance, in his statement, P-2027 stated that Mr Ngaïssona gave him money in Cameroon; that Mr Ngaïssona had helped him before in Bangui, that he did this 'out of the goodness of his heart' and helped a lot of people like this, including pensioners in Bangui; and further stated that he felt no obligations towards Mr Ngaïssona nor like he 'owed' him anything because of the money he gave him. In court, P-2027 said that Mr Ngaïssona would help people in need, including 'retired people who had unpaid arrears', and that Mr Ngaïssona 'wanted to calm down the Anti-Balaka' and give them money to not cause disorder. For example, the witness was asked about an exchange in which two individuals said that P-2027 had received a 'large' sum of money and had to be watched because he was a danger for their movement, or that P-2027 was mandated to meet with 'white people'. Having assessed P-2269's testimony holistically, in light of the Defence's allegations and in relation to other evidence before it, the Chamber concludes that it is nonetheless generally credible. P-2269 had a vast amount of first-hand knowledge about the events in 2013, especially about the various groups in Gobere, including his own, the movement of some of these groups towards Bangui and their participation in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. The Chamber did not consider this evidence unique in that others like him, including FACA members, testified about the events starting from the formation of Anti-Balaka groups in Gobere and their participation in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. In the view of the Chamber, P-2269 appeared forthcoming and truthful about his own involvement in the Anti-Balaka and his actions in 2013. P-2269's account was largely internally consistent, and he was able to explain the differences in his interview with the Prosecution sufficiently.

Turning to specific inconsistencies raised by it, the Chamber considered that those regarding P-2269's presence in Gobere were minor and did not throw into question the fact that he himself was present there. This is particularly supported by the detailed account P-2269 provided on the base set up in Gobere, the different groups present there and the activities they carried out. Similarly, the Ngaïssona Defence's arguments concerning the list provided by P-2269 and his handwriting are based on speculation and do not make the remainder of his evidence unreliable. As regards the remaining inconsistencies raised concerning his account, in particular on the leadership structure in Gobere and his concrete role in the movement, as well as regarding financial and materiel support, the Chamber has assessed P-2269's evidence together with other evidence before it.
As regards the Yekatom Defence's arguments, the Chamber has assessed P-2269's claims about Mr Yekatom crossing to Zongo together with other evidence in its evidentiary analysis below.
Overall, the Chamber has assessed the reliability of P-2269's information on a case-by-case basis and within the context of other evidence before it. ######

paragraph_text_preview: Having assessed P-2602's testimony holistically, in light of the Ngaïssona Defence's allegations and in relation to other evidence before it, the Chamber concludes that it is generally credible. P-2602 had a vast amount of first-hand knowledge about the events in 2013, especially about the various groups in Gobere, including his own, and the attacks in the Bossangoa region. As to the latter, the Chamber finds that the inconsistencies raised by the Ngaïssona Defence concerning the exact circumstances of the attacks on the villages were minor, especially since P-2602 was not present in all of the attacks and did not claim to list them exhaustively in his account. In the view of the Chamber, P-2602 appeared forthcoming and knowledgeable about his own involvement in the Anti-Balaka and his actions in 2013. P-2602's account was largely internally consistent, he appeared to be generally able to distinguish between the sources of his knowledge and was able to explain the differences in his interview with the Prosecution sufficiently. Overall, the Chamber has assessed the reliability of P-2602's information on a case-by-case basis and within the context of other evidence before it. ######

The Chamber considers that the witness's in-court testimony was coherent with his prior recorded statement, and that his openness and explanations about why certain individuals did not trust him, as well as admitting that he might have received false or misleading information, reinforced the witness's credibility. Furthermore, the Chamber notes that the witness provided differentiated answers and made clear that some of the information he received from others turned out to be incorrect, but that he usually attempted to cross-check the information he received. P-2673 was also clear about which events he experienced himself, and distinguished own experiences from matters he heard from others, often specifying sources of the information he received. The Chamber also considers that, in this instance, the fact that these individuals might have had a negative opinion about P-2673 is not in itself sufficient to undermine the witness's credibility overall. The Chamber also considers the Ngaïssona Defence's argument about P-2673's demeanour to be speculative.

As to the Ngaïssona Defence's claim that P-2673 was part of a scheme to falsely incriminate Mr Ngaïssona, the Chamber notes, as further detailed below, that it is essentially based on the evidence of D30-4914 and D30-4197, whom the Chamber considers not credible in this regard. Furthermore, in this instance and taking into account its findings in the preceding paragraph on the witness's candour, the Chamber does not consider that P-2673's testimony was 'rehearsed' or that it lacked spontaneity simply because he 'repeatedly' referred to or stood by his prior recorded testimony during his examination in court, but rather merely referred to information which he already provided.

The Ngaïssona Defence relies on Brice Stanislas Mohi's evidence to demonstrate the presence and circumstances of Mr Ngaïssona's stay in Cameroon in 2013 and to contest the claim that Mr Ngaïssona financed transportation of elements to the Cameroonian border.
At the outset, the Chamber notes that Brice Stanislas Mohi stayed in Douala, visited Mr Ngaïssona's house and directly interacted with Mr Ngaïssona and his family in 2013.

As set out below, having reviewed his evidence, the Chamber notes that Brice Stanislas Mohi was not forthcoming in his testimony and limited the scope of his knowledge on the events throughout the testimony. In particular, the Chamber finds that the witness downplayed the frequency and nature of his interactions with Mr Ngaïssona in Douala and thereafter in the CAR. At the same time, the witness also overemphasised Mr Ngaïssona's involvement in football-related activities at the time, admitting either not knowing or having heard about Mr Ngaïssona's involvement in anything but football-related activities during the relevant time. In the view of the Chamber, the witness's claims, in and of themselves, are highly improbable and contradicted by other evidence before it.

For example, in his statement, Brice Stanislas Mohi said that in Douala, he would see Mr Ngaïssona 'often', one or two times per month, including on Saturdays, during the weekend. In court, asked about his visits to Mr Ngaïssona, the witness said that they did not take place often and that '\[s\]ometimes', he would go there on Saturday or Sunday, if there was nothing to do at home.

paragraph_text_preview: P-2049 P-2049, a Muslim civilian from Bossangoa, testified fully live with in-court protective measures. He testified about the Anti-Balaka attacks on and near Bossangoa in 2013, including the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013. In particular, he provided evidence on the identities of victims of these attacks.

The Prosecution relies on P-2049's evidence in support of some of its arguments. The Ngaïssona Defence argues that the witness is not credible as his claims are contradictory, implausible, insincere, biased and inconsistent with other reliable evidence. It also submits that his evidence about the death of individuals in the various attacks in Zere, Benzambé and Bossangoa is unsubstantiated, untruthful and based on anonymous hearsay; and further argues that P-2049 and his family were associated with the Seleka.

In the view of the Chamber, P-2049 was clear about how he became aware of the events that occurred in and around Bossangoa, and explained his sources of knowledge. The Chamber notes that throughout his testimony, P-2049 differentiated clearly between his personal experiences and the information he came to learn from others. For example, P-2049, when asked about an individual selling gris-gris, stated that he 'did not see those products with \[his\] own eyes' and that his information on this was based on what he had heard. P-2049, when asked about 'Caporal Ndangba', said that he had 'heard people talk about him', and explained the source of his information. P-2049, when asked if he was 'informed about everything that was happening' in Bossangoa at the time, said that one had to 'make a distinction' and that, at the École de la Liberté, it was possible for him to receive information because he was present but could not receive information about what was happening in their area or in the bush.

The Ngaïssona Defence heavily relies on D30-4608's evidence to counter the arguments made by several witnesses on the events that occurred in Bossangoa in 2013 and 2014. The Ngaïssona Defence heavily relies on D30-4608's evidence to counter the arguments made by several witnesses on the events that occurred in Bossangoa in 2013 and 2014. The Prosecution argues that some of D30-4608's evidence is not reliable as it is based on hearsay, such as claiming that it 'was common knowledge' that there were arms stored in the mosques.

As set out below, the Chamber considers that D30-4608's claims and opinions concerning the Seleka and the Muslims, when assessed together, indicated a strong bias against the Muslim community in Bossangoa, so much so that they threw into question his evidence on key aspects relevant to the Chamber. Furthermore, these claims were not supported by any other evidence before the Chamber.

D30-4608 made broad generalisations about the Muslims in Bossangoa and was unable to explain the source of his knowledge or opinion. For example, D30-4608 stated that Muslim civilians were armed, even the women, even before the Seleka arrived, such as with Kalashnikovs; that there had always been arms stored at the mosques, even before the rebellion of 2003; and that the Seleka gave arms to the Muslims to protect themselves, and also protected the traders. He further stated that some Muslim civilians joined the Seleka, providing some names, including that of a woman. During his testimony, when asked whether he had seen Muslim civilians with arms back then, he said that he saw '\[n\]otably young people', that he remembered one by face and name, and that 'all the young Muslims of Bossangoa, even traders, they all had weapons'. When asked whether he saw other women besides the one he mentioned in his statement who had weapons, he said that he had 'heard of that' and that 'many people' had seen the woman he mentioned. When asked how he learnt that there were arms stored in the mosques, he said that 'everybody knew that', that it was 'common knowledge', that he had discovered 'a lot of weapons in the mosque of Paoua' and that '\[i\]n Bossangoa, everybody talked about it'. When asked whether his statement that all the Muslims, even the women, were armed, was a generalisation, he said that 'it was more the majority of women', that it was 'known even in the town of Bossangoa' and that '\[p\]eople knew that'. He also said that Muslim civilians at the École de la Liberté were armed and 'walked around with their arms', 'always' carrying them.

paragraph_text_preview: P-2475 P-2475, a former alleged 'child soldier' and Anti-Balaka element, testified fully live with in-court protective measures, and received Rule 74 assurances. He reported being forcibly recruited by Mr Yekatom's group in Boeing in or about July 2013, and having actively participated in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. He also reported being stationed with Mr Yekatom's elements at an Anti-Balaka base at Yamwara following the attack on Bangui. He later participated in the 'child soldier' demobilisation process in Pissa in August 2014, conducted by Enfants sans frontières (hereinafter: 'ESF' and the 'ESF programme', respectively), was present at the 'centre de transit et d'orientation' (the 'CTO') in Mbaïki, and appears on the list prepared by ESF officials containing the names of children that participated at the Mbaïki CTO (the 'ESF List').

paragraph_text_preview: The Yekatom Defence has raised several challenges to the reliability of P-2475's account and argues that P-2475's 'obvious lack of regard to his oath' requires 'the exclusion of his evidence'. In particular, it argues that P-2475 falsified his identifying details, namely his age; the death of his mother; his membership in Mr Yekatom's group; as well as his testimony in respect of (i) his abduction; (ii) the presence of child soldiers in Mr Yekatom's group; (iii) Muslims being killed and buried at Yamwara; and (iv) the killing of Djido Saleh by the Anti-Balaka. Further, the Yekatom Defence argues that P-2475 provided an inconsistent account concerning, inter alia, his section chiefs, the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, and P-1839's role in this attack. Moreover, it asserts that P-2475 is connected with the certain officials 'in relation to his false testimony', and alleges that P-2475 was motivated by monetary gains to provide an unreliable account.

footnote_content: Certificate, CAR-OTP-2128-1197, at 1198. P-2475, confronted in court about the apparent overwriting on the year of birth, said that he had never seen this document. P-2475, shown Certificate, CAR-D29-0013-0004, a copy of his baptism certificate obtained by the Yekatom Defence mentioning the year of birth '1994' and Baptism register, CAR-D29-0014-0065, maintained that he was born in 1999 and not in 1994. *See* P-2475: T-133, p. 70, line 19 -- p. 74, line 6. *See also* Certificate, CAR-D29-0013-0096.
paragraph_text_preview: Having considered the documents presented to demonstrate P-2475's age, the Chamber finds the attendant challenges to their reliability and authenticity well founded. First, the year of birth on P-2475's baptism certificate '1994' appears to have been overwritten with '1999' and does not correspond with the purported original copies of the baptism certificate obtained by the Yekatom Defence. Second, P-2475's school certificate appears to have been issued by someone who did not have the authority to do so. Third, another one of P-2475's school certificates appears to contain a correction in white ink and overwriting on the years of attendance as '2011-2012', and D29-6011, who issued this certificate, stated that this correction was not done by him. For these reasons, the Chamber cannot rely on these documents to enter any findings relating to P-2475's age.

D29-6036 testified fully live and knew P-2475. They met in the period between the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 and the arrival of the Anti-Balaka in Pissa. The witness played football matches with P-2475 in the period after 5 December 2013 when the Seleka were still in Pissa. The witness said that he would meet P-2475 during this period, and would visit P-2475's family during this time. The witness said that he was with P-2475 when the Anti-Balaka entered Pissa. He also said that after the Seleka's departure and after the Anti-Balaka entered Pissa, P-2475 would give water to the Anti-Balaka stationed at the checkpoint in the vicinity of the gendarmerie. According to the witness, during this time, P-2475 continued his activities and meeting each other. The witness said that he never saw P-2475 within the Anti-Balaka movement.

Having assessed P-2476's testimony in light of the submissions by the parties, the Chamber finds that there are indeed significant inconsistencies when it comes to his experiences within Mr Yekatom's group.

As discussed in detail below, the Chamber by majority, Judge Chung dissenting, finds P-2476's account to be wholly unreliable. In the view of the Chamber by majority, Judge Chung dissenting, these inconsistencies are irreconcilable with his remaining account and other evidence before the Chamber, namely, the length of time he spent in Mr Yekatom's group, when and how he joined it, and observing Cœur de Lion's role and actions in relation to Mbaïki and Boda.

Judge Chung considers that these inconsistencies were of a minor nature, especially given P-2476's age at the time of the events and his own admission that he was too young at the time to remember all the details correctly.

The majority appreciates that P-2476 did not need to remember all the details having to do with his experience in Mr Yekatom's group coherently and consistently, especially given his purported age at the time. However, in the view of the majority, the inconsistencies in his testimony were crucial to his account as an alleged child soldier, and such that the majority was unable to resolve the bold claims made by P-2476 about Cœur de Lion's actions with his inability to place himself in time in relation to the latter's death. The same held true for the amount of time that P-2476 allegedly spent in Mr Yekatom's group.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes the significant challenges to V45-0001's identity that were raised and finds them well-founded. Following the testimonies of V45-0001 and V45-0002 (the 'CLRV1 Witnesses') in September 2023 and during its threat and risk assessment of these witnesses, the VWU discovered material concerning their identities and brought this to the attention of the Chamber. Upon order by the Single Judge, the VWU filed a report in which it stated that it found several indications on V45-0001's phone that suggested that his identity was not 'Dimitry Socrate Mongo' but 'Dimitri Socrate Molouba' and that he was Wilfred Molouba's son. In support, the VWU reported that there had been exchanges between V45-0001 and a phone number used by Wilfred Molouba in which the former used the word 'papa'.

In this regard, the Chamber also considers that V45-0001's identity-related documents contain discrepancies that he was unable to reasonably explain in court and as such were not reconcilable with other evidence on the record. Additionally, as discussed further below, the Chamber also observed serious inconsistencies in his testimony concerning his alleged experience within the Anti-Balaka.

As regards his identity-related documents, V45-0001, shown the reconstitution of the birth certificate of 'Mongo Dimi Socrate' born on '13 August 2003' and parents named 'Jean-Baptiste Mongo' and 'Stella Mitiami', testified that he recognised this document and confirmed that it was a court ruling handed down subsequent to an application made on his behalf.

As regards his identity-related documents, V45-0001, shown the reconstitution of the birth certificate of 'Mongo Dimi Socrate' born on '13 August 2003' and parents named 'Jean-Baptiste Mongo' and 'Stella Mitiami', testified that he recognised this document and confirmed that it was a court ruling handed down subsequent to an application made on his behalf.

However, the Chamber notes that the information in this judgment purportedly reconstituting V45-0001's birth certificate is not consistent with his testimony, nor is it consistent with other evidence before it.

First, while V45-0001 maintained that his date of birth was 13 August 2003, it is not consistent with other documents on the record. V45-0001's victim application form and the declaration of identity contained therein state that his date of birth is 13 June 2002. Asked whether he had told Kevin Mborolo, the person who took down the information to fill the victim application form, his date of birth, V45-0001 said that he had told this person that he was born on 13 August 2003. When confronted with the dates as they appear on his victim application form, V45-0001 said that he did not know a lot about it because he had indicated that it was 13 August 2003 and his statement was not read back to him after they took it and perhaps that is where the problem came from.

Fifth, and relatedly, V45-0001's testimony suggests that his reconstituted birth certificate was issued without his knowledge of the process. Asked about the administrative process of issuing the aforementioned document, V45-0001 said that his counsel obtained it so that his birth certificate could be issued. V45-0001 agreed that he himself gave the information on the basis of which this document was issued. V45-0001 was not aware if any supporting documents had been filed before requesting this document as he was not present before the tribunal to obtain the ruling. Asked if he gave the reason for filing an application for this document, V45-0001 said that his counsel wanted to have his passport issued and therefore asked for his birth certificate, however, his birth certificate did not have a counterfoil; and at the tribunal, they did not have access to his birth certificate and this is why they decided to issue a new birth certificate. When asked about it, V45-0001 agreed that he had never said that his birth certificate had been stolen and nor had he provided any information sheet in support of a reissue of his birth certificate.

In this regard, the Chamber notes that V45-0001 said that he did not know this person's (Wilfried) surname, but recognised the individual depicted in a photograph, as Wilfried, the focal point of the ESF. V45-0001 himself refuted the suggestion, on the basis of various documents, that he was in fact this person's son and that his identity had been fabricated by Kevin Mborolo, working in tight cooperation with this person. Further, he stated not knowing the children of this person and Prisca Mbongo or, that they had children together. V45-0001 did not recognise anyone in photographs shown to him, which, according to the Yekatom Defence, depict individuals also related to Wilfried Molouba.

paragraph_text_preview: Having reviewed V45-0001's baptism documents and health records submitted by the CLRV1 in support of his identity and age, the Chamber finds them inauthentic and unreliable.
For these reasons, the Chamber is convinced that V45-0001 was not who he claimed to be.

Furthermore, and in any event, as set out below, the Chamber found V45-0001's account inherently unreliable as it contained significant discrepancies insofar as it concerned his alleged experience as 'child soldier' and Mr Yekatom's alleged acts.

In his victim application form, V45-0001 mentioned being taken by force by Nganazoui and Sartana and being given bullets by Sartana to threaten him not to leave the Anti-Balaka. However, during his testimony, V45-0001 did not mention Nganazoui or Sartana and said that it was Mr Yekatom who gave him the two bullets.

In his victim application form, V45-0001 mentioned being taken by force by Nganazoui and Sartana and being given bullets by Sartana to threaten him not to leave the Anti-Balaka. However, during his testimony, V45-0001 did not mention Nganazoui or Sartana and said that it was Mr Yekatom who gave him the two bullets.

The Chamber finds that V45-0001 was unable to offer a reasonable explanation for this discrepancy. Asked about this difference, V45-0001 said that Kevin Mborolo did not read back to him his account when interviewing him for the victim application form. V45-0001 did agree that it was incorrect that Sartana handed him the bullets; according to V45-0001, if Mborolo had read out what he had written down, they would have realised this mistake, but unfortunately he did not. The Chamber considers it unlikely that the victim application form would omit mention of Mr Yekatom's actions had he mentioned them to whoever was taking down the notes, and instead would have recorded a completely different name.

Similarly, V45-0001's victim application form mentions two bullets which states that he kept until the date on which he filled out the form, while during his testimony, V45-0001 said that Mr Yekatom gave him the bullets once, one to him and one to another person, and that V45-0001 then gave those bullets to ESF. From a further answer, it is unclear whether a bullet was given just to V45-0001 or also to another person. In addition, V45-0001 was unclear about when he gave the bullets to ESF: while agreeing that he gave the bullets to ESF in 2018 while signing his victim application form -- which states that he still had the bullets -- in 2021, V45-0001 said the victim application form contained incorrect or false information, while his account given to CLRV1 -- as read back to him, but not signed -- was the correct one. According to V45-0001, when asked more generally about the differences between his victim application form and his testimony, he said that his counsel did ask questions to find out where the differences were, and that he told them that the statement made at ESF was different because 'we didn't read our statements in -- it wasn't in Sango so that we could provide the necessary corrections and recount the accurate situation of what happened'.

Overall, the Chamber concludes that while V45-0002's date of birth seems less contested, the above raises such doubts as to his real identity that the Chamber is not in a position to rely on V45-0002's evidence. This is so also because aside from such doubts, and in any event, the Chamber finds that V45-0002's account is replete with discrepancies that throw into question the remainder of his evidence, in particular his claim that he was an element of the Anti-Balaka. Some of these discrepancies are set out below.

During his testimony, V45-0002 agreed that he joined the Anti-Balaka before 5 December 2013 in Bangui-Bouchia, after which he went to Mogné forest before going to Kapou forest and then going to fight in Boda; following this, he agreed that he was deployed to the Mbaïki checkpoints. However, V45-0002's victim application form suggests that he joined the Anti-Balaka in March 2014 and that the events described in the form took place between March and August 2014. When asked how long he remained within the Anti-Balaka, V45-0002 testified that he left the group in 2015, after the 'last battle in Boda'.

In this regard, the Chamber notes that V45-0002 appeared to provide some general details about the ESF programme that do not comport with the other evidence concerning this programme. In particular, asked about the selection process, V45-0002 first testified that some ESF staff initially met with the mayor of Pissa, Okoua-Penguia, and asked to be shown the 'child victims' so they could be demobilised, re-educated and no longer be integrated into any armed groups. He then said that before being selected, he was asked questions by an ESF staff member, after which a date was fixed for a vehicle to take them to Mbaïki. According to V45-0002, there were many of them at the time of the discussions which took place at the town hall, and at which, he agreed, Didier Beninga was also present. He further said that once in Mbaïki, Kevin Kakpayen came from time to time providing them with food and telling them what to eat, while he agreed that he also saw Kevin Mborolo in Mbaïki.

The evidence suggests that there were indeed procedural irregularities in the manner in which the ESF programme was launched. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo, the prefect of the Lobaye prefecture at the time, when asked about ESF, confirmed that he learned that ESF had received funding but did not know where it came from. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo said that the terms of reference of the ESF programme were not filed with him and that ESF was not able to provide all the required documentation -- 'no reference document and no report' -- that the authorities would have needed to know the objective of the project. The witness also said that they 'did not insist' on these procedures because he personally wanted to satisfy the needs of the population and help the community.

In this respect, the Chamber has considered the evidence by the prefect of the Lobaye prefecture at the time, Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo, who indicated that he received complaints that 'some NGO heads', including ESF, were named as being those who tried to play in favour of some people and to the detriment of the others.

Nonetheless, the Chamber finds that these irregularities do not discredit the entirety of P-1974's testimony. While certain individuals may have tried to benefit from the ESF programme through their proximity with P-1974, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that this was a deliberate scheme, rendering P-1974's testimony unreliable as a whole.

Having assessed P-1974's testimony overall, in light of the Yekatom Defence's allegations, the Chamber finds that P-1974 is, nonetheless, generally credible insofar as the general administration and purpose of ESF is concerned. However, noting his limited oversight role over the ESF programme, the Chamber notes that P-1974 was unable to provide any first-hand information on the specific children that participated in it, their ages, let alone their membership or role within Mr Yekatom's group. In light of this, the Chamber cannot rely on his account to establish the ages of the children that participated in the ESF programme. As regards his claims of seeing children at the Pissa and Sekia checkpoints, the Chamber has assessed them in light of other evidence received before it in its evidentiary analysis below. ######

paragraph_text_preview: The Yekatom Defence argues that P-2018 was part of the ESF 'fraudulent scheme', raising a number of arguments in relation to P-2018's actions and documents authored by him.

The Chamber first turns to P-2018's testimony concerning how children were identified and how their ages were verified for the purposes of the ESF programme. According to P-2018, children under the ages of '18 years' within Anti-Balaka groups were identified during 'identification missions' by P-2018 and Anti-Balaka chiefs purportedly acting on instructions by Mr Yekatom. P-2018 testified that identification forms drafted by UNICEF were filled out by the Anti-Balaka chiefs. He also testified that within their group, they had a secretary who would go from one locality to the next to help fill out these forms and was in charge of filling out the forms; Mr Yekatom had the secretary do this. The Chamber did not have access to any of the purported filled out identification forms and therefore, no assessment can be carried out on how and whether they were duly filled out. According to P-2018, these forms were submitted to UNICEF where they remain to this day.

Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo resided in Mbaïki when Mr Yekatom's group arrived there and also when the ESF programme took place. He provided evidence about, inter alia, events that occurred in Mbaïki at the relevant time, including the meeting held at the St Jeanne d'Arc Church with Mr Yekatom, the fleeing of Muslims from villages to Mbaïki and therefrom to other locations, Djido Saleh's death, and the ESF programme.

The Chamber sets out below its assessment of the evidence submitted and discussed before it at trial with respect to each of the findings of fact identified above in Section II ('Findings of fact'). In particular, the Chamber details below the evidence which supports each of those findings of fact, and explains how any such finding was reached in light of the available evidence -- and the arguments made at trial -- both in support of and against that particular finding, as appropriate. This also includes instances when findings on the facts and circumstances described in the charges are reached by way of inference -- thus, through facts which are of 'intermediate' or 'subsidiary' nature -- on the basis of circumstantial evidence. At the same time, the Chamber clarifies that while it structures its discussion below delineating its analysis of evidence with respect to each individual finding of fact, evidence may be relevant to more than one factual finding even if not necessarily reiterated in each instance, and all evidence submitted and discussed before it at trial has been considered holistically.The conflict in the Central African Republic between 2012 and 2014 The formation of the Seleka, its advance to and takeover of Bangui, and ensuing violence The formation of the Seleka Around August 2012, a coalition of armed groups opposing then-President François Bozizé emerged in the Central African Republic (CAR) under the name of the 'Seleka', led by CAR citizens and including elements from Chad and Sudan. Michel Djotodia became the leader of the Seleka.

At the outset, the Chamber considers it of import to briefly outline some of the evidence illustrating events and circumstances providing the background to the crisis in the CAR during the period relevant to the charges. While this is not to provide a fully exhaustive account of events, the Chamber is of the view that some understanding of the context leads to a better understanding of the events directly relevant to the charges.

As aptly put by Catherine Samba-Panza, the former president of transition of the CAR, it is important 'to realise that the \[CAR\] has been experiencing political instability for 30 years and \[...\] had a number of crises -- a political crisis, social crisis, military/political crisis -- \[which\] weakened the state considerably and have caused problems within the people in terms of social cohesion and national cohesion'.

The Chamber notes that the CAR Panel of Experts similarly concluded that the conflict which broke out in 2012 and culminated in the overthrow of François Bozizé on 24 March 2013 was the most recent escalation in a series of crises that the country experienced over 40 years. *See* CAR Panel Interim Report 2014, CAR-OTP-2001-0835, at 0843, paras 14-17, 19.

Further points of contention concerned the fraud allegations surrounding the 2011 elections following which François Bozizé remained in power, as well as the suggestion that regions in the north and north-east of the country, predominantly inhabited by Muslims, were considered to be neglected by the Bozizé regime. Specifically, Nicolas Tiangaye, former prime minister of the CAR, testified that he and others in the opposition contested the 2011 election results and created a movement calling for an annulment and re-organisation of the elections. According to Nicolas Tiangaye, this seizure of power and management of the country's assets created conditions for violence and the rebellion by the Seleka. The panel of experts on the CAR set up pursuant to a UN Security Council resolution (the 'CAR Panel') similarly noted a deep fragmentation of the political landscape, combined with increased activities of a multitude of rebel groups that took control over large parts of the territory. paragraph_text_preview: The evidence before the Chamber indicates that the overall relations between Muslims and non-Muslims within the CAR before the crisis relevant to the charges were positive. For example, P-1666 testified that they lived in 'perfect harmony' in Mbaïki until power was taken by the Seleka. As P-2232 put it, when the Seleka advanced towards Bangui, Muslims and Christians used to live in 'symbiosis'. Similarly, P-2657 testified that before the arrival of the Seleka in Bossangoa, life was peaceful, harmonious, without problems, and they cohabited peacefully. Michel Ningando equally stated that before the events of the Seleka, Christians and Muslims in Bossangoa were 'getting along'. P-0967 also testified that prior to the coup, there were no concerns and difficulties between the different religions, her mother -- Christian, and her father -- Muslim, lived in perfect harmony, as did Christian and Muslim communities, and there were no problems or tensions, which started only in 2013. P-2325 stated that before the conflict, there were around 70,000 Christians and around 20,000 Muslims living in Berbérati and both communities lived in peace.

paragraph_text_preview: Specifically, Catherine Samba-Panza testified that the coup by the Seleka started in August 2012 in the north-east part of the CAR. According to her, some people thought they were not considered true citizens of the CAR because the areas they lived in had been neglected, and gradually the demands became very political in nature, with people mixing up these with demands from religious communities and ultimately a rebel group emerged, called the Seleka. This group combined various individuals and, coming from the north-east of the CAR, decided to descend upon Bangui, becoming larger as it did, with people joining from some prefectures, as well as from Sudan and Chad. Catherine Samba-Panza explained that the Seleka movement was run by CAR citizens of Muslim faith but became quite a mixture in their advance, being supported by troops originally from Chad or Sudan, bandits, 'no-accounts', people who had no work, young Peuhl, Muslims, Christians.

Specifically, Catherine Samba-Panza testified that the coup by the Seleka started in August 2012 in the north-east part of the CAR. According to one NGO report, the Seleka formed in 2012 when at least four different rebel groups came together to create a united front against François Bozizé.

Other witnesses described the context in which the Seleka was formed, such as Tenebaye Massalbaye, who spoke of various security problems which could not be solved by François Bozizé, and a strong anti-Chadian sentiment taking shape in 2011, with the majority of the commercial circuits in the CAR held by Chadians. Roger de Martial Yagao also described how he received information about a rebel coalition forming in the north of the CAR through following the radio communications on the gendarmerie network, as well as international and national media. The Seleka advance towards Bangui Starting in late 2012, the Seleka advanced towards Bangui. The Libreville agreement, concluded in January 2013, presented an attempt to end the crisis, leading to a government including representatives of various factions, with François Bozizé remaining president and Nicolas Tiangaye as prime minister, Michel Djotodia as deputy prime minister and minister of defence, and Mr Ngaïssona as minister of youth, sports, arts and culture. At the same time, the widely reported advance of the Seleka, and violent acts and abuses committed in this context, including against civilians, sparked reactions within the civilian and political sphere: 'Coalition citoyenne d'opposition aux rébellions armées' (COCORA) and 'Comité d'organisation des actions citoyennes' (COAC) were two organisations which were active in mobilising support for François Bozizé in light of the Seleka advance. They erected checkpoints or roadblocks at which passers-by and vehicles were checked, with the objective of identifying Seleka infiltrators and people deemed to be associated with or in support of them, including Muslims. The individuals manning these checkpoints were armed with bladed weapons and, in some cases, with AK-47s. Seleka advance and Libreville negotiations

paragraph_text_preview: The Libreville agreement provided, inter alia, that (i) the president would remain in function until the end of his mandate in 2016 and could not run for another term; (ii) an inclusive government was to be set up for 12 months, tasked with restoring peace and security, organising legislative elections, re-organising defence and security forces, as well as territorial administration, reforming the justice system, setting up a process of DDR and a reform of the security sector, and undertaking economic and social reforms; (iii) the Seleka coalition forces would withdraw from occupied villages and abandon the armed struggle, with militias to be dissolved across the national territory and armed elements billeted in locations to be agreed upon; and (iv) the member states of the Communauté économique des États de l'Afrique centrale (CEEAC) would endeavour to progressively withdraw all foreign troops on the basis of the development of the security situation.

At the same time, the evidence indicates that François Bozizé also failed to implement recommendations agreed upon in Libreville, including by announcing on 15 March 2013 his intention to run in the following presidential elections. COCORA and COAC

Within the context of the Seleka advance and the Libreville negotiations, the Chamber assesses the evidence before it concerning the activities of two organisations, COCORA ('Coalition citoyenne d'opposition aux rébellions armées') and COAC ('Comité d'organisation des actions citoyennes') at that time. As outlined further below, the evidence shows that these organisations were set up to mobilise civilians in support of François Bozizé and to resist the Seleka advance. COCORA was involved in organising the rally in December 2012 at PK0 at which François Bozizé spoke. The evidence suggests that COCORA and COAC on the one hand, and the (re-) creation of self-defence groups in light of the violence committed by the Seleka regime on the other, were related.

The Ngaïssona Defence submits that COCORA's aim was to protest and protect the population through peaceful means, and that there is no evidence that COCORA and COAC would have excluded Muslims or propagated anti-Muslim animus. The Chamber does not follow this argumentation. First, the Chamber notes that the evidence before it shows that individuals said to be manning COCORA checkpoints and roadblocks were armed, at least with bladed weapons, and that abuses were reported. Second, the Chamber notes the evidence of Jean-Jacques Demafouth, who stated that in the context of the Libreville negotiations, Levy Yakété made a statement on behalf of COCORA, issuing public threats that if the Seleka dared coming towards Bangui, he had put his militia on alert and COCORA was ready to defend Bozizé's regime. Third, in the Chamber's view, the evidence as outlined above shows that while the COCORA roadblocks and checkpoints may have been looking for 'Seleka infiltrators' at the outset, this was clearly equated with 'Muslims' or 'non-Sango' speakers more generally.

paragraph_text_preview: From some media statements which seem to have been issued by Steve Yambété, it appears that COAC was also active at roadblocks and checkpoints with a view to checking passers-by and vehicles, in support of the Bozizé government. Several witnesses drew a link between COCORA or COAC and the later (re-)emergence of self-defence groups which would eventually form the Anti-Balaka. P-2232 noticed that the youth in the neighbourhoods became gradually more mobilised before the Seleka arrived in Bangui and stated that while the Anti-Balaka did not exist when COCORA or COAC were operational, there were no longer leaders to organise the young people when the leaders of these movements fled upon the Seleka take-over, and this vacuum was filled by the emerging Anti-Balaka. P-0889 similarly confirmed that certain youth that had been with COCORA or COAC later joined the Anti-Balaka. P-1847 testified that some senior officials of COCORA, such as Papa Javon Zama and David Banga, and some other members of the KNK, were involved in the Anti-Balaka movement.

The Chamber refers to its discussion of the speeches made in the context of this rally below as well as of Steve Yambété's radio address on 22 March 2013.

On the basis of the above, the Chamber concludes that COCORA, led by Levy Yakété, and COAC, led by Steve Yambété, were two youth organisations with direct links to François Bozizé, the KNK and Bozizé's government, including Mr Ngaïssona at least while he was minister therein, which were active specifically between the end of 2012 and the end of March 2013, when the Seleka took power. They erected checkpoints and/or roadblocks at which passers-by and vehicles were checked, with the objective of identifying Seleka infiltrators and people deemed to be associated with or supportive of them, including Muslims. The individuals manning these checkpoints were armed with bladed weapons and, in some cases, AK-47s. The take-over of power by the Seleka On 24 March 2013, the Seleka took control of Bangui. Michel Djotodia proclaimed himself President of the CAR.

It is undisputed that Seleka elements advanced on Bangui in the period leading up to 24 March 2013 and took control of the city and power over the country on this day. Indeed, the Chamber has received consistent evidence in this regard, as further outlined below. It also appears from the evidence outlined below that this arrival was welcomed at least by parts of the population who thought the Seleka would bring about a desired change.

paragraph_text_preview: Nicolas Tiangaye testified that on 22 March 2013, Seleka elements crossed the demarcation line in Damara and advanced towards Bangui, passing the Bossembélé axis where they successfully procured a significant number of weapons. He stated that another 'army' came from Bossembélé and on 24 March 2013, these two groups united their forces at PK12. According to the witness, when the Seleka arrived in Bangui, they already had weapons, combat attire, and uniforms. Nicolas Tiangaye called the army general chief of staff at the time, General Jules Bernard Ouande, who said that he was only a simple general without troops and that Bozizé in his quality as commander-in-chief was absent, and the general at the head of the army did not take any action. According to the witness, the then-FOMAC commander also told him that they could not fight the Seleka which had 7000-8000 fighters, and the CAR did not possess any operational combat planes to address the situation.

paragraph_text_preview: A number of other witnesses described their experiences of the Seleka entering Bangui on 24 March 2013.

Jean Louis Yamodo stated that when the Seleka entered Bangui, people stood on the side of the road clapping and cheering since they thought that the Seleka would be a good change for the country. Similarly, P-0884 testified that people initially applauded the Seleka when taking power because François Bozizé, at a certain point, 'lost it' with his government: he surrounded himself with people from his own ethnic group, there was nepotism, he was accused of keeping everything to himself, his family and close relatives. He testified there was a certain marginalisation of some people, Vakaga and others, and for Muslims in Vakaga, Birao, and Ndélé, there were problems of a lack of government structure. Similarly, P-2324 stated that before the conflict started, most people were already fed up with the Bozizé regime, and people were happy with the arrival of the Seleka because of the idea that high positions in the government were reserved for people of the Gbaya ethnic group, and many non-Muslims felt that way too because they were not Gbaya.

In addition to the evidence regarding the actual take-over of Bangui on 24 March 2013, the Chamber also received evidence on aspects of what happened immediately following the coup.

Specifically, Jean-Jacques Demafouth was in Bangui around the time of the 24 March 2013 coup, at Camp M'Poko, the FOMAC military base, and, since Nicolas Tiangaye and Mboli-Goumba were also at the camp, could directly follow the developments of how a new government would be made and how François Bozizé was received by the Cameroonian authorities. According to the witness, the night when François Bozizé lost the battle and came back to Bangui, he held a meeting with the entourage, particularly officers from the military and those responsible for COCORA, and gave them instructions as regards armaments, weapons, and resources to create complete disorder in the country, and asked some of them to be ready so he could call upon them and they could join him. Jean-Jacques Demafouth said that when François Bozizé understood that his army had lost, he sent an instruction that all the arms from all the soldiers who came from the front be recuperated, but those weapons were never in the state armoury, they simply disappeared and were re-distributed to people who did not have an entitlement, for example, members of the militia such as COCORA, and supporters of the KNK to defend themselves. Jean-Jacques Demafouth said that he met various people at Camp M'Poko, including generals, the protocol man of Bozizé, the director of the training school, Mokom; and that, at that moment, no one regarded him as an enemy, so they talked. In the camp, the witness already had information that resistance was being organised, and contacts started to be made at that point.

Adrien Poussou, who was not in Bangui when the Seleka entered, went there three days after the coup and spent seven days in the city, of which five were at the Hotel Ledger, the centre of power at the time where he exchanged with Crépin Mboli-Goumba, the minister of state and minister of public works, and met Nicolas Tiangaye, Michel Djotodia and others. The Seleka violence After the Seleka took control of Bangui on 24 March 2013, they committed violence and abuses in various localities across the CAR, in particular against individuals considered to be associated with François Bozizé, his Gbaya ethnic group, his government's security forces, and non-Muslims. Mr Ngaïssona's properties in Bangui were looted. However, the Muslim civilian population was not entirely spared from this violence. The Seleka included fighters in particular from Chad and Sudan. It was led by Central African Muslims. Due to the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and in light of its perceived composition, tensions in particular between Muslim and non-Muslim communities increased.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber has received a significant amount of evidence concerning the violence committed by members of the Seleka following the take-over of Bangui, in the city itself and other locations across the CAR territory. That the Seleka committed abuses following their take-over of Bangui is indeed not disputed between the parties. It transpires from the evidence before the Chamber that, certainly at the outset, the violence targeted in particular supporters of the former regime or individuals perceived to be so, including members of the regular armed forces, including FACA, police and gendarmerie, members of the Gbaya ethnic group, or inhabitants of neighbourhoods and areas in which supporters of François Bozizé were generally thought to be living.

Catherine Samba-Panza testified that once the Seleka entered Bangui, they committed many acts of violence and abuse, theft, as well as destroyed public and private property, and religious buildings. The witness agreed with the suggestion that the Seleka targeted non-Muslims, particularly Gbaya and people suspected of being close to François Bozizé, and that many people deemed close to François Bozizé were in Boy-Rabe, which was regularly attacked by the Seleka. Catherine Samba-Panza stated that the Seleka thought that the people in Boy-Rabe were pro-Bozizé and resisting its attacks to disarm elements, so she had to intervene to provide assistance. The witness agreed with the suggestion that crimes by the Seleka did not come to an end when she became president in January 2014, at which time the armed forces had practically disappeared and internal forces were trying to ensure the defence, security and protection of the people, and the international forces, given their numbers, could not be everywhere and could not protect the civilian population everywhere.

P-2050 testified that on 27 April 2013, she visited Mr Ngaïssona's house in Boy-Rabe, an area which she was told the Seleka had punished for being close to François Bozizé, coming three or four times to pillage. P-2050 could see that Boy-Rabe had been heavily looted: houses were empty, doors were destroyed, loose elements were wandering around looking for food, including some men in Seleka uniforms. P-2050 was told by one of her sources that there were militiamen of Bozizé in Boy-Rabe at the time and that Mr Ngaïssona, before he fled Bangui, had ordered a militia be set up. P-2050 testified that Mr Ngaïssona's residence was the biggest in the area and she knew it was his because the 'askari' (guard) at the gate confirmed it to her. It had the biggest gate with a lot of bullet holes visible on it and P-2050 was told that the Seleka targeted the house before looting it. P-2050 described the inside of the house as totally chaotic, finding Mr Ngaïssona's personal files and private pictures between the mess, everything gone, even the mattresses, just the couch was still there. P-2050 noticed quite a number of bullets in the compound and five or six young boys, probably aged between 12 and 18, in flip-flops, were living between the remains. The 'askari' told P-2050 that Mr Ngaïssona was in Douala or Yaoundé and paid him to protect the property and afterwards took her just around the corner from Mr Ngaïssona's compound to show her a warehouse belonging to Mr Ngaïssona that had also been looted.

Other witnesses described Seleka abuses in their respective localities. The evidence suggests moreover that Muslims and ethnic groups other than Gbaya were also not always spared from the violence.

The Chamber notes all this evidence, but is of the view that no further detailed discussion thereof is apposite for purposes of adjudicating the allegations before it. Overall, it is clear from this evidence and the evidence outlined below that at the latest by October 2013, the situation in the CAR had reached such a state that the UN Security Council expressed concerns about violations of international humanitarian law and human rights in particular by Seleka elements and also other armed groups, demanding that all Seleka and other armed groups immediately lay down their arms.

In the context of the Seleka violence, it is of import for the determinations of the Chamber to analyse the impact of such abuses on the CAR communities. In this regard, the Chamber turns to the composition of the Seleka and proportion of foreign elements within it, which is discussed by numerous witnesses.
The Ngaïssona Defence argues that Sudanese and Chadian mercenaries formed the backbone of the Seleka forces and that mercenaries were the 'overwhelming majority' within the Seleka.

Numerous witnesses testified about the Seleka including individuals from Chad or Sudan, as well as some considered to be Janjaweed, often in reference to Seleka elements not speaking Sango or French, but only Arabic.

paragraph_text_preview: The report presented by P-2926 concluded that the Seleka included fighters from ethnicities of the north of the CAR, including Gula, Runga, Sara, Kara, Peul, and others, as well as park rangers of Bamingui-Bangoran, diamond collectors such as Abdoulaye Hissène and Abakar Zakaria, to which were added Chadian and Sudanese combatants, such as Moussa Assimeh, leader of the Janjaweed. An NGO report found that the extended force of the Seleka included local people from the CAR, as well as foreign mercenaries and poachers. Kasper Agger testified in this regard that while there were senior members and commanders of the Seleka who were from Sudan, for example Assimeh, a well-known former member of the Janjaweed, it was still his impression that the majority of the Seleka were Central Africans. The CAR Panel similarly concluded that the Seleka included Chadian and Sudanese combatants, but that this was not unique, in that the rebellion led by François Bozizé in 2003 was also comprised of substantial amounts of foreign fighters, mostly from Chad. Yet any reference to a 'foreign invasion' in the panel's report simply conveyed the statements brought to their attention in which that term may have occurred. Indeed, the Seleka was often perceived as being in the majority 'foreign', without however there being concrete information on the Seleka's actual composition, let alone how many actually foreign fighters it may have included. Catherine Samba-Panza testified that the Seleka was led by Central African Muslims. P-1577 was also aware of the names of significant high-level Seleka commanders who were from the CAR.

P-2841 confirmed that once the Seleka arrived in Bangui in March 2013, their numbers grew significantly since with this type of movement, young unemployed people would join, and a lot of damage was caused in Bangui due to these young people who knew the city well. Adrien Poussou similarly testified that when he was a member of government, Michel Djotodia said that the elements which continued to commit violations in Bangui were made up of youth who had joined the Seleka on their way to Bangui and in Bangui, not only Muslims, but also Christians. The witness did not know the relative number of people that joined the Seleka in Bangui or on the way down from Birao; they ('we') had no idea of the number of people who officially belonged to the Seleka and those who joined later.

The Chamber is of the view that the numbers in the evidence before it diverge to such an extent that it cannot reach a conclusive finding as to how many elements the Seleka may have counted at specific times in 2013. However, the Chamber can conclude, on the basis of the evidence before it, that the Seleka counted several thousand elements at the time of the take-over of power in March 2013, growing significantly over time and until the end of the year. Les individus concernés et leurs activités au Cameroun et en République démocratique du Congo Après que la Séléka a pris la ville de Bangui et le contrôle en RCA, François Bozizé, Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona, Bernard Mokom et d'autres ont fui au Cameroun. Maxime Mokom, Alfred Yekatom et d'autres ont fui à Zongo, en République démocratique du Congo (RDC). Grâce à des réunions tenues au Cameroun et à des communications avec des individus à Zongo, en particulier Maxime Mokom, qui assurait ensuite la liaison avec des personnes et des groupes à Bangui et dans les provinces, François Bozizé, Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona, Bernard Mokom et d'autres ont planifié les mesures à prendre pour répondre aux violences commises par la Séléka en RCA et pour s'assurer du retour de François Bozizé au pouvoir, par tous les moyens possibles, y compris par la violence armé. Durant la période où il n'a pas été en RCA en 2013, Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona a participé activement à la planification des mesures à prendre pour répondre aux violences commises par la Séléka en RCA et pour s'assurer du retour de François Bozizé au pouvoir, en se réunissant et en assurant la liaison avec François Bozizé, Bernard Mokom et d'autres, afin de discuter de leurs stratégies et plans, en prenant contact avec des individus en dehors de RCA afin de rallier du soutien à leur cause, et en apportant une aide financière aux personnes désireuses d'appuyer leurs activités. Dans ce contexte, Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona s'est rendu jusqu'à la frontière entre le Cameroun et la RCA en vue de rencontrer des groupes censés les aider dans leurs projets. Il a continué à apporter une assistance financière également après les attaques coordonnées du 5 décembre 2013. En même temps, Alfred Yekatom s'est rendu brièvement à Zongo en 2013 puis a commencé à former un groupe, dont il a pris le contrôle, avec Freddy Ouandjio, également appelé Cœur de Lion, et Habib Beina, en vue de planifier une réponse aux violences commises par la Séléka et de chasser Michel Djotodia et la Séléka du pouvoir. Maxime Mokom était en contact avec des individus et des groupes au Cameroun, à Zongo et à l'intérieur de la RCA, y compris avec son père, Bernard Mokom, avec Alfred Yekatom et avec des groupes qui se formaient dans les provinces, et ce, en vue de coordonner les activités et une possible marche sur Bangui. Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona a apporté des contributions financières et a mené des activités liées à l'organisation et à la coordination de groupes dans le but de faciliter la commission d'actes criminels visant la population musulmane, notamment les crimes constatés plus loin. Cameroun

Les éléments de preuve dont dispose la Chambre, tel que décrits davantage plus loin, montrent qu'après la prise du pouvoir par les forces de la Séléka, de nombreux individus ont cherché refuge à un certain nombre d'endroits au Cameroun, surtout à Yaoundé, Douala, Bertoua et Garam-Boulaï. La Chambre a entendu des témoins présents au Cameroun durant des périodes de durée variable qui ont donc pu expliquer qui d'autre s'y trouvait et quels contacts avaient pu être établis, tant au Cameroun qu'en RCA ou dans d'autres localités, avec certaines personnes, notamment P-0884, Joachim Kokaté, P-2673, Adrien Poussou, P-1847 et P-0974. Comme indiqué plus en détail plus loin, certains témoins ont parlé de réunions tenues au Cameroun, en présence de François Bozizé, de plusieurs de ses fils, de Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona, Bernard Mokom et d'autres. Les éléments de preuve tels que décrits plus loin montrent que François Bozizé et plusieurs de ses fils, ainsi que Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona, Bernard Mokom et de nombreux autres individus ont fui la RCA après la prise de pouvoir de la Séléka pour se rendre au Cameroun.
La Chambre relève à cet égard qu'un passeport au nom de Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona contient un visa pour une entrée en Afrique du Sud le 27 mars 2013 ou vers cette date, émis à Yaoundé 19 mars 2013.

P-1847 a fui avec François Bozizé à Yaoundé et est resté avec lui jusqu'à ce que celui‑ci se rende en Ouganda. Un certain nombre de Centrafricains qui avaient fui le coup se trouvaient au Cameroun ; beaucoup appartenaient à la même ethnie, les Gbaya, mais étaient aussi des partisans du KNK. Beaucoup de « déserteurs » des forces armées se trouvaient à la frontière entre le Cameroun et la RCA ; ils ont récupéré toutes les armes qu'ils pouvaient et les ont emportées jusqu'à une base militaire à Bertoua. L'État camerounais a pris les armes et les a restituées après 2014. Les soldats présents au Cameroun comprenaient le colonel Ngoya et le capitaine Koudemon, dont les hommes étaient nombreux, sont venus avec beaucoup d'armes jusqu'à la frontière camerounaise et ont été cantonnés à Bertoua.

Joachim Kokaté est allé à Yaoundé à un moment où Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona était déjà arrivé au Cameroun, après avoir eu avec lui des contacts téléphoniques. Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona lui a dit qu'il avait fui au Congo Brazzaville puis au Cameroun. D'après Joachim Kokaté, de nombreux Centrafricains, y compris des civils, des soldats et des membres de la famille de François Bozizé, avaient fui au Cameroun , en RDC et au Congo Brazzaville. De nombreux soldats ont fui au Cameroun, et Joachim Kokaté a entendu dire qu'ils étaient rassemblés dans un camp ou centre à Bertoua. Parmi les soldats présents à Yaoundé, il y avait ceux qui vivaient avec François Bozizé et Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona : Eric Danboy, Franklin Bozizé et d'autres. Certains membres de son groupe, le Collectif des officiers libres, étaient également au Cameroun, certains à Douala et d'autres à Yaoundé.

P-0884 lui aussi est allé au Cameroun. Lorsqu'il y est arrivé, Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona et d'autres s'y trouvaient déjà. D'après P-0884, Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona est d'abord allé à Yaoundé, mais lorsque P-0884 est arrivé à Douala, Kevin Kpefio, avec qui il avait été en contact depuis Bangui et qui était venu avec quelques soldats pour le récupérer à l'aéroport, l'a conduit à l'hôtel Lumière où on leur a dit que Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona avait été là mais venait tout juste de partir. P-0884 a déclaré qu'à Yaoundé, il était resté la résidence de Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona, mais que celui‑ci était toujours en déplacements. P-0884 a passé un certain temps chez Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona à Yaoundé, jusqu'à ce qu'il retourne à Bangui après trois semaines ou un mois. Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona était souvent absent, voyageant pour des activités liées au football, de sorte que P-0884 habitait dans la résidence avec ses « soldats ». Ces deux soldats étaient le capitaine Lamkague et Koudemon Olivier, également appelé Bangouma, que P-0884 connaissait tous les deux et qui étaient d'anciens « liberators ». Koudemon se trouvait au Cameroun avant même que la Séléka ne prenne le pouvoir, ayant fui Bossangoa. Il voyageait régulièrement entre Yaoundé et Douala et était très connu des Centrafricains à Douala.

D30-4914, un membre de la Gendarmerie à l'époque, était posté à la frontière, à Beloko, en octobre 2013. D'après lui, Michel Djotodia et ses partisans avaient créé un système « imperméable » visant à empêcher tout départ dans le secteur de Garam-Boulaï, Berbérati, Gamboula et Beloko. Il a dit qu'ils étaient allés à Bouar puis à « Garoua-Boulaï », avant de se rendre à Yaoundé, au camp de réfugiés de Bertoua. De nombreux membres des forces de sécurité centrafricaines se trouvaient en exil au Cameroun ; ceux qui avaient travaillé avec François Bozizé avaient été contraints à l'exil, et n'avait pas le choix s'ils voulaient rester en vie. D30-4914 a expliqué que Gbangouma et Ganazoui avaient également traversé la frontière et que Guerson Nganadekoe se trouvait à Yaoundé en 2013 ; il est venu à la frontière deux ou trois fois peut-être pour voir ce qui se passait, mais il n'a donné à D30-4914 aucun conseil ni aucune instruction. Martial Wango a passé environ un mois et demi à « Garoua-Boulaï » avant de se rendre à Bangui.

Communication et coordination dans le pays et au‑delà de la frontière ######

Réunions à YaoundéComme la Chambre le précisera plus loin, les éléments de preuve dont elle dispose montrent que des ressortissants centrafricains ont participé à différentes activités au Cameroun, notamment à des réunions à l'hôtel Hilton de Yaoundé, en présence entre autres de François Bozizé, de Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona, de Bernard Mokom, et d'autres personnes. Leurs conversations ont d'abord porté sur la critique du coup d'État de la Seleka, ainsi que sur les premières mesures à prendre pour assurer le retour à « l'ordre constitutionnel », ce qui signifiait le retour au pouvoir de François Bozizé -- par tous les moyens possibles.

paragraph_text_preview: La Défense de Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona soutient que i) Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona n'a pas suivi François Bozizé au Cameroun, ne lui a pas rendu régulièrement visite ni n'a vécu à sa résidence ; ii) la proximité alléguée entre Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona et François Bozizé ne saurait être déduite du fait qu'ils sont de la même ethnie ; iii) Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona n'a pas participé à la mobilisation des jeunes ; iv) Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona n'a jamais exprimé de sentiment antimusulman ni n'a semé la division au sein de la population centrafricaine ; et v) Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona n'a pas participé à des réunions avec François Bozizé au Cameroun.

Elle soutient que l'Accusation n'a pas établi que François Bozizé avait l'intention de reprendre le pouvoir à tout prix et que les éléments de preuve concernant les réunions tenues au Cameroun ou en France ne permettent pas de déduire que les intéressés avaient un dessein criminel. Elle affirme également que l'Accusation n'a pas établi que François Bozizé avait participé au mouvement anti-balaka, que ce soit en le créant, en l'organisant ou en le finançant, et qu'en raison du manque de précision dans l'identification du « cercle immédiat » qui gravitait autour de François Bozizé, il n'est pas possible d'établir un niveau minimal de coordination.

Sur la base des éléments de preuve, comme cela est précisé ci‑après, la Chambre considère que les arguments de la Défense de Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona à cet égard sont sans fondement, y compris s'agissant de l'expression d'un sentiment « antimusulman ».
La Chambre va d'abord se pencher sur les réunions tenues à l'hôtel Hilton auxquelles Joachim Kokaté et Adrien Poussou ont participé en personne, et sur celles dont P-1847 a entendu parler.
