One of the documents which appears to be an attachment to this is entitled 'Protocole d'accord politique pour la création du Front pour le retour à l'ordre constitutionnel en Centrafrique (FROCCA)'. This document lists a number of goals, namely i) re-establishing as quickly as possible constitutional order destroyed by 'enemies of the nation' who inflicted, with 'Islamist mercenaries', violence on the CAR population; ii) restore and consolidate security; and iii) re-assure Central African people, economic operators and development partners for swift resumption of activities. The measures to be taken to achieve return to constitutional order include: (i) on the political level, make political parties, NGOs, intellectuals, opinion leaders (youth, women, ...), confession and spiritual leaders adhere to cause; (ii) on the diplomatic level, exhibit diplomatic intelligence on all levels; (iii) on the strategic level, take all measures necessary to avoid further suffering of people, specifically acquiring human, material and financial means to achieve goals, finding communication means which cannot be decrypted by intelligence services, preferably Thurayas, setting up smooth and practical coordination for swift and effective strategic actions, rebuilding confidence and aligning elements of security apparatus that only wait to address the 'affront' inflicted by 'envahisseurs islamistes sans foi ni loi'; and (iv) on the communication level, 'très fondamental d'éviter des déclarations frisant la haine, la vengeance et la division'.

Jean-Serge Wafio took part in the meeting that established FROCCA. Adrien Poussou had not seen the FROCCA political agreement before, but it is in keeping with the decision taken during the first meeting establishing FROCCA. According to the witness, the role attributed to Mr Ngaïssona in this document, as being responsible for domestic affairs and associations, was related to his activities, since he said he was in regular contact with a number of people who had remained in the country, with associations referring to the groups in the field, like COAC. Looking at the document was the first time Adrien Poussou had seen that such level of responsibility and such function had been attributed.

Joachim Kokaté had also not seen the FROCCA political agreement before and stated that he did not know the plans and strategies of FROCCA because he was not a member. He indicated that Jean Serge Waffio is a politician from the CAR but that he did not know why he would be a party to this agreement; Mazoungou was a member of Bozizé's government; Thierry Bongolo was working at the economic and social council during Bozizé's time. Joachim Kokaté maintained not having been aware of the positions people occupied within FROCCA, never having been a member of FROCCA and having no information about what happened in FROCCA. Joachim Kokaté insisted not knowing anything about FROCCA. According to Joachim Kokaté, when he spoke on television, Africa 24, he denounced Djotodia's government speaking as a Central African who was against the seizing of power by force and the Seleka violence, but not on behalf of FROCCA. When he spoke on television for the first time, he was in telephone contact with Mr Ngaïssona and they talked about that. Frequently when he made statements it was after discussions between himself, Mr Ngaïssona, other compatriots, because Joachim Kokaté was not present in Bangui.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes in this regard that the evidence before it shows that Joachim Kokaté was clearly a member of FROCCA and involved in planning its activities, as shown by his attendance to the meetings and by the evidence of other witnesses who attribute to him a specific role in this group. The Chamber notes in this regard that the witness seems to have been well familiar with Lin Banoukepa, who appears to have been legal counsel of the CPJP while Joachim Kokaté was involved therewith. On this basis, the Chamber considers not credible the claim of Joachim Kokaté that he was not a member of FROCCA and would not have played any role in it.

The Chamber considers of no further consequence that D30-4720 stated never having received or been informed of any FROCCA drafts, press releases or communications. Indeed, the witness herself indicated that she did not have an email account at the time. Overall, in light of the witness's clearly limited knowledge of any activities of FROCCA, and bearing in mind the Chamber's above discussion on this witness's evidence, the Chamber considers the evidence of D30-4720 of little assistance for its determinations regarding FROCCA.

The Chamber has before it a typed document which purports to contain a collection of FROCCA press releases. In what is called 'Communiqué de presse no 001' of 5 August 2013, the Seleka coup and violence are addressed, the creation of FROCCA is announced, before concluding, 'Tout en s'imposant le devoir de chasser, par les moyens légaux, les criminels de la Séléka du sol centrafricain qu'ils ont souillé et profané, le FROCCA interpelle la conscience collective centrafricaine en vue d'une adhésion sans condition à cette lutte légitime de libération nationale'. The second statement, dated 16 August 2013, also denounces the Seleka violence, and expresses the support of FROCCA for solutions envisaged by the UN Security Council to re-establish peace, democracy and stability in the CAR 'à la seule condition du retour à l'Ordre Constitutionnel en Centrafrique', before concluding: 'Le \[FROCCA\] appelle l'ensemble des forces politiques et sociales centrafricaines à faire plus que jamais preuve du nécessaire esprit de responsabilité pour préserver l'unité nationale et obtenir sans délai, le rétablissement de notre président élu, qui doit garantir la poursuite du processus démocratique dans notre pays'.

The statements are followed by what is said to be an interview with Lin Banoukepa who is reported as stating, inter alia, that the aim of FROCCA is to '\[r\]établir l'ordre constitutionnel, établir un pouvoir laïc, démocratique respectant les libertés et droits des individus. Un pouvoir ayant pour fondement le droit et non les dogmes religieux salafistes'.

The Chamber considers of importance to note within which temporal context these statements were set. Specifically, they were issued at a time when self-defence groups were organising in the CAR, emerged into the Anti-Balaka, and started to advance towards Bangui, engaging in hostilities during this advance. In particular the statement of 18 September 2013 was issued the day after an attack on Bossangoa.

The Chamber notes that while in France, Mr Ngaïssona did not only participate in the meetings regarding FROCCA as outlined above. Rather, Adrien Poussou also learned -- he did not recall from who -- that Mr Ngaïssona, when in France, sent money via Western Union to the field, said to be for the upkeep of the elements in the field; and when Adrien Poussou was later in the government, he became aware of Western Union receipts on which he recognised some of the names of Central African soldiers. Michel Djotodia showed Adrien Poussou a number of money transfers and gave him a number of names, including that of Mr Ngaïssona as being one of the people sending money to their accomplices in Bangui, but the witness did not specifically see the name of Mr Ngaïssona on a money transfer. According to Adrien Poussou, it was not necessary for Mr Ngaïssona to go himself to a Western Union office; for example, when Adrien Poussou was in New York on a FROCCA mission with Yvon Songuet, it was not François Bozizé himself who went to a bank to send money to them, neither one of his sons, he would send somebody else. People like Yvon Songuet and others might have resorted to other people to send this money. Once Michel Djotodia resigned, they did not hear about this matter any further. On the receipts which Djotodia showed him, Adrien Poussou could see amounts ranging from 800,000 to a million, and he saw that some of the amounts were sent to Olivier Koudemon, not remembering any other names.

paragraph_text_preview: In an email from 'Alfred le Grand Ngaya' to 'npatriceedouard' of 16 July 2013, the sender states that he communicates the composition of the coordination recently created with a view to mobilising the population for protest actions against the Seleka exactions, with the ultimate goal being the withdrawal of Djotodia and return of François Bozizé to power; further states that the members are highly motivated but lacking means, and asks whether such means would be expected from the addressee's side; further saying that the population, mainly in Bangui, is ready to go to the streets to protest and it is sufficient to just start the process; concluding that he knows the addressee is capable of presenting the situation to the president for steps to be taken. In another email Alfred le Grand Ngaya' sends to 'npatriceedouard' on 13 August 2013, included in the same email chain, the sender indicates that he attaches a copy of the 'tract' they are disseminating in the city of Bangui on that day. This email is forwarded by Mr Ngaïssona to Adrien Poussou on the same day, and appears to contain in its attachment a typed document with a FROCCA header entitled 'Appel patriotique', which points to the positive situation under the Bozizé rule, denounces the exactions of the Djotodia regime with criminal disciples and mercenaries imported from Chad and Sudan, claims that the latter wants to 'Islamise' the CAR and asks, in this light, and bearing in mind the appeal of Bozizé on 10 August 2013 on RFI, the interview discussed above, that 'tu dois te lever, résister et rejeter l'oppression que t'impose NDOTODJIA et sa horde de séléka', and to mobilise 'comme un seul homme', to take out Djotodia and demand from international community 'return to constitutional order'.

paragraph_text_preview: Alfred Legrand Ngaya stated that he knew that FROCCA was set up by Bozizé's lawyer, Lin Banoukepa, after Bozizé left the CAR, with deputy Mr Ngaïssona. Alfred Legrand Ngaya communicated with Mr Ngaïssona briefly to find allies and share information, their goal was to restore Bozizé in power legally. Levy Yakété was a member of FROCCA. They ('we') shared the same vision as FROCCA, had to liberate the country through a popular uprising and wanted something to indicate to the international community, that was why they walked about the front for the return to the constitutional order.

paragraph_text_preview: The exchanges between Mr Ngaïssona and Alfred Legrand Ngaya in relation to FROCCA did not end here. In response to a FROCCA 'communiqué' sent by Alfred Legrand Ngaya on 13 August 2013, Mr Ngaïssona indicated that 'the authority' would like to read and approve the document before publication, and suggests drafting a 'communiqué' accusing the Seleka of using the FROCCA name for diversion purposes, and that he as focal point waited for the central coordination in Paris regarding the actions to take, which will be read to the 'patron'. Alfred Legrand Ngaya reacted, stating that a text would be proposed, and asking for advice on how to prompt the FROCCA executive coordinator for a preliminary view on the tract.

Mr Ngaïssona reached out again to Alfred Legrand Ngaya on 17 September 2013, asking for news, to which Alfred Legrand Ngaya responded that the situation in the country remained alarming, with Bossangoa, Bouca, Batangafo in distress, stating that preoccupied with FROCCA lines of action to allow envisaging actions on the national level, and asking whether Mr Ngaïssona could give some indication for which actions to propose. In response, Mr Ngaïssona stated that given the situation in the country, they ('we') have men on the ground that manoeuvre, asking Alfred Legrand Ngaya to 'accentuer la dégradation dans Bangui et faire généralisée sur une bonne partie du territoire \[sic\]', and further asking whether he could get workers in the public and private sector involved. Alfred Legrand Ngaya followed up stating that the proposals would be examined to find appropriate actions, but that people were afraid, though they were thinking 'with the others' and would keep informed. Mr Ngaïssona in turn responded saying that matters were urgent, and whether a response could be done as quickly as possible, 'le Grand BOSS attends \[sic\]'.

Alfred Legrand Ngaya explained that he contacted Mr Ngaïssona for FROCCA action because the situation was really chaotic and they hoped for something to happen. According to the witness, any discussions on manoeuvring would have concerned mobilisation of the population, political actions, citizen actions. It was systematically through Mr Ngaïssona that Alfred Legrand Ngaya obtained information about FROCCA. The witness did not know what Mr Ngaïssona meant with people on the ground, he could not suspect Mr Ngaïssona as being someone who was in favour of war; his correspondence with Mr Ngaïssona was related mainly to popular movements, associations; the idea was to persuade popular movements to do something; they ('we') were hoping that FROCCA would put pressure at the level of Paris. Alfred Legrand Ngaya understood the proposals to be within the framework of the actions they had been carrying out, that is, to mobilise association leaders. The witness did not recall exchanging messages with a Facebook account of 'Bangui FROCCA'; in any event, their ('our') actions were extremely discreet and he was therefore not aware whether other persons were working under the name of FROCCA. At their level, there was an increasingly generalised awakening of consciences, such as concert of pots.

Adrien Poussou explained that in the meeting at the hotel close to the Champs Élysées he was nominated to go to New York with Yvon Songuet for a lobbying mission, especially by virtue of the fact that the witness attempted to sensitise others for the need to favour political and diplomatic solutions to the ongoing crisis. François Bozizé dealt with financial and military matters together with his son Francis, who used to be minister with special responsibility for defence matters. To Adrien Poussou, it seemed clear that there was a military branch, even though there was no formal link between it and FROCCA as such. According to the witness, while he sent Adrien Poussou to New York, François Bozizé did not believe in these diplomatic initiatives and was not counting on them to regain power. They ('we') were convinced that the solution would be diplomatic, and to satisfy them, and maybe to get rid of them as well, they were sent to New York -- proof of this being that on their return, no one met with them for them to be able to report on their activities. When they came back from New York, they talked, if only to tell Bozizé's inner circle about their impressions of what people told them there, but Adrien Poussou had no further communications with François Bozizé. According to the witness, he did not go to New York representing FROCCA, the messages transmitted were not in the name of François Bozizé, even though he financed the mission, and no memorandum was object of a discussion with François Bozizé whom they told it was important to go to New York to meet people and speak with them about the situation in the country.

As regards further activities of FROCCA following the meetings in Paris as outlined above, the Chamber notes, from the evidence outlined below, that its members seemed to attempt to gain support from individuals or groups that they considered could contribute to FROCCA's stated cause. However, the evidence on record does not show that there would have been a concerted alignment of groups with FROCCA.

First, Joachim Kokaté testified about being approached by Francis Bozizé who drafted and sent to him a document of the 'Collectif des Officiers Libres', which he wanted the witness to validate at the request of his father, and which Joachim Kokaté accepted, thereafter publishing it on social media. According to the witness, this was just for the purpose of having his name on the document, it was a strategy of François Bozizé, but Joachim Kokaté had no role. The strategy of attack of Bozizé with others was planned by FROCCA. At the lunch they said they had an attack plan, a strategy, which they were going to work on, but Joachim Kokaté was not involved and could not give details; as former soldier, Joachim Kokaté considered that talking about 'attack' means going to war and he thought this was what FROCCA decided to do. At the same time, the witness maintained that he was a supporter, sympathiser of the Anti-Balaka, but never on the ground; he never gave a single order and did not have that competence. According to Joachim Kokaté, he understood after the meeting with Franklin Bozizé, Mr Ngaïssona, Bernard Mokom, Eric Danboy, Rodrigue Bozizé in Yaoundé that they were the deciders of the military wing of FROCCA. Mr Ngaïssona was determined to see that Bozizé come to power with him and Mr Ngaïssona told Joachim Kokaté that he organised and coordinated military actions in the field. Joachim Kokaté stated that his statement on BBC Radio on 22 August 2013 was in the context of knowing that the Seleka was made up of Central Africans and mercenaries from Chad and Sudan, and in any event not a statement, but the opinion of the written media.

paragraph_text_preview: P-1847 testified that he was informed by François Bozizé, in South Sudan, that he was leaving for Paris, where he then met up with his lawyer Banoukepa, Yakété, Kokaté, Adrien Poussou and other members of the Central African diaspora that supported Bozizé, and they created FROCCA, with Kokaté as spokesperson. Aurélien Llorca interviewed François Bozizé on 6 June 2014 in Entebbe, Uganda, occasion on which Bozizé denied commanding the Anti-Balaka in the CAR, any involvement with what was happening there, and stated not understanding why people would say he was responsible. Bozizé explained that the Anti-Balaka took control over Bossangoa in September 2013 when he was in Paris and thus he could not have been involved, and that the fact that a lot of people involved in that insurgency were close to him was a coincidence. Bozizé also said in relation to the telephone call tapped between him and Yvon Konaté that he had called Konaté at the request of the US State Department to prevent further violence, and that the leak of the conversation coincided with internal struggles within the Anti-Balaka movement for leadership, which Aurélien Llorca supposed was referring to the power battles between Bara, Kokaté, Mr Ngaïssona, Wenezoui and others. Bozizé said that he never played any coordination role for the Anti-Balaka and had never called any Anti-Balaka commander before that particular call, saying that the Anti-Balaka were a grassroots reaction to the crimes committed by the Seleka and that he welcomed the election of Samba-Panza. Bozizé also said that his political movement, FROCCA or KNK, had no relation with the Anti-Balaka. Aurélien Llorca believed Bozizé was not necessarily personally involved; during their meeting, which lasted quite long, Bozizé did not receive any phone calls, which indicated to the witness that he was not very busy.

According to P-2926's report, François Bozizé went to France following stays in Yaoundé and Nairobi, seen there in summer 2013 and staying until September, coinciding with the re-emergence of his supporters and the creation of FROCCA announced on 5 August 2013, coordinated by Lin Banoukepa, composed of people close to Bozizé, including Mr Ngaïssona, Levy Yakété, Joachim Kokaté. In releases and media interventions, the FROCCA coordinator took up the rhetoric of Bozizé's circles from the beginning of the conflict in relation to the 'forced Islamisation of the CAR' and an attack launched by 'Islamist Muslim mercenaries coming in more than 15,000 from Chad and Sudan', which was perfectly illustrated by the 'communiqué' of 18 September 2013, which stated that the Seleka was systematically destroying public buildings, churches, houses of worship all across the CAR with the sole political aim of 'de-Christianising' the CAR to allow introduction of the Koran and forced Islamisation -- it conceptualised the fight against the Muslims by bringing forward the notion of 'Centrafricanité', borrowing from the Ivorian political context. This notion related to the argument that Seleka were not really citizens, and its promoters linked it to linguistic, cultural and religious aspects, in that people had to speak Sango, be part of the CAR culture (in particular through language), and not be Muslim. The agenda of FROCCA was return to the constitutional order, meaning the return of François Bozizé, playing the role of indirect spokesperson of Bozizé who was in hiding and stayed discreet. Through Lin Banoukepa, FROCCA also claimed the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, encouraging the youth to rise up against the 'foreign Djihadists' and considering this attack as a return to the constitutional order.

The evidence as outlined above shows that FROCCA, founded in Paris in August 2013, was meant to advocate for the return to the constitutional order, which signified the return of François Bozizé to power. The evidence equally shows that Mr Ngaïssona was part of this group, active in its discussion, and that its executive director Lin Banoukepa did not work in isolation. Indeed, any steps undertaken in the context of FROCCA were part of broader-scale attempts to ensure François Bozizé's return to power and must be seen in the context of steps and coordination efforts undertaken as discussed above, as well as of activities unfolding on the ground, as discussed in the following section. Formation of groups in different localities and emergence of the Anti-Balaka Against the backdrop of the violence committed by the Seleka, and in parallel to the activities in Cameroon and Zongo, self-defence groups in various localities across the CAR formed or re-activated from previous existence very quickly following the take-over of power by the Seleka. Individuals within those groups also obtained amulets or gris-gris. Some of these individuals and local groups converged onto and joined together in Gobere, north-east of Bossangoa. In Gobere, civilians and former members of the Central African armed forces (FACA) and Presidential Guard gathered, and (i) organised into various sub-groups with a leader each; (ii) set up or maintained contacts with groups and individuals in other locations, including Maxime Mokom in Zongo, who was considered to be a coordinator of operations; (iii) organised trainings in weapon handling and combat by FACA members; and (iv) made further plans with a view to descending onto Bangui and removing the Seleka and Michel Djotodia from power. At the same time, former members of the FACA and Presidential Guard also in other localities created new or joined pre-existing self-defence groups, organising themselves into military-like structures and assuming or sharing command over them. Initially having formed separately, these groups started out with a common enemy and increasingly coordinated their activities, thereby essentially forming one movement. This movement came to be known as 'Anti-Balaka'. The armed groups forming at the time were armed mainly with makeshift and bladed weapons, hunting rifles, service weapons retained by members of the FACA, and weapons they seized from the members of the Seleka after engaging them in hostilities. Self-defence groups in various localities

While efforts were undertaken in localities outside of the CAR as outlined above, individuals within the CAR, in particular in the provinces, did not remain passive. Rather, as further outlined below, the evidence before the Chamber shows that, in light and in the context of the violence committed by the Seleka as outlined above, groups composed mainly of civilians formed in various localities across different provinces of the CAR as well as in Bangui with a view to defending against the abuses perpetrated by the Seleka. It appears from this evidence that, in many localities, self-defence groups already existed in the past to fight against road bandits and poachers and that such groups were either re-activated or re-purposed with a view to defending against the Seleka.

The evidence before the Chamber, as further outlined below, shows that information on self-defence groups forming with a view to defending themselves against the abuses committed by the Seleka was widely available.

Indeed, Catherine Samba-Panza testified that the information she received once she became head of the transition government indicated that the Anti-Balaka were youth organised to defend their locality against robbers and bandits, using artisanal weapons, knives, non-fire arms to defend themselves, which then organised to defend their interests in light of the Seleka abuses. It appears from the evidence that while the above were among the initial motives, this did not include, in the early stages, advocating for the return of François Bozizé to power, or indeed having wider political ambitions. For example, P-1193 explained that after the collapse of the 'Seleka government', the population expected a change, a return to peace, to constitutional order. Vivien Beina stated that initially, the goal was to get rid of the Seleka, they had no political ambition and the idea of taking Bangui came later. Similarly, P-2841 stated that the Anti-Balaka was not created to 'take power', it was a spontaneous self-defence movement at first, politics came later. Alfred Legrand Ngaya confirmed that the objective of the Anti-Balaka groups was to defend themselves against the Seleka and that these groups were not set up with the aim of bringing Bozizé back to power -- indicating that at that moment they were not thinking of Bozizé because he had abandoned them. D30-4848 testified that the Seleka was a danger for the country and that it was necessary for them to leave, so everyone was making efforts to 'drive them out by all means possible'.

The question of gris-gris -- amulets -- being used by Anti-Balaka is widely discussed in the evidence before the Chamber. While it is clear that also Seleka may have worn gris-gris, as well as individuals not necessarily associated with the Anti-Balaka, it is equally clear that gris-gris in the context of the conflict within the CAR and certainly following the Seleka takeover and the emergence of self-defence groups were commonly associated with the Anti-Balaka. The evidence mentions the acquisition of gris-gris in Gobere and other areas. The evidence also indicates that not all Anti-Balaka elements necessarily wore gris-gris.

Several witnesses, as further outlined below, testified to the formation of self-defence groups in specific localities, including in particular in the Ouham prefecture. At least some of these groups would eventually gather and join together in Gobere.

For example, Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana stated that he was the secretary-general of the Anti‑Balaka in his village in the Bossangoa area, directing operations to attack the Seleka in the bush, with him having a hunting rifle and them making their hunting cartridges out of ammunition seized from the Seleka. They also seized weapons from Seleka they defeated. The witness also traced the origins of the group back to previous groups that had defended against road bandits and poachers, stating that they started calling themselves Anti-Balaka when François Bozizé was still in power, when armed Peuhl acted as road bandits and they defended themselves. Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana thought there were other groups which fought against highway bandits; in fact, there were self‑defence groups for each locality, for example, Godonam Richard was part of the self‑defence group in Ouham, there was somebody else in Bogangolo and other localities close by. He also indicated that on one side they were called Anti-Balaka while in another region they were called 'Anti-Zarguina'.

Similarly, P-2269, who had initially crossed to Zongo, stated that when his mother was killed, he got very angry and wanted to avenge her death, so he crossed back to Bangui with over 100 men, going through the bush to Bossangoa. P-2269 went to Bossangoa with his men 'to prepare the rebellion' -- he knew some of the men from the 2003 rebellion, some were from Bangui, Bossangoa, and a mix of other areas, and they were all in the camp in Zongo with him. According to P-2269, 'Mokom' told him to fight the Seleka, to help lead the rebellion. Similarly, P-0475, an imam in Bangui at the time, explained that before the Anti-Balaka formally emerged in Bossangoa and Bangui, young people of Bossangoa formed defence groups, as the local population had no other way of protecting itself against the Seleka violence. In September 2013, P-0475 went with Archbishop Nzapalaigna and others to Zere to try to persuade the young people to put down their weapons. There, P-0475 saw a group of around 20 or more young people, including women, with amulets and gris-gris, hunting rifles, makeshift guns and machetes, who were adamant and determined about attempting to enter Bangui, taking over governmental power, and said that they wanted to overthrow the Seleka because they had done a lot of harm, killed their parents, destroyed their homes and markets. P-0475 said there was tension because of him being Muslim. In a photograph taken during the visit, P-0475 identified the young people who called themselves Anti-Balaka, drawing a distinction with individuals in another photograph who, according to him, were civilians, not soldiers.

paragraph_text_preview: When P-1577, a photojournalist, travelled to Bossangoa and its surroundings in early November 2013, he encountered individuals that identified themselves as Anti-Balaka. The majority of weapons that P-1577 saw at that time were artisanal, fabricated in local villages, machetes carried in a sleeve, and a few Kalashnikovs. When they met the local population, it was clear there was some hierarchy because they were always taken to a spokesperson or chief of the Anti-Balaka, who identified as such, they were in charge, there was a clear hierarchy on who they would speak to and who not. According to P-0974, a former Anti-Balaka member, the second resistance to Seleka took place in villages around Bossangoa, in Zere, and in Bozizé's native village of Benzambé, and the resistance movement became widespread, larger operations were carried out, and many Seleka were killed, as P-0974 heard on RFI. Each of these resistance groups had their own gris-gris, and the group in the south led by 'Rombhot', Cœur de Lion and 'Habib' crossed the river with gris-gris from the DRC. The largest area with gris-gris was Bouca-Batangafo, led by Andjilo who was the most powerful marabout-fighter in the area; and Damara was led by 12 Puissances, who took his power from DRC. In the west, Anti-Balaka in Ouham-Pende prefecture used gris-gris; and in Bouar, the Anti-Balaka -- as the resistance became known later --, was led by three Ndales, General Ndale, Colonel Ibrahim Ndale, and Adamou Ndale. Belo was another Anti-Balaka first active on the Bouar-Bohon axis, then based in Abba. After General Souleyman was killed, the Seleka retreated north from Berberati, Carnot, Baoro, Bouar, Bocaranga, facing resistance the whole way from the Anti-Balaka, in Ndale, Belo.

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that members of the FACA and civilians, including those who had already organised in self-defence groups, gathered in Gobere, administered traditional rituals, organised and structured the groups, trained in handling weapons, and strategised with a view to advancing through the provinces towards Bangui in order to drive Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power. Arrival to Gobere and reasons for going thereSeveral witnesses testified about the circumstances in which they decided to go to Gobere, and how they reached the location.

At the outset, the Chamber notes the Ngaïssona Defence's submission that '\[i\]nformation on the location of G\[obéré\] camp is confusing and inconsistent'. The Chamber considers that the evidence of three witnesses who were at Gobere and provided sketches or marked maps with a view to indicating the location in fact largely overlaps. Indeed, P‑2602, Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana and P-2658 all located Gobere to the north, north-east of Bossangoa, with maps also showing 'Bonguere' as a separate location south thereof. That the location indicated by these three witnesses is not exactly the same is, in the Chamber's view, immaterial for reaching a conclusion on the approximate location. Indeed, the Chamber considers it reasonable for individuals walking in areas otherwise unfamiliar to them to not subsequently pinpointing the locations of these areas on maps or aerial imagery shown to them. This is with the exception of the information provided by P-2251, who located Gobere further south-east of Bossangoa. In light of the other evidence before it, the Chamber does not rely on P-2251's evidence concerning the location of Gobere.

The Chamber notes in this regard that Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana described the area of Gobere as mountainous, and further stated that the only place they spent a lot of time at was Gobere, and once they left, they moved forward heading in the direction indicated to them. On the first point, and recalling that Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana and P-2658 placed Gobere in similar areas towards the north-west of Bossangoa, the Chamber considers this discrepancy concerning its description as mountainous to be immaterial. On the second point, and noting that no other witness specifically mentioned a group staying in 'Gbonguere', the Chamber recalls the specific circumstances of P-2658's stay with the groups around Gobere, that he was with them for some weeks having been abducted and therefore likely not informed of all details of the group's workings, while at the same time noting Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana's evidence that at some point, the group split up. In light of this, the Chamber does not consider the witnesses' accounts to be contradictory on its face, and relies on their descriptions of the groups and their activities accordingly.

P-2658 recalled Herman, Regbai, Desire, Togbo among the Anti-Balaka gathered in Gobere. The elements were divided into six groups, led by Andjilo, corporal Dangba, 12 Puissances, Nambozouina and Akim. Dedane met with the group leaders every morning in Gobere. The group leaders joined during the exercises with the elements at Gbonguere, where Nambozouina, 12 Puissances and Akim came every morning to greet Dedane as chief on the hill, at which time Andjilo was no longer there. Andjilo had already gone to Bouca and Dedane was in the habit of calling him over the telephone. P-2658 saw Andjilo in Gobere two days after his arrest. Dangba was a chief corporal in the army and had many elements, Nambozouina, a FACA, and P‑2658 grew up together, Akim used to be a driver in Bossangoa and people called him 'Massa Akim' or 'chef', but he had no elements under his control. When P-2658 was arrested, Akim said in Sango that they did not have to keep an Arab alive, they were killing Arab people, but 12 Puissances said the commander had given instruction to keep P-2658 alive. Moundjou (meaning in Sango 'light skin') was an Anti-Balaka element, not a commander, he was working under 12 Puissances. 12 Puissances was an Anti-Balaka commander; Dedane told P-2658 that 12 Puissances was a hunter. P-2658 did not know the names of Ndomaté, Alfred Ngaya, Wenezoui, Yvon Konaté, Modibo and did not hear the names of Houronti Dieudonné, Richard Bejouane or Modibo. P-2658 had heard the name of Marabout Lundi, but did not recall his real name, everyone would call him marabout.

paragraph_text_preview: In a video interview of Dieudonné Houronti, the latter described that they started 'the movement' in Bossangoa, walking through the bush to get there, where they then also encountered military who had gone there from Bangui, 16 in total; that they created their Anti-Balaka base in the bush, at around 40 kilometres from Bossangoa and 15 kilometres from Benzambe, called Gobere; that there were about 2,000 people there, which would be trained by the soldiers in tactics, combat, how to advance and fight; that they also had 'marabouts'; and that they fought even though they did not have any weapons, only machetes.

Individuals who were not present in Gobere themselves also provided information on the persons who were there. For example, P-2232 testified that Gobere was a village where Dedane went for the first attack to Bozoum, they regarded this village as the 'password' for the Anti-Balaka and from Gobere, they regrouped to go to other villages and organise other attacks. Other individuals in Gobere included Mauri, Azounou, Marabout, Richard Bezouane, Corporal Inga; Konaté was not yet with them during the first attack, he joined them afterwards. These people were like ComZones, they commanded troops, supervised them, were in the front and also looked at how they should attack the villages. Asked whether any ammunition was brought to Gobere, P-2232 denied, stating when they left Bozoum to go to Gobere, they did not have any support, they started receiving support after the fight in Ndjo, so their used their own means to fight, recovered arms and ammunition on the ground. P-2232 stated that everybody who belonged to this group were former hunters, others were highway bandits, they were used to handle hunting guns, machetes, arrows, but did not really teach someone how to use a machete, you learn that by yourself.

P-0884 heard that when the Seleka were advancing to take over the country, Gbaya soldiers went to Gobere and were in contact with Maxime Mokom. There were 17 of them, they started using the term Anti-Balaka, taking advantage of pre-existing groups that fought against the Peuhl's cattle, destroying fields and against road bandits, and that used traditional training to reinforce them to lead them to fight -- going into towns, they trained other people, until they arrived in Bangui. All the Central Africans talked about it; when they went there it was to protect themselves with the supernatural powers so as to become invulnerable. Dieudonné Houronti, a gendarme, was among the 17, as were Bama Clement, Mokpem, Dangba. P-0884 confirmed that Ouapoutou Benjamin (civilian), Thierry Lebene aka 12 Puissances (civilian), Guy Mazimbelet (military), Yadjoungou, Mokpem (military), Donoh (military), and Houronti were all in Gobere. The military themselves told P-0884 that they were in Gobere when they came to Bangui in December, saying that when the situation was difficult, 17 soldiers went to Gobere to create the Anti-Balaka movement with Maxime Mokom as coordinator. P-0884 did not know how long they were in Gobere. ######

Activities in Gobere and plan to advanceThe evidence outlined below shows that the Anti-Balaka in Gobere were organised. The individuals present in Gobere were registered on arrival and organised into various groups.

Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana testified that he was in charge of registering new recruits and informing them about the principles to be respected: 'do not steal, do not attack civilians', if an Anti-Balaka was caught stealing, the thief would be tied up and beaten and the witness personally sanctioned several such punishments. His men respected his orders and would be punished if not, by whipping them and making them stand up all night. The instructions given to those who joined were, 'don't kill or steal, don't touch the Muslim women. And if the Seleka attack, you can defend yourself'.

Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana described that they were divided into 14 companies, each company with between 500 and 1,000 persons and divided into four sectors, dispatched to areas according to the province of origin of their elements, and he was a deputy chief before becoming a chief of company. The witness gave a list of elements in Gobere to ComZone Kema since as one of the few literate men, he was asked to keep the register of companies and their members, with Kema then forwarding the lists to Maxime Mokom. It appears from Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana's testimony that lists were more or less regularly updated as the various groups moved around. ComZone Kema kept the list of all elements in Bossangoa and forwarded them to the leader, Kema told them that once he found some coverage, he would give the names of the people. Each group had a secretary, and the witness re-transcribed all lists and prepared a clean copy before forwarding. Dedane was responsible for communicating the lists, but at one point the group split up and Kema would send the information to Dedane, who would send it on. It was a matter of recruiting them into the army later and people who were not on one of the lists were not considered to be part of the movement: it appears from Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana's testimony that integration into the army was considered to be the reward for protecting the country, while the soldiers in the movement, in case of victory, might get one rank higher.

Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana testified that when they arrived at Gobere, there were no weapons, it had 'all been a lie', and had he known, he would have stayed in his village to fight. The witness did not leave because, according to him, once one joined the movement, one could not go out freely and leave until authorisation was given, but then he stated it was no longer possible for him to find his way back to his village. When they left Bossala, the objective was to get weapons and ammunition in Bossembélé, so they could go to Bossangoa with weapons, yet they left Bossangoa without weapons and in Bossembélé they received a fresh supply of weapons, ammunition, grenades to head to Bossangoa a second time. There were rumours about tanks and war arsenal, but when they reached Gobere they did not see any; at Ndjo, they saw people had 'DKN' and AK-47s, but at Gobere they did not see any tanks or arsenal, while they had one DKN and a 'lance-roquettes', and the soldiers had AK-47s; once they arrived in Benzambé, they started to have some conventional weapons, gradually as they advanced they retrieved those.

The evidence before the Chamber, as discussed below, shows that training on how to handle weapons was provided by the former FACA elements to the civilians. While they were low on weapons and living conditions overall were challenging, civilians in the groups received some training on handling weapons by the FACA members present. With discussions being had on how to move the groups' activities forward, as further outlined also below, Gobere was in essence a regrouping and vantage point for groups to coordinate and discuss their further steps to be taken for them to be able to advance to Bangui and eventually remove Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power.
Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana stated that there were training and exercises in Gobere, they did simulations with sticks.

P-0975 described Gobere as a place of refuge, training, regrouping for youngsters to fight the Seleka, who were a scourge on the country. P-0975 spent two months in Gobere receiving training from FACA members who had fled into the bush, including on self-defence techniques, the use and assembly of weapons, for those who had any; they mainly used traditional hunting rifles, 'saguets' and machetes, and did not have automatic weapons; they were also taught how to differentiate the different sounds of weapons and protect themselves. According to P-0975, there were only about four to five FACA members who trained them in Gobere, their overall objective was to 'free \[their\] brothers and sisters' from the Seleka.

P-2658 testified that Gobere was a big training place for the Anti-Balaka; Gobere is near Boukatou, in the bush; there were no proper buildings but there were about 17 huts; he saw many people being trained there and he also saw more people coming for training. P-2658 did not spend much time in Gobere, the base existed before he was there. Only subsequently the Anti-Balaka group divided into two, one went to Bouca and the Dedane group, including P-2658, set up in Gbonguere, before they went to Bossangoa. Two weeks after P-2658's arrest, Dedane gathered all his men at Gbonguere when he returned from Bossangoa. In Gbonguere, P-2658 saw training; there was a former FACA by the name of Kokofere who had two weapons in his hands, shot and wanted to kill everybody, which created confusion and he was killed. The largest base was in Gbonguere. They went to Gobere on a regular basis because Dedane was a chief; they might go in the morning and then come back. The elements stayed with their leaders and around the main camp of Gobere, meeting at one place during training or for the group meeting; a river called Gobere was running through the camp. The training was like a military training; they were divided into two groups, each with a leader or commander, and P-2658 could see them running, walking around; some wore military uniform; after the training, their commander Dedane gave them practical instructions, but P-2658 was too far to know which. They were taught how to handle weapons, shown what being a soldier was all about, they did sports. P-2658 did hear Dedane give instructions to the elements, mainly those in charge of the training, on how to train them regarding some military tactics and how to attack. P-2658 could also see former soldiers -- those who wore military uniform during training, staying away from the other elements that were being trained, and seemingly leading other elements -- carrying guns. In Gbonguere, the soldiers gathered in the morning and chat, with P-2658 remaining at a respectful distance. As for training, they gathered together, on occasion did some sporting activities and went running together, but P-2658 was not close enough to know exactly what kind of training they were doing.

paragraph_text_preview: P-2658 explained that Dedane used to communicate on the phone when he was at the hill at Gbonguere, communications during which he would hear three names: Charli, Komas, Yongo. Dedane always complained about the lack of ammunitions, said that his elements and him were ready to get out for the attack; Charli, Komas, Yongo were putting pressure on Dedane and asked him what he was waiting for; Dedane responded that he wanted to divide his elements into different groups so he could deploy them but he did not have enough ammunitions and weapons; he said he would go to Bossangoa to look for more ammunition and on return would proceed to divide the Anti-Balaka elements into three groups.

P-2658 explained that Dedane used to communicate on the phone when he was at the hill at Gbonguere, communications during which he would hear three names: Charli, Komas, Yongo. Dedane always complained about the lack of ammunitions, said that his elements and him were ready to get out for the attack; Charli, Komas, Yongo were putting pressure on Dedane and asked him what he was waiting for; Dedane responded that he wanted to divide his elements into different groups so he could deploy them but he did not have enough ammunitions and weapons; he said he would go to Bossangoa to look for more ammunition and on return would proceed to divide the Anti-Balaka elements into three groups.

According to P-2658, Dedane went to Bossangoa at least three times. The first time he went for ammunition and captured a young person called Cisco who seemingly promised knowing where the ammunition was; the second time he went with Cisco, but they were not successful in getting ammunition. It appears that Dedane split the group for purposes of attack after the third trip to Bossangoa. Dedane talked about his elements on the phone; he spoke to Andjilo whom he sent to Bouca. Dedane transmitted the information about the location of his elements to someone else, village per village. Dedane provided information to Charli, P-2658 did not know the other people Dedane spoke to. P-2658 denied that Dedane transmitted lists of elements to someone over the phone, he did not hear him talk about a list. According to P-2658, the chiefs who spoke about lists were not next to Dedane; in Gbonguere, the team was divided into groups and each group had their own list.

In light of various witnesses mentioning at least Dedane, and some other leaders, being in a position to communicate through telephone, the Chamber disregards P-2251's indication that he did not know if the chiefs in 'Ngobere' communicated with others as he never saw anyone speaking on their phone while they were there. In any event, the Chamber notes that P-2251 does support other evidence when stating that at 'Ngobere', they organised, with elements from each town sleeping together in their own zone, leaders staying in the centre of the different zones and exchanging ideas and strategies. P-2251 also recalled some gatherings at 'Ngobere' where they all stood in front of the chiefs such as Konaté, Lebene, Dangba, Dedane and Andjilo, and they spoke to them, telling them to stay calm and not be afraid, that God would help them exit the bush, that they had no choice but to have fled to 'Ngobere' to save themselves, but that a time would come when they would be able to exit the bush and drive the Seleka away.

paragraph_text_preview: P-2658 testified that he stayed with the Anti-Balaka at Gbonguere for some weeks and during his entire stay there, the elements constantly told him that they did not want the Seleka and Muslims around; they said the Seleka and Muslims were the same and that they want to deal with the Muslims and the Seleka. Groups mainly based around FACA and/or PG

In addition to self-defence groups centred around civilians forming in the provinces, a number of former FACA and PG elements also gathered individuals around them. Importantly, it is clear from the evidence as outlined that in the same vein as self-defence groups which formed in different localities and eventually pursued the same cause, also these groups, while initially founded separately, communicated and found together on the basis of pursuing one goal. The evidence before the Chamber shows that the various groups operated in conjunction with other groups and were eventually all associated with the Anti-Balaka.

One of these groups was the 'Front de resistance pour l'alternance pour le peuple Centrafricain' (FRAPPE). P-0954 explained in this regard that he started out of a group of around 10 serving FACA in June 2013 with purpose of protecting themselves and the civilians, and many civilians joined them, with P-0954 seeing his obligation to defend his country as also implying to defend its citizens from the attack of foreign Seleka and strangers. P-0954's evidence suggests that this group evolved and grew over time, including with civilians joining who were part of autonomous self-defence groups, taking the stated name in November 2013 on the basis of Léopold Bara's idea, after 'the French' had told him that they did not like the name Anti-Balaka since the Anti-Balaka had made too many blunders. The group had a clear structure, with P-0954 communicating clearly that they were to protect the population and not create disorder, and had Bonaventure Guiyegba as secretary-general, Léopold Bara as spokesperson and Lieutenant Kengwa as chief of staff. P-0954 had gone into the bush with the aim of identifying Seleka and kicking them out of his area, he wanted to protect Bimbo, and as ComZone later, when Djotodia left, he wanted to protect the entire community, including Muslims, and to avoid armed robberies, pillaging, people settling scores. P-0954 agreed that he took action because (i) there were still Seleka in the area, (ii) there was still general chaos, and (iii) there were no domestic and not enough international forces to manage these problems.

P-1858 stated that the group was a politico-military organisation created by Basile Mbomon and Léopold Bara-Dessi between the end of March and September 2013, with the objective to overthrow the Djotodia government. When Bara came to visit, they discussed how the different groups could come together; at that time FRAPPE was not part of the Anti-Balaka yet; they heard about different Anti-Balaka groups but they were all located in different areas; this was during the period between September and November 2013. P-1858 agreed with the suggestion that the name 'FRAPPE' was not known, and everybody from the outside was referring to them as Anti-Balaka. From September to November 2013, they stayed in the bush preparing to overthrow the Seleka; the FACA in the group trained the civilians in combat strategies and on how to use weapons -- involving to call them, align them, show them discipline, teach them how to behave, to say 'on your guard'. The elements of the group were using traditional weapons while the FACA of the group had automatic weapons, some also had grenades. P-1858 agreed with the suggestion that he and others felt an obligation to defend the country. There was another group that came from Pissa on foot and they set up a base at 'Yanwara' school in Boeing; these were the elements of Rombhot, whose 'full name is Alfred Y\[ekatom\]', and 'real name is Alfred S\[aragba\]'.

paragraph_text_preview: Brice Emotion Namsio stated that at some point the Seleka started tracking down the FACA and to save their lives, these were obliged to join the Balaka they had heard of, and Balaka leaders gave them also gris-gris to protect themselves and the peaceful population. The witness stated that Konaté had also said he was spokesperson of the 'Siriri', meaning peace, and that he and his elements were leaving Bangassou to move to Bangui to liberate the Central African people. Others were called 'Anti-Balaka' from the hinterland, before the Bangui Attack was the CLPC was demanded by Maxime Mokom, and after that attack, 'they' insisted to change the name from Anti-Balaka to CLPC, but that did not work, so it was dropped and they continued under the name Anti-Balaka.

In addition to these groupings which appeared before 5 December 2013, P-0974 also testified about, thereafter, taking control of a disorganised Anti-Balaka group north of the airport, near Damala, with former FACA members, civilians from the provinces, the 8^th^ arrondissement, Combattants, roughly a few hundred people with P-0974 and sous-lieutenant 'Doze' being the only officers. P-0974 took the decision to lead the group which they divided people into sections like in the army with about 50-60 men each, with a former FACA as leader of which section and a civilian who had proven himself capable of fighting as his deputy, and each section organising its own training, including in the use of weapons, how to take cover, how to behave, led by a lower level former FACA elements. They made their base at the OCRB in Damala which they took over from the Seleka. Their objective was to prevent the Seleka from making excursions into their area; they could attack from north and west through exits to PK12, so they put military outposts at all the exits. P-0974's role as 'ComZone' was to defend his zone, each Anti-Balaka group defended their own zone, in a defensive, not offensive, role. P-0974's men did not patrol outside their zone as they would have gotten in trouble for that with the other zone, if they needed to go into another zone, they would tell the ComZone before and enter without weapons. They obtained weapons and ammunition in the context of fighting -- according to P-0974, senior officials of the Seleka had many arms and ammunition stocked at their residences, which they had pillaged from arms depots. When the Anti-Balaka entered Bangui, they attacked houses belonging to Muslims and who were of the Seleka, who had fled and abandoned their weapons and ammunition -- there was no other way to obtain ammunition for P-0974's group. According to P-0974, they tried not to communicate via mobile phones at the time because they knew they were tapped, so they sent messages through people. Not all ComZones worked this way; for example, in the 8^th^ arrondissement, the Anti-Balaka from Boy-Rabe and from Combattants attacked at different times, believing that the Seleka chiefs who lived there hid weapons in their homes. P-0974 in his zone gathered their men and told them not to attack the population, not to use weapons against those without weapons, and that an investigation would follow if they did. If someone broke the rules, they were whipped; P-0974 did not have to use more severe punishment as his group was very disciplined. They were not waiting for instructions from another individual to apply disciplinary measures in their group. If a soldier misbehaved, he could be put into prison; another type of sanction was to make them stay at a guard post for an indefinite period of time.

According to P-2841, 'Commander' Ngremangou played a very big role in the idea of the FACA joining the civilian Anti-Balaka, and the FACA chiefs and Anti-Balaka chiefs had telephone contact to organise the resistance, though P-2841 did not know how they organised everything practically speaking. In each zone there was a commander, such as Kema, Andjilo, Douze Puissances; from Bangui, Ngremangou would have been in contact with the Anti-Balaka chiefs. Regrouping took place where the military had means available, but finally they failed; this officer did play a role in the mobilisation of the military in that particular fight. Soldiers are trained, organised, disciplined, but the Anti-Balaka were mostly people who relied on mystical powers with gris-gris. P-2841 agreed with the suggestion that from the perspective of the FACA, it was necessary to protect the population. According to P-2841, in 2013 the Anti-Balaka were all mixed up and not very well structured, but used mystical powers and in a way were more powerful than the military and often led, instead of being led by, the military men amongst them. There were various groups and each one tried to defend itself as best it could, but within each group there was some hierarchy -- but it was the coordination at the general level which did not exist. P-2841 stated that it was clear that officers may have been mobilising people, but at the same time foot soldiers had fled Bangui and it was easy for them to join the traditional Anti-Balaka groups which were already beginning to be active in the villages; looking at the Anti-Balaka who fought on the ground, liberating villages, these were the villagers themselves who were then subsequently joined by foot and rank soldiers and not officers; that is why the officers were involved in some other kind of development.

Jean-Jacques Demafouth testified that he first became aware of the Anti-Balaka becoming operational in terms of military capacity around the months of June, July 2013. He had an informant known as Pabandji who was in contact with Ngaikosset in DRC and also had some informants in Cameroon who provided them with information -- Jean-Jacques Demafouth was convinced that the Anti-Balaka were putting in place a military-type structure for the purpose of recapturing power; all the soldiers at Camp M'Poko and FACA soldiers close to François Bozizé had left, were no longer visible, and the understanding was that they had gathered at a location to reorganise themselves.

paragraph_text_preview: P-2602 stated that the movement of the military started in light of the Seleka advance and takeover, the name was first 'Armée du Territoire blindé', created because the Seleka killed military. The report of P-2926 concluded that some self-defence groups were organised and coordinated by FACA members to march to Bangui and engage in the attack of 5 December 2013, some soldiers infiltrated the west of the CAR from Cameroon and emerged as Anti-Balaka fighters at the beginning of 2014. Links between self-defence groups and members of regular forces

It is clear from the above discussion that various self-defence groups in different localities, including in Gobere, were also joined by or integrated with members of the FACA or PG who led, trained and helped developing organisational structures. The Chamber has received additional evidence in this regard, which is outlined below.

For instance, Catherine Samba-Panza testified that as head of the transition government, she received information that the Anti-Balaka were at some point structured by the FACA members who joined the movement, and most of the army members who fled the military during 'the events' went back and joined the Anti-Balaka, training and structuring them, making their organisation more logical.

P-2232 explained that Ngaikosset was taken to Kinshasa after 'DGM' discovered that he organised the distribution of leaflets against the Seleka violence, and Ngaikosset contacted 'Mokom' from there; during the advance of the movement, 'Mokom' was coordinator of operations, Dedane, who was 'the core or the beginning', was still in town and they sometimes communicated, and 'Rambo' carried out manoeuvres from his side until and up to 5 December 2013. When Andjilo and 'the others' got together, they made Maxime Mokom coordinator, some people got to know Maxime through Dedane, and thereafter Mokom organised everything, though P-2232 was not with him then and did not know details. Whenever Dedane heard that a group had been formed in a village, he would try to contact their leader to organise the members and link them up with Mokom. People such as 'Abel Dinganan', Emtenou Euzebe, his younger brother Edya all crossed the river and linked up with the teams on the hill; these career soldiers were there to train the civilians with a view to winning the battle. Other FACA members who were never in Zongo also joined the movement, including Corporal Inga, Dedane, Andjizékané Tchakpa Blaise. At some point the Seleka were looking for soldiers; these soldiers fled and joined the movement in Damara and wherever else possible, some crossing the river and later returning to Bangui to join. The soldiers took their own weapons and were taken in as leaders when joining the movement.

paragraph_text_preview: Thierry Tribunal Ndokobanda, a military himself, described how approximately two weeks after his arrival to Zongo, which he put in approximately September 2013, they heard the news about an ambush against the Seleka in Ouham-Bac, close to Bossangoa according to Maxime Mokom. Maxime Mokom said that he would find out who was behind the ambush and get in contact to help them, and he called relatives from Bossangoa to find out what was happening. As Maxime Mokom found out that those behind the ambush were civilians, he asked the witness as military officer to advise them on how to progress and set up a military ambush. Maxime Mokom came to Thierry Tribunal Ndokobanda's house and asked on behalf of the civilians that staged the ambush for advice, and what they could do to help 'the children'. P-1847 testified that Achille Godonam told him that he had been in contact with Bernard Mokom who was going to take over all the activities in the area to counter-attack the Seleka. He went to meet Mokom and later also went with the Anti-Balaka coordinator Ndale to Bouar to meet Danzoumi. On their way back, Ndale stopped by and told P-1847 that they had been given a little bit of money and he was going back to see how things would be organised in Ngaoundaye, Bozoum, to sensitise the Anti-Balaka who were in the area so that they could start the attacks; Achille came back to Garam-Boulaï, the base, and they informed P-1847 that Col Daz and his troops were now dealing directly with 'Rambo', former FACA on the other side of the river towards Zongo, and that they were getting ready to attack the Seleka. The former PG who were in Bossangoa and Bouar were under the command of Dedane, P-1847's cousin; his cousin contacted him and told him that they had received orders from François Bozizé to descend on Bangui and attack, and that was how they started to attack the towns from Bossangoa, then Ndjo, Bossembélé and other locations.

The Chamber recalls its observations regarding the prior recorded testimony of P-1847, introduced pursuant to Rule 68(2)(d) of the Rules, and has considered P-1847's evidence on this topic in the context of the other evidence before it. P-1847 stated that certain FACA officers, in particular of the PG in Bossangoa, joined the Anti-Balaka, for example Florent Kema, Bama Clément, Dedane. He stated that there were FACA officers in Douala, Anatole Ngaya and Lamtague, with the Anti-Balaka financed by Marcelin, they participated in the meetings with Marius and Yvon Songuet, with the aim of supporting the Anti-Balaka on the ground; Marcelin talked about them to P-1847. P-1847 heard from Tchikaya, who was close to Pascal Koyagbele, that the latter held meetings with Anatole Ngaya and some young FACA elements who were in Douala, bought food and provisions for the Anti-Balaka in Bozoum, and Tchikaya also accompanied a woman who said she was the sister of Martin Ziguélé to the border to bring supplies. The meetings in Douala took place at restaurant Balet or the Meridien hotel where Yvon Songuet, Marius and Goke Boston usually stayed.

Adrien Poussou specified that he knew this because he was part of FROCCA, and it was public knowledge in the CAR that Koudemon Olivier alias Gbangouna, Semdiro and others, who were said to be leading the Anti-Balaka, were close to Bozizé. Adrien Poussou did not know how they procured weapons or anything about contacts between people close to François Bozizé and any of the self-defence groups in the time frame of April, summer 2013. Adrien Poussou explained that in her interview, Ghislaine Dupont had put a question on Eugène Ngaikosset, one of François Bozizé's close entourage and former officer of the PG, who had found refuge on the other side of the river, and that might have led people to believe that those close to Bozizé were on the other side of the river.

Adrien Poussou testified that after his return to France, he was in constant contact with Socrate Bozizé and in touch with Joachim Kokaté, and between his stay in Yaoundé and the arrival of François Bozizé in France, the Anti-Balaka came into being. According to Adrien Poussou, Levy Yakété, Mr Ngaïssona, Joachim Kokaté were very close and spoke to each other on a regular basis, so he supposed they had been in contact. According to Adrien Poussou, he did not take very seriously what Kokaté was telling him, due to his 'tendency to tell lies and fabulate', but Kokaté claimed he was heading an organisation by the name of free officers who were 'hell-bent', had enough equipment to launch an attack and only lacked financial means to pay for things like food. Socrate Bozizé did not discuss military matters with Adrien Poussou; as Socrate was not a military man himself, the witness thought he was not associated with anything of that, and military matters were also not very interesting for Adrien Poussou as he was in favour of a political process.

The Chamber notes the Ngaïssona Defence's argument that rather than being a 'top-down organisation', the Anti-Balaka was a 'myriad of self-defence groups that spontaneously rose out of the Seleka's heinous and continues crimes against the civilian population'.

paragraph_text_preview: In this regard, the Chamber further notes that the CAR Panel concluded at the time of its 2014 interim report that the Anti-Balaka was not an armed group with a centralised structure and effective command and control over its elements, but a 'myriad \[of\] different militias that either identify themselves as part of the movement or are or were associated to it by default'.

However, Aurélien Llorca explained that while this was the starting point, it gradually, through the use of emissaries, formed into some structure. Indeed, as the 2014 interim report also made clear: 'The re-emergence in the second half of 2013 of what was initially a self-defence group with the aim of protecting civilians and communities against the perceived State-sponsored oppression of non-Muslims culminated in a wider, better-structured and organised movement against the Séléka. It also gave an opportunity to former elements of the Central African armed forces to take much-awaited revenge against those who had defeated them during the March 2013 coup'.

Jean-Jacques Demafouth testified that the resistance he heard about already had a structure which could be used: the first what they called self-defence in the hinterland, young people, usually KNK militants, recruited by mayors of local communes, with first mobilisation started by those in the prefecture in Ouham, M'Poko, Ouham-Pendé and Lobaye, who would then be joined by COCORA militia and Bozizé's PG who would flee Bangui on foot to join them. They started to have meetings in Cameroon with others who had joined him there or were already outside the country, and he started to set up an organisation. Ngaikosset fled to the DRC and set up a structure of military nature there, and also in Landja, a place in Central Africa a bit upstream, they started to set up a structure and create the command links between them. The Chamber is of the view that the illustration of the Anti-Balaka as 'myriad' of different groups is only partially accurate. Indeed, the Chamber agrees, as the evidence above and below also shows, that self-defence groups were formed in various localities across the CAR. The Chamber further agrees that their objectives included rising against the atrocities committed by the Seleka and removing Michel Djotodia as well as the Seleka from power, and that such objectives evolved over time. The Chamber notes in this regard also its discussion on the efforts to structure the Anti-Balaka as a whole further following the attacks of 5 December 2013.

paragraph_text_preview: However, the Chamber disagrees that the various self-defence groups pursued their objectives in isolation and without coordination. The Chamber also disagrees with the suggestion that the Anti-Balaka would have been divided into separate 'clusters'. The evidence before the Chamber clearly shows that self-defence groups in various localities communicated, with each other and also with individuals in other localities in the CAR and abroad, and coordinated with a view to descending towards Bangui and eventually launching the coordinated attacks against Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013. Further, in the Chamber's view, and as is also clear from a holistic assessment of the evidence before it, the fact that groups initially started out separately does not exclude their coordinated action thereafter. On the contrary, the evidence on record is unequivocal in showing that these various groups, in sharing a common enemy, set aside whatever individual motivation may have existed -- whether of political, financial, or otherwise opportunistic nature -- and through coordinated efforts acted towards the same goals.

As discussed in detail below, this is further exemplified by the various super-imposed interests coming into play especially following the resignation of Michel Djotodia in early January 2014: while such interests informed the discussions and activities as well as tussles for leadership when it came to being considered by the transitional government, in the end, the various streams within the Anti-Balaka continued to cooperate, coordinate and align during the period relevant to the charges. Objectives and policies of the Anti-Balaka The self-defence groups initially forming in the provinces aimed at defending against the abuses and violence committed by the Seleka, within which framework some considered necessary to remove Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power. Due to the religious and ethnic commonalities between the Muslims in the CAR and the Seleka, the Anti-Balaka perceived the former as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka. On this basis, as the Anti-Balaka emerged and coalesced in pursuit of its core objective, its elements targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, killing and dislocating them. The implementation and execution of the Anti-Balaka's core objective was primed by anti-foreign sentiments and inflammatory rhetoric openly expressed by François Bozizé and others, which incited vigilance against those perceived to support the Seleka, in particular Muslim civilians. Such rhetoric was reflected in meetings of François Bozizé, Mr Ngaïssona and others in Cameroon and repeated in a radio statement issued by FROCCA on 5 December 2013 in relation to the attack on Bangui, which referred to the attack as '\[l\]e rétablissement de l'ordre fonctionnel' and further stated that the Anti-Balaka 'sont des Centrafricains pour aller libérer leur pays des jougs des djihadistes venus du D\[arfour\], du T\[chad\], du S\[oudan\]'. Mr Yekatom knew that the Anti-Balaka perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis. Mr Ngaïssona knew that the Anti-Balaka perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis. Mr Ngaïssona made his contributions fully aware that the Anti-Balaka would violently target the Muslim civilian population in the west of the CAR, committing the widespread attack that ultimately took place from September 2013 through February 2014, including the seminal coordinated Anti-Balaka attacks of Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013.

The evidence before the Chamber as outlined above shows that the Anti-Balaka emerged from self-defence groups that formed with a view to defending against the Seleka violence, and started coordinating and organising in order to remove Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power. Individuals like François Bozizé, Mr Ngaïssona and others instrumentalised these Anti-Balaka groups to ensure that the removal of the Seleka from power would be followed by the return of François Bozizé to power.

It appears from the evidence that while the above were among the initial motives, this did not include, in the early stages, advocating for the return of François Bozizé to power, or indeed having wider political ambitions. For example, P-1193 explained that after the collapse of the 'Seleka government', the population expected a change, a return to peace, to constitutional order. Vivien Beina stated that initially, the goal was to get rid of the Seleka, they had no political ambition and the idea of taking Bangui came later. Similarly, P-2841 stated that the Anti-Balaka was not created to 'take power', it was a spontaneous self-defence movement at first, politics came later. Alfred Legrand Ngaya confirmed that the objective of the Anti-Balaka groups was to defend themselves against the Seleka and that these groups were not set up with the aim of bringing Bozizé back to power -- indicating that, at that moment, they were not thinking of Bozizé because he had 'abandoned' them. D30-4848 testified that the Seleka was a danger for the country and that it was necessary for them to leave, so everyone was making efforts to 'drive them out by all means possible'.

paragraph_text_preview: At the same time, and as outlined above, the Chamber received evidence according to which individuals, especially those gathered in Cameroon, started using the self-defence groups forming in the provinces with a view to pursuing a super-imposed political goal, in particular the 'return of the constitutional order', meaning the return of François Bozizé to power, by all means.

The Chamber is of the view that it is immaterial for purposes of its determinations whether the reinstatement into power of François Bozizé was the agreed aim of some or all Anti-Balaka groups, at one time or another. Indeed, as stated below, the Chamber does not consider that the Anti-Balaka had to be a monolithic entity and/or ideologically homogeneous at any stage of the events. It remains that the express and overriding aim upon which all the self-defence groups that then coalesced as the Anti-Balaka were united was the expulsion of Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power in the CAR.

In the view of the Chamber, of crucial importance for the current discussion is how this aim was understood and implemented in practice. On the basis of the evidence before it, as outlined below, the Chamber concludes that, against the backdrop of the violence committed by the Seleka in particular against the non-Muslim population and the perceptions this created, the Anti-Balaka equated the Muslim civilian population with the Seleka and its actions, and targeted it accordingly.

At the outset, the Chamber recalls its discussion of the violence committed by the Seleka, in particular against the non-Muslim population, of the composition of the Seleka, which included Chadian and Sudanese mercenaries, and of the perceptions the aforementioned created among the non-Muslim population. The Chamber considered this as one of the factors that cumulatively played into the evolution of the Anti-Balaka and its objectives and policies. Concretely, the Chamber considers that the abuses and violence committed by the Seleka following its coup not only confirmed the fears forewarned by François Bozizé, as discussed below, but also reinforced communal distrust, grief and feelings of revenge among the common population against the at that stage known 'enemy', the Seleka.

As the evidence outlined below shows, several witnesses testified as to how, within this context, the Anti-Balaka started targeting the Muslim civilian population, describing how the latter were seen as accomplices of the Seleka and responsible for the violence and human rights abuses reportedly perpetrated by the Seleka. In this overall framework of Seleka violence and resulting perceptions, the Anti-Balaka equated the Muslim civilian population with the Seleka and its acts, targeting it accordingly. This was another factor considered by the Chamber that cumulatively played into the evolution of the Anti-Balaka and its objectives and policies.

Catherine Samba-Panza testified that 'generally speaking, \[the Anti-Balaka\] wanted retaliation, reprisals against the Seleka and those in favour of the Seleka, and the Muslims who had helped the Seleka to take power and those who had committed all those crimes which we all deplore', testifying that 'the majority of the Anti-Balaka, they were moved in this spirit of revenge' and 'above all' wanted to ensure that the Seleka, who were responsible for crimes, would no longer hold power. The Prosecution argues that this speech of Bozizé is set within the context of Bozizé and members of his government and the KNK, including Mr Ngaïssona, 'stepping up efforts to mobilise support for the regime, resorting to nationalistic appeals discriminating against, and targeting Muslims', with the speech at PK0 'stok\[ing\] fear and engender\[ing\] ethno-religious animus toward the country's Muslim population, falsely portraying his political opponents as the product of a foreign Muslim invasion'.
