In the Chamber's view, the content of the speeches and how they were understood, as outlined below, cannot be interpreted in the manner suggested by the Ngaïssona Defence. Instead, it is clear from the statements discussed that François Bozizé meant to mobilise the population into a state of preparedness to fight, if necessary, against 'foreigners', including those living, at that time, in 'fenced compounds' within the CAR.

Speaking at the rally on 27 December 2012, François Bozizé called on the support of France and the US for assistance in pushing back the Seleka to their former positions and for continued dialogue in Libreville. François Bozizé warned those at the rally of the precarious situation the country was in, referring to the approaching Seleka as being comprised of foreigners and stressing the differences between the CAR population and Seleka rebels, stating that the latter did not speak Sango or French, included Janjaweed and 'Toroboro', and sought to take over power in the CAR, exploit the country's resources, and kill Central Africans: Des étrangers cherchent à s'accaparer de notre pays; Pourquoi s'empressent-ils de venir tuer les gens, ils ont pris des J\[anjaouid\] \[...\] Des T\[oroboro\] et consorts pour venir prendre le pouvoir à B\[angui\]; Ce sont tous des étrangers. Il y a beaucoup de J\[anjaouid\] parmi eux; beaucoup trop de J\[anjaouid\]! Il n'y a aucun Centrafricain parmi eux \[...\] Voilà, ils ne parlent pas sango, ils ne parlent pas français; Ce n'est pas une guerre justifiée, mais plutôt une tentative de vol de notre pétrole, de vol de notre uranium, de vol de notre or à \[N\]dassima, de vol de nos diamants, de vol de notre forêt.

The Chamber considers of import in this context that François Bozizé knowingly provided false information in his speech when stating that the Seleka were 'tous des étrangers' and included 'aucun Centrafricain'. In the view of the Chamber, this is a further illustration of how François Bozizé wanted the Seleka to be seen: as being exclusively 'foreign', including its members, or purported supporters, that were in fact citizens of the CAR.

Indeed, the evidence shows that the Muslim community in particular understood the speech accordingly, including that the reference to 'fenced compounds' referred to Muslims. For example, P-0967, a Muslim civilian, testified that Bozizé led people to understand that the enemy was fast approaching and was not from the CAR, but foreign, and therefore the citizens of the CAR had to be alert and vigilant. According to P-0967, after this speech the people's understanding of the country changed, in that the population thought that the rebellion was managed by the Muslims and were disappointed vis-à-vis the Muslims.

In light of the above, the Chamber considers this speech of François Bozizé a clear call for vigilance of 'Central Africans' towards all 'foreigners', which, on its face and in the words used by François Bozizé, included individuals 'living' in 'fenced compounds' within the CAR. The speech played on and heightened an already prevailing climate of fear and suspicion and was meant to mobilise the population into supporting his regime. Far from being a mere innocent call for peaceful demonstrations, as suggested by the Ngaïssona Defence, the Chamber is of the view that this speech was meant to set the tone of preparedness for the possibility of 'real' Central Africans fighting, to their death, against anyone who was considered to be 'foreigner'. This speech was made in full knowledge of the Seleka, in their essence, having come to the fore through a coalition of Central African groups opposed to the Bozizé administration, and in this knowledge falsely claimed that the Seleka included exclusively 'foreigners', and not a single Central African.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that this speech did not directly refer to Muslims within the CAR in general, and that this speech, on its own, did not make Muslims out to be the enemy. However, the Chamber recalls how the speech and in particular the reference to 'fenced compounds' was understood and considers that it primed its audience, setting the tone with references to 'foreigners' to include also those considered 'foreign' within the CAR who would support the Seleka. This is not negated by François Bozizé also calling, at that stage of the conflict, for peaceful protest.

The speech of François Bozizé held on 27 December 2012 was not the only address to the population in the context of the advancing Seleka. The Chamber considered in this context as a further cumulative factor that François Bozizé's message was widely known and drew sectarian lines well before the coup and the events in the latter half of 2013 because of its repetition by others and its dissemination prior to the Seleka coup in March 2013, including the support expressed by Mr Ngaïssona as outlined below. The Chamber considered as an additional cumulative factor that certain youth organisations took on François Bozizé's appeal to vigilance by setting up roadblocks and checkpoints 'to find hidden Seleka and their accomplices', targeting Muslims and CAR ethnicities associated with Muslims.

Mr Ngaïssona, attending in his capacity as minister of youth, sports, arts and culture, pledged to François Bozizé the support of the Central African youth in 'defending their endangered homeland'.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber considers this to be underscored by then-ambassador of the CAR to Cameroon Louis Oguéré who, on the same day, stated that the war of occupation that the country was experiencing had been predictable, because foreigners had installed themselves in the country, fraudulently becoming Central Africans and, due to the resources of the CAR, were interested in gaining political power, and that the people in question had been welcomed but now wanted to take the country.

The Chamber concludes that the context given by the then-ambassador, who also participated in meetings with François Bozizé and Mr Ngaïssona in Cameroon after the Seleka coup, makes clear that he was not merely referring to foreign elements of the Seleka, but in fact to those considered 'foreigners' in their own country, the CAR.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes the Ngaïssona Defence's argument that there is no evidence that Mr Ngaïssona instructed Steve Yambété to make an address on his behalf and that, in any event, this address was a call for appeasement and not violence. The Chamber agrees that there is no evidence on the record indicating that Mr Ngaïssona instructed Steve Yambété to make the above radio statement. At the same time, the Chamber notes that Steve Yambété clearly indicated in this address that he was giving it on behalf of '\[his\] minister' and thus, in the least, wanted the audience to think that this was the case. Further, the evidence pointed to by the Ngaïssona Defence in this regard is inconclusive. P-1847 testified that Mr Ngaïssona did not issue any messages himself, but that Steve Yambété did, and further indicated that he had not heard of the specific message of Steve Yambété reflected above. Alfred Legrand Ngaya testified that Mr Ngaïssona was not present in the CAR at the time of the Seleka coup, as did P-2232, who added that those mobilising or organising the young people in Bangui were Levy Yakété and Steve Yambété, among others.

In any event, the Chamber disagrees that the message delivered by Steve Yambété was merely a call for peace. While telling the 'youth of the CAR' to remain calm, the message continued to state that once they would be told that their lives are in danger 'tu peux faire tout ce que tu veux' and that '\[d\]ès que le besoin se fait sentir, on te fera appel'. In the view of the Chamber, far from being a simple appeasing call, this message implied a state of alert, and that the youth could -- and would -- be called on as needed.

More generally, Adrien Poussou considered that 'the rhetoric of the government was to get Christian Central Africans to understand that foreigners were coming and taking their country away from them \[and\] if \[they\] allowed the Seleka rebellion to enter Bangui, it would mean that the foreigners, the Chadians and the Sudanese, would come and take control of the country', a rhetoric which resonated with the population given that ten years earlier, Bozizé had orchestrated a coup with the support of the Chadian army, that brutalised people in the 2013 to 2014 crisis, 'behaving as an occupying force'.

paragraph_text_preview: P-1847 testified that the Bozizé government began marshalling supporters against the Seleka rebellion, frequently and widely circulating information on the radio and in papers about the Sudanese and Chadians encroaching into the CAR territory and committing offences, for example via David Banga, director-general of the Central African radio and Jevon Papa Zama, who had a daily radio programme in which he denounced the Seleka violence and broadcast messages in support of François Bozizé against the 'Islamists', such as asking the population to be vigilant.

Adrien Poussou also referred to this programme, stating that Radio Centrafrique was 'the voice of the government at the time', and mentioning a programme called 'Ye so a lingbi ti inga' hosted by Abakar Piko, Séverin Vélé Yamindi and Javon Papa Zama, which would openly attack opponents of the regime.

The Ngaïssona Defence argues that the speeches and radio statements made in December 2012 and March 2013 by François Bozizé and others, including the broadcasts of the radio show mentioned above, merely denounced the Seleka violence, encouraged dialogue, and discouraged violence.

In the view of the Chamber, this is an overly trivialised reading of the messages given. While it is clear that calls for peaceful demonstrations and refraining from violence such as throwing stones against individuals or people were made, all of the above also unequivocally called for 'vigilance' of the addressees, thereby maintaining the Central African population in a state of alert against 'foreigners'. The references to 'foreigners' have to be seen in the context of the Seleka not being in fact a 'foreign invasion', even though it used combatants from Chad and Sudan, as well as in light of the fact that they were made in direct connection to 'foreigners' living in the CAR and supporting the Seleka, in contrast with 'real' or 'authentic' Central Africans.

The Chamber furthermore notes as another cumulative factor its discussion of the creation and activities of FROCCA, which marshalled support against the Seleka regime with express pleas to return to 'the constitutional order', signifying François Bozizé's return to power. Adrien Poussou testified that within FROCCA, the prevailing rhetoric was that Christian Central Africans 'were being robbed of \[their\] own country by Muslim invaders. And it just so happens that the Seleka regime was made up of \[their\] fellow citizens of the Muslim faith', and that this was sort of language was also being used by Mr Ngaïssona. According to this witness, FROCCA used 'hate speech or hateful language' in its communications with the goal of spreading incendiary information, such as the alleged planned 'Islamisation' of the CAR, to 'step up the antagonism between Christians and Muslims \[...\] to push Christians to defend their country against the invaders, to resist by violent means'.

paragraph_text_preview: The press releases issued by FROCCA employed a similar rhetoric. The first release of 5 August 2013 stated that the Seleka's takeover and human rights violations were 'l'heure du triomphe des commanditaires extérieurs et leurs complices locaux \[sic\]'. Lin Banoukepa was reported as stating in that same interview at the time that the coup had been carried out with 'la participation très active des mercenaries islamistes de confession musulmane \[...\] du Tchad et du Soudan'. FROCCA further denounced the Seleka raids and criminal acts of the Seleka in general, referring to the transitional regime as anti-democratic and Islamic. FROCCA continued to decry alleged plans for a forceful Islamisation of the CAR, calling on the international community 'to see the genocide that is under way', and requesting the unconditional withdrawal of the Seleka from power and the CAR territory. Lin Banoukepa was further reported as calling on the Central African people to rise up and drive out Islamists and jihadist terrorists who came with the aim of 'Islamising' the CAR.

Nous nous revendiquons l'espace, l'organe politique, pour sauver nos citoyens, au FROCCA. Et nous revendiquons aujourd'hui notre part auprès de vos jeunes frères et sœurs qui, eux, sont en action. Donc nous sommes ensemble, et nous sommes la tête politique. Si le peuple se soulève, nous sommes derrière le peuple. Les A\[nti-Balaka\] sont des Centrafricains pour aller libérer leur pays des jougs des djihadistes venus du D\[arfour\], du T\[chad\], du S\[oudan\]. Vous savez que les évènements de B\[angui\] ne sont pas une rébellion comme la S\[eleka\] l'est. C'est un peuple indépendant qui ne veut pas être soumis, qui veut mettre fin aux crimes impunis. \[...\] En ce jour du 5 décembre, j'appelle tous les Centrafricains à se lever comme un seul homme pour bouter hors de notre territoire la composante islamique étrangère, envahissante, criminologène \[sic\] qui sévit, qui humilie. Et l'objet de notre appel au soutien de l'action de libération de ce 5 décembre de nos jeunes sœurs et frères du B\[alaka\].

In the view of the Chamber, this statement of Lin Banoukepa on behalf of FROCCA is a good illustration of how matters unfolded at the time: the Anti-Balaka groups fought on the ground, with political ambitions and frameworks, such as FROCCA, making use of these actions to further their motives.

Overall, the evidence before the Chamber shows that the Anti-Balaka groups which engaged in hostilities against the Seleka in earnest from September 2013 onwards equated the Seleka with the Muslim civilian population in general, perceiving Muslim civilians, due to their religious or ethnic affiliation, as collectively responsible for the crimes committed by the Seleka, or as complicit with, or supportive of, the Seleka.

The evidence before the Chamber also shows that this was widely known, including to the Anti-Balaka leadership and Mr Ngaïssona therein. The Chamber thus considered as a last cumulative factor that each stage of the evolution of the Anti-Balaka objectives and policies was public knowledge, and that it was instrumentalised by François Bozizé, Mr Ngaïssona and others to further their political or personal agenda.

As outlined below, the Chamber is of the view that Mr Ngaïssona was aware of the context and how it developed already through the meetings he participated in while in Cameroon, and at the latest in discussions concerning FROCCA. Further, Mr Ngaïssona was informed of the attacks taking place as from September 2013. Similarly, Mr Yekatom, given his own history with the Seleka and flight to Zongo, knew about the context and how members of his group, irrespective whether they were trained FACA members or not, did not distinguish between Muslim civilians and the Seleka. Yet, Mr Yekatom as leader of his group did not demand or emphasise the need for such distinction when instructing his elements in preparation of the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, in Yamwara, or when his group advanced along the PK9-Mbaïki axis.

Importantly, in a very public visit to Mbaïki on 12 February 2014, following the dislocation of Muslims therefrom, Catherine Samba-Panza, then-transition president of the CAR, denounced the violence and killings committed by the Anti-Balaka, warning the group it would pay should it continue. This had been prefaced by a statement of the commander of the Sangaris, Francisco Soriano, who declared that the Anti-Balaka were 'enemies of peace'. This was followed by the Anti-Balaka coordination, under lead of Mr Ngaïssona, complaining about the characterisation of the group in what it called 'incendiary declarations', while at the same time acceding that inquiries needed to be made within the movement to find those responsible for possible violence.

paragraph_text_preview: Moreover, this rhetoric did not stop there. Indeed, in a document dated 11 February 2014 issued under Mr Ngaïssona's name, the background to the conflict is recalled by stating that 'la population, victime des exactions des S\[eleka\] à travers la Centrafrique depuis le 10 décembre 2012, a regagné les rangs des Antibalaka avec un esprit de vengence \[sic\] envers les ex-Séléka est \[sic\] les sujets musulmans qui ont soutenu les Séléka durant leur occupation de la RCA'. Similarly, a press statement of the same day appears to criticise that 'Muslims', in general, were speaking up against the Anti-Balaka, who are described as 'dignes fils du pays' which engaged in an 'œuvre salvatrice'. In an interview later in February 2014, Mr Ngaïssona stated: 'We cannot accept the attacks by the Muslims'. Even later in 2014, Mr Ngaïssona continued using rhetoric similar to that used by François Bozizé in mid-March 2013, when stating: '[Un étranger qui vient dans notre pays, pour faire de l'occupation]{.underline}, prendre des armes et tuer les enfants du pays, nous ne pouvons pas accepter cela et voir les enfants du pays souffrir' (emphasis added). In another interview at a time of general peace efforts, in which he stated that he was against violence, Mr Ngaïssona also reiterated, against his better knowledge, that at least 90% of the Seleka were foreigners from Chad and Sudan, and that the Seleka's goal was to transform the CAR into an Islamic state: 'Mais nous, on ne peut pas accepter alors que nos frères sont seulement peut-être à 8% de la population qui peuvent prendre toute une 92% de la population en otage'.

paragraph_text_preview: This lack of distinction was equally present within Mr Yekatom's group. Indeed, as outlined below, Mr Yekatom must have been aware of the statements against Muslims, in general, made by elements and leaders of his group under his command, and, when giving instructions to his group, himself did not draw an appropriate distinction between targeting Seleka members or individuals belonging to the Muslim civilian population. In fact, the evidence before the Chamber indicates that Mr Yekatom himself expressly instructed the elements under his command to attack Muslim civilians, in the context of events relating to crimes as charged in this case. Mr Yekatom not only issued such instructions to elements under his command, but also personally participated in related attacks which targeted not only Seleka members, but also Muslim civilians. Further, leaders in Mr Yekatom's group under his command echoed his instructions to the elements of the group, while elements of the group participated in the targeting of Muslim civilians. Mr Yekatom must have known that, as a consequence of his specific instructions resulting in the targeting and killing of Muslim civilians, the latter would flee the attacked areas. Hostilities during the advance towards Bangui The Anti-Balaka groups, which had formed in the provinces and in part gathered together at Gobere, started their advance towards Bangui, with the ultimate objective to attack the capital in order to remove Michel Djotodia from power and oust the Seleka from the CAR. In this advance, various Anti-Balaka groups started engaging in attacks against the Seleka from September 2013 onwards. Such attacks were not limited to Seleka forces, but included attacking localities with Muslim civilians. These groups going into different localities communicated with each other and individuals abroad, including Maxime Mokom, with a view to coordinating such attacks. Attacks were launched around Bossangoa and in Bouca (Ouham prefecture), in Ndjo, Bossembélé, Boali and Gaga (Ombella-M'Poko prefecture), as well as in Bouar (Nana-Mambéré prefecture). As part of these attacks, Anti-Balaka elements attacked Bossangoa on 17 September 2013. Throughout the advance and during these attacks, Anti-Balaka groups targeted Muslim civilians. This information was widely known across the CAR and abroad, including in Cameroon. The advance of the Anti-Balaka groups and hostilities on the way culminated in coordinated attacks in Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013. From his involvement in coordinating his own group's advance through the provinces towards Bangui for purposes of the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, Mr Yekatom knew of the advance of the Anti-Balaka groups through the provinces towards Bangui, including the hostilities, as well as killings and dislocation of Muslim civilians, taking place in this context. Mr Ngaïssona knew and was informed of the advance of the groups towards Bangui as well as of the hostilities during this advance, including the killings and dislocation of Muslim civilians from the locations mentioned above. Two or three companies could be sent to the same town, and Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana's company, the last to leave, was sent to Benzambé with the group of 'John Rombhot'.

Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana stated that, when they arrived near a village, they would send someone in the night to do 'reconnaissance' to determine how many 'Seleka' were present, confirm if people had fled to the bush and whether there were women or not. The witness further stated that they searched houses and mosques for weapons to determine if a house was a Seleka house, they had to enter and look for weapons. According to Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana, it was easy to identify Seleka houses as they usually lived together in a group fenced off from the rest.

The Chamber is of the view that the evidence of Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana as outlined above has to be seen against the background of the overarching policy exhibited by Anti-Balaka groups at the time. This is indeed underscored by how the witness framed the description of their activities himself: while averring that not all Muslims were considered Seleka, the witness also stated that those who did not fight had to be put together in a 'safe place', without specifying for which reason he considered this necessary if such individuals were civilians. Similarly in this context, in his view Muslims needed to be 'help\[ed\] to get out of there'. In addition, while stating that they could not destroy 'everything' because they wanted the population to return, he also stated that to avoid being shot by a Seleka, all 'Seleka' houses were destroyed, with such houses for search for weapons being identified on the basis of the assumption that 'Seleka' usually lived in a group fenced off from the rest. The Chamber is of the view that the activities of Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana's group, even as described by the witness himself, were clearly not informed by a genuine distinction between actual adversaries, i.e. members of the Seleka or individuals engaged in hostilities in case there were any, but rather focused on what, in the group's perception, a 'Seleka' would be.

paragraph_text_preview: Jacob Mokpem-Bionli further explained that gradually the Anti-Balaka started organising themselves to come to Bangui walking up to 300 kilometres through the bush, some from across the river from Zongo. The rest of the Anti-Balaka, including the witness, who had remained in Boy-Rabe, like Emmanuel Rekhbohanam, Antoine Kenga, and many others, were in contact with the people coming from Bozoum and the provinces. Jacob Mokpem-Bionli stated that the people from the provinces arrived first and information was given to the people from across the river Oubangui to join; he recalled that the leaders of the youth from the provinces were two brothers with last name 'Ndangba' from Bossangoa, the younger of the two a soldier; there was Yvon Konaté, a FACA who was close to François Bozizé and had gone to Bossangoa; there were also people from Ombella-M'Poko going towards Lobaye who were from the 'forest area'. The witness stated that 'Rambo' led the group from Ombella-M'Poko; Brice Emotion Namsio was in contact with him and told the witness about it. Jacob Mokpem-Bionli was in contact with the people from across the river from Zongo, including Emotion, his brother-in-law and leader of the group from Zongo, Mokom and a third whose name the witness forgot. The witness thought that the leader of the resistance in Bouca was Djim and that Batangafo must have been led by Andjilo. Jacob Mokpem-Bionli was in permanent contact with Djim Adoum, ComZone in Bossangoa and part of those who discovered the traditional magic in Gobere; Djim was tasked with dispatching information. Bossangoa and surroundings, including Bouca (Ouham prefecture)

In what follows, the Chamber has first assessed the Anti-Balaka organisation, strategy and movement, including the attacks in localities around Bossangoa and Bouca in September 2013, before turning to Mr Ngaïssona's involvement with respect to these groups during this time. Attacks in localities around Bossangoa and in Bouca in early September 2013

In line with the strategy of attacking smaller locations in the Bossangoa area and Ouham prefecture more generally, as outlined above, the evidence further outlined below shows that in early September 2013, Anti-Balaka groups launched several coordinated attacks in the surroundings of Bossangoa, followed by an attack against Bossangoa itself on 17 September 2013.

paragraph_text_preview: As set out below, witnesses specifically talked of attacks taking place simultaneously in several villages in the Bossangoa area, including in Bowaye, Zere, Benzambé, Ouham-Bac and Koro-M'Poko.

P-2453 mentioned simultaneous attacks on Bowaye, Zere, Benzambe, and Ouham-Bac on 6 September 2013, the first of which he was a victim to, the other two of which he heard about. P-2453 also heard later at the 'École Liberté' in Bossangoa from people from Bowaye, Benzambé and Koro-M'Poko that attacks had occurred on the same day. Similarly, P-2049 testified to attacks on Bowaye, Zere and Benzambé on 6 September 2013. P-2462 also heard from people at the École de la Liberté at Bossangoa who were from villages such as Zere, Benzambé, Ouham-Bac and Koro‑M'Poko that they had fled from the Anti-Balaka in September 2013. P-2453 heard that mainly Muslim civilians were killed in Bowaye, Zere and Benzambé, and that after the attacks, Muslims did not stay in Zere and the Anti-Balaka controlled the town and location. P-2200 heard that between August and October 2013, the Anti-Balaka attacked several villages in the Bossangoa area at the same time, on a Friday, killing numerous Muslims in each village, including Benzambé, Boue, Zere, 'Karamboko', Sajo, '15Km' and 'Ouham-Bac 45Km'.

A statement seemingly issued by the CAR government on 11 September 2013 mentions that Beboura, Bohong and Ngaoundaye in the Ouham-Pendé prefecture and Bossangoa, Bouca, Benzambe, Lere and 'Bowaie' in the Ouham prefecture were theatre of violent clashes between Seleka elements and 'gangs' presented either as 'archers', as Anti-Balaka organised in self-defence groups, or as supporters of François Bozizé, leading to the death of Muslim families, houses and granaries burnt, and civilian population fleeing to the bush. The CAR Panel concluded in its 2014 interim report that a group of Anti-Balaka carried out the military offensive on the front line in the area of Benzambé, in particular in Bouca, alongside a group commanded by Andjilo Ngaïbona alias 'Angelo', and in Dékoa, with reinforcements from Bozoum and Bossembélé, clashing on a regular basis with the forces of Alkhatim Mahamat, appointed in Ndélé as deputy chief of staff of the 'new' Seleka.

paragraph_text_preview: A statement seemingly issued by the CAR government on 11 September 2013 mentions that Beboura, Bohong and Ngaoundaye in the Ouham-Pendé prefecture and Bossangoa, Bouca, Benzambe, Lere and 'Bowaie' in the Ouham prefecture were theatre of violent clashes between Seleka elements and 'gangs' presented either as 'archers', as Anti-Balaka organised in self-defence groups, or as supporters of François Bozizé, leading to the death of Muslim families, houses and granaries burnt, and civilian population fleeing to the bush. The CAR Panel concluded in its 2014 interim report that a group of Anti-Balaka carried out the military offensive on the front line in the area of Benzambé, in particular in Bouca, alongside a group commanded by Andjilo Ngaïbona alias 'Angelo', and in Dékoa, with reinforcements from Bozoum and Bossembélé, clashing on a regular basis with the forces of Alkhatim Mahamat, appointed in Ndélé as deputy chief of staff of the 'new' Seleka.

In the following, the Chamber outlines the attacks on various locations in the wider Bossangoa area, and related movements of different Anti-Balaka groups that were coordinating their activities. ######

In turn, P-2658 was in the Anti-Balaka group that was to attack Bowaï (Bowaye), which also included Richard, Dolpig and Chagata. P-2658 said that Bowaï is not far from Bossangoa and Dedane said to his elements that after attacking there, the elements should continue to Bossangoa. P-2658 saw two trucks that had been attacked in Bowaï and in Kaboro, just before Bowaï, and some of the village inhabitants told Dedane that five people were killed in the first truck and that some Muslims and Seleka elements buried the bodies at the site of the attack. The same villagers from Kaboro told them that another truck was attacked by the Anti-Balaka which then retreated after they encountered the Seleka of Bowaï, and that the driver, Rachid Mouzambil, and the owner of the truck, were captured by the Anti-Balaka but the passengers fled; they also said that later the Seleka took the truck to Nana-Bakassa. P-2658's group took goods and some engine oil, diesel fuel from the truck which Dedane said they would use to clean their guns. They heard that the Anti-Balaka that went to Bowaï continued to Ndorombouli, hence Dedane, P-2658 and Dedane's aides-de-camp returned to about 17 kilometres from Bossangoa where Dedane had positioned his elements.

The Chamber does not consider this information to be diminished by Screening note, CAR-OTP-2078-0132-R01, at 0134, or Compilation, CAR-OTP-2088-1673-R01, at 1704, which suggest that there were less than 10 victims during this attack (*see* P-2049: T-102, p. 33, line 2 -- p. 36, line 6). The first provides information of an individual that also does not seem to have been in Zere at the time of the attack, without providing a source for the information, while the second is a compilation of anonymous 'statements', with the specific 'statement' in question not providing any source for the information and in fact being unclear on whether it even relates to the same event. P-2049, due to his position at the time and contacts with the imam, as well as talking to individuals at the *École de la Liberté*, had more immediate, even if still indirect, information on the victims of the attack. Similarly, the Chamber does not consider the information impacted by the suggestion that a video, which is not available to the Chamber and that according to P-2049 shows the burning of Djouli Djibrila, would have been taken in March 2011 (*see* T-102, p. 40, lines 6-17; [Ngaïssona Defence Closing Brief](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/nx7gero0/), ICC-01/14-01/18-2736-AnxA-Corr-Red, para. 318, n. 1113 *referring to* Metadata, CAR-D30-0008-0087). Indeed, P-2049 made clear that he did not record the video but received it from someone else, that he knows Djouli, visible on that video and burned on the street during the events in Zere, and that at the time of his testimony, he was in the same camp as Djouli's brothers and other members of his family (*see* P-2049: T-102, p. 38, line 8 -- p. 42, line 7). The Chamber similarly cannot conclude whether the event described in Report, CAR-OTP-2110-0915, at 0920, para. 31 is the same as that depicted on video, as the identity of the victim supposedly shown on the video described is redacted and identified by persons as imam or village head. In relation to the latter report, the Chamber further notes that the Defence argued lack of relevance and probative value in a different context (*see* Annex 1 to Defence Response to the Prosecution's "Request for the Submission of Evidence from the Bar Table regarding the Prevalence of Sexual and Gender Based Violence", ICC-01/14-01/18-1278-Conf-Anx1, pp. 74-75; Annex A to Yekatom Defence Response to the Prosecution's "Request for the Submission of Evidence from the Bar Table regarding the Prevalence of Sexual and Gender Based Violence", 4 January 2022, ICC-01/14-01/18-1233, ICC-01/14-01/18-1279-Conf-AnxA, pp. 20-21). As the Chamber has only examined this report in the context of specific witness testimony, and not relied on it in the context of its evidentiary analysis, the Chamber does not consider necessary to address these arguments further.

The Chamber notes that also P-2251 provided details on how the Bouca attack unfolded, stating that after retreating from Bossangoa, everyone went to attack Bouca, and they were instructed to do the same thing there, to 'shout loudly to drive the Seleka out'. In Bouca, P-2251's chief had also been part of the attack on Bossangoa. P-2251 recalled that some Anti-Balaka members died during the attack but did not know if any Seleka died. In this regard, the Chamber also notes that P-2251 stated not seeing any Muslims in Bouca and not knowing where they were. Bearing in mind its credibility assessment of this witness, as well as the evidence outlined below indicating the presence of Muslim civilians during the attack, the Chamber has not relied on this part of P-2251's evidence. This is underscored by P-2251 himself stating that in places like Bossangoa, Bouca and Bogangolo, Muslims 'associated with' the Seleka were killed.

The Chamber notes that Achta Moussa Animer testified that her husband, Ajdo Ibrahim Moussa also known as Mahamt Abdel Karim, did not return when one Thursday, which the witness thought was a month before the 5 December 2013 attack in Bangui, he went with his vehicle to take people to Benzambé for a weekly market despite a warning from neighbours not to do it because the 'malefactors', which to the witness were the Anti-Balaka, were around in that locality. Achta Moussa Animer later learned that her husband's vehicle, which transported Christians and Muslims, was stopped, after which she fled with her family, with the help of some neighbours, to Sibut and then Bangui. The witness did not know what happened to her husband's remains or what happened to the bodies and vehicle. While the witness was unable to provide further details in relation to the death of her husband, the Chamber concludes from the general context provided that this concerned events in Benzambé taking place during the advance of Anti-Balaka groups through the provinces.

Following the various attacks in smaller localities in the wider area of Bossangoa, in coordination and in accordance with the plan outlined above, an Anti-Balaka group eventually attacked Bossangoa town early morning on 17 September 2013.

At the outset, the Chamber notes the evidence of witnesses who were involved in the Anti-Balaka moving about and engaging in attacks in the wider Bossangoa area, as discussed above, and who described their movements and re-grouping before the attack on Bossangoa in September 2013. Specifically, following the attacks in Bowaye, Zere, Benzamble, and Bouca, the Chamber notes that Dedane's group continued planning a further attack in Bossangoa.

P-2658 said that Dedane's group remained in the bush near Bossangoa for three days after the Zere attack, during which Dedane went to Bossangoa, bringing back ammunition and weapons. P-2658 said that Dedane said they should wait for Andjilo, adding that Andjilo would finish attacking Bouca and come to Bossangoa; Dedane and his men wanted to join him so that they could attack Bossangoa together. Dedane told the group that he was speaking with Andjilo on the phone. P-2658 said that, after Zere, they went to a place around 12 kilometres from Bossangoa where they waited to hear from Andjilo, who, following Dedane's instructions, took the direction of Zere from Bouca. Dedane told Andjilo to wait for his instruction in Zere because he was going to look for the group that had attacked Bowaye, and on finding them he returned and said they had 'all arrived to attack Bossangoa'.

The Anti-Balaka attacked at several locations at the same time, with witnesses hearing shots and explosions from several directions, in different neighbourhoods.

paragraph_text_preview: It was suggested that Adjaro Gara would have been part of a Muslim self-defence group who was killed in battle. The Chamber notes in this regard that the related information was taken from an unsigned screening note of an individual who did not testify before the Chamber. Considering further P-2049's insistence that this suggestion was incorrect, his family relation with Adjaro Gara, and given his evidence that he had information only about civilians, the Chamber relies on P-2049's evidence in relation to this person that he was not a member of a self-defence group and was killed by the Anti-Balaka.

Following the attack, individuals went to the 'École Liberté', where they felt safer because it was protected by the FOMAC Congolese contingent. P-2453 stated they had very limited resources at the school, so MSF and UNICEF provided some basic hygiene amenities, water and medical care. Individuals also went to the house of the imam. P-2200 stated that four days after the attack, the Seleka came to him to say that order had returned and the conflict had moved in direction of Karanboko; P-2200 heard that some Anti-Balaka had withdrawn to the bush and others to the Catholic mission; calm returned to Bossangoa, but the Anti-Balaka and Seleka continued to fight in the neighbouring villages.

Several witnesses travelled to Bossangoa and surroundings in the aftermath of the attack and described their impressions.

For instance, Michaël Zumstein travelled to Bossangoa on 22 September 2013, where they were told that 25,000 people were gathered around a church in fear of attacks and looting by the Seleka, while an estimated 1,000 Muslim civilians were gathered at the École de la Liberté, fearful of revenge attacks from Christians. The witness went again to Bossangoa between 28 and 30 September 2013, seeing looted and destroyed villages on the way, with people telling them that the houses were looted and destroyed by the Seleka. Michaël Zumstein noticed Muslims fleeing on trucks in the opposite direction, away from Bossangoa but did not know where they came from. Both in Bossangoa and in the small villages around it, the witness's general feeling was that everyone was displaced at the time: Muslim Peuhl herders were being attacked by Christian farmers, Christians were fleeing from the looting Seleka, farmers would sleep in the bush and Peuhl abandon their cattle, Muslims fearing the Anti-Balaka were gathered in the bush or fleeing to Bangui. Buses and trucks often belonged to Muslims and would take on fleeing Muslims.

P-1576 went to Bossangoa in the second half of November 2013, with information circulating that there was a humanitarian crisis and about 40,000 displaced Christians. On the route to Bossangoa, some villages had been completely destroyed. P-1577 was similarly present in Bossangoa in November 2013 and observed that the road from Bangui to Bossangoa, normally quite busy, was extremely overgrown, while many of the villages along the way were empty. paragraph_text_preview: Nicolas Tiangaye testified that the Anti-Balaka excesses against the Muslim civilian population in Bossangoa were quite significant and he travelled there on behalf of the government around 17 October 2013 to bring humanitarian assistance to those at the bishop's residence. Nicolas Tiangaye met thousands of displaced persons at the bishop's residence, living under extremely difficult circumstances, no water, food, health care. The Muslim population was already suffering reprisals from the Anti-Balaka, but the Seleka were also committing acts of violence against non-Muslims. The first victims were those who had come under abuses from the Seleka, and the Anti-Balaka organised themselves to carry out reprisals against the Muslims; the witness did not hear any testimony as such, but he experienced these things personally, he spoke to victims at the bishopric. Nicolas Tiangaye did not have details on the perpetrators of the excesses committed by the Anti-Balaka. The witness insisted that he made only one trip to Bossangoa.

P-2416 heard about an attack on Bossangoa by the Anti-Balaka after he had returned from Mecca in October 2013, and in a more recent conversation in Garam-Boulaï, P-2416 heard that the person was present during the attack and that some of his relatives were killed, as were many Muslim civilians, and also the wife and children of a wholesale customer of P-2416. In late February 2014, P-2416 talked with three Anti-Balaka from Bossangoa located in Yaloké who told him that they were Anti-Balaka, though P-2416 saw that they were not wearing gris-gris like many of the other Anti-Balaka, and that they had travelled from Bossangoa to Yaloké, had been trained in Rwanda or Uganda to kill people, and they said to P-2416 'Nzapa a bata mo, nzapa a bata ala kwé so álá ngbá gé' ('God spared you, God spared all of you remaining here'), that 'Our plan was to kill all Muslims but we came to Yaloké and found you here. In light of the evidence as outlined above, illustrating in particular that information on the attack in Bossangoa in September 2013 was widely available at the time, the Chamber concludes that also Mr Ngaïssona must have known about the attack on Bossangoa in September 2013, including the deaths and dislocation of Muslim civilians that took place as a result of the Anti-Balaka attack there. Attacks between mid-September and December 2013

The evidence shows that, following the attacks in the Bossangoa region in the north, as discussed above, the movement of the Anti-Balaka expanded by October 2013 to other regions of the CAR. This included to Bouar in the west, in Nana-Mambéré prefecture and towards Bangui in the south, through Ndjo, Bossembélé, and Boali in Ombella-M'Poko prefecture. This is exemplified by the attacks that took place in these locations respectively.

P-2251 descended with a group led by Bama Clement aka 'Flame de Guerre', taking about four days to walk from Bouca to Bogangolo, through Marali and Bobatoua. In the bush outside Bogangolo, P-2251 met Lebene, Kolongo, Benjamin and Tex. Lebene was the chief of Kolongo, but in turn had chiefs above him who gave him orders that he implemented; these were Kems, Andjilo, Benjamin. P-2251 heard Benjamin telling Lebene that now they had taken back their native village, he should tell his elements to work for peace and send a message to people hiding in the bush to return. In Bogangolo, they clashed with Seleka which eventually fled to Ndjo and Bossembélé. P-2251 left Lebene and Benjamin in Bogangolo and went with Kolongo to Boban the same day; the Seleka had already left Boban. In Bona, another chief called Gaba acted as Kolongo's deputy; he had been with them in Ngobere, but became a chief only in Bouca.

In addition to this, these attacks and their chronology show a clear overarching and coordinated movement of Anti-Balaka groups from the Bossangoa region in the direction of Bangui in advance of 5 December 2013. The Chamber has assessed these attacks in turn below. Ndjo

The Chamber notes that Ndjo, which is on the road between Bossangoa and Bossembélé, right at the prefecture lines dividing the Ouham and Ombella-M'Poko prefectures, was mentioned by witnesses describing their advance towards Bangui in accordance with the agreed plan and assigned locations. It is also one of the locations mentioned in the email sent to Mr Ngaïssona on 7 October 2013, transmitting the needs expressed by Lakouetene and Doguela.

paragraph_text_preview: P-1779, an Imam from Gaga, stated that two weeks before the first attack of the Anti-Balaka in Gaga, a Christian gold digger warned the population and advised to evacuate the women and children, which the Christians immediately did. The Muslims did not believe him. The attack took place on a Friday, starting at around 05:00 and continuing until 12:00. P-1779 did not see the attackers, but heard shots and left his property only once to see the body of Yaya, a Muslim, who was lying covered in blood. P-1779 knew of three more victims, one Seleka and two more civilians, Adoum, who was killed in the street, and Ibrahim, a Peuhl, killed on the north side of the village where the attack started -- all Muslims talked about the deaths of Adoum and Ibrahim. At around 11:00, still hearing firing, P-1779 left his family property and started looking for means to flee, he heard from a taxi driver, that Ardo Saidou, village chief of Gaga 3, instructed the Muslims to evacuate because the Anti-Balaka outnumbered the Seleka. P-1779 stated that the Seleka in Gaga were joined by Muslim youth from the village armed with bow and arrow that usually protected the village against road bandits to counter the Anti-Balaka. P-1779 later saw the village deserted, houses of Muslims burnt, all in Gaga 1 on the north side of the village, where the attack started. P-1779 also saw looted shops, while the mosques and churches of the village had not been touched. After this attack, the Muslims no longer trusted the Christians who stopped visiting them, and P-1779 was afraid of going about in the village and no longer went out.

At around 11:00, still hearing firing, P-1779 left his family property and started looking for means to flee, he heard from a taxi driver, that Ardo Saidou, village chief of Gaga 3, instructed the Muslims to evacuate because the Anti-Balaka outnumbered the Seleka. P-1779 also saw looted shops, while the mosques and churches of the village had not been touched. After this attack, the Muslims no longer trusted the Christians who stopped visiting them, and P-1779 was afraid of going about in the village and no longer went out.

Zenaba Oumar, a Muslim resident of Yaloké at the time, did not recall when the first attack on Gaga occurred, but it was more than a month prior to the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. On the day Gaga was first attacked, the witness was in Yaloké and her cousin Odélon, called Odi, a gold miner working in the Gaga minefields, called the witness and told her that at about 03:00 the Anti-Balaka came from the bush, injured a Seleka that later died, then the Seleka drove the Anti-Balaka back into the bush and commenced killing all Christian civilians in Gaga. Having travelled to Gaga the same morning, Zenaba Oumar saw at least 100 dead bodies, men and some children, all appeared to have been shot with the gun, not chopped with machete. The witness was told that many Christian merchants from Bangui were killed by the Seleka during this attack, she was told all the dead were Christians. On the way back to Yaloké, on the road from Gaga to Zawa, Zenaba Oumar saw other dead bodies which she later learnt to be the Christians who were fleeing Gaga and were shot and killed by the Seleka; the bodies had not been there when she went to Gaga.

Having regard to the above, the Chamber finds that the Anti-Balaka attacked Gaga in October 2013 in the early hours of a Friday, clashing with the Seleka there, which resulted in many civilian deaths, both Muslim and Christian, and Muslims fleeing to other locations. Bouar

The Chamber now turns to the attack in Bouar in the Nana-Mambéré prefecture. The Prosecution submits that an attack on Bouar took place on 26 October 2013 during which the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim population as a whole, resulting in the deaths of at least 20 civilians and the displacement of over 10,000 people. It argues that Mr Ngaïssona provided 'the Bouar group' with organisational support, funds, ammunition and Thurayas. It also argues that P-1847's testimony establishes that Mr Ngaïssona and Bernard Mokom ordered the Bouar attack.

Nicolas Tiangaye did not remember what happened in Bouar; there were some soldiers who did not remain in Bangui, elements of the army who were scattered across the country and joined the Anti-Balaka and provided training for them to carry out the counter-attack on Seleka elements. The witness explained that Bouar is of strategic importance because it was a French military base, with Camp Leclerc; it is some 150 kilometres from the Cameroon border and merchandise coming through the Douala port was taken to the CAR through this route; it is also not too far up north, if going through Bocaranga, which is quite close to Chad; from Bouar one can go to Cameroon through Garam-Boulaï and to Chad by passing through Paramba.

The Chamber further notes its discussion of the evidence showing that Mr Ngaïssona and Bernard Mokom travelled to the Cameroon-CAR border with a view to liaising with the groups led by Achille and Ndale.

Bearing in mind the evidence outlined above, the Chamber considers without merit the arguments of the Ngaïssona Defence in relation to Mr Ngaïssona's role in advance of the Bouar attack. Indeed, D30-4914's generalised claim that it is 'absolutely wrong' that Mr Ngaïssona or Bernard Mokom would have coordinated the attack on the basis of them being civilians is inconsequential. Involvement in preparations of an attack in a coordinating role is not excluded by mere virtue of the fact of someone not having a military role or background. Further, the Chamber's conclusions in this regard are based on witnesses with knowledge of the events, rather than solely Facebook messages and witnesses' comments thereon.

Another journalist, Michaël Zumstein, travelled on the road to Sibut, a town 100 kilometres from Bangui, on 1 December 2013 and saw a convoy of three Seleka vehicles going in direction of Sibut, with the Seleka all nervous. Having seen around five wounded Peuhl children at a hospital in Bangui who, they were told, had come from Boali where they were attacked by 'Christians', Michaël Zumstein went to Boali; on the road from Bangui to Boali on 4 December 2013, they met both Muslims and Christians, all fearing inter-communitarian violence; for example, they met a Christian at PK47 and met the Muslim community in Bougoula. The witness stated that, when he returned to Bougoula a month later, there were 'no Muslims left'; near Bougoula, further down the road to Boali, they met a fleeing Christian, pushing a cart with his families' belongings, who told them that they had been attacked by Peuhl. Michaël Zumstein found several destroyed houses in Boali; they were told that they belonged to Christians; whilst at the Boali mosque, 'Muslim men' armed with bows and arrows and machetes were gathered to protect the mosque, fearing that the mosque would be destroyed if they did not guard it.

P-2546 went to Bangui and sometime after the 5 December 2013 incident in Bangui saw on France 24 that the situation in Boali had gotten worse and some Peuhls had been killed; the parish priest of Boali, Abbé Arnold Xavier Fagba, also spoke on France 24 and Afrique 24 and said he had taken in some Peuhls and had to stand between them and the Anti-Balaka to stop the Peuhls from being killed.

Having regard to the above, the Chamber finds that the Anti-Balaka attacked Boali, resulting in the killing of Muslim civilians, especially the Peuhl, and fleeing of these populations to other locations. This attack was widely covered by the media. Mr Ngaïssona was directly informed of this attack and the involvement of the Anti-Balaka in 'killing the Seleka'. In light of these arguments, the Chamber has considered the evidence regarding meetings that took place at Yamwara at the end of December 2013, as provided by individuals who attended these meetings.

The Chamber finds that the meetings attest to the emerging individual political ambitions of the various Anti-Balaka group leaders following the Bangui Attack. They also show that, at this time, not every Anti-Balaka leader may have had a sustained interest in supporting the return of François Bozizé to power. At the same time, the Chamber considers that the meetings do not attest to a divided movement or separately existing movements. Rather, the meetings show attempts at pivoting the Anti-Balaka's combined force towards securing political leverage and, in some cases, ministerial positions in a potential future government.

The evidence as outlined attests to the emerging individual political ambitions of the various Anti-Balaka group leaders following the Bangui Attack and that, at this time, not every Anti-Balaka leader may have had a sustained interest in supporting the return of François Bozizé to power. At the same time, the Chamber considers that the meetings do not attest to a divided movement or separately existing movements. Importantly, the Chamber is of the view that the various Anti-Balaka groups did not have to be a monolithic or singular entity and/or ideologically homogeneous at any stage of the events. Indeed, as outlined above, despite apparent political or personal viewpoints and ambitions, the Anti-Balaka groups coordinated their actions around their core objective of removing Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power. That this was the common core is also amplified by the discussions at the meetings at Yamwara as outlined, which centred around what would happen once this core objective would have been achieved -- and indeed did not question it as common baseline. The Chamber therefore considers that the suggestion that Mr Yekatom's purported objective was 'not to fight for Bozizé's return' does not mean that Mr Yekatom's group was not Anti-Balaka, or that it did not share the core objective of wanting to remove Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power, including the way in which this objective was pursued and achieved on the ground. Continued liaison by Mr Ngaïssona in the lead-up

The evidence before the Chamber as outlined below further shows that Mr Ngaïssona remained informed of continued activities related to the Anti-Balaka during the period between the coordinated attacks of 5 December 2013 and his return to Bangui on 14 January 2014.

Alfred Legrand Ngaya agreed with the suggestion that before and just after the attack on Bangui, the Anti-Balaka did not have any political aims, just wanted to get rid of the Seleka, and said that, after the attack, they had to try and find some 'point of contact'. Alfred Legrand Ngaya said that after the attack, they had a meeting in Boeing, at which he was not present, with Wenezoui, Ngremangou, at which the Anti-Balaka asked Sébastien Wenezoui to be their spokesperson. Alfred Legrand Ngaya said that people wanted to position themselves as representative, on a political level, and also Léopold Bara suggested to them he should be one because he had been to the summit in N'Djamena. The witness agreed with the suggestion that the absence of leadership and people juggling for positions contributed to the lack of discipline and commission of opportunistic crime. The witness further agreed with the suggestion that in December 2013 and beginning 2014, before Mr Ngaïssona arrived, the Anti-Balaka tried to organise slowly and began to shape political demands, they had to get out of the crisis which would not be done if one did not have some degree of organisation, and there were some roughly 50,000 young people with some familiarity of handling weapons.

In one email of 28 December 2013, Alfred Legrand Ngaya sent two CLPC documents, stating that this is transmitting 'the documents of our little ones' ('les documents de nos petits') which will be subject of possible negotiations, and that Mr Ngaïssona's reaction on the CLPC demands is expected.

The first document which appears to have been attached to this email is entitled 'Communiqué de presse no 01', dated 27 December 2013, with the typed name of Brice Emotion Namsio at the bottom. It states that the CLPC, generally called 'Anti-balaka' wants to make some points, including that (i) since the start of the hostilities by the nebulous Seleka coalition, composed essentially of Chadian and Sudanese mercenaries, the Central African populations mobilise to oppose and denounce exactions, while MICOPAX helped the Seleka take power; (ii) since March, Michel Djotodia and the Seleka persecute the defenceless population; (iii) in light of the desperate situation, young villagers and some elements of the FACA took their responsibility, without any appropriate means, to fight Michel Djotodia and the Seleka; (iv) the CLPC regrets that during its military operations, there were some innocent victims; (v) the CLPC is available to start a dialogue with the international forces in Bangui to think about conditions for the return to peace and security; (vi) attention of these international institutions is drawn that any attempt to kerfuffle or not take into account the Central African populations 'meurtries' over the preceding nine months would only 'poison' an already chaotic situation ('ne fera qu'envenimer une situation déjà chaotique'); (vii) the CLPC remains convinced that only the involvement of true representatives of the Central African population, within the dynamic of inclusive negotiation, could get the CAR out of this cycle of violence ('implication des véritables représentants de la population centrafricaine, dans une dynamique de négociation inclusive, pourra sortir la République Centrafricaine de cette ornière de violence').

The Chamber has before it a typed document apparently drafted for the 'Mouvement des Combattants "Antibalaka"', dated 12 January 2014. This document welcomes the withdrawal of Michel Djotodia and Nicolas Tiangaye, recalls that the aim of the Anti-Balaka movement was fighting for the restoration of peace and security across the CAR, and further makes the following points: (i) the national transitional council in its current composition does not meet the requirements of equality and objectivity necessary to designate the new transition president in a satisfactory manner since, while the Seleka is represented, the Anti-Balaka is not, and because the composition was contested already at the time at which it was set up; and (ii) it is impossible to organise the vote for a new transition president in such imbalanced conditions, at the 'risk' of giving rise to 'other conflicts' ('au risque de faire germer d'autres conflits'), considering that this needs to be resolved before setting up a transparent and equitable mechanism to designate a new transition president. The document ends by saying that any new 'slips' could easily make 'us' tumble into another 'spiral of violence', which is not the intention of the Central African people ('tout nouveau dérapage pourrait facilement nous basculer dans une autre spirale de violence, ce qui n'est pas du tout la volonté du peuple centrafricain').

Leading towards the discussions in N'Djamena, the Chamber has further considered the testimony of Joachim Kokaté, who described how towards the second week of December 2013, he was in contact with Abakar Sabone about the latter's statement calling for the division of the country, eventually leading to Joachim Kokaté being informed that Idriss Déby wanted him to come to N'Djamena to have discussions. The witness informed Mr Ngaïssona, who had contacted him, that he was going to N'Djamena, with Mr Ngaïssona saying to him that he would tell the others about this, meaning talking about it to François Bozizé. Joachim Kokaté explained that he never did anything without telling Mr Ngaïssona because he knew Mr Ngaïssona was very close to Bozizé, and because Mr Ngaïssona used to tell them that whatever Bozizé said was mostly said to Mr Ngaïssona, so he could not travel to N'Djamena without informing Mr Ngaïssona, he was not the leader of the Anti-Balaka and could not go there on their behalf. While Mr Ngaïssona initially approved, he said a few days later that he did not trust Déby and would therefore not come, but he told Joachim Kokaté to contact a number of people, including Ngremangou, providing their phone numbers. Joachim Kokaté confirmed he talked to Levy Yakété about the meeting as he was also a member of the Anti-Balaka.

Catherine Samba-Panza explained that during the Djotodia administration, the CAR was going through 'an extremely difficult time' and was 'plunged into chaos', with no state, no administration, no economy, no health system, no school, no education, no justice, no army, it was 'total chaos'. Just after the return from N'Djamena, a delegation of eight women from a multi-faith religious platform came to see the witness and told her they wanted 'a woman at the leadership who can replace Michel Djotodia', and eventually the witness accepted their proposal. Elections were organised by the national transitional council, and on 20 January 2014, Catherine Samba-Panza was elected, running against eight men. On the day of her election, Catherine Samba-Panza received an SMS stating, 'It's in your best interest that you win the elections, because if you don't, we will burn everything down. You really can't afford to have a Seleka or a Muslim overtake you'. The witness felt disproportionate hope was invested in her as many other candidates had resources and ran a campaign, which she did not, so when she received this message, she smiled but could not know who was sending it because so many people had her phone number.

paragraph_text_preview: The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that after Catherine Samba-Panza was elected as new transition president, and the new transition government was sworn in on 23 January 2014, several meetings took place between her and representatives of the Anti-Balaka, at which the latter presented demands as to the representation of the Anti-Balaka within the new transition government.

In the view of the Chamber, the circumstances of these meetings as well as the requests made by the Anti-Balaka are another illustration of the Anti-Balaka structure taking further shape in the context of different political and personal ambitions of various individuals. It is clear from the evidence as further outlined below that in particular Mr Ngaïssona, at the time of the initial meetings freshly installed general coordinator of the Anti-Balaka, exhibited ambitions which developed to no longer centring around bringing François Bozizé back to power, but rather around personal interests combined with wanting to represent the Anti-Balaka which were still a party to the conflict to be taken into account, and thus, in the general political dynamics, an influential factor to be reckoned with.

It is within this context that the Chamber recalls its conclusion that the various Anti-Balaka groups did not have to be a monolithic or singular entity and/or ideologically homogenous at any stage of the events. The Chamber is of the view that different Anti-Balaka groups, of 'north', 'south' or other designation, coming together to be represented towards the new transitional authorities and international forces does not signify that there were many different groups. Rather, as is clear from the evidence before the Chamber as outlined above and below, groups which did have varying super-imposed interests were not only perceived to be one movement, the 'Anti-Balaka', from the outside, but also presented themselves as such with a view to being taken into account as party to the conflict.

Concretely, Catherine Samba-Panza explained that she called on the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka to lay down their arms and join forces with her to build the country and install national cohesion. She received a delegation of about 15 people of the Anti-Balaka at her home. According to Catherine Samba-Panza, General Essongo and General Garcia were 'managing this period', and the latter organised this meeting.

Joachim Kokaté said that Catherine Samba-Panza told the Anti-Balaka that she was counting on them to comply with her policies, meaning to appeal to the Anti-Balaka to put down their weapons and take the side of legality, that she did not want disorder in Bangui and the rest of the country. P-0974 testified that there was a mediation by the Congolese contingent to create a single coordination, and that they referred the matter to Catherine Samba-Panza. He said they had a meeting with Catherine Samba-Panza at which she asked why they had split, told them they should be one, asked for them not to sow any trouble but work in collaboration with her, and told them she would continue to work with them for peace to return. P-0974 stated that at this meeting, Mr Ngaïssona explained that although he had been out of the country during the fighting, he still had been active with the movement, that while he was still in Cameroon, he had organised meetings with former FACA and been in telephone contact with people in the provinces to establish the movement. P-0974 testified that was the reason which Mr Ngaïssona gave to say that he was a 'legitimate choice' to be the Anti-Balaka coordinator. According to P-0974, Bara gave 'his own version of the facts', explaining that the activities of the Anti-Balaka surfaced in various neighbourhoods 'spontaneously as a way of resisting the Seleka', they objected to the narrative that 'one single individual' created the movement -- they had fought very hard to see the departure of Djotodia, and Mr Ngaïssona returned one week after Michel Djotodia left power. No one contradicted Mr Ngaïssona as regards the mentioned contacts; there was no objection from his side of the coordination against the statement that he was at 'the foundation' and 'involved right from time back'. P-0974 further seemed to say that Catherine Samba-Panza asked them to have one single coordinator to ensure coordination for the movement, and that after the meeting Mr Ngaïssona became the sole coordinator.

P-1839 testified that in the context of 'reconciling' Mr Yekatom's group with that under Mr Ngaïssona, the Congolese general facilitating the meeting said that Mr Ngaïssona had a 'red folder' ('un dossier rouge'), a reference that the witness did not understand, and Mr Yekatom said that 'he has had a lot of positions' and was there 'to see' what posts he could have in the future. The president received them on the same day as they had met at Boganda. From what the witness understood, Samba-Panza asked that they control their 'men', and the witness did not remember the response of the leaders. Mr Yekatom did not speak, only said at the end that he was 'for the peace'. The witness agreed with the suggestion that at this meeting, and at the meeting with General Essongo, Mr Yekatom defined his group with the term 'Révolution des forces armées centrafricaines pour le peuple'. The witness thought that Leopold Narcisse Bara indeed said that he was the 'spokesperson' of Mr Yekatom's group. They talked about the elements and their situation, the process, about how to go about disarming them in the long term.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes in this regard that radio broadcast of an interview with Mr Ngaïssona of 27 February 2014, in which he, inter alia, complained about MISCA's attempt to arrest him, stating that he was not an enemy of the state or of peace, but returned to the country to help 'these children' to have a voice ('ses enfants à porter leurs voix'), yet they had no one to listen to it ('on n'a pas d'interlocuteurs pour écouter la voix de ces enfants'). He continued that he was the general coordinator of the Anti-Balaka, and that the children left the hinterland, arrived on foot, had already used weapons, and they were now being asked to return to where they came from, but if they were to return with their weapons, this would mean insecurity in the hinterland, and the only solution to eradicate this was to regroup them to have them lay down their weapons and return to the hinterland empty-handed. He said that he talked to 'these children' a lot so there would be no 'slips' ('dérapage'): 'Mais ceux qui font des exactions au nom des A\[nti-Balaka\], mais si ensemble avec les autorités, nous nous mettons ensemble, on peut lutter contre ces braquages, lutter contre des délinquants qui se prennent pour A\[nti-Balaka\] et aujourd'hui tous ces dérapages-là sont imputés à A\[nti-Balaka\]'. Mr Ngaïssona further explained the chain of command of the Anti-Balaka was him as general coordinator and, before, Kokaté was military coordinator, who took other options, emphasising that he had control: \[...\] Lui, il a pris d'autres options, lui-même il peut vous expliquer, et que tout se passe sous mon contrôle. En principe, s'il y a des discussions, il y a des débats, c'est moi qui devais être présent à ces débats ou s'il y a des ... des choses à discuter avec les autorités, en principe, ça devait être moi. On ne sait pas quand on parle d'autres fractions par-ci, par là, ça me gêne un peu, et pour quelles raisons ? Est-ce qu'on veut chercher rapidement à avoir ... manger ou est-ce qu'on veut rapidement avoir le poste, est-ce que c'est ... pour quelles raisons, ces fractions ? Mais dommage que ceux qui se disent peut-être fraction ceci cela, ne peuvent pas aller sur le terrain demander à leurs éléments de ... par exemple, de se retirer. C'est malheureux qu'on trompe le public, qu'on trompe certaines autorités, et qu'on trompe l'opinion internationale.

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that the first meeting at Catherine Samba-Panza's residence did not remain the only one.

Specifically, another meeting took place at the president's office on 25 January 2014. The delegation was led by Joachim Kokaté. On this basis, the Chamber considers that on the evidence before it, the question of there being different 'streams' within the Anti-Balaka, such as those denominated by being from 'the south' or 'the north' has no impact on the Anti-Balaka groups acting in a coordinated fashion in pursuit of their core objective even beyond Michel Djotodia's resignation. Indeed, it is clear from the evidence before it, as also further outlined below, that the various Anti-Balaka groups, whether 'south', 'north' or of other designation, continued to cooperate with a view to being represented towards the new transition government and international forces. It is also clear from the evidence before the Chamber, as outlined above and below, that during the time relevant to the charges, the person representing the Anti-Balaka for such purposes was Mr Ngaïssona.

The Chamber further considers that within this context, any direct relations between Mr Ngaïssona and Mr Yekatom are, on the facts, irrelevant. Mr Ngaïssona contributed to the activities of the Anti-Balaka as one movement, whereas Mr Yekatom acted clearly under that same umbrella, even if not sharing the initially held interest of Mr Ngaïssona to bring François Bozizé back to power which, as discussed, Mr Ngaïssona in any event left behind at a certain point. Moreover, and as will be discussed further below, the Chamber does not consider that any 'north' and 'south' streams within the Anti-Balaka acted entirely independently and separately from each other at any time during the period relevant to the charges.
It is within the context of the above that the Chamber has considered the evidence before it on the position and role of Mr Yekatom's group within the Anti-Balaka in 2014.

Second, the evidence before the Chamber shows that Mr Yekatom enforced discipline within his group. Specifically, P-1193, who was with the group in 2014, stated that 'Rombhot' disciplined his men when he was not under the influence of alcohol, and that he never saw anyone opposing 'Rombhot'. Similarly, Gérard Ouambou, who could observe the group closely at the beginning of 2014, stated that 'Rombhot's' elements listened to him and those who did not, those that were disciplined by him, left the group. Vivien Beina testified that Mr Yekatom's group was very well structured, there was military discipline, and Mr Yekatom respected the military rules and their ranking. The witness testified that Mr Yekatom's group included many that were not soldiers, and they were all subject to the same discipline because they were part of the group. P-1858 testified that he had seen 'Rombhot' giving orders and threats, it seemed to him that his elements, even FACA, were afraid of him and his orders were obeyed without question, and if one did not obey, Mr Yekatom 'would hit you or you would be killed'. Jacob Mokpem-Bionli stated that Mr Yekatom was a FACA member who was part of the Anti-Balaka, had his base on the route of Mbaïki, and had a significant number of elements under his control which he led with an iron hand ('une main de fer') and disciplined as necessary, including sanctioning when needed. Roger Okoa-Penguia stated that he was present one day when Mr Yekatom addressed his elements and told them to behave appropriately, adding that Mr Yekatom maintained discipline within his elements.

paragraph_text_preview: In this context, the Chamber has considered specific examples which illustrate Mr Yekatom's control over his group and the area he was in. Mr Ngaïssona's role in the Anti-BalakaThe evidence before the Chamber shows that following his return to Bangui and taking up the position of general coordinator in a more formalised structure of the Anti-Balaka, Mr Ngaïssona remained involved with the group's activities.

At the outset, the Chamber notes that the evidence before it, as further outlined below, shows that the knowledge of Mr Ngaïssona and his activities in the context of the Anti-Balaka before he became general coordinator of the movement in January 2014 depended on the perspective and role of each individual testifying thereto. In particular, it is clear from the evidence discussed below that elements on the ground advancing through the provinces in late 2013 may not necessarily have been privy to Mr Ngaïssona's activities at the time, while persons more directly concerned with his actions were.

In the view of the Chamber, the fact that some individuals did not know of Mr Ngaïssona's involvement with the Anti-Balaka before he became general coordinator in January 2014 does not mean that such involvement did not exist.

The Chamber recalls that Mr Ngaïssona became general coordinator of the Anti-Balaka immediately upon his return to Bangui on 14 January 2014. In the Chamber's view, this is, by itself, an indication that Mr Ngaïssona was familiar with and involved in at least parts of the movement before his officially becoming coordinator.

paragraph_text_preview: Furthermore, Alfred Legrand Ngaya stated that when Mr Ngaïssona returned to Bangui, the witness saw that he knew the Anti-Balaka very well, and realised that Mr Ngaïssona had links with the military because he saw him with FACA members. For example, on the day of the meeting with the transition government in January 2014, Alfred Legrand Ngaya went to Mr Ngaïssona's house where he saw him with 'Lieutenant Konaté', and it was clear that they knew each other from before that day. The witness also stated that Mr Ngaïssona was 'very popular' and 'generous'. Position within the Anti-Balaka

At the outset, the Chamber emphasises that the question of Mr Ngaïssona having been in control of the Anti-Balaka as a whole or parts thereof is, in the context of the charges in the present case, immaterial. The Chamber has considered the evidence as outlined below, which shows that Mr Ngaïssona in fact did exercise control over the Anti-Balaka as an additional factor to assess his contributions to the Anti-Balaka's activities.
First, various witnesses testified about Mr Ngaïssona being the person to contact when it came to representing the interests of the Anti-Balaka.

Specifically, and most importantly, Catherine Samba-Panza, the transition president at the time, testified that from the Anti-Balaka side, and from January 2014 onwards when she took her position, she had 'no other person' to contact but Mr Ngaïssona, with whom she had her contacts. Aurélien Llorca stated that in the view of the CAR Panel, Mr Ngaïssona was indeed coordinating the Anti-Balaka groups from 'a political point of view', and Maxime Mokom was 'in charge of military operations'. Kasper Agger testified that while different personalities tried to portray themselves as leaders of certain groups of the Anti-Balaka; at the time of his interview with Mr Ngaïssona in February 2014, he referred to himself as 'the coordinator of the Anti-Balaka in a general term', portrayed himself in that role, and was looked at as 'an interlocutor'; and the witness found Mr Ngaïssona's place in Bangui by asking for 'Mr Ngaïssona, the coordinator of Balaka'.

Third, the Chamber has considered the evidence, as further outlined below, that Anti-Balaka groups stayed within, and used for their purposes, Mr Ngaïssona's properties in Bangui.

Specifically, P-2050 stated that on their way to the interview in which she met with 'Emotion Gomez' on 28 February 2014, they were stopped at a roadblock at the entrance of Boy-Rabe, 'Emotion' arrived with an AK-47 and all of the Anti-Balaka at the roadblock saluted him, it was clear he had some sort of authority over the Anti-Balaka there. P-2050 stated that at the gate, she recognised the place she had been to in 2013, and 'Emotion' told her that it was the Anti-Balaka headquarter and confirmed it was the minister's, Mr Ngaïssona's house, saying, 'yes, this is the house of our boss', calling him 'coordinateur'. P-2050 stated that '12 Puissances' came from the private house on the left side, and in the garage 'young boys' were dancing around a prisoner, torturing him. P-2050 stated that she wrote in her notes that '12 Puissances' was directing 'military operations' because he was the 'highest man' in the compound, when she told 'Emotion' that she did not want to talk to the spokesperson but to the one in command, he took them to '12 Puissances'. P-2050 stated that '12 Puissances' did not tell her which area he controlled, but when she later called him about dead bodies found in the 8^th^ arrondissement, he said he was not in control of that area. P-2050 stated that she recorded from the moment they entered the gate probably until the moment '12 Puissances' became upset, it was clear he was not very happy to see them. P-2050 commented on her recording, explaining inter alia, that they talked to the prisoner who gave his name as 'Larma-Soum', and that '12 Puissances' explained to someone on the telephone that they had put their hands on the 'fake' Anti-Balaka responsible for exactions in the 3^rd^ and 8^th^ arrondissements. P-2050 thought in relation to '12 Puissances' ending the call with 'merci beaucoup, c'est moi qui te remercie. D'accord', that he told her afterwards that the 'chef' had been calling, but she could not hear it in the audio. P-2050 testified that when she asked who their boss, coordinator was, 'Emotion Gomes' mentioned Mr Ngaïssona by name, and further explained that when '12 Puissances' was on the phone, it was very clear from his very submissive body language and his submissive way of talking in French that a superior in the chain of command had called.
