paragraph_text_preview: Fourth, the evidence before the Chamber suggests that Mr Ngaïssona was in a position of influence over Anti-Balaka groups also in 2014, both before and following the coordination set up in June 2014.

In this regard, Aurélien Llorca stated that when he met Mr Ngaïssona on 3 May 2014, he came across commanders from the provinces and Bangui who had come for a coordination meeting. The witness stated that during their earlier talk, Thierry Lebene had mentioned Mr Ngaïssona as political coordinator, and that Mr Ngaïssona himself presented as the coordinator of the 'liberators', explaining that he represented them politically to defend their rights as 'freedom fighters', and further stating that his role as the coordinator, in which he had addressed Catherine Samba-Panza on her election, would be confirmed in a general assembly. Aurélien Llorca stated that he concluded, based on repeated confirmation to that effect, that Mr Ngaïssona and Maxime Mokom regularly sent Anti-Balaka elements into the provinces, and that he heard that Mr Ngaïssona sent money to local commanders of groups that would then be added to a list of 'Anti-Balaka commanders' with their 'Anti-Balaka element'. The witness testified that Mr Ngaïssona told him that, in his view, the Anti-Balaka were not represented sufficiently in the transition government, and that there was a desire 'to exert pressure on the government through the Anti-Balaka' to 'obtain political leverage'. Aurélien Llorca stated that, in his analysis, someone like Mr Ngaïssona was trying to have 'more personal political leverage by buying allegiance from these local groups' since the more elements one had, the stronger the voice with government, UN, etc., and the more relevant he would become -- the higher the number of Anti-Balaka under his coordination, the more power he would receive from that; and that is why he needed to maintain contact with the provinces. Aurélien Llorca stated that Mr Ngaïssona responded affirmatively to the witness' question whether he was in control of the Anti-Balaka groups for example in Boy-Rabe, Combattant, Boeing, Castor, which in the panel's analysis were indeed in control of the Anti-Balaka in 2014.

The Chamber notes the evidence which suggests that the Anti-Balaka coordination under Mr Ngaïssona's lead may not have been in full control of all actions of the various Anti-Balaka groups. As stated above, the Chamber does not consider any inability of Mr Ngaïssona to control Anti-Balaka groups to be of relevance for its determinations. In any event, the Chamber refers to its discussion of the general functioning of the Anti-Balaka within the framework of its structure evolving over time. Financing
One of the factors which the Chamber considered for purposes of assessing Mr Ngaïssona's contributions to the Anti-Balaka in 2014 relates to the question of providing financial assistance.
The Ngaïssona Defence argues that there is no credible evidence showing that Mr Ngaïssona financed the Anti-Balaka after the attack of 5 December 2013 for the purchase of weapons and ammunition.

However, the evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that Mr Ngaïssona continued to provide financial assistance to the Anti-Balaka also following his return to Bangui in January 2014. In this regard, the Chamber considers that the specific purpose of providing money for purchase of weapons or ammunition is not alone determinative for concluding on Mr Ngaïssona's actions in relation to the charges. It has therefore considered the evidence before it also in relation to provision of financial assistance for other purposes.

Therefore, and on the basis of the evidence as outlined, the Chamber concludes that Mr Ngaïssona continued to provide financial assistance to the Anti-Balaka for various purposes in 2014. The Chamber concludes that these purposes included the purchase of weapons and ammunition.

Further recalling its discussion of Mr Ngaïssona's financial contributions to the activities of groups coalescing into the Anti-Balaka in 2013, the Chamber concludes that Mr Ngaïssona's financial contributions to the Anti-Balaka activities during the period relevant to the charges were regular and related to the Anti-Balaka manoeuvering or continuing to function. In this way, even if the financial contributions aimed also, or even mainly, at daily subsistence or reimbursement of travel costs for meetings, they inter-locked with the inter-operability of the Anti-Balaka. This is not contradicted by the argument that the 'daily subsistence' was conceived as a means to avoid looting or other criminal acts. Knowledge and awareness

The evidence before the Chamber shows that Mr Ngaïssona knew of the activities the Anti-Balaka engaged in, including the hostilities during their advance towards Bangui, the Bangui Attack, the Bossangoa Attack and the continued hostilities in 2014, and that this included the targeting of the Muslim civilian population.This is evidenced also by the repeated attempts, despite the above-mentioned knowledge, to absolve the Anti-Balaka from any responsibility for any violent acts, while only seemingly admitting to some Anti-Balaka elements possibly engaging in isolated acts of theft and looting. First, that the Anti-Balaka committed violent acts was common knowledge in the CAR at the time. Indeed, Catherine Samba-Panza testified that the existence of the various enclaves, 'evacuations' of Muslims from there, the attacks were public knowledge, people were waiting for the transport trucks so that they could attack them.

Thus, and in light of the above evidence, the Chamber considers that Mr Ngaïssona was aware, throughout the period relevant to the charges, of the activities of the Anti-Balaka and the violent acts committed by them in light of the fact of this being (i) common knowledge in the CAR at the time; (ii) raised with Mr Ngaïssona by the transition president; and (iii) reported internally in the Anti-Balaka. ######

General functioning of the Anti-Balaka in 2014In what follows, the Chamber has assessed the structure and positions within the Anti-Balaka national coordination and its evolving structure and tussles for power. In examining, its structure, the Chamber assessed the evidence it received in relation to the roles of ComZones, Anti-Balaka bases in Bangui, their number, meetings between them, badges issued to them as well as the media statements made by the coordination. The Chamber has also assessed, in this context, the arguments concerning the 'fake' Anti-Balaka. Structure of and positions within the national coordination

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that over time, positions within the Anti-Balaka and who held them evolved. However, when the structure of the Anti-Balaka formalised following Mr Ngaïssona's return to Bangui in the immediate aftermath of Michel Djotodia's resignation, specific positions were assigned to individuals who acted accordingly.

Evolving structure and tussles for leadership

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below illustrates that the Anti-Balaka was, in 2014, subject to certain discussions as to who should be its leader. In the view of the Chamber, such discussions were but a further illustration of various individuals super-imposing different personal and political ambitions on the group. At the same time, the person who eventually prevailed in leading the Anti-Balaka was Mr Ngaïssona, and the Anti-Balaka were represented as one movement at peace negotiations and in contacts with the national authorities and international community. Importantly, the Chamber notes, in this context, its conclusion on the continuation of hostilities between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka until the end of February 2014. Thus, the discussions about leadership happened after the events as charged in the current case took place. Therefore, any discussion of a possible split within the Anti-Balaka as an organisation is, at best, of indirect relevance to the determinations of the Chamber.

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that Sébastien Wenezoui challenged Mr Ngaïssona for his leadership of the Anti-Balaka. Whilst Sébastien Wenezoui proclaimed himself coordinator of the Anti-Balaka at a meeting in Pissmiss in May 2014, following mediation by the NGOs Mouda and PARETO, Mr Ngaïssona prevailed as general coordinator in June 2014, Sébastien Wenezoui being installed as his deputy. The Chamber notes in this regard its conclusions as to the hostilities between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka until the end of February 2014.

Importantly in this regard, P-0884 confirmed that there was no Anti-Balaka 'south', no Anti-Balaka 'north', but one Anti-Balaka with one objective, namely to 'drive Djotodia and his mercenaries out'. He explained that there was discontent among the ranks, including because of Kokaté on the radio describing the Anti-Balaka from the south as the 'good' Anti-Balaka and the others not, as well as because they thought the movement was being used for political purposes. P-0884 stated that Sébastien Wenezoui wanted to draw Mr Ngaïssona's attention as they had no information about what was going on and he should not just have political considerations but also think of the fighters and DDR, so Mr Yekatom 'Rambo', Kamezolai and Wenezoui held a meeting at PK9, wanting to dismiss Mr Ngaïssona and designate Wenezoui or 'Yagouzou' as the general coordinator of the Anti-Balaka to provoke a reaction, but since some people did not come, they designated Wenezoui as coordinator. P-0884 stated that they had invited people from Boy-Rabe, but neither Ngremangou nor Mr Ngaïssona were there because they knew 'full well' what the intention was.

The Chamber has before it video footage of the gathering on 15 May 2014, discussed extensively with various witnesses. In his speech at the meeting, Sébastien Wenezoui stated that they created the Anti-Balaka with everyone, that they tried to organise with 'Rombhot Yekatom', Kamezolai, Ngremangou and all brothers, while 16 soldiers based in the Bossangoa area formed the hard core of the Anti-Balaka and arrived to Bangui with them, where they fought well ('ils sont arrives à Bangui avec nous, et nous avons bien combattu'), but if someone came from abroad and wanted to take advantage, they would not sit idly and watch them destroy the movement which did not have a political character. Léopold Bara also spoke at the gathering, stating that there could be no unified coordination without involving 'the other side', speaking in favour of a unified coordination with reference to the previous coordination set up under Mr Ngaïssona's lead, and reiterating not to forget that it was responsible for the Anti-Balaka exactions, and crimes within the jurisdiction of the ICC were 'imprescriptible'.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber considers this incorrect on the basis of the evidence before it, as is shown by the various coordination efforts before, during and following the Bangui Attack. This evidence shows that even without formalised 'coordination' as an organisational entity, the Anti-Balaka coordinated their activities. The Chamber is of the view that even if there was no formalised coordinated entity with a pre-existing hierarchical structure, and even if various political and personal interests superimposed the activities over time, and especially in the aftermath of Michel Djotodia's resignation, this did not mean that the Anti-Balaka groups did not engage in coordinated activities. It is clear from the evidence before the Chamber that the Anti-Balaka was no static structure that already existed before the time relevant to the charges or remained unchanged throughout that period. However, it is also clear from the evidence that during the period relevant to the charges, the Anti-Balaka groups exhibited clear signs of structure, operational capability and coordination that remained present even if evolving in its details over time.

paragraph_text_preview: P-0876 stated, when asked about a 'structure' of the Anti-Balaka for the attack on 5 December 2013, that at the bottom were the elements, followed by ComZones, about a hundred though these included about 30 main ones, then intermediaries who looked for money to feed each group, one or two military coordinators on the ground, including Konaté, '12 Puissances', 'Rombho', Kamezolai, all this headed by Ngremangou who was in contact with those abroad, including Maxime Mokom in Zongo and 'les Bozizé', with the political structure including François Bozizé, Lin Banoukepa, Levy Yakété, Pascale Koyagbele, Francis Bozizé, Kokaté, Mr Ngaïssona. P-0876 qualified this by stating that there would not have been a pyramid structure of the Anti-Balaka general coordination, his answer concerned self-defence groups coming together for the purpose of defending villages and the empirical representation, which was not a structured entity as such. P-0876 testified that between January 2014 and June 2014, there was no coordination that brought together the 'two camps', but Mr Ngaïssona continued making statements as general coordinator, even when ComZones said that some individuals acted on their behalf, 'whereas they had no interaction with the elements on the ground'.

P-1193 testified, speaking of the time following the setting up of the June 2014 coordination, that ComZones came from Bangui and the provinces for meetings at which they received messages from the coordination, concerning that 'the war was over', that 'everyone should be accepted as brothers', and they 'were to get ready for the elections'. P-1193 testified that they did not have all the information because no ComZones said what they had done and even if they heard over the radio that certain things happened, people in the hinterland would deny it systematically. P-1193 testified that there was no possibility of forcing a ComZone to a meeting if they refused, the coordination was in some way a means to unify people who had 'goodwill and wanted to pass on the message'. P-1193 agreed with the suggestion that the coordination did not have the means for example to disarm, but did have 'the communications to avoid the crimes and work towards peace'. P-1193 further agreed with the suggestion that at the time, there was a vacuum in security authority in the CAR.

paragraph_text_preview: P-1521 testified that the role of the coordinator was to represent them on a political level, but also agreed with the suggestion that the chain of command was not respected, this was set up to control the 'true' Anti-Balaka under certain chiefs. P-1521 testified that there were about 20 ComZones in Bangui when including Bimbo and Begoua, about eight zones across Bangui plus two on the Damara and Bouali axis, and numerous ComZones outside of Bangui. P-1521 also mentioned 'prefectural coordinators'. P-1521 testified that they decided to have a coordinator of operations to 'investigate and control' ComZones. The Chamber does not consider credible the witness's suggestion that Mr Ngaïssona would in the beginning have been against the creation of the position of an operations coordinator because he did not think it was necessary and that it was only given to Maxime Mokom so there would not be 'too much frustration'. It is clear from the evidence before the Chamber, as outlined above, that Maxime Mokom was, without question or hesitation, designated to be operations coordinator upon Mr Ngaïssona's return to Bangui and the initial steps to formalise the structure of the Anti-Balaka. P-1521 testified that between January and June 2014, it was the same structure which continued to function because the ComZones were each responsible for their elements, even when Mr Ngaïssona came to represent them, he did not have control of the movement, did not 'master' all the ComZones or elements. paragraph_text_preview: The evidence before the Chamber concerning the number of Anti-Balaka elements across the CAR in 2014 varies, but suggests that overall, by February 2014, there would have been approximately 50,000 Anti-Balaka elements in Bangui and across the provinces. Meetings

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that in 2014, meetings of Anti-Balaka leaders and ComZones were convened by and held at Mr Ngaïssona's properties as well as at the Azimut hotel, as paid for by Mr Ngaïssona. While the evidence is unclear as to the frequency of such meetings, it is clear that meetings were held to discuss a variety of matters.

For example, P-2232 described attending a meeting following his return from Zongo at Mr Ngaïssona's residence in Boy-Rabe which was attended by various Anti-Balaka leaders, including 'Inga', 'Leroi', 'Bawa', 'Dongodo', 'Ngoyace', 'Andjilo', 'Mazimbele', 'Bernard Mokom', Mr Ngaïssona, but not Mr Yekatom, and many ComZones, including from Bangui and the provinces. P-2232 said that the coordinator asked for the needs of all ComZones, in particular in relation to health, to see the status of the combatants and who has injured. P-2232 testified that Mokom asked the ComZones to present an assessment of their needs, particularly their weapons, and promised that he would visit them at their various bases. P-2232 further testified that when Mauri asked to be reimbursed for his expenses, 'father Bernard' answered, 'We have not yet reached our objectives. We cannot reimburse you now. P-1962 talked of a meeting in June 2014 to which Mr Ngaïssona called Habib Soussou and the commanders in Boda, and P-1962 went with Habib Soussou, Roddy Mbossé, Moraise Sendé. P-1962 stated that many Anti-Balaka were present at this meeting, including Maxime Mokom, Wenezoui, '12 Puissances', and Anti-Balaka commanders from Bambari, Sibut, Bossangoa, Kaga Bandoro, Carnot and Berberati ('Chiki Chiki'), Gamboula, Gazi (Rodrigue), Yaloke ('Le Bleu'), Bossembélé, Bossemptélé, Boali and Damara; apart from the coordinators from Boda and Bambari, the others were all ComZones; it was their first time meeting each other. P-1962 said that at the meeting, Mr Ngaïssona said 'to lay down' their weapons and 'to reconcile with the Muslims' who were born in the CAR since they are 'brothers', and 'not to kill the Muslims', to 'bring back peace', and to 'wait for the DDR'. P-1962 testified that he never heard Mr Ngaïssona advocating for or encouraging crimes against the Muslim population. P-1962 stated that a strategy for disarmament was also discussed, but not everybody was in agreement, with some refusing to put down their arms. P-1962 stated that the day after the meeting, Mr Ngaïssona officially appointed Habib Soussou as coordinator of Boda and P-1962 as his deputy.

Aurélien Llorca stated that the Anti-Balaka from the provinces met Mr Ngaïssona in Bangui during coordination meetings, often openly staying at Hotel Azimut, the owner of which the witness learned to be connected to the Anti-Balaka, but he was not aware of coordination meetings before May 2014. 'Fake' Anti-Balaka
The Chamber received a significant amount of evidence on the discussions about so-called 'fake' Anti-Balaka.

The Ngaïssona Defence argues in this regard that the existence of 'fake' Anti-Balaka 'impeded the effective demarcation of the Anti-Balaka groups', which makes it 'impossible to know who allegedly committed crimes and if those crimes were committed as opportunistic acts, or within the alleged shared intent of the group'.

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that the concept of 'fake' Anti-Balaka was used in varying contexts and for varying purposes throughout the time relevant to the charges. In particular, it was used by Anti-Balaka leaders such as Mr Ngaïssona to suggest that violence and abuses attributed to the Anti-Balaka would instead have been committed by individuals not linked to the Anti-Balaka, who used its name for purposes of committing such violence.

Aurélien Llorca stated that when he interviewed Mr Ngaïssona in March 2014 and asked him about violence and exactions committed by Anti-Balaka elements, Mr Ngaïssona responded that this was done by uncontrolled elements or 'fake' Anti-Balaka, explaining that he had asked the international forces in a press release to arrest the 'fake' Anti-Balaka, but not having himself taken 'any specific measures' since he was not able to stop said acts. The witness testified that in the CAR panel's analysis, an Anti-Balaka element became 'uncontrolled' when acting 'out of bounds', such that an element could have been 'controlled' in the evening before, but became 'uncontrolled' the day on which they committed some exaction or a particular act. Aurélien Llorca testified that one needed to distinguish between political coordination and military structure of the organisation, in that, some acts might have been 'uncontrolled' because one could not ascribed some political responsibility for them, but they still fell under a military strategy consistent with their execution.

Various witnesses talked about the difficulty to distinguish between 'real' and 'fake' Anti-Balaka. The Chamber considers the testimony of Catherine Samba-Panza instructive in this regard, in her agreeing that it was not always possible to identify the 'true perpetrators' of exactions since not all armed civilians were Anti-Balaka, and neither journalists nor the population could always distinguish. Yet, she also clarified that generally speaking given the context and events in specific areas, it was quite likely that the people who were attributed with the crimes 'were the ones indeed', and that it depended on the location, the time, and the general political and security backdrop.

The Chamber considers that the fact of the concept of 'fake' Anti-Balaka being used to blame violent acts and abuses in falsely attributing them to 'outsiders' is clearly illustrated by the example of Andjilo. The Chamber is convinced that the evidence before it shows that Andjilo was one of the initial members of the self-defence groups that coalesced into the Anti-Balaka, recalling in this regard its discussion on the groups forming in the Bossangoa area. The Chamber further recalls that Andjilo was one of the individuals who, with a group that he led, descended through the provinces towards Bangui, and participated in attacks, including against Muslim civilians, in this advance. The Chamber also refers to its discussion that, following this advance to Bangui, Andjilo was one of the individuals who, with a group that he led, participated in the coordinated attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013.

Overall, the Chamber considers that the existence of 'fake' Anti-Balaka as a generalised concept is immaterial to its determinations for purposes of the charges insofar as the Chamber discusses the specific individuals involved and their place or role within the Anti-Balaka in relation to each charged incident, as well as in relation to the hostilities during the advance in 2013, and in early 2014. Furthermore, the Chamber is of the view that the generalised concept is immaterial on a broader level insofar as the existence of individuals allegedly operating under the name of the Anti-Balaka does not, in and of itself, negate the existence of (i) a structure or organisation within and among those that considered themselves to be 'real' Anti-Balaka; (ii) the shared core objectives of those that considered themselves to be 'real' Anti-Balaka; and (iii) the hostilities engaged in by Anti-Balaka elements to such extent as to amount to an armed conflict with the Seleka. The Chamber further notes that these hostilities are not claimed to have been engaged in by 'fake' Anti-Balaka, indeed, in particular as regards the hostilities during the advance in 2013, the generalised concept of the 'fake' Anti-Balaka was brought up only much later in 2014. Anti-Balaka badges

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that at some point in 2014 and thereafter, the Anti-Balaka national coordination, under Mr Ngaïssona's lead, decided to issue badges to Anti-Balaka elements.

The Chamber has before it a number of different items which appear to be Anti-Balaka badges or ID cards. One format, visible on a card issued in the name of Mr Yekatom and bearing his picture, bears an Anti-Balaka logo, name, function, nationality and address of the bearer, an ID card number, stamp and signature. This same format is visible in other examples, including in an electronic blank version obtained by Kasper Agger in February 2014 that he called 'template', and as photographed by P-2050 in February 2014, as well as by the CAR Panel in March 2014.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber has before it various media statements attributed to the Anti-Balaka, for the most part seemingly signed by Mr Ngaïssona in his capacity as Anti-Balaka general coordinator since his return to Bangui.

In a press release of 1 February 2014, reference is made to recent violence in Bangui and in the hinterland, 'often wrongly attributed' ('souvent imputée à tort') to the Anti-Balaka movement, with the wish to clarify that the ultimate aim of the movement was to 'deliver the Central African people' from the 'claws of the bloodthirsty'('griffes des sanguinaires') Seleka, which is now reached. It refers to confusion between 'fake' Anti-Balaka which infiltrated the movement with bad intentions, the Anti-Balaka combatants who had committed not to steal or loot, to whom cases of looting and theft were attributed. Further, Kasper Agger testified that during his interview on 25 February 2014, Mr Ngaïssona referred to the Seleka having taken power of the country, and being mainly a Muslim group, particularly on the command level, with Muslims from the northern CAR, Sudan or Chad, and speaking Arabic; they would be more friendly towards their local Muslims, while there was more resistance from the FACA, mainly in the central and western part of the country, being non-Muslims; and when the FACA started to organise the resistance against the Seleka together with the Anti-Balaka, members of the PG, in particular that were close to François Bozizé, they 'obviously' would 'target Muslims' and 'Muslim communities' as well; what Mr Ngaïssona expressed to the witness was that it was 'a form of resistance' and that these were 'self-protection groups' from the local populations against the Muslims: 'We cannot accept the attacks by the Muslims'.

In the view of the Chamber, it is clear from this that Mr Ngaïssona, at a time at which the Anti-Balaka under his lead as general coordinator appeared to be calling for peace and reconciliation, continued to see 'Muslims', in general, as 'the foreigners' in the country against whom the Anti-Balaka had 'defended'. This is also made apparent by the billeting and emergency assistance project proposals of February 2014, which clearly refer to Anti-Balaka elements including individuals being motivated by revenge and acting against both Seleka and Muslims considered to have supported the Seleka.

Various statements were issued by the Anti-Balaka coordination under Mr Ngaïssona's lead after February 2014. The Chamber refers in this regard to its conclusions as to the duration of the active conflict in the CAR in 2014. The Chamber has therefore considered these statements in the specific context of the Anti-Balaka coordination, under Mr Ngaïssona's lead, engaged at that time in negotiations with the government and international authorities.

In an RFI interview published at the beginning of April 2014, Mr Ngaïssona is presented as head of the 'coordination des combattants pour la paix en Centrafrique', 'differently put the wing of the Anti-Balaka which is not represented in the government', and which, 'according to him' constituted the majority of the movements controlling the south of the country. The article reports Mr Ngaïssona as saying that the Anti-Balaka control almost the entire country, Bangui and the hinterland, and that this movement, which was born since the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, now waits for the CAR government to recognise this 'acte de bravoure de ces enfants' and to reach out for dialogue 'parce que les anti-balaka, à partir d'aujourd'hui, ont décidé de ne plus continuer les hostilités'. When asked about the 'wing' under Joachim Kokaté, Mr Ngaïssona is reported as stating: \[l\]es anti-balaka que je coordonne sont un seul et même mouvement qui est réparti sur tout l'étendu du territoire. Quand je donne l'ordre à ces enfants, je pense que c'est immédiatement suivi d'effet. Donc, si on veut que la paix revienne définitivement dans ce pays, il faut dialoguer avec la coordination -- son staff -- pour qu'il y ait la paix definitive en République centrafricaine.

The article reports Mr Ngaïssona as saying that the Anti-Balaka control almost the entire country, Bangui and the hinterland, and that this movement, which was born since the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, now waits for the CAR government to recognise this 'acte de bravoure de ces enfants' and to reach out for dialogue 'parce que les anti-balaka, à partir d'aujourd'hui, ont décidé de ne plus continuer les hostilités'. In another press release of 29 May 2014, the events at Fatima church the day before are condemned, stating that the 'enemies of the CAR' struck again, and criticising the 'complacent and lax, if not complicit' attitude of the international armed forces, in particular MISCA, whose mandate it is to oversee the cantonment of Muslims in KM5, yet allows them to leave their camp armed to commit such major atrocities. The Chamber considers this document to be another illustration of the Anti-Balaka and its national coordination, led by Mr Ngaïssona, equating Seleka or other violence-committing individuals with Muslims in PK5 in general. It is of note that this statement was made at a time when the Anti-Balaka national coordination had repeatedly expressed its commitment to peace and security in the CAR. Yet clearly the underlying mindset remained the same.

In June 2014, at a time when most of the Seleka had retreated to the north or were billeted in camps in Bangui and parts of the Muslim civilian population especially in the west of the CAR had been forced to leave their localities, the Anti-Balaka coordination also presented a project concerning the peace process, outlining the general context of Seleka violence that had pushed the Central African youth in towns and the hinterland to organise into self-defence movement, and the Anti-Balaka, to protect the CAR population and following their advance through the provinces, eventually reach Bangui for the attack of 5 December 2013. It criticises that despite the Anti-Balaka's enthusiasm for the new transition authorities, they were seen as enemies of peace and tracked down by international forces, yet the meeting at the presidency on 17 April 2014 restarted the dialogue with the government, and states that while the implication of the Anti-Balaka coordination in the new dynamic of dialogue allowed to manage the security situation in Bangui, in certain localities in the provinces, the counter-productive behaviour has once again emerged in the Anti-Balaka ranks ('dans certaines localités de provinces, des comportements contre-productifs sont encore relevés dans les rangs des Antibalaka'). The document further criticises the favourable treatment of Seleka and not being taken into account despite the engage of the Anti-Balaka to cede hostilities since the election of Catherine Samba-Panza, as well as the international forces, and outlines steps for a communication and sensitisation programme to achieve peace.

paragraph_text_preview: In an interview around this time, Mr Ngaïssona outlined his view of his role as Anti-Balaka coordinator, having been asked how he came to be national coordinator of the Anti-Balaka since the previous December, and stated that the Anti-Balaka came into being 'parce que des étrangers ont accompagné les S\[eleka\] qui étaient de vrais Centrafricains lors de leur entrée dans B\[angui\] et que ceux-ci ont fait beaucoup du mal au peuple centrafricain'. The Chamber considers the importance of the context well illustrated by the evidence of Vivien Beina. While describing how grateful the people in the Lobaye were to Mr Yekatom for his efforts and stating that this was why they elected him as member of parliament, Vivien Beina further testified that during those elections there were practically no Muslims in the Lobaye, and even Christians who had converted refused to vote because they were afraid.

Among the activities engaged in by the Anti-Balaka, and by Mr Ngaïssona and Mr Yekatom more specifically, the Chamber notes the press statement issued by the Anti-Balaka general coordination, as signed by Mr Ngaïssona, on occasion of Catherine Samba-Panza's election as new transition president.

Further, the evidence before the Chamber as outlined below shows that the Anti-Balaka coordination requested billeting of the Anti-Balaka elements comparable to the billeting of Seleka in Bangui, leading to frustration when this did not happen. The question of billeting Anti-Balaka elements was also related to the issue of organised disarming, neither of which in fact took place during the period relevant to the charges.

The Chamber has before it two documents which appear to be project suggestions for billeting and aid projects for the Anti-Balaka, prepared around February 2014. The first document traces the origins of the Anti-Balaka to self-defence groups that set up due to the Seleka violence, progressing to and reaching Bangui with the attack on 5 December 2013, and eventually leading to the dismissal of Michel Djotodia and Nicolas Tiangaye. Importantly, the document continues: Aussi, la population, victime des exactions des S\[eleka\] à travers la Centrafrique depuis le 10 décembre 2012, a regagné les rangs des Antibalaka avec un esprit de vengeance envers les ex-Séléka est \[sic\] les sujets musulmans qui ont soutenu les Séléka durant leur occupation de la RCA. Avec la généralisation du mouvement « Anti-Balaka » à cette frange de population centrafricaine victime des Séléka, les dérapages sont constatés dans les rangs des Antibalaka en sachant que beaucoup de délinquants et de déviants ont grossi les rangs du Mouvement. L'effectif global de ces Jeunes antibalaka est aujourd'hui évalué à environ 50.000 combattants, repartis sur les différents sites d'implantation du Mouvement à Bangui et dans l'arrière-pays. Pour freiner et enrayer la propension aux dérapages des combattants Antibalaka « mélangés », le cantonnement, la prise en charge et l'alimentation des combattants Antibalaka constitue une urgente nécessité en vue de consolider le processus du pacification et de normalisation en cours en République Centrafricaine. Cette opération permettra de préserver les communautés centrafricaines.

Moreover, Alfred Legrand Ngaya testified that he drafted the projects on instructions of Mr Ngaïssona, explaining that the figure of 50,000 elements was an approximation on the basis of what the ComZones were telling them. Alfred Legrand Ngaya said that there were two similar projects with different themes, concerning emergency assistance and return to villages, as well as billeting. The witness testified that the projects were sent to the transition government and international forces and organisations, but there was never any reaction. As stated, the Chamber has considered the evidence in the overall context of the information before it. In particular, the Chamber considers that while the Anti-Balaka, and specifically Mr Ngaïssona and Mr Yekatom, did engage in activities also aimed at peace and reconciliation, these were set in the context of broader peace negotiations with the CAR government and international authorities as well as at a time when no more large-scale active hostilities took place, when the Seleka had mostly retreated to the north or was billeted, and when Muslim civilians especially in the west of the CAR had been forced to leave their localities. The continuation of hostilities Continued hostilities and peace negotiations Notwithstanding the retreat of the Seleka following the resignation of Michel Djotodia and the setting up of a new transition government in January 2014, the main hostilities between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka which had started in earnest in September 2013 continued largely unabated until the end of February 2014. Hostilities thereafter did continue, but subsided considerably. The UN Security Council recurrently dedicated attention to the security situation in the CAR in 2013 and 2014. Several attempts to bring about the cessation of hostilities failed, including the 16 June 2014 PARETO mediation agreement, the 23 July 2014 peace agreement signed by the Seleka and the Anti-Balaka in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, and the agreement signed in Nairobi in April 2015. The number of internally displaced persons and refugees outside of the CAR decreased in the course of 2014, but overall remained in the hundreds of thousands throughout the year. Continued hostilities

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that between September 2013 and the end of February 2014, and despite the resignation of Michel Djotodia, the subsequent withdrawal of the majority of the Seleka troops from the CAR, and the election of a new transition president in January 2014, the hostilities in the CAR involving the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka continued. The continuing hostilities led to significant numbers of CAR civilians being forced to leave from their homes. As the evidence outlined below demonstrates, hostilities between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka from March 2014 onwards amounted mainly to skirmishes and low-intensity tactical struggles.

At the outset, the Chamber notes in this regard its discussion of hostilities between Anti-Balaka groups and the Seleka starting in September 2013, in the context of the advance of Anti-Balaka groups through the provinces. In addition, the Chamber refers to its discussion of continued hostilities in localities in western CAR in January and early February 2014. The Chamber also notes its discussion of the hostilities in the context of the coordinated attacks in Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013.

The evidence before the Chamber as further outlined below shows that several summits were held and agreements signed with a view to creating dialogue, achieving peace and ceasing the hostilities in the CAR between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka, as well as other warring factions concerned. It appears that those attempts were met with limited, if any, success.

paragraph_text_preview: Second, a forum on national reconciliation in the CAR was held in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, in July 2014, mediated by President Denis Sassou Nguesso. paragraph_text_preview: Witnesses testified that the violence in the CAR continued despite the change in government and the peace talks. Catherine Samba-Panza testified that the violence and reprisals continued throughout the CAR even after she was appointed as transition president and in fact until the end of 2015, in the presence of international forces, Sangaris, African Union forces, describing the CAR as being 'in a situation of total chaos'. Specifically in relation to Boy-Rabe, the witness testified that even though the Seleka was no longer present, tensions still existed and people sought to protect themselves with weapons, re-confirming that the crisis lasted until the end of 2015. P-0876 also testified that after the resignation of Djotodia and the departure of the Seleka from power, the violence continued, and the CAR continued to face disorder and remained in a state of chaos beyond the control of the transition government. He asserted that from the time that the CAR fell into a state of chaos on 10 December 2012, the violence was in fact still ongoing at the time of his testimony in December 2021. Hostilities in western CAR in January and February 2014 As part of the Anti-Balaka's pursuit of its core objective, in the context of which its elements targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, due to the Anti-Balaka perceiving the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka, the Anti-Balaka continued to target the Muslim civilian population in 2014 across the western CAR prefectures, including in the second half of January and early February 2014 in Ombella-M'Poko (Gaga, Zawa, Yaloké), Ouham-Pendé (Bossemptélé), Nana-Mambéré (Baoro), Mambéré-Kadéï (Guen, Carnot, Berbérati) and Lobaye (Boda). The attacks followed a pattern with Anti-Balaka groups killing and injuring Muslim civilians, looting and destroying their belongings, and often placing them in enclaved positions under difficult circumstances, eventually leading to many Muslims having to leave the respective areas.

P-2416 stated that before this first major attack, about one or two days after the meeting of Sangaris with the Muslim community, there were rumours that the Anti-Balaka were coming from everywhere to attack and kill the Muslims in Yaloké, there was widespread fear in the Muslim community at this time and they knew they were coming for them, the Anti-Balaka would taunt them saying 'get prepared we are coming to kill you'; it was as if these Anti-Balaka were planning these main attacks in Yaloké with the assistance of Anti-Balaka from other areas.

P-2416 stated that on the day of the first major attack, he was at home and heard gunfire from the direction of 'Quartier Sous-Manguier'. P-2416 stated that he later heard from the imam that the Anti-Balaka had killed the president of the Islamic community, and another person; P-2416 saw their bodies at the central mosque, with one appearing to have gunshot wounds to the stomach, back and chest. P-2416 stated that he also saw people injured with gunshot wounds during this attack. P-2416 stated that the only people who had guns in the area were Sangaris and Anti-Balaka, and the people he saw had not been shot by the Sangaris; all those injured said they had been shot by the Anti-Balaka. P-2416 thought that over an hour after the attack commenced, the Sangaris arrived back in Yaloké. Zenaba Oumar, a Muslim woman from Yaloké, stated that after the attacks on Gaga and Zawa, she was told by someone whose son was in the Anti-Balaka, that the Anti-Balaka were en route to Yaloké to launch an attack. The witness stated that the community also received the same information and she knew that the Anti-Balaka had 'surrounded' Yaloké because she could hear gunfire in the air 'coming from all directions'. Zenaba Oumar stated the Muslims gathered in the mosque and other compounds.

The evidence as outlined below shows that the situation in Yaloké did not calm down following these two attacks. Rather, various groups of Muslims remained confined to specific properties in Yaloké and outside of Yaloké for weeks, under threat of violence by the Anti-Balaka. This was followed by hundreds of Muslims being removed from Yaloké.

The evidence as outlined below shows that in addition to the attacks within Yaloké, the Anti-Balaka also attacked a large group of Mbororo/Peuhl near Gaga and Yaloké, keeping them first in Gaga and then in Yaloké, where the group stayed for more than two years.

footnote_content: The Chamber notes that in this context the designations Peuhl and Mbororo seem to often be used interchangeably (*see* P‑2546 Statement, CAR-OTP-2114-0402-R01, at 0408, para. 23; P-2416 Statement, CAR-OTP-2106-0489-R02, at 0493, para. 13).
paragraph_text_preview: Specifically, Adama Djigaou, a Mbororo woman, described in detail how her large group of Mbororo was attacked by the Anti-Balaka in the bush when talking towards Yaloké, leading to people being injured and killed, including 12 members of their family. The witness stated that when the group then walked further towards Gaga, they again encountered the Anti-Balaka, whom she later learned were 'Colonel Richal's' men, who looted their remaining cattle and walked them to Gaga, where 'Colonel Richal' said that he would protect the Mbororo from being killed by the Anti-Balaka as he had trained them, that he was sorry for what he had done in the towns, and therefore had instructed his Anti-Balaka not to hurt the Mbororo. Adama Djigaou stated that the Mbororo group remained in Gaga for approximately one month and was then transferred to a big compound in Yaloké centre, where it was overcrowded and they spent approximately one month. The witness stated that the Anti-Balaka guarding the compound was unarmed and they could pray in the open, but that the Anti-Balaka groups from other towns present in Yaloké would have harmed them because they wanted to kill the Muslims. Adama Djigaou stated that the Mbororo were later moved by MISCA to the Yaloké town hall where they remained for two years, still receiving unsuitable food, which led to some deaths; she eventually decided to go to a refugee camp in Cameroon. The witness heard that all the Muslims had fled from Yaloké and that none of the Muslims' shops were open and saw that some of the shops had been destroyed.

P-2546 stated that 20 Peuhls from the hospital were accommodated by Le Bleu at the compound opposite his compound, approximately 100 Peuhl men were in the bush in Djobeu surrounded by Anti-Balaka, and Peuhl women and children were in Gbawi. P-2546 said that the Peuhl men told him they had lost everything and were in terrible living conditions and lacked food. P-2546 stated that 'General Richard' took all Peuhls from the bush to the compound opposite Le Bleu's compound and asked the archbishop to take care of them, with surveys giving numbers of 800 and then 918 Peuhl men, women and children there. P-2546 stated that the compound was not large enough and the sanitary situation was appalling, and the Peuhls were moved to the administrative buildings, where their living conditions improved and MINUSCA were responsible for protecting them. P-2546 stated that initially there was tension between the Peuhls and local population, with the latter feeling victimised because they had not received any humanitarian aid, as opposed to the Peuhls. P-2546 stated the Peuhls were eventually moved to a camp in 2015 and most of them went to Cameroon.

D30-4914 also stated that Rocca Mokom came to see him from time to time and tell him that his elder brother Maxime had called for news.

The Chamber therefore concludes that an Anti-Balaka group, following instructions of 'the authority' from Yaoundé, including Mr Ngaïssona and Bernard Mokom, attacked the Seleka in Beloko on 20 January 2014. ######

P-0595 stated that on 5 February 2014 at around 08:00-09:00, Dieudonné Gomitoi, the Guen mayor, Emmanuel Boybanda, Beina, Maturin and all other Christians of Guen surrounded his courtyard with armed Anti-Balaka elements. P-0595 stated that they demanded that everyone leave the house and in response all men, around 70, came out while the women, children and injured stayed inside. P-0595 stated that the Anti-Balaka elements searched and pillaged everything, including the merchandise of his shops. P-0595 said that at the same time, Beina divided the group of Muslim men into two, a group of 50 men was taken 500 metres away and the Anti-Balaka made them lie down on the ground. P-0595 stated that one or two minutes afterwards, they heard a lot of gunshots, cries and the Anti-Balaka crying out in joy. P-0595 would also later see the body of Hamadou Djada who had been one of the 50 men that were taken from his house; he recognised his clothes.

P-0732 stated that she later sought shelter at chief Ali's house. She stated that many Muslim men sought shelter with chief Ali, and that the Anti-Balaka specifically targeted Chadians. P-0732 stated that one morning at chief Ali's house, the Anti-Balaka asked all the men at the house to go outside, there were about 132 men. P-0732 stated that Beina then divided the men into two groups, putting one group aside and ordering his men to kill the other group. P-0732 stated that she did not see the killings, but could hear the shootings and hacking noise of the machetes as the Anti-Balaka were killing the men. P-0732 stated that the men from the second group managed to escape, some ran to the Djomo village church, others to the bush. P-0732 stated that Beina was present during the killing, she heard another Anti-Balaka element named 'Koya' was also present. P-0732 stated that in the afternoon of the killings she went to see the bodies and recognised that of her husband.

P-1598 stated that he was informed on 4 February 2014 by the mayor and CB that people had been killed. P-1598 stated that he arrived in Guen at around 15:30 and saw bodies piled on the side of the road and that some had been dismembered. P-1598 stated that the CB, mayor, councillor Bandjoukou and a few others counted 43 dead bodies. P-1598 said that the CB and the mayor told him that the Anti-Balaka had visited the Ali Garba and Bandjoukou sites of displaced persons, chosen some men, shot them dead and prohibited their burial. P-1598 deduced from the fact that Beina and his group were present and prohibited the burial that they were responsible. P-1598 thought that the victims were all Muslims since the Anti-Balaka had sought them out at sites where there were only Muslims. P-1598 said that Bandjoukou told him that there were also people killed in the bush. P-1598 sought and gained permission from ComZone Beina to bury the bodies, warning of a risk of an epidemic like cholera.

P-0595 stated that the morning after the attack, around 05:30-06:00, the women, children and injured, close to 200 people, left his house and walked to Djomo, around nine kilometres away, accompanied by the chief from Zarao-Yanga and some Anti-Balaka elements. P-0595 said he gave 50,000 CFA to Beina for protection and remained hidden at his house for two to three weeks with his wife and Mamadou. P-0595 said that Beina informed him that the mayor, Dieudonné and the neighbourhood chiefs wanted P-0595 killed because he knew what had happened. P-0595 stated he was scared for his life and organised a transfer of 500,000 CFA so Beina would help him flee with his wife and Mamadou, and they left Guen on 19 February 2014 on a moto given to P-0595 by Beina, eventually leaving the CAR with the MISCA escort for Cameroon around 28 or 29 February 2014. P-0595 stated that he lost everything when he left Guen.

P-1598 stated that on 6 February 2014 at 10:25, 163 displaced Muslims from Guen arrived at the Catholic mission in Djomo without any belongings, and escorted by a large number of Anti-Balaka, including Beina, Armand, and Mathurin. P-1598 stated that Beina told him that the displaced would be better off with P-1598 in his parish and gave him 30.000 CFA to provide them with food; some of the displaced people also had money on them to buy food. P-1598 stated that hygiene conditions were very precarious in the parish, the displaced were crammed into a small space, they had no water in the parish, but P-1598 insisted they have access to the pump in Djomo town without paying. In the evening of 6 February 2014 at approximately 20:00, P-1598 was threatened by two Anti-Balaka elements from Ngaboua for protecting 'ferocious beasts', i.e. the Muslims in the parish. P-1598 stated that on 28 February 2014, the Anti-Balaka came to the parish to kill a Peuhl. P-1598 stated that the Anti-Balaka tolerated Muslims but they strictly refused to welcome Peuhls because of their close collaboration with the Seleka. He heard a gunshot and the Anti-Balaka asked the displaced to bury the Peuhl man. P-1598 stated that on 6 March 2014 at 8:30, the Anti-Balaka, including Jean, nicknamed Gbaara, killed the imam of Djomo.

P-1598 stated that on 12 February 2014 at 17:00, MSF arrived in Djomo and, reassured by their presence, a wave of displaced Muslims and non-Muslims also arrived in Djomo from the surrounding villages. P-1598 stated that on 13 February 2014, there were 519 displaced Muslims in the parish, and 309 non-Muslims in Djomo, with others arriving later. P-1598 stated that the Muslims did not want to return to their homes and preferred to go to Carnot or Cameroon because they were afraid and scarred by the killings. P-1598 stated he knew from former Djomo parishioners that the Muslims of Djomo and Guen have not yet returned.

P-0732 stated that many Muslims who were staying at Ali's house moved to the church in Djomo village after the pastor from the church asked them to do so. She went with her children to the house of Gbandjoukou for a week before the Anti-Balaka took him away and killed him. P-0732 stated that the Anti-Balaka took her, her children and other people to the house of Abdoulaye Sodiam who was in Bangui at the time. She heard from the Anti-Balaka who were at Sodiam's house that at Gbandjoukou's house they had killed a handicapped boy named Ousseini and an older Mbororo woman. P-0732 stated that Beina left four Anti-Balaka elements to guard Sodiam's house, including Kefiou, Bruno, and the chief of mission. P-0732 stated that the Anti-Balaka who were guarding them had machetes and hunting rifles or 'Ngba na ngonda' in Sango, and the chief of mission was carrying a 'kala'. P-0732 stated that they were not allowed to leave Sodiam's house and stayed there for approximately two months. She heard that her aunt tried to leave and was buried alive with a Mbororo woman. P-0732 stated that they were harassed for money and sexually assaulted at Sodiam's house by the four Anti-Balaka guarding them and other Anti-Balaka who came from Mbaina village. She stated that Bruno and the chief of mission raped her. P-0732 stated that Sodiam arranged for them to leave his house after he heard that threats that were being made against Muslims by another group of Anti-Balaka that had come to Guen. They arrived in Mambere, and MISCA took them to the gendarmerie where they remained for about a month, before being taken to a big church in Berbérati where there were many Muslims from Berbérati but also from surrounding villages where they remained for about a month before MISCA Cameroon took them to Kenzou.

Carnot -- early February 2014The evidence before the Chamber as outlined below shows that in early February 2014, Anti-Balaka elements entered Carnot, and killed Muslim civilians, looted properties, and created conditions which led to the majority of the Muslim population leaving.P-0289, a priest in Carnot at the relevant time, stated that rumours that the Anti-Balaka would attack had multiplied before the attack, and the Seleka left at the end of January 2014 when the Anti-Balaka were at 30 kilometres from Carnot. P-0289 stated that the majority of Muslims from Carnot left at the same time as the Seleka, while Muslims from surrounding villages, especially from Yaloké, Bossembélé, Bozoum, Baoro, Bossemptélé, sought refuge in the parish.

P-0289 stated that Anti-Balaka elements entered Carnot in a column formation on 2 February 2014. P-2132, the mayor of Carnot at the time, described that he saw the Anti-Balaka coming towards the centre of Carnot in a column formation on 3 February 2014. P-2393, a Muslim civilian residing in Carnot at the time of the attack, stated that he saw the Anti-Balaka entering Carnot in military columns on 5 February 2014. Barthélémy Namsenmo agreed that the attack on Carnot took place in the first week of February 2024. He also stated that more than a thousand Anti-Balaka elements entered Carnot. The witness testified that the Bossangoa group, along with that of Baoro, went to attack Carnot.P-2556, who was among the Anti-Balaka group entering Carnot, stated that some of the elements were armed, carrying bows, arrows, knives, big knives called 'dankanarés' and machetes.

The evidence shows that the Seleka left Berbérati on 7 February 2014, before the arrival of the Anti-Balaka.

P-2325 stated that he heard around 13:00 on 8 February 2014 that another Anti-Balaka group was about to enter the town, which Mokom confirmed, stating they were more violent and suggesting that Muslims should hide in a safe place. P-2325 stated that this second group was large and came from surrounding towns like Carnot, Gadzi, Guen, Sassele and Bekadili, he recognised some as former scouts and heard some speak dialects from those places. P-2325 stated that the group, wearing gris-gris, wigs, horns on necklaces, started operating at around 13:30 on 8 February 2014, going directly to Poto-Poto and starting to chase the Muslims, looting from houses and shops of Muslims, and he believed them to be familiar with the area because they knew where to find the Muslims. P-2325 stated that the next group was led by a local street seller called 'Chiki-Chiki', who explained to P-2325 that he had lost everything because of the Seleka and had gone north to get his 'vaccination' and returned to seek revenge against the Muslims since all Muslims were accomplices of the Seleka, so he wanted to chase them out/kill them. P-2325 stated that 'Chiki-Chiki' had about a hundred elements under his control. P-2325 stated that an Anti-Balaka group based in Poto-Poto seemed to have some autonomy, but was under orders of 'Chiki-Chiki'.

P-2324 stated that at around 18:00, he went to the mosque for evening prayer when he was told by a Red Cross person that it was not safe because the Anti-Balaka were killing people in the Muslim neighbourhoods. P-2324 stated that he returned home to collect his brother and departed, seeing hundreds of young Anti-Balaka elements attacking the houses of Muslims, destroying walls, and leaving with mattresses and furniture. P-2324 stated that his house was looted and the fence around the property was destroyed, and he learned that some of his neighbours participated in the looting. P-2324 stated that in Poto-Poto, all houses were completely emptied, some destroyed, some had roofs or windows removed. P-2324 stated that the Anti-Balaka said publicly that their goal was to destroy everything so the Muslims would leave and never come back. P-2324 stated that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslims' shops and spared the Christians', his shop was looted and damaged, but his Christian neighbours' were not. P-2324 stated that he heard the Anti-Balaka destroying the mosque in Sambanda.

He further testified that the attack involved more than a thousand Anti-Balaka elements.

The evidence before the Chamber, as outlined below, shows that after the withdrawal of the Seleka from Boda in early 2014, non-Muslim and Muslim communities attacked each other, leading to deaths and destruction of property. The evidence shows that following these clashes, the non-Muslim community wanted the Muslim community to leave Boda. The evidence further shows that the Anti-Balaka launched an attack in Boda in support of the non-Muslim population soon thereafter.

Joachim Kokaté confirmed that a red line was drawn up and the Muslims were protected by the French elements and the Sangaris forces, and that after the confrontation between the two communities, the Muslims found themselves enclaved in Boda.

As regards the Yekatom Defence's arguments that Mr Yekatom was not aware of the 'broader' operation concerning the Bangui Attack, the Chamber finds that the alleged coordinated nature of the Bangui Attack does not rest on Mr Yekatom's awareness of its broader contours. Given the mode of responsibility attributed to him, Mr Yekatom would not have needed to be aware of the 'respective or collective' nature of the Bangui Attack or the conduct of the other groups or leaders that participated in it. Admittedly, in theory, while Mr Yekatom's awareness of the 'broader' Bangui Attack would have been a factor positively demonstrating coordination, the lack thereof does not mean that the Bangui Attack was not otherwise coordinated.

Accordingly, in assessing the evidence in light of the Defence's challenges, the Chamber has first addressed the coordinated nature of the Bangui Attack and then turned to the actions attributed to Mr Yekatom and his group. As set out below, the coordinated nature of the Bangui Attack is indeed demonstrated with and without having regard to Mr Yekatom's purported awareness. In the early morning hours of 5 December 2013, the Anti-Balaka mounted a coordinated attack on Bangui, including in Boeing and Cattin. The plan to mount an attack on Bangui existed at least as of 30 November 2013. Anti-Balaka elements and groups travelled from the provinces to arrive close to Bangui before 5 December 2013. During their move from the provinces to Bangui, Anti-Balaka chiefs communicated across their groups, kept and maintained records or lists of elements, armed themselves, and waited at common locations and prepared for an attack on Bangui. Mr Ngaïssona provided funds to Anti-Balaka elements that participated in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. By the beginning of December 2013, several thousand Anti-Balaka elements had arrived at the outskirts of Bangui to participate in an attack. News about an impending attack on Bangui circulated in various circles within the Anti-Balaka leadership. Mr Ngaïssona knew that an attack would take place on Bangui. The Anti-Balaka participating in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 shared the same goal, which was to target Seleka positions in Bangui with a view to 'getting rid of Djotodia' and 'chasing out the Seleka', which included systematic targeting of Muslim civilians. Various Anti-Balaka groups that participated in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 had common leaders, who coordinated their actions and instructed them. Anti-Balaka groups that reassembled close to Bangui prior to the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013 were each assigned a specific target within Bangui and instructed to begin the attack on the respective targets at 05:00 on 5 December 2013. The attack was carried out as planned, resulting in clashes between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka in several locations in Bangui, including Boeing, with the Anti-Balaka beginning to retreat around 10:00 the same day. Later that day, FROCCA issued a radio statement in relation to the attack on Bangui, referring to it as '\[l\]e rétablissement de l'ordre fonctionnel' and stating that the Anti-Balaka 'sont des Centrafricains pour aller libérer leur pays des jougs des djihadistes venus du D\[arfour\], du T\[chad\], du S\[oudan\]'. The attacks on Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 were coordinated with each other.

Turning to the first indicator of coordination, the Chamber finds that a plan to attack Bangui existed, at least, as of 30 November 2013, of which Mr Ngaïssona was aware.
The Chamber finds that, in November 2013, Mr Ngaïssona and Bernard Mokom met certain individuals in Yaoundé, Cameroon, in relation to a future attack on Bangui.

Joachim Kokaté described a meeting that he himself attended, towards the 'end of November' 2013, with Mr Ngaïssona, Eric Danboy, Franklin Bozizé and Bernard Mokom, during which Mr Ngaïssona stated that it would not be long before 'his troops' attacked the Seleka, of which they would be notified in due time, telling them that there would be 'an imminent attack on Bangui'.

P-0884 testified that he would talk to Mr Ngaïssona 'during this period'; P-0884 told Mr Ngaïssona that the situation was difficult and that the Seleka were continuing to attack the population, to which the latter answered, 'when I come back \[...\], one day God will allow the country to be freed'. The Chamber further notes Adrien Poussou's phone call with Mr Ngaïssona around 30 November 2013 after the witness was appointed as a minister in Michel Djotodia's government. Adrien Poussou said that, in his conversation with Mr Ngaïssona, the word 'attack' was not used, but everything Mr Ngaïssona was saying, the references he was using, insinuated that there would be an attack -- Mr Ngaïssona said the regime was going to topple in a short time, and asked what the witness was going to Bangui to do. Adrien Poussou based his conclusion on his experience within FROCCA and what they imagined that François Bozizé and his entourage were up to, as well as information of public knowledge that François Bozizé was organising his supporters with a view to attacking Bangui. In the witness's view, it was impossible to imagine Michel Djotodia falling in a peaceful way, or at least falling and being replaced by François Bozizé in a peaceful manner. Adrien Poussou did not discuss with Mr Ngaïssona the latter's sources or how he came to know about this.

Turning to the second indicator of coordination, as set out below, the Chamber finds that various groups of Anti-Balaka elements began moving from the provinces to Bangui before 5 December 2013.

The Prosecution submits that under Maxime Mokom's coordination, Anti-Balaka groups from Gobere, Bossangoa, Bouca, Bouar, and Bossembélé marched south to carry out the Bangui Attack. The Ngaïssona Defence argues that the evidence is inconsistent on the groups' progression out of Gobere and the subsequent attacks in the region.

paragraph_text_preview: At the outset, having regard to the agreed maps, the Chamber notes that there are two primary roadways from the northern Bossangoa region to Bangui (through Bouca -- Damara and Bossembélé -- Boali), and one from Bouar through Yaloké -- Bossembélé -- Boali. From the southern end of Bangui, the river Oubangui runs between the CAR and the Democratic Republic of Congo with Zongo on the immediate other side of the river. On the western side of Bangui lies the M'Poko airport and the M'Poko river. Bimbo lies on the southwest end of Bangui.

The Chamber has first assessed evidence concerning the elements entering into Bangui from these directions and then examined where these elements gathered, or otherwise reassembled, prior to the Bangui Attack.

Describing generally the movement of Anti-Balaka elements, P-0884, a Gbaya from Bossangoa who received information directly from actors in the field, testified that, for the attack, people came from 'everywhere', including from Bossembélé, Bossangoa, Bambari, Sibut, Bogangolo and Damara. P-0884 said that these people, some of whom went on foot, arrived from the north-east, north and south of the country, and that 'their convergence point was Bangui'. P-0876 also said that, before the Bangui Attack, 'people continued to come in from the hinterlands, on foot, on dirt tracks, through the forest as they converged on Bangui'. P-1847 said generally that the young Anti-Balaka of the Bossangoa area, supported by members of the PG, walked towards Bangui for the Bangui Attack. Alfred Legrand Ngaya said that he did not know how the young people from the villages all knew to come to Bangui on 5 December 2013, and did not know in advance that they were coming.

The evidence shows that some of these individuals had organised themselves in distinct groups within their respective provinces with varying compositions, and then began making their way to Bangui in advance of the Bangui Attack, merging with other groups along the way. The Chamber has considered the movement of some of these Anti-Balaka groups, as discussed further below, from the provinces to Bangui to assess the level of organisation and coordination prior to the Bangui Attack.

paragraph_text_preview: In what follows, the Chamber finds that while these groups progressed at a different pace and took different routes to reach Bangui, this movement occurred along specific axes ending at Bangui.

From the north, groups that were based around Gobere and Bossangoa travelled through villages along two main axes, discussed separately below. P-2269 said that individuals that were in Gobere had divided themselves into groups, each with their own chief, and took different routes to go to Bangui; some groups went to other towns to attack areas controlled by the Seleka, like Bouca and Bossangoa; however, not every group went to Bangui, some people stayed behind at the Gobere base and in Bossangoa. P-2602, one of the group leaders at Gobere commanded by Danboy Dedane, stated that military and civilians at Gobere were joined by other people from the villages on the way to Bangui. P-0889, who was himself not in Gobere, put it more simplistically insofar as he claimed that 'all Anti-Balaka leaders' met in Gobere to get gris-gris and then went into different directions, to reach Bangui on 5 December 2013.

footnote_content: The Chamber notes P-2658's evidence that the elements at Gobere were divided into six groups with many people each (*see* P-2658 Statement, CAR-OTP-2126-0012-R02, at 0027, para. 97). The Chamber further notes that P-2658 noticed 'Dedane' meeting with other chiefs of groups there 'every morning' but said that he himself was not present during those meetings and could only see them speaking from a distance (*see* P-2658: T-135, p. 42, lines 6 -- 25, p. 44, line 6 -- p. 45, line 15). The Chamber considers that this difference in the number of groups at Gobere is inconsequential for the purposes of the present discussion.

P-0954 also denied that his group intended to attack Bangui on '6 December' 2013 (*see* P-0954: T-167, p. 46, lines 17-23). paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that witnesses Brice Emotion Namsio and P-2232 were among those in Zongo at the time and who crossed over to Bangui to participate in the Bangui Attack, facilitated by Maxime Mokom.

P-2232 said that Maxime Mokom asked people in Zongo to cross over to Bangui, towards Saint Paul, after which they went up to Ndress to get to 'their various bases'. P-2232 explained how they crossed the river from Zongo to Bangui and how many persons crossed to participate in the attack. P-2232 named, among others, Lieutenant Bruno Semdiro and Brice Emotion Namsio, as soldiers that crossed from Zongo to Bangui to participate in the Bangui Attack. He indicated that civilians also joined them and crossed to Bangui to participate in the fights. P-2232 said that Maxime Mokom paid 500 CFA per person to a canoeist, brought provisions and other material, and the canoeist helped them cross over; they arrived near the French Embassy, from where, they walked towards Ndress, and then Boy-Rabe. P-2232 said that Maxime Mokom made soldiers in Zongo cross to the other side to go to Bangui and 'all the soldiers' came to Zongo in order to ultimately go to Bangui. P-2232 said that there were quite a lot of civilians in the Anti-Balaka, so the intention was to coordinate the Bangui Attack ('sur le mouvement anti-balaka, il y avait beaucoup plus que des... des civils, donc, l'intention, c'était de coordonner l'attaque du 5 décembre').

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that Mr Yekatom was also in Zongo at the end of 2013 but crossed over separately to form his group and set up a base in Gbangba. Level of communication between the Anti-Balaka chiefs across the various groups during their advance to Bangui

Turning to the third indicator of coordination, as set out below, the Chamber finds that members of these Anti-Balaka groups were in communication with each other about their location, size, and operational needs during their movement from the provinces to Bangui prior to 5 December 2013. Communications between 'chiefs' on the ground

Chiefs in the provinces and those in Zongo were in regular contact with each other before their groups began their descent to Bangui. For example, P-2269, who was in Zongo before coming to Bossangoa, said that he would call Andjilo from Zongo and they 'spoke many times', agreeing to meet in Bouca. P-2269 also called 'other chiefs' like Thierry Lebene, Konaté, Richard Bejouane, Dedane, Benjamin Ouapoutou, and others, asking them to meet near Bouca. P-2269 also describes meeting and discussing with other chiefs in Gobere on what to do, receiving information from informants, listening to the radio, deciding to go to Bangui, and discussing tactics.

In assessing the frequency and the quality of communication that was possible amongst the various groups and their chiefs before and during their descent to Bangui, the Chamber also considered the circumstances in which such communication was taking place. For example, some witnesses have described the difficulty in accessing telephone networks in the bush. P-2251 said that there was no possibility of telephone communication in the bush because there were no networks; it was only until they reached Bangui on 5 December that people started having telephones to be able to communicate. P-1521, a combatant in Andjilo's group, agreed that before the Bangui Attack, he did not have any communication tools, including a Thuraya. P-2027, a senior FACA member who had trained both Dedane and Ndangba before the conflict, stated that, when he was in Yaoundé, he spoke to both of them over the phone, and they were calling him from Bossangoa because that is where they could pick up a phone signal, but they had no more phone contact until after they reached Bangui.

During their descent to Bangui, chiefs of the various Anti-Balaka groups communicated with each other, sometimes in person, along the way to exchange information. For example, when P-2602 was coming from Bossangoa to go to Bossembélé, he stopped at Bogangolo to give instructions to those 'coming from Bouca before they could continue to Bangui', including that they were 'not to attack Damara' but 'leave straight for Bangui', as the group that was in Sibut would attack Damara; P-2602 stated that those who had come from Bouca had walked for a long distance and were tired, and had among them 'those who knew their thing very well' and they 'had to maintain the energy in order to attack the capital'. P-2602 stated that they were all heading to Bangui.

The Chamber does not find Didier Ouebio's testimony credible on this aspect. Didier Ouebio's opinion that military tacticians were the only ones to manage what was happening in the country does not accord with his earlier unfiltered words on Facebook that Mokom and Mr Ngaïssona intended to manage military actions. The witness specified that he knew the names of those who were in Gobere since he was the one who was responsible for drawing up the lists of companies.

Turning to the fifth indicator of coordination, as set out below, the Chamber finds that the Anti-Balaka groups that were moving to Bangui reassembled and waited at common locations close to Bangui and prepared for an attack. The fact that these Anti-Balaka elements and groups assembled in common locations prior to the attack was, in itself, a strong indicator of the planned nature of the Bangui Attack.

The Prosecution submits that the Anti-Balaka elements that were marching south for the Bangui Attack assembled mostly behind the Boy-Rabe hill, also known as the Bas-Oubangui hill or Gbazabangui hill, but also elsewhere, including in Boeing. It submits that civilians joining along the way were put under the command of Anti-Balaka leaders.

P-0876 testified that he did not know whether all the elements were present during that first meeting or whether the intention was 'to create an impression' in the second meeting, but that nonetheless there had been a significant increase in the number of elements (*see* P-0876: T-085, p. 34, line 21 -- p. 36, line 1; P-0876 Interview Transcript, CAR-OTP-2046-0324, at 0336, lines 412-414). The Chamber has considered these estimates when appreciating the level of organisation and coordination it would have required of their chiefs to ensure that an attack take place as planned, in that a higher number speaks to a higher level of organisation required. In the view of the Chamber, considering the number of elements from different locations descending approximately at the same time, gathering at the same locations, preparing and being ready to attack on a specific date, demonstrates a very high level of coordination and organisation. Financing, arming and efforts to obtain weapons and ammunition along the way to Bangui

Turning to the seventh indicator of coordination, as set out below, the Chamber finds that Mr Ngaïssona provided funds to Anti-Balaka elements that participated in the Bangui Attack. It finds that the Anti-Balaka groups were arming during their move from the provinces to Bangui.

The Prosecution argues that Mr Ngaïssona was involved in financing and arming Anti-Balaka elements in October 2013, and, from November 2013 onwards, financing the Anti-Balaka elements from Cameroon and Zongo to arrive in Bangui for the Bangui Attack. The Prosecution submits that Mr Ngaïssona 'promised financial support' for the Bangui Attack.

paragraph_text_preview: The evidence discussed below shows how the Anti-Balaka elements were armed and how some of the weapons and ammunitions were obtained prior to the Bangui Attack. P-0884 was also in contact with Mr Ngaïssona around this time.

Jean-Jacques Demafouth testified that he knew about the attack on Bangui before it happened. At the time, he was advisor for security, had his old intelligence network, and had also infiltrated the Anti-Balaka network because they were beginning to encircle Bangui, PK12, on the hills surrounding Bangui, and Mbaïki, in Bimbo, at Cattin, Boeing, 7^th^ arrondissement. He personally started getting worried and wondered what was happening in the country. Jean-Jacques Demafouth said that there were people who were said to be 'Anti-Balaka leaders' and whom he knew, and they talked to him, in particular Léopold Bara whom the witness thought to be one of the leaders in Bangui at the time. The witness had seen them give a press conference at the Ledger hotel talking on behalf of a 'revolutionary organisation that was about to arrive'. Léopold Bara later told the witness that these were the 'Anti-Balaka', told him about sites in PK12, and gave him names of some leaders, of FACA who were in the movement.

In light of this, while the Chamber cannot reach a conclusion on the exact reason the Bangui Attack appears to have been postponed from 1 to 5 December 2013, there is no doubt that information about an imminent attack on Bangui was circulating at various organisational levels within the Anti-Balaka.

This was also true of certain circles outside the Anti-Balaka. In this regard, the Chamber has considered evidence from witnesses, who were not part of the Anti-Balaka circles, that showed that 'rumours' about an impending attack by the Anti-Balaka were circulating in Bangui. To the Chamber, this depicted the prevailing sentiment, particularly amongst the Muslim population.

P-1521, who was present when the decisions of when and where to attack were taken, said that there were Seleka bases at PK12, so some groups would try to attack them at '36 Villas' and 'Gobongo'; these locations were chosen because Seleka elements were based in the areas that they targeted. P-0876 explains that he later heard that the Anti-Balaka's plan was to target several Seleka positions at the same time: Camp Kassai, the Sapeurs-Pompiers base, the camp Béal, the base in Don Bosco near the airport, among others.
