The evidence shows that the attack was to begin between 04:00 and 05:00 on 5 December 2013. For those that were on the hills behind Bangui, this meant that the descent had to begin in time to reach Bangui at the designated time. P-0306 said that they stayed on the back side of the hills in Bangui until 5 December 2013 when they received the decision to enter Bangui. P-0306 indicated that the 'programme' or 'plan' to attack Bangui on 5 December was set up from 1 to 3 December 2013; but it was on 4 December that 'everybody came down' to attack Bangui. P-0306 said that on 5 December 2013, after receiving instructions to enter Bangui, they took up the 'light weapons' they had taken from the Seleka and entered Bangui very early in the morning. According to P-0975, the Anti-Balaka group posted on Boy-Rabe hill entered Bangui at 04:00 on 5 December 2013. P-0965 also said that the attack started at 04:00 in the morning of 5 December. Brice Emotion Namsio, who was on the hill behind Boy-Rabe on 4 December 2013, stated that the elements left their base around midnight to come down to Bangui, and that it was a two-hours walk; the attack took place in the early morning, it had been decided that the attack would start at 05:00.

The Chamber has noted the routes adopted for the attack that were in keeping with the pre-decided locations and targets. The Anti-Balaka coming in from the north proceeded in three main directions: towards PK12 (direction northwest), towards 4^th^ arrondissement (direction south), and Camp Kassai (direction southeast).

footnote_content: P-2251 Statement, CAR-OTP-2093-0045-R01, at 0059, para. 93; Map (annotated by P-2251), CAR-OTP-2093-0084.
paragraph_text_preview: P-2251 and P-1521 annotated maps showing the routes taken by the Anti-Balaka elements that were attacking from the northern side of Bangui. P-2251 marked a map with (i) the route that his group took from Nguito; (ii) the route that Andjilo's group took through the 4^th^ arrondissement in Bangui, attacking 36 Villas and retreating to Cité Jean XXIII; (iii) the route that the group who went to Camp Kassai took over the hill; (iv) the route of the group that attacked PK10 and PK12 leaving from Kpata. P-2251 thought that these targets - notably Boy-Rabe, Camp Kassai and PK12 - were picked because they were informed that this were where 'the Seleka were harassing population'. P-1521 also annotated a map showing the 'plan' of the Bangui Attack, that mirrors the main directions taken by the different groups that day. P-1521 described one group going directly to 4^th^ arrondissement and another to Camp Kassai toward Camp de Roux, and the third going to PK12, said that 'these three directions' were the ones they needed to attack; he added that everyone was to engage 'where they can fight' and that it was 'all a bit mixed up'.

Turning to the thirteenth indicator of coordination, as set out below, the Chamber finds that the Bangui Attack was carried out as planned, with the instructions to start at 05:00 on 5 December 2013, resulting in clashes between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka in several locations in Bangui, with the Anti-Balaka beginning to retreat around 10:00 the same day.
The Prosecution submits that at around 10:00, the Anti-Balaka withdrew in face of the Seleka, notably behind the Bas-Oubangui hill, located behind the Boy-Rabe neighbourhood.

P-0975 stated that at 10:00 on 5 December 2013, Andjilo instructed them to retreat to the Boy-Rabe hill because the Seleka were too strong, he himself was with Andjilo when they retreated to Boy-Rabe. Brice Emotion Namsio agreed that around 10:00 the attack was considered as 'ended' and the attack itself did not last, given the resources that the Anti-Balaka had in their possession and given the arsenal used by the Seleka; in the witness's opinion, 'the Balaka could not do anything so the Balaka decided to avoid a bloodbath so that the effects should not fall once again on other people'. The witness, commenting on a photograph of what appear to be dead Anti-Balaka in front of the National Assembly, said that many Anti-Balaka used sticks and all of this happened after the reprisals were carried out by the tank battalions of the 'firefighters' brigade'. P-2251 stated that a lot of people from his group were killed or injured during the Bangui Attack and that it was very difficult; his group went through Boy-Rabe to the National Assembly and that is where the Seleka attacked them 'seriously', after which he managed to 'escape' to Camp Obrou. P-2251 agreed that on 5 December 2013, his group was so disorganised and ill-equipped and they did not have military equipment for the fighting, except for hunting rifles and pots, while, on the other hand, the Seleka had heavy weaponry and military vehicles so they could not really face up to them; he thought that since the Anti-Balaka had a strategy of making noise with pots and pans, they were able to 'succeed' and said that the Anti-Balaka were fighting while retreating and that is why there were many people that were injured and even killed.

Conclusion

Having regard to the conclusions for each of these indicators, the Chamber finds that the Bangui Attack was highly coordinated. Furthermore, having regard to its conclusions on the Bossangoa Attack, the Chamber finds that the Bangui Attack and the Bossangoa Attack assessed together also reflect a similarly high level of coordination with each other.

Before turning to the arguments by the Defence challenging the coordinated nature of the attack, the Chamber recalls some of its conclusions based on the evidence thusfar. The Chamber found that a plan encompassing the Bangui Attack existed as of 30 November 2013. The Anti-Balaka elements from the provinces that had been moving towards Bangui were mobilised by their chiefs to arrive in Bangui prior to 5 December 2013. These comprised of both FACA members and civilians and more joined as the groups moved towards Bangui. During this time, the various Anti-Balaka chiefs of these groups remained in regular contact amongst each other to share information, materiel, and elements. A significant number of these chiefs were in contact with Maxime Mokom directly over the phone. Some Anti-Balaka groups started keeping track of the elements within their groups by maintaining lists that were shared with their chiefs. By the end of November 2013, the Anti-Balaka groups started gathering around the perimeter of Bangui in preparation for the Bangui Attack.

The gathering occurred in a manner permitting the Anti-Balaka elements to be able to enter Bangui from the north, north-east, south-west and south. While the exact number of elements at this stage of the events is not known, it ranged in the thousands. Information about an impending attack began to circulate as early as end-November 2013 and initially, the Bangui Attack was planned for 1 December 2013, but this was postponed to 5 December 2013. Meanwhile, an attack took place in Boali on 3 December 2013, which was reported in the news. Between 1-5 December 2013, the Anti-Balaka elements, along with their chiefs, prepared, planned, and decided on specific locations to target in Bangui. These locations corresponded to known Seleka bases. Elements from the provinces were paired with those that were familiar with the neighbourhoods in Bangui to be able to find their way. The purpose of the attack shared among the elements was to 'get rid' of the Seleka.

The Anti-Balaka elements gathered together and completed their final preparations in the night of 4 December 2013 to begin the attack from all directions to enter Bangui by 5:00 on 5 December 2013. They then carried out the attack along pre-decided routes, reaching the target locations and starting the offence at the same time. The Seleka repelled the attack successfully, forcing the Anti-Balaka to retreat within a few hours.

The Chamber further recalls that later that day, on 5 December 2013, FROCCA issued a radio statement in relation to the attack on Bangui, referring to it as '\[l\]e rétablissement de l'ordre fonctionnel' and stating that the Anti-Balaka 'sont des Centrafricains pour aller libérer leur pays des jougs des djihadistes venus du D\[arfour\], du T\[chad\], du S\[oudan\]'.

The Chamber finds that these attacks were highly coordinated despite claims of certain witnesses that the various Anti-Balaka groups were independent, and came from 'everywhere', not knowing each other, and did not have a political aim or agenda.

First, the Chamber draws a distinction between (i) the coordinated nature of the Bangui Attack; (ii) the coordination of the Anti-Balaka as a movement; and (iii) the 'national coordination' setup formally in the months after the Bangui Attack.

The Chamber grants that the existence of an underlying cohesive (or coordinated) movement of political ideology could have positively demonstrated a coordinated attack. The reverse is not true. A political movement lacking in coordination does not demonstrate that individuals and groups cannot actualise coordinated action. Nonetheless, the Chamber has considered the rhetoric of how uncoordinated the Anti-Balaka were as a movement prior to the Bangui Attack, but it did not change the Chamber's conclusions that the attack itself was coordinated.

Second, in the Chamber's view, some level of self-organisation within groups of civilians, or with the involvement of FACA members, is not mutually exclusive to there being an overarching coordination at a 'higher' level, political or otherwise. While the evidence does point to civilians self-organising in the provinces, there is a wealth of evidence showing that, at least as of November 2013, these civilians, together with FACA members, had been actively mobilised in preparation for an attack on Bangui. Indeed, a combined reading of the evidence in light of the Defence's arguments demonstrates that the purported self-led movement by civilians in the provinces was in fact channelled into common action by placing on it a common task.

paragraph_text_preview: Il y a trop de concïdences. C'est pourqoui je suppose que ça a été planifié quelque part. \[...\] Bon, si on disait: « Bon, un groupe a attaqué le matin vers 8 heures et d'autres ont été attaqués vers 11 heures \[phon.\] », là, on peut dire que : « Bon, peut... peut-être ça a suivi celui-là \[phon.\], ils ont vu que ça attaquait là-bas, on peut attaquer ici. » Mais c'etait le même jour, à la même heure, ils ont commencé tout...Fourth, in the view of the Chamber, coordination is not a function of singular command, as suggested by P-0876, neither is it prefaced on strict military hierarchy or political leadership. By its very definition, 'coordination' implies different elements that are organised to work together by one or more entities. In this respect, the Chamber has considered several indicia based on mutual assistance, cooperation, communication, and implementation within an overarching goal -- all of which are shown to exist on the facts and prior to the Bangui Attack. Therefore, in the view of the Chamber, the setting up of the Anti-Balaka national coordination formally only after 5 December 2013 did not mean that the Bangui Attack was not coordinated.

Lastly in this respect, the Chamber considers that the coordinated nature of the Bangui Attack was not premised on its success. The Chamber finds that, on the basis of the totality of the evidence discussed above, the manner in which the Bangui Attack was organised and carried out was highly coordinated. In this instance, even a failure to overpower the Seleka spoke to the unachieved yet common goals and targets. Involvement of Mr Yekatom Mr Yekatom's group coordinated with other Anti-Balaka groups to participate in the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013. In the months leading up to this attack, Mr Yekatom and his group armed and trained in the bush. The movement of Mr Yekatom's group in the bush, when superimposed onto those from other groups who proceeded towards Bangui along the same time frame, shows that this coordination had begun well before November 2013. In the afternoon of 4 December 2013, Mr Yekatom chose some of his elements and instructed them to move towards Bangui. The same day, the group arrived in Projet, situated near the M'Poko airport in Bangui. Mr Yekatom's instructions to his elements concerning the attack on 5 December 2013 were to fight the Seleka and included targeting sectors where 'Muslims' were to be found. Mr Yekatom's instructions were understood by the elements to accept that Muslim civilians would be killed as a result of the fighting based on his elements not having been trained or instructed to apply the principle of distinction during combat and bearing strong anti-Muslim sentiment and feelings of vengeance against the Seleka.

The Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom and Maxime Mokom may have been in contact during their time prior to the Bangui Attack. While the Chamber notes the Prosecution argument concerning the CDR between the numbers attributed to Mr Yekatom and Maxime Mokom, it cannot conclude anything about the actual contents of these calls and whether any exchanges indeed took place.

The Chamber also considers that Mr Yekatom's return to the CAR, grouping in locations close to Bangui, and arming prior to the Bangui Attack is similar to many other FACA members, some of whom have testified. In the Chamber's view, P-1339, a civilian element in Mr Yekatom's group, continued to conflate the Seleka with the Muslims in how he understood Mr Yekatom's instructions.

Having regard to the above, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom's instructions to his elements were to fight the Seleka and that it included targeting sectors where 'Muslims' were to be found. The Chamber also finds that Mr Yekatom's instructions were understood by the elements to accept that Muslim civilians would be killed as a result of the fighting. Prominently, Mr Yekatom did not instruct his elements to refrain from attacking civilians or civilian property.

Noting the above, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom was aware of how his elements would interpret his instructions to 'target those sectors where Muslims were to be found' and not restrict their attack to the Seleka. Mr Yekatom was aware that his instructions would be understood as also targeting Muslim civilians. The Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom was aware of the fact that his elements had not been trained in or instructed to apply the principle of distinction when engaging in combat. Accordingly, Mr Yekatom was aware that his elements would not apply the principle of distinction during combat.

In addition to the above, there is audio-visual evidence showing that elements of Mr Yekatom's group expressed anti-Muslim sentiments and conflated the Seleka and Djotodia with Muslims. The Chamber recalls that there is no evidence on the record indicating the date on which these videos were shot. Nonetheless, the Chamber has assessed this material together with what witnesses have said about them.

To ascertain whether there was coordination, the Chamber was not guided by a standard requiring perfect lines of communication between all levels, whether they be chiefs or elements, or requiring that information be shared democratically or fully across all groups. It was sufficient that these lines of communication existed and were used. The fact that information was being transmitted faithfully would have added to the Chamber's assessment. However, imperfect communication between chiefs and elements across different groups did not take away from the Chamber's conclusion that these groups were being coordinated in relation to the Bangui Attack. Conclusion
Having regard to the evidence discussed thus far, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom's group coordinated with other Anti-Balaka groups to participate in the Bangui Attack.

The Chamber has had regard to the fact that Mr Yekatom formed his group, composed of FACA members and civilians, following his return from Zongo. Mr Yekatom's group armed and trained in the bush and gathered on the south side of Bangui close to Projet, at the outskirts of Bangui. On the eve of the Bangui Attack, Mr Yekatom's group conducted reconnaissance missions to prepare for an impending attack the next morning. Mr Yekatom's group joined other groups coming from the Bossangoa area at Projet, and Mr Yekatom instructed his elements in advance of the attack. Mr Yekatom's group then launched the attack at the exact same time as the groups in other locations in Bangui at a pre-decided location where the Seleka were supposed to be present. Across the various Anti-Balaka groups, including Mr Yekatom's group, attacking the Seleka positions was also understood by the elements to target Muslim civilians.

The Chamber finds that the movement of Mr Yekatom's group in the bush, when superimposed onto those from other groups who proceeded towards Bangui along the same time frame, shows that this coordination had begun well before November 2013. Attack on Boeing Boeing Market On the night of 4 December 2013, Mr Yekatom and some of his elements visited the market in Boeing to assess its precise geographical location and conduct reconnaissance. The same night, Mr Yekatom instructed his elements to target Seleka positions along the Boeing-Cattin-PK5 direction. These instructions encompassed attacking the Muslim traders at the market in Boeing before moving along the route to PK5. In the early morning of 5 December 2013, Mr Yekatom launched the attack on Boeing by firing an automatic pistol in the air when his group reached the market in Boeing. The armed elements in the front continued and advanced together and fired at the Muslim traders who were present there. During this time, Mr Yekatom's elements shot in all directions. Those that were inside the shops fled. Mr Yekatom's group attacked the market in Boeing during their advance towards PK5 following Mr Yekatom's orders.

The Chamber now turns to the circumstances of Hassan's death.

The Prosecution submits that none of the Muslim traders Mr Yekatom and his group killed during the attack on the Boeing Market were fighters or actively took part in hostilities. The Yekatom Defence disagrees and submits that there is a 'reasonable inference' to be drawn that Hassan and the other traders at the Boeing Market were directly participating in hostilities on 5 December 2013. The Yekatom Defence argues that Hassan, having received information about 'the impending Operation', opted to spend the night at the market instead of at PK5 and would have shared this information with the other traders. The Yekatom Defence asserts that Hassan and the traders would have 'decided to take up a position at the market', 'equipped with Seleka firearms', given their 'membership (or at the very least, material links) with the Seleka'. This, it argues, does not allow for a finding that their use of firearms was 'merely in the exercise of their right to self-defence'.

paragraph_text_preview: The evidence outlined above shows that certain Seleka officials frequented Hassan's shop before 5 December 2013, and that they were known to personally interact with each other at the Boeing Market. The Chamber does not read the evidence of P-1339 and P-0884 to mean that Hassan was a member of the Seleka at the time of the Bangui Attack, or indeed before that attack. Further, the Chamber considers D29-4011's suggestion regarding Hassan being a member of the Seleka to be based on what she generally heard, and in any event unsupported by any other evidence.

paragraph_text_preview: The evidence outlined above shows that certain Seleka officials frequented Hassan's shop before 5 December 2013, and that they were known to personally interact with each other at the Boeing Market. In this regard, the Chamber recalls that Hassan was the delegate of the male Muslim traders at the Boeing Market at the time and that his duty, as described by P-2682, was to represent the traders before the authorities. The Chamber does not read the evidence of P-1339 and P-0884 to mean that Hassan was a member of the Seleka at the time of the Bangui Attack, or indeed before that attack. Further, the Chamber considers D29-4011's suggestion regarding Hassan being a member of the Seleka to be based on what she generally heard, and in any event unsupported by any other evidence.

Having regard to the above, the Chamber finds that Hassan personally interacted with certain Seleka officials prior to 5 December 2013 in his role as delegate of the male Muslim traders at the Boeing Market. The Chamber does not conclude on the basis of such interactions by themselves, and in light of the above evidence, that Hassan was a member of, or otherwise affiliated with, the Seleka at the time of his death on 5 December 2013.

Turning to the presence of the traders of the Boeing Market at their shops immediately before the events, P-2682 recalled that her husband had told her on the evening of 4 December 2013 that he would not go back to PK5 that night because 'there was a lot of tension in the air, \[...\] the information going around wasn't good and so he would rather stay there in order to protect his shop'. This accords with P-1339's recollection that during the night visit to the Boeing Market prior to the attack, most shopkeepers were sleeping inside their shops. The Chamber therefore infers that Muslim traders at the Boeing Market were sleeping in their shops in fear of 'rumours' about an imminent attack on Bangui. At the same time, the Chamber notes that Gaston Sallo mentioned that following an incident of robbery at the Boeing Market which took place before the Seleka arrived to Bangui, traders at the market ensured the security of their shops by watching over them and spending the nights there.

The Chamber notes that P-2682 described to the Chamber the impact that losing her spouse had on her life. P-2682 said that after the death of her husband, 'everything' was 'over'; she said that she could not stop thinking about him, especially when she is alone and reminisces about their life together; she recalled his generosity, especially towards her family, feeling lucky to have him as part of their family; she described becoming 'practically sick' when she lacks something and thinks about what he would do if he had been present. P-1339 recalled not being in a position to observe everything that was happening, as he himself was towards the back.

The Chamber notes the Yekatom Defence's submissions that P-1339's account 'remains inherently unreliable' since he initially stated that Mr Yekatom's group was 'not involved in the destruction of the Mosque' and subsequently reversed his position, thereby 'negating the probative value of either version'.

At the outset, having considered the Yekatom Defence's arguments in light of the charges, the Chamber notes the difference between an attack on the Boeing Mosque and its subsequent purported destruction. The Chamber recalls that Mr Yekatom is charged with 'directing an attack against a building dedicated to religion' pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(iv) of the Statute. In the view of the Chamber, whether and by whom the Boeing Mosque was later destroyed, dismantled, or otherwise taken apart, is not material to the charges.

Indeed, P-1339 drew a similar distinction during his testimony between the attack to the mosque -- which he attributed to Mr Yekatom's group -- and its subsequent destruction or dismantling -- which he said was carried out by the civilian population. In the view of the Chamber, this explains why P-1339, when repeatedly asked who destroyed the mosque, said that it was the civilian population, while at the same time maintained that it was Mr Yekatom's group that attacked the mosque. For example, and as discussed in further detail below, P-1339 confirmed that he had told the Prosecution that 'Alkanto shot a rocket' and the walls were 'destroyed by the population'.

Importantly, the Chamber considers that the subsequent destruction or taking apart of the Boeing Mosque by the population does not, in any way, exclude the possibility that Mr Yekatom's group attacked it first.

In light of this, the Chamber considers without merit the Yekatom Defence's submissions that P-1339 initially stated that Mr Yekatom's group were 'not involved in the destruction of the Boeing Mosque' and thereafter reversed his version. Likewise, it considers without merit the Yekatom Defence's submissions that 'P-1339's testimony in regard to 'the destruction of the Boeing Mosque' contains two irreconcilable accounts: one that would put the population 'solely responsible for the destruction of the Mosque', and another 'partially blaming' Mr Yekatom's group.

In light of the above, and contrary to the Yekatom Defence's submissions, the Chamber considers that Gaston Sallo's account of the Boeing Mosque being 'progressively dismantled by the civilian population' confirms the veracity of P-1339's account. Indeed, P-1339 indicated that he saw how the local population 'destroyed' the Boeing Mosque as the group withdrew, but at no point indicated that the mosque was fully destroyed that day. Regarding D29-4011's claim that the Boeing Mosque was intact when she arrived to her house on the day she witnessed the destruction of the mosque, the Chamber notes that while the witness stated that she passed by the 'église néo-apostolique' -- located close to the Boeing Mosque --, she did not specifically state that she walked close to or by the mosque or paid any particular attention to it. The Chamber further notes that from her house, D29-4011 did not seem to have full visibility of the entirety of the mosque's building. It is therefore of the view that D29-4011's account does not contradict that of P-1339 nor that of Gaston Sallo.

The Chamber now turns to the impact of the attack on the Boeing Mosque. The Chamber notes that Salehou Ndiaye provided the following explanation when asked how the memories of the Boeing Mosque emotionally affected him: It's difficult to explain what I feel within. It's difficult to describe what I feel, because I don't see why. When there is a problem, why is it that religious buildings are destroyed? For what reason? No matter what the problem might be, these are places where people take refuge when there are problems. And when I see this, it's true, it hurts. It's very \[...\] sad to see the house of God destroyed. This is my opinion. I might be wrong, but if there are problems and if someone goes to a religious place, a church or a mosque, in principle, the action should stop. But to destroy it, a church or a mosque, to my mind, that makes no sense. That's what I feel. When I see it, it brings back all the memories of everything that was destroyed.

Salehou Ndiaye said that about a year before giving testimony before the Court, his deputy, who stayed 'there', resumed prayers at the location of the Boeing Mosque by setting up a tent. The witness indicated that the Boeing Mosque has since been reopened.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber recalls the Prosecution's allegation that Mr Yekatom and his group attacked Boeing and Cattin, with the goal of advancing towards PK5, the predominantly Muslim neighbourhood in the third district.

The Prosecution submits that while attacking the Cattin neighbourhood in the morning of 5 December 2013, elements of Mr Yekatom's group 'killed at least one Muslim civilian, who was not actively taking part in the hostilities' in the execution of Mr Yekatom's 'orders to attack the Muslim civilian population on the eve of the attack'. Having regard to the above, the Chamber, for the reasons set out below, finds that 'the Anti-Balaka' killed a Muslim man in Cattin.

The Chamber considers that Salehou Ndiaye was unequivocal about the identity of the alleged perpetrators as 'the Anti-Balaka', clearly distinguished between 'the Anti-Balaka' and the local population and did not attribute the incident to the latter. While the witness was not able to observe the body of the victim when the Anti-Balaka elements beat him, he heard a man pleading for help and saw wounds on the body lying on the ground when he later saw the body. The Chamber notes that the witness saw the body lying on or close to the place where he had seen the Anti-Balaka elements. As to the wounds the body sustained, while the witness could not describe them in detail nor ascertain whether the man lying wounded on the ground had indeed died, it is clear from his description that these wounds were not sustained because of an exchange of fire. The description was consistent with Salehou Ndiaye's own impression that this man had been beaten by the Anti-Balaka.

Further, given the words used by the assailants and their description, the Chamber finds that the four Anti-Balaka elements that Salehou Ndiaye saw indeed targeted this Muslim man on the basis that he was an 'Arab'. Having regard to what the witness later learnt about this person, the Chamber infers that the victim eventually succumbed to the injuries inflicted on him by the Anti-Balaka.

The Chamber further considers Salehou Ndiaye's description that the man was lying on the ground when the Anti-Balaka approached him. The witness did not mention seeing any weapons or arms on or around the body. On this basis, the Chamber finds that this man was not armed at the time of his death nor otherwise engaged in combat.
The Chamber now turns to whether 'the Anti-Balaka' referred to by Salehou Ndiaye was a reference to elements in Mr Yekatom's group.

The Yekatom Defence disputes that Mr Yekatom's elements could have been present there at the same time that Salehou Ndiaye observed the killing. Referring to audio-visual evidence, the Yekatom Defence submits that members of Mr Yekatom's group were engaged with the Seleka forces on the Cattin road at 08:00 'latest' and that the Seleka pursued Mr Yekatom's group 'around the Cattin crossroad along the Dameca road, past the Dameca factory' by 08:51 and westward from Cattin to M'Poko Bac river by 10:29. It also argues that since there were 'multiple groups' of Anti-Balaka present in and around Boeing at the time, including Modibo and his group, this killing cannot be 'automatically' attributed to Mr Yekatom's group.

While the Yekatom Defence points to evidence from P-0884, Brice Emotion Namsio and P-1521 regarding the presence of other Anti-Balaka groups 'in an around Boeing, both before 5^th^ December and afterwards', the Chamber finds that such evidence does not support its assertion. P-0884 recalled Modibo and his group specifically not being in Boeing on 5 December 2013 but attacking the National Assembly. P-0884 further recalled Ngremangou's group composed of 'military men' being in Boeing before 5 December 2013 and remaining there 'until Djotodia left', which the Chamber understands to be a reference to Mr Yekatom's group. The same holds true for Brice Emotion Namsio, who stated that some of Mr Yekatom's elements were in Boeing on that day and 'attacked' KM5 and PK9. P-1521 did not have direct or accurate information about Mr Yekatom's group or the 'Boeing team' that attacked on the '6^th^ or the 7^th^' of December 2013. Asked 'who led the Boeing group', P-1521 recalled certain names generally, including Ngremangou, Mr Yekatom, Sylvestre Yagouzou, Sebastien Wenezoui, Bertin Nganabeam, Bama Clement and Modibo; and said that on the 5^th^, 6^th^, or the 7^th^, 'we did not have any contact with them'. The Chamber also has regard to P-0889's evidence concerning the presence of certain Anti-Balaka in Boeing, including Modibo Honoré, Yvon Donoh, Sylvestre Yagouzou, and Sébastien Wenezoui. P-0889, asked specifically if these groups were in Boeing 'before' 5 December 2013, said that he could not confirm and that he would not have known if they were there, because he was in Zongo at the time; he clarified that his sketch of the Anti-Balaka bases in Boeing was made in relation to when he went to Boeing 'after' 5 December 2013.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber now turns to the Prosecution's allegation that someone reported the killing of a Muslim civilian by Anti-Balaka in Cattin during the attack on 5 December 2013. The Chamber finds that without further evidence, it is unable to conclude that this alleged killing took place or that it refers to the same event as described by Salehou Ndiaye.

Lastly in respect of the events in Cattin, the Chamber notes that the Yekatom Defence challenges 'P-1339's uncorroborated account of the killing of a moto-driver in Cattin'. In this regard, it notes that P-1339 testified that during the Bangui Attack, seemingly in Cattin, 'a young Muslim who was on a motorcycle' fell during a skirmish and 'they' killed him and torched his motorbike. In the absence of any further information about the alleged victim and perpetrators, as well as on the circumstances of the alleged killing, the Chamber is unable to reach any conclusion in this regard. Dislocation of Muslims from Boeing and Cattin From 5 December 2013 onwards, the majority of Muslims of Boeing and Cattin, including Salehou Ndiaye and P-2682, fled to PK5 in Bangui, while some others fled to other parts of the CAR, in the context of the attack by Mr Yekatom's group on Boeing and Cattin. Muslim persons who fled to PK5 continued to fear for their security because of the presence of the Anti-Balaka around PK5 and Bangui generally. With the influx of Muslims fleeing the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, PK5 became overcrowded, practically uninhabitable, and unsafe. As a result, some Muslims, including Salehou Ndiaye and P-2682, then fled to neighbouring countries fearing for their safety.

The Chamber notes that the Prosecution points to two sets of events attributed to Mr Yekatom's group that led the Muslims to flee from Boeing and Cattin on 5 December 2013 to PK5. First, Mr Yekatom's 'attack against the Muslim civilian population of B\[oeing\] and C\[attin\] on 5 December 2013'. Second, 'the crimes that his elements continued to commit, under his leadership, against this population' while based at Yamwara. The Prosecution submits that Muslims from Boeing and Cattin fled to PK5 as this was 'the only safe place' for them in Bangui, and to other parts of the CAR and neighbouring countries. The Prosecution submits that most of the displaced Muslims at PK5 were eventually evacuated to neighbouring countries, including Chad and Cameroon, in convoys secured by heavy military escorts. The Prosecution argues that the 'forced departure of the Muslim civilian population from Bangui' was one of the 'objectives' of the Anti-Balaka who took part in the attack, including Mr Yekatom and his group.

In assessing the circumstances relevant to the allegations concerning displacement, the Chamber has considered (i) fear and threats to physical security; (ii) the lack of freedom of movement; (iii) the living conditions at PK5; and (iv) the fear of being identified as a Muslim following the events.

As regards the climate of fear and threats to physical security, the Chamber finds that Muslims who fled to PK5 continued to feel threatened by the Anti-Balaka's presence around PK5 and Bangui generally. P-1865, who sought refuge at PK5 at the time, stated that they could not exit PK5 as they were afraid of the Anti-Balaka, who were in the other neighbourhoods of Bangui.

P-2472 indicated that after the Bangui Attack, there were 'continuous attacks by the Anti-Balaka' against the Muslim population in Bangui for about three months, the Muslims living in PK5 were 'encircled' and could not get out, and they spent months unable to sleep, 'in constant fear of being attacked'.

On the basis of the above, the Chamber finds that the majority of Muslims, including Salehou Ndiaye and P-2682, fled Boeing and Cattin to PK5, while some others fled to other parts of the CAR, in the context of the attack by Mr Yekatom's group on Boeing and Cattin. Muslim persons who fled to PK5 continued to fear for their security because of the presence of the Anti-Balaka around PK5 and Bangui generally. With the influx of Muslims fleeing the attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013, PK5 became overcrowded, uninhabitable, and unsafe. As a result, some Muslims, including Salehou Ndiaye and P-2682, then fled to neighbouring countries fearing for their safety. In this regard, the Chamber recalls the abundant evidence on the case record pointing to the massive displacement of the Muslim population of Bangui to PK5 and to other parts within and outside of the CAR, in the context of the Bangui Attack.

During this period, the people who fled endured the loss of their family members, loss of their home, loss of their belongings, and sense of material and non-material unsafety for prolonged periods. During their stay in PK5, they lived through uninhabitable living conditions that aggravated this loss. P-2682 mourned her husband in this environment.

Unfolding of the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 On 5 December 2013, in coordination with the Anti-Balaka attack on Bangui on the same day, Anti-Balaka elements, divided into two groups led by Florent Kema and Théophile Ndangba, respectively, carried out an attack on the town of Bossangoa. The attack started at approximately 13:00 and lasted until the late afternoon or early evening. During the attack, the Anti-Balaka targeted residential areas, including the Boro neighbourhood, generally known as the Muslim neighbourhood in Bossangoa, with the intention of showing that the Anti-Balaka were attacking not only Bangui but also in the provinces, and to 'free' the town from Seleka and all Muslims, thereby targeting Muslim civilians and drawing no distinction between them and the Seleka. During the attack, the Anti-Balaka was well armed, with some AK-47s and RPGs, as well as hunting weapons.

The Anti-Balaka from Gobere arrived near Bossangoa a few days before the Bossangoa Attack. Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana, an Anti-Balaka element who participated in the Bossangoa Attack, stated that he was secretary for chief Alexis Mandago (also known as 'Sol Sol'), who told them that their group was going with Florent Kema and Ndangba to Bossangoa. The witness testified that the Anti-Balaka arrived 30 kilometres away from Bossangoa between 2 and 3 December 2013 and, as they did not expect to attack Bossangoa on 5 December, had a three-day fast to ask for God's blessings prior to fighting.

The evidence before the Chamber shows that the goal of the Bossangoa Attack, conducted in coordination with the Bangui Attack, was to chase away the Seleka as well as all Muslims from the town, and from the Ouham prefecture more generally.

Bearing in mind that it is unclear on which basis the witness made these assertions, while Jo-Brice Ouabira Dana in contrast had direct insight into this Anti-Balaka's group's objectives, the Chamber does not rely on D30-4608 in this regard.

There is evidence that the Anti-Balaka perceived the Muslims in Bossangoa as being associated with or part of the Seleka, as well as armed. The Ngaïssona Defence submits in this regard that a 'substantial number' of individuals in the Muslim population in Bossangoa joined the ranks of the Seleka or collaborated with them, that Muslim civilians bore arms in the months before the Bossangoa Attack, and mixed up with the Seleka. The Chamber finds that while some Muslims may have joined the Seleka and some collaborated, the great majority of Muslims in Bossangoa did not join and were not otherwise armed at the time of the attack.

The evidence before the Chamber shows that the Anti-Balaka groups that had come to Bossangoa, upon hearing that the Bangui Attack had taken place, started their attack in Bossangoa to ensure both attacks were coordinated.

In particular, Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana testified that at 05:00 on 5 December 2013, they heard over RFI radio that Bangui had been attacked. P-2602 similarly stated that before they attacked Bossangoa, they heard about the Bangui Attack and that some of their men had died.

In relation to whom the Anti-Balaka attacked while advancing through Bossangoa, the Chamber notes the evidence of Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana, an Anti-Balaka element who participated in the attack, according to which they assumed that if someone stayed in a house as opposed to fleeing, the person had a weapon to defend himself. According to Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana, the attack was against the Seleka who were bearing arms, but he could not know who was military or civilian and fought all individuals bearing arms. The Chamber considers this evidence in the context of the same witness's explanation according to which 'whoever was a Muslim was a Seleka' in Bossangoa, and that for Christians of Bossangoa to 'live in peace' and go 'back to their lives', the Anti-Balaka 'cleansed' the houses in Bossangoa because the houses were 'dirty of the Seleka'. It can be inferred from the evidence of this witness, who participated in the attack, that no distinction was made between Muslim civilians and members of the Seleka.

On the basis of the above, and contrary to the Ngaïssona Defence's argument that a large proportion of Muslim civilians actively participated in the Bossangoa Attack, the Chamber finds that while some Muslim civilians may have been armed during the Bossangoa Attack, the large majority were not, as is also evidenced by their fleeing in great numbers to the École de la Liberté in the face of the attack. Attack near the Imam Naffi's residence in the Boro neighbourhoodThe residence of the imam of Bossangoa, Imam Naffi, was located near the Boro neighourhood, in the 'Arabe' neighbourhood. P-2049 described the location of the imam's residence and estimated that it could take between seven and 10 minutes to walk from the mosque in Boro to the imam's house.

Imam Naffi was warned about the Bossangoa Attack before it started. P-2049 testified that Imam Naffi said that FOMAC had warned him about the attack and to take refuge at the École de la Liberté where the FOMAC elements were securing displaced persons at that time.

Other witnesses provided similar evidence. P-2200 stated that at around 12:00 on 5 December 2013, 'UDAC' soldiers from Guinea and Cameroon came to the neighbourhood to advise Muslims to shelter in the school. P-2200 stated that about 40 or 50 people first sought refuge at his residence. P-2200 stated that from 13:00, they began to hear detonations and around one hour afterwards went to the school as the soldiers had advised. P-2200 stated that they were escorted by the 'UDAC' soldiers and by the Seleka and it took them around 15 minutes by foot to reach the school. P-2657 testified that, as there were gunshots, she ran into a house of some people who lived along the road and locked herself up inside. P-2657 stated that seven men came into the house and talked to each other, discussing whether P-2657 should be killed. One of them proposed that she should be taken 'to their leader Ngaïssona'. P-2657 also heard them talk about Charly, who was a prominent individual and was well-known in the villages around Bossangoa. P-2657 stated that they were all armed and some were in military outfits while others were not, and they were speaking Gbaya and Sango. P-2657 stated that she recognised one of them as Armand from Ouham-Bac, whose father was a pastor in Ouham-Bac and close to her father. P-2657 stated that Armand pretended not to know P-2657 and after a while, five of them went out and Armand and another man who remained raped her. P-2657 stated that after they had raped her, they left her in the house and left.

Other witnesses support P-2462's and P-2657's accounts. P-2049 testified that his wife, P-2657, and his 'sister', referring to P-2462, were raped. P-2453 stated he learned from a woman he worked with that the Seleka rescued two women who were with Koursi Abdelrahim when he was killed: Aichatou Mahamat and Fane Adjaro. P-2453 further stated that neither of them ever told him what happened to them in the bush but 'when men take women into the bush, the assumption is that they force them to have sexual intercourse' and because of that rumour, Fane Adjaro is still not married because no man is interested in her now.

On the basis of this evidence, and as further outlined below, the Chamber concludes that the identified victims were civilians and not engaged in hostilities, who were killed by the Anti-Balaka during the Bossangoa Attack. The arguments presented by the Ngaïssona Defence in this context are without merit.

In this context, the Chamber also notes the Ngaïssona Defence's suggestion that the fighting would have been 'particularly intense' at the imam's house, for which reason 'it is impossible to discount the possibility that the alleged victims might have been unfortunately killed in cross or friendly fire'. First, the Chamber recalls P-1577's evidence according to which the closest Seleka base in relation to the imam's residence was three to four kilometres away, and that indeed he did not see any Seleka close to the imam's house when he left the Peuhl family there, as well as its finding that the Seleka base at Boro school was there only temporarily during September 2013. Second, the Chamber recalls that while P-1577 saw Seleka driving in the direction of the imam's residence, he could not say if they in fact went there. Third, the Chamber finds that P-1577's reference to an 'intense battle' in the area of the imam's house was made in relation to the number of spent cartridges he found on the ground, the bullet holes in walls, and the blood spatter on ground and walls a few days after the attack, and not because he was aware of a battle taking place at that location. Fourth, and in any event, the suggestion that victims would have been killed 'in cross or friendly fire' is, with nothing further, purely speculative. On this basis, the Chamber does not follow the Ngaïssona Defence's argument that intense fighting between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka would have taken place in the area of the imam's residence.

The final argument of the Ngaïssona Defence in relation to the attack having been 'proportionate' fails on its flawed submission that proportionality is shown when comparing the number of the alleged victims with the number of civilians who managed to seek shelter at the École de la Liberté. First, this assumes that a legitimate military objective was attacked in the area of the imam's residence which, as stated above, the Chamber does not find to have been the case. Second, the argument fails due to the comparative basis being used: even if a legitimate military objective is targeted, proportionality of such targeting is not assessed by comparing the possible civilian casualties with any -- civilian -- individuals that were spared.

As regards the Ngaïssona Defence doubting Khadidja Adjaro's role at the time of her death on the basis of her alleged affiliation with the Seleka, the Chamber notes the Ngaïssona Defence's reliance on Odette Namsona, who stated that she did not see Khadidja Adjaro taking up arms, but 'knew' that Khadidja Adjaro organised marriages between the Seleka and 'local girls' in Bossangoa, which the witness stated knowing because she 'kn\[e\]w those women quite well' and heard from some of 'our elements' who reported to her about who was organising which event. In contrast, P-2462 denied that Khadidja Adjaro could have been part of the Seleka as she was a woman, while P‑2453 denied knowing whether Khadidja Adjaro was armed during the Bossangoa Attack. As Odette Namsona's hearsay evidence is not supported by any other evidence, the Chamber does not find that Khadidja Adjaro was affiliated with the Seleka.

On the basis of the evidence before it, the Chamber concludes that Khadidja Adjaro was not a member of the Seleka, not engaged in fighting against the Anti-Balaka on 5 December 2013, but was shot and killed while seeking refuge from the attack. The Chamber finds that Khadidja Adjaro was a Muslim civilian killed by the Anti-Balaka during the Bossangoa Attack.

Koursi Abdelrahim: At the outset, the Chamber notes that the charges as confirmed by the Pre-Trial Chamber list Koursi Mahamat and Koursi Abdelrahim as two individuals killed during the Bossangoa Attack, while both the Prosecution and the Ngaïssona Defence argue that they are the same person. In this regard, the Chamber notes that P-2462 stated that Koursi Mahamat, also called Koursi Abdelrahim, was a trader and deputy mayor of Bossangoa, while P-2453 testified that Koursi Mahamat Abdelrahim is one and the same person, representative of the traders. D30-4608 stated that 'Koursi Mahamat or Koursi Abdlerahim' or 'Kourcy Abdlerahim' was a trader in his 40s or 50s who was also councillor at the town hall, and that he heard Koursi had weapons at his home and was killed by some young self-defence persons when he was trying to steal cattle (*see* D30-4608 Statement, CAR-D30-0017-0004-R01, at 0016, para. 92, at 0017, para. 96; D30-4608: T-291, p. 55, lines 7-25; T-292, p. 54, lines 11-24).

In relation to the Ngaïssona Defence's challenge to Koursi Abdelrahim's role at the time of this death in light of his supposed affiliation with the Seleka as well as him attacking young men and his wives bearing weapons on 5 December 2013, the Chamber notes that Faustin Ngamesse stated that Koursi Abdelrahim pointed out Christian traders to the Seleka, while Nestor Wiabona said he knew that Koursi financed the Seleka because he had some means during this period. In contrast, P-2453 stated that, because of the pillaging by the Seleka, the imam asked Koursi Abdelrahim as representative of the traders to talk with the Seleka about their bad behaviour, and that he did not get on with the Seleka in any way. P-2462 stated that Koursi Abdelrahim, a trader, did not belong to the Seleka. As the hearsay evidence of Faustin Ngamesse and Nestor Wiabona is not supported by any other evidence, and in light of the evidence to the contrary, the Chamber does not find that Koursi Abdelrahim was affiliated with the Seleka. Even if there had been such affiliation, the evidence before the Chamber does not support that Koursi Abdelrahim was armed or engaged in active hostilities at the time of his death.

Abdel, also known as Adaye, Abakar: P-2657 testified that the name of her sister-in-law's husband is 'Abdel Abakar', and while she did not see who killed him, she saw him get shot, along with her mother-in-law, and saw his body. paragraph_text_preview: P-2200 stated that 18 people were killed during the Bossangoa Attack, including three women, giving the names of Khadidja Adjaro, Koursi Abdelrahim, Koursi Mahamat, Abdallah Mahamat, Abdelkhadir, Mariam Yawha, Amadou Oumarou, Djime Atahir and Abdaye, while not remembering the names of the other victims that day. P-2200 stated these Muslims were neither Seleka nor soldiers, and not armed or fighting when they were killed. P-2200 also explained that once the Seleka had transported the bodies to the school site, he participated in their burial the day following the attack, seeing the bodies of 18 victims with wounds and blood on their clothes. As it was too dangerous to leave the school, they did not have clean shrouds in which to wrap the bodies, nor was there the usual washing of the bodies. The 15 men were buried in one communal hole, while the three women were buried in another. P-2200 stated that the they could not access the usual cemetery because the Anti-Balaka were still around in the town.

'C-17', a taxi driver: P-2453 stated that at some point during the attack, the Anti-Balaka came very close to the École de la Liberté, they started shooting in their direction, killing one of the FOMAC soldiers and one of the displaced Muslims, a 23-year-old moto-taxi driver named Husseni, alias 'C-17'. He was P-2453's friend, not involved with the Seleka, and never carried a weapon. P-2049 testified that 'C-17', a young man from Bossangoa, was killed just in front of the mosque during the Bossangoa Attack. P‑2049 could not say whether 'C-17''s real name was Abakar Moussa and denied knowing whether 'C-17' was armed and fighting along the Seleka. An HRW report also mentions a 'popular motorcycle taximan' called 'Hamidou "Seize-Dix-Sept"' among the killed. The Chamber notes the Ngaïssona Defence's argument that P-2453 did not in fact witness the killing. However, the Chamber considers that even if P‑2453 did not see the actual killing of 'C-17', he specified that the individual was his friend and he described the circumstances in which he was killed. Therefore, and in light of the evidence before it, the Chamber finds that 'C-17', a taxi driver from Bossangoa, was a Muslim civilian killed by the Anti-Balaka during the Bossangoa Attack.

P-2453 stated that on 5 December 2013, he was living in the École de la Liberté and heard the explosions outside from 14:00 to 16:00 and that the Anti-Balaka approached the premises of the school but the soldiers of FOMAC pushed them back. P-2453 testified that the Anti-Balaka even killed a Congolese soldier, but no refugee or displaced person was injured inside the school as they were protected by the Congolese soldiers. P-2453 similarly stated that the Congolese commander at the school called for reinforcement. P-2453 testified that he could not see what was happening outside since the people inside the École de la Liberté were ordered to lie down on the ground. P-2453 stated that at around 16:00, the Seleka managed to fight back, took Boro back from the Anti-Balaka, and the Anti-Balaka retreated near the bush at the entrance of Bossangoa, on the side of Boro.

It appears that following the Bossangoa Attack, also some Seleka remained in Bossangoa. P-1577 stated that as he was circulating the town on 7 December 2013, the Seleka groups had been told to stay in their camp, and he did not see any military in the centre of town.

However, the Seleka did eventually leave the town. Indeed, Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana testified that they heard on the radio that Michel Djotodia had resigned when he and his group were heading towards Bossangoa, they took a path close to the airport and headed towards the bishopric to set up post in Bossangoa. Once they controlled Bossangoa, he was asked by FACA ComZone Florent Kema to write a mission order to allow some FACA Anti-Balaka to establish checkpoints in Bossangoa. Similarly, Michel Ningando stated that the Seleka disappeared from Bossangoa overnight at the time of Michel Djotodia's resignation, and even the Sangaris did not know how the Seleka had left. While Roger de Martial Yagao did not recollect the date, he also stated that the armed Seleka left town one night, with Bossangoa remaining under control of the Congolese contingent of MISCA, which was subsequently replaced by the Chadian MINUSCA contingent, the Sangaris, police and the gendarmerie. He further stated that the Anti-Balaka in Bossangoa were living in the 'Camp Chic' neighbourhood behind the municipal stadium, not far from the church where the displaced Christians were staying, occupying the houses of civilians who had fled to the church. Roger de Martial Yagao got to know the spokesperson of the Anti-Balaka nicknamed 'Atakoli' in Sango or 'Koko' in Gbaya, which means grandfather, because he introduced himself as such during meetings.

Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana stated that after the Bossangoa Attack, they were recovering in Benzambé and learned that they had been given 500,000 CFA to buy food and medicine and that this money came through the Cameroon border to Bouar. The witness further stated that they organised a meeting of chiefs and Florent Kema decided that two chiefs should be sent to collect the money. When the two chiefs returned, only 180,000 CFA was left as they had used some of the money to buy solar panels to charge cell phones, leading to anger and a huge dispute among the elements. Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana stated that he never found out who the money came from. The witness stated that later in Bangui, there was a dispute between Dedane and Andjilo over the money; Andjilo, who was under Dedane, was angry at not having received his share and Andjilo's younger brother killed Dedane. The witness stated that he was in Benzambé when this happened and asked to inform his family, so he wrote a letter to Sidony Danboye, Dedane's sister. Expert witness Lars Bromley analysed satellite imagery with images taken before and after the Bossangoa Attack, 4 and 12 December 2013, concluding that 'the image from 4 December \[2013\] includes hundreds of structures that exhibit signs of destruction but would need comparison with a previously acquired image for verification'. The witness further concluded that indications of burning were 'relatively frequent' on both assessed dates and 'at least a few destroyed structures were burned', the image of 4 December 2013 included 'hundreds of structures' exhibiting 'signs of destruction', and 'at least 17 structures were destroyed in various areas \[...\] by 12 December 2013'. Further analysis of satellite imagery from 5 December 2013, 22 January 2014 and 28 February 2014 concluded on 227 destroyed buildings (probable) by 5 December 2013, an additional 893 destroyed buildings by 22 January 2014, and a further 114 destroyed buildings by 28 February 2014, leading to a total of 1,234 destroyed structures. The CAR Panel concluded accordingly that '1,007 buildings were destroyed between 5 December 2013 and 28 February 2014'.

P-1577 visited an area in the vicinity of the imam's residence on 5 December 2013, at which time buildings there were not destroyed, while several of these buildings had been destroyed by the time he returned to the same area around 7 December 2013. Indeed, P-1577 provided photographs showing signs of burning and destruction which, according to their metadata, were taken on 8 December 2013. P-1577 explained that the photographs were taken at the buildings very close to the imam's house, and he was told that the Anti-Balaka had looted and set them on fire during the attack on 5 December 2013. P-1577 stated that there was a recent burning smell and it was very clear that it was a recent fire. P-1577 testified that the area close to the imam's house was very clearly a Muslim district and Muslims lived in those homes as when he visited there in the morning of 5 December 2013, it was filled with individuals who identified themselves as Muslims, other residents also identified this area as the Muslim neighbourhood, and when he returned, there was evidence of Arabic writing on papers strewn around the floor and the names on identification documents had Muslim sounding names. The location which P-1577 believed to be a Muslim school, with tablets for teaching children the Koran, was almost razed to the ground, with no roof and all of the walls blackened. P-1577 further explained that he found bullet shells and unexploded ammunition in the Muslim trading area quite close to the imam's house, and that shops were looted and items taken. P-1577 did not know who was responsible for the looting but was told that it was the Anti-Balaka on the day of the Bossangoa Attack.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that P-2049 commented on a video which shows the destroyed and burnt mosque and residential buildings in Bornou and Foulbé neighbourhoods. P-2049 explained that he received the video from another person and thought that it was filmed after the Bossangoa Attack as he believed that the mosque shown in the video was destroyed two or three days after 5 December 2013. Lars Bromley agreed that the damage to the buildings appearing in the video was consistent with the type of damage he saw in the satellite imagery for Bossangoa, with indications of burning and frequent roofless structures, and stated the video may have been taken some time afterwards, so some of the blackened soot would have washed away in the rains. P-2453 stated that the video showed several places within Boro, explaining that the white house at 00:07:01 was his and that the roof was damaged, and naming owners of the other houses depicted in the video. P-2453 further stated that the houses would normally have had roofs, doors and windows and that in his assessment, the video was filmed after the Bossangoa Attack, as it was only after that attack that the houses in the Boro neighbourhood, intact until 5 December 2013, were pillaged and damaged. On the basis of this evidence, the Chamber concludes that the video was filmed at some point after the Bossangoa Attack, without being able to conclude on the specific date.

Further, the Chamber concludes that the central mosque had been destroyed by February 2014.

Muslim population at the École de la Liberté and its eventual transportation mainly to Chad During the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, the Muslim civilian population of Bossangoa fled the attacked neighbourhoods to seek shelter at the École de la Liberté, where their numbers rose into several thousands.

In light of the consistent evidence above according to which Muslims at the École de la Liberté were specifically advised not to leave the school for risk of being attacked by the Anti-Balaka, the Chamber does not consider credible the account of D30-4608 who alleged that Muslims were not threatened since the Seleka were roaming the city, while Christians at the bishopric had no possibility of leaving. This same witness also stated that the Anti-Balaka conducted attacks on the École de la Liberté after the Bossangoa Attack, according to him targeting the Seleka who had withdrawn around the school for fear of the Muslims possibly being attacked. Similarly, and also bearing in mind the dire living conditions at the school as further outlined below, the Chamber accords no weight to Faustin Ngamesse's suggestion that the Muslims stayed at the school even though it was not dangerous for them to leave. It is clear from the evidence before the Chamber that the Muslims at the school did not remain there having been in a position to genuinely choose between remaining or not. The Ngaïssona Defence's argument that Muslim civilians had the possibility to leave the school premises and that there is no evidence that Anti-Balaka elements were the reason why they remained in the school is dismissed in this same context.

The Chamber concludes from the above evidence that while there may have been meetings with representatives of various groups and organisations, they clearly remained without result, and certainly did not lead to the creation of conditions which would have allowed Muslims confined to the École de la Liberté to return to their homes. Eventually, in light of the prevailing insecurity as well as the dire and cramped living conditions at the École de la Liberté, all Muslims staying at the school were transported away from Bossangoa to Chad in two separate convoys, leaving in February and April 2014, respectively, following which Bossangoa was emptied of its Muslim population.

As regards the approximate number of elements staying at Yamwara at the relevant time, the evidence suggests that there were approximately 1,000 elements present at Yamwara in December 2013, including those from Mr Yekatom's group. In its assessment, the Chamber has used the estimates provided by P-1786, Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili and P-1839 about the sizes of their respective sections and companies. According to P-1786, there were about 1,000 Anti-Balaka elements at Yamwara. He further stated that there were 10 companies with four sections each and each section had about 30 men. Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili stated that there were about 120 people in his company but said that there were 'thousands' of 'Anti-Balaka' at Yamwara and most of them lived at the school compound, and did not know how many companies there were. P-1839 gave the example of Alkanto, who was the chief of the 1^st^ company, 1^st^ division and was commanding 30 people in his section.

As part of its submission that Mr Yekatom's group was not 'a strict military structure with Mr Yekatom as the commander-in-chief', the Yekatom Defence raises several arguments concerning the hierarchy of command and interpersonal relations between Mr Yekatom and Cœur de Lion. In particular, the Yekatom Defence (i) disputes that Cœur de Lion was Mr Yekatom's 'deputy', de facto or otherwise; and (ii) asserts that there was functional independence between their respective units. In respect of the latter, the Yekatom Defence further submits that each unit had the capacity to operate independently from the other, Cœur de Lion's elements were 'strictly loyal to him', conducted separate operations, and there was friction between Mr Yekatom and Cœur de Lion. Specifically in relation to Yamwara, the Yekatom Defence submits that Cœur de Lion operating independently was also seen in relation to 'decisions taken at Yamwara', in that Mr Yekatom 'did not occupy a building at the base', 'very rarely visited the base', and 'when he did visit, it was for brief periods of time'.

Notably, Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili, a FACA member who was at Yamwara in December 2013 within Mr Yekatom's group said that '\[t\]he deputy at the time was the late Ouandjio'. P-1839, a civilian member of the group, but close to Mr Yekatom in late December 2013 and early 2014, recognised Cœur de Lion as Mr Yekatom's 'deputy' during the time at Yamwara. P-1786 also said that, aside from Mr Yekatom, he did not know of another chief that would give instructions to elements in Yamwara; there was only Mr Yekatom who could give instructions to 'Habib', who would then relay them. P-1786 said that Mr Yekatom was the 'topmost commander' and that his 'deputy was Cœur de Lion'.

Notably, Cœur de Lion's own words to a journalist at Yamwara in December 2013 show that he was the deputy of the 'movement' ('C'est moi qui suis adjoint de ce mouvement'); relatedly, he is seen saying to another element that he must seek authorization from his chief ('Il fallait que je demande l'authorisation d'abord. Je ne peux pas faire ça à mon niveau, il faut que je demande mon chef d'abord').
The Chamber furthermore notes the evidence on Cœur de Lion being considered as Mr Yekatom's deputy also in other locations and contexts.

In light of this, the Chamber is not persuaded that Cœur de Lion's 'more years of military service' than Mr Yekatom and his assignment to an 'elite' PG reversed, or otherwise changed, the dynamics of the relation inter se, or the perception of the members of Mr Yekatom's group, of which Cœur de Lion himself was part. The Yekatom Defence has pointed to no reason why, despite its assertions as to Cœur de Lion's higher or comparable authority vis-à-vis Mr Yekatom, their own elements would consistently testify to Cœur de Lion being the 'deputy'. This is regardless of the purported formality of the title 'deputy' or whether military and non-military members understood it differently. In both formal and informal sense, military or civilian, it conveys the same and unambiguous directional flow of authority.

As regards the Yekatom Defence's arguments concerning Cœur de Lion's 'repeated disagreements' with Mr Yekatom and the resulting friction between them, the Chamber considers that such a dynamic is premised on an expectation on Cœur de Lion to follow, or otherwise implement Mr Yekatom's orders. Training at Yamwara At Yamwara, Mr Yekatom's group, including civilian elements, received training of military nature. There was no training in international humanitarian law at Yamwara.

The Prosecution submits that, through his commanders, Mr Yekatom organised military training for the new recruits at Yamwara which would take place in classrooms, and that Mr Yekatom 'permitted outsiders to provide limited training to some of his elements' on international humanitarian law, but not including the principle of distinction.

The confirmed charges concern four men and three Muslim women being stopped at a checkpoint, after which they were taken to Yamwara by Anti-Balaka members and mistreated, resulting in the death of Saint Cyr Lapo N'Gomat (hereinafter: 'Saint Cyr') at the end of December 2013.

The Chamber heard from all, except one, of the direct victims of the Yamwara Incident in court, namely P-1704, P-1705, P-1716, P-0967, and P-1811 (the 'Five Witnesses'). Some were related to Saint Cyr by blood: P-1705 was Saint Cyr's younger brother and P-0967 was Saint Cyr's maternal aunt. Others were related by marriage: P-1704 was Saint Cyr's brother-in-law and, at the time, married to Saint Cyr's sister. P-1811 was Saint Cyr's aunt by marriage and considered him to be her nephew. P-1716 was P-1705's friend and familiar to the Lapo N'Gomat family.

The Chamber notes that all witnesses were eyewitnesses to all or parts of the Yamwara Incident and have coherently described their respective experiences. The Chamber found them generally reliable and credible.

The Chamber considered the discrepancies within and among these testimonies concerning the Yamwara Incident which are discussed in detail below. In this regard, the Chamber appreciates the time that has elapsed since the Yamwara Incident and its traumatic nature, and is of the view that a majority of these inconsistencies were either minor or did not concern facts material to the allegations. Therefore, they did not undermine the credibility of these witnesses generally. On the contrary, these inconsistencies, when assessed in their totality, suggested to the Chamber that the witnesses' accounts were genuine and not rehearsed, or otherwise agreed upon prior to their testimony before the Chamber, contrary to the Yekatom Defence allegations concerning contamination. In places, where these discrepancies did concern material factual allegations, these have been discussed in detail below.

Having regard to this, the Chamber turns to the specific Yekatom Defence allegations concerning contamination of the evidence. First, the Yekatom Defence submits that both P-0967 and P-1705 read the Letter and that it influenced their evidence: while P-0967 modified her statement during the witness familiarisation process, P-1705 changed his testimony to include Mr Yekatom's interactions with P-1654, which did not feature in his original statement. Second, the Yekatom Defence submits that 'the Lapo Family Group witnesses were each aware of one another's involvement in these proceedings' and no efforts were undertaken to minimise witness contamination, as the witnesses had exchanges with each other about their potential testimony, altering their evidence.

Given the openness of the witnesses when answering the questions about their contacts with each other and having considered their respective answers, the Chamber finds the nature of these contacts genuine, understandable, and even reasonable. The Chamber is not persuaded that these contacts, in themselves, meant that the witnesses contaminated each other's accounts.

In particular, as regards the witnesses' contacts in the context of their interviews with the Prosecution, the Chamber is not convinced that them meeting the Prosecution within the same timeframe caused contamination, as such. The witnesses were able to explain the circumstances of their meeting with the Prosecution, including how some accompanied each other for the interview. While P-1811 said that P-0967 called her about giving a statement to the Prosecution, P-0967, in turn, did not recall who had called her to be interviewed by the Prosecution, while understanding that P-1654 had approached the investigators. P-0967 stated having heard some information from the other witnesses, but was open about the source of her knowledge. The Chamber has taken it into account when evaluating her evidence. Further, P-1704, P-1705, and P-1716 confirmed that they were interviewed individually by the Prosecution. Overall, the Chamber finds that there is nothing in the respective witnesses' testimonies which suggests that they would have agreed with any of the other witnesses on certain facts in advance of their respective interviews.

The Chamber has taken these factors into account when assessing their evidence holistically, in light of the discrepancies that emerged during their testimonies.

Lastly in this respect, the Chamber has had due regard to the passage of time in assessing the evidence concerning traumatic events. The Five Witnesses were testifying approximately ten years after the events, and it is understandable that they did not recall all the details with precision.

paragraph_text_preview: The Five Witnesses described travelling together in an ambulance from the hospital, through PK5 to Boeing, and during this trip, they were stopped, at least once, at a post close to the Lapo N'Gomat family house in Cité de la Paix. Some witnesses remembered that those who stopped the ambulance said that they were checking vehicles for Seleka elements and weapons. After they searched it and saw the body of the deceased, the ambulance was allowed to carry on. When they arrived at the Lapo N'Gomat house, the dead body was taken out and the family continued preparing for the funeral.

footnote_content: P-1811: T-115, p. 5, line 20 -- p. 6, line 2, p. 7, lines 7-13; P-1716: T-148, p. 14, lines 9-15; P-1704: T-128, p. 31, line 12 -- p. 32, line 2; P-1716: T-148, p. 15, lines 6-23, p. 18, line 25 -- p. 19, line 7; P-1811 Statement, CAR-OTP-2058-0003-R05, at 0006, paras 18-22; P-1716 Statement, CAR-OTP-2053-0062-R05, at 0066, paras 22-23; P-1704 Statement, CAR-OTP-2054-1136-R05, at 1140, para. 23. The Chamber notes that some witnesses testified about being stopped at Seleka checkpoints when passing through PK5 to Boeing. However, P-1705 denied going through any Seleka roadblocks in PK5 but was clear in stating that they were stopped at 'Avicom', which is close to Yamwara (*see* P-1705: T-212, p. 15, lines 15-19). P-1811 also denied that they went through Seleka checkpoints (*see* P-1811: T-115, p. 10, line 17 -- p. 11, line 3). The Chamber also notes that there appears to be a discrepancy between the accounts on where and how many times the vehicle had to stop at checkpoints along the way. However, the Chamber considers that these details are not material to the factual allegations concerning the Yamwara Incident, neither is the number of times the vehicle was stopped *before* it arrived in Boeing. The Chamber has also considered that P-0967 seemed to think that no one stopped them along the way and also did not appear to remember well who was sitting in the vehicle. However, the Chamber notes that she was sitting behind in the ambulance and said that it was very difficult to see what was happening outside (*see* P-0967: T-200, p. 25, lines 8-14, p. 30, lines 2-19). Further, given the time that has passed and P-0967's general coherence and detailed description of the subsequent events, the Chamber considers her account on this aspect not materially discrepant from those of others.

The Five Witnesses and Oumi (collectively, the 'six persons'), together with Saint Cyr, left the Lapo N'Gomat house somewhere between 13:00 and 16:00. Elements from Mr Yekatom's group apprehended these seven persons at a checkpoint led by Alkanto close to the Lapo N'Gomat family house and to Yamwara. Alkanto pointed to the women as belonging to the family of Mamour and Michel Djotodia in the presence of the elements in his group. Alkanto's identification of the women being related to Djotodia and Mamour as well as being Muslims, combined with Alkanto's negative feelings centred around a desire for revenge against the women, predisposed Alkanto's group to perceive the seven persons as 'Muslims'.

P-0967 said that after he recognised P-1811, whom he knew very well, Alkanto also knew that they were 'Muslims \[...\] and that is why he stopped us'. The Chamber further notes that the four men accompanying the three women were, in fact, not Muslim by faith.

According to the Yekatom Defence, Alkanto's 'vigilance' was heightened by 'personal grievances' and 'vendetta' towards P-1811. It argues that Alkanto's group suspected the seven persons of being 'Seleka informants' after 'Seleka cards' were found on the men during the searches at the checkpoint; and that these were the reasons they were brought to Cœur de Lion at Yamwara.

The evidence shows that Alkanto may have indeed borne negative feelings against P-1811 and the Mamour family, and also made them known to the elements at the checkpoint. All witnesses remembered Alkanto saying out loud that he had previously worked with Mamour. Some of them remembered that Alkanto also spoke about his friend having been mistreated by the Mamour family and wanting revenge.

paragraph_text_preview: The evidence shows that Alkanto may have indeed borne negative feelings against P-1811 and the Mamour family, and also made them known to the elements at the checkpoint. All witnesses remembered Alkanto saying out loud that he had previously worked with Mamour. Some of them remembered that Alkanto also spoke about his friend having been mistreated by the Mamour family and wanting revenge.

Based on this and what follows, the Chamber finds that it was a combination of Alkanto's negative feelings centred around a desire for revenge, the women being identified as related to Djotodia and Mamour, as well as being Muslims, that predisposed Alkanto's group to their perception of the seven persons. This was despite the fact that the men in the group were non-Muslims. Following Alkanto's identification of the women, his elements started to threaten the group with death, telling the group that they would be 'skinned like a papaya'. The expression 'peeling' or 'skinning' the 'papaya' was used by elements in Mr Yekatom's group in relation to the treatment of captured persons suspected of being Seleka.
As set out below, the evidence shows that, following Alkanto's identification of the women, his elements started to threaten the group with death.

P-0967 said that Alkanto said that '\[w\]hen it rains, it's the period to sow seeds, and today we are going to sow some seeds'. P-1811 understood this to mean that 'since the soil is wet, it would open and they would bury them' there. P-1811 said that the group told the seven persons that it was the end for them and they would not survive. P-0967, P-1705, and P-1704 said that Alkanto's elements gathered around the group and said to them that they were going to be 'skinned like a papaya'. P-0967 explained what this phrase meant to her: '\[...\] somebody who carries a machete and doesn't have any fruit in his hands, it's an image which shows that the fruit or, rather, the plant which should be sown today would have been us \[...\] a very strong image. It was quite clear to us that it meant that we would be buried that day'.

Mr Yekatom himself used this phrase at least once in his phone call with P-0954, and is seen in a video responding to one of his elements about a certain captured person and the expression 'faire sa papaye'. Alkanto ordered his elements to search the male captives at the checkpoint. Alkanto's elements beat P-1704 and P-1716 and accused them of being traitors. None of the seven persons posed a threat to Yamwara or the security of the elements placed there. In fact, the nature and the purpose of them being together and close to Yamwara was linked to the funeral of Saint Cyr's older brother.
