paragraph_text_preview: P-0967 and P-1716 recalled that Saint Cyr had a 'military card' that the Anti-Balaka found and according to them he was a soldier serving in the FACA. P-1705 recalled that the military card was found on Saint Cyr when the group was searched after their arrival at Yamwara. In the view of the Chamber, both of these inconsistencies were minor and explainable by the passage of time and the traumatic nature of the events. The transfer from Alkanto's checkpoint to Cœur de Lion's house in Yamwara took a few minutes. P-1704 said that it did not take much time to go from the roadblock to Yamwara. P-0967 thought it was 'bit far'; they left the main route and walked roughly the same distance as between the Lapo N'Gomat house and the main road to reach Yamwara. There, in Cœur de Lion's presence, elements in Mr Yekatom's group, including Bojos, interrogated the four men individually on their identity, ethnicity, and reasons for being there with the women, also demanding the captive men to speak in the dialect associated with their respective ethnicities. Saint Cyr and another captive, who were Boffi from their father's side and Goula from their mother's side, gave their ethnicity but neither could speak their dialect. Saint Cyr said that he was 'Boffi' but could not speak in this language. When Saint Cyr was unable to do so, elements in Mr Yekatom's group accused him of being 'Goula', and therefore associated with Djotodia. The elements in Mr Yekatom's group kept the women apart from the male captives but close by, under the veranda of Cœur de Lion's house. Mr Yekatom was not present at Yamwara during the group's arrival there or during the said interrogation at Cœur de Lion's house.

The Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom was not present at Yamwara during the group's arrival there or during the said interrogation at Cœur de Lion's house. Only P-1704 recalled him being present and described (i) the captives being presented to Mr Yekatom when they arrived at Yamwara; and (ii) Alkanto telling Mr Yekatom that the captives were from General Mamour's family.

The Chamber notes, in this regard, that the Prosecution does not rely on his account to establish Mr Yekatom's presence at Yamwara at this point, and that the Yekatom Defence argues that P-1704's testimony is contradicted by all other witnesses who were present at the scene. Having assessed the evidence holistically, the Chamber finds that P‑1704's account is not reliable in relation to the two aspects mentioned and therefore, does not rely on it. Following the men's interrogation, the elements in Mr Yekatom's group forced them to undress, searched them again, threatened them with death, and found no weapons on any of them. Upon another search of the captives, an element in Mr Yekatom's group recovered a SIM card in the trousers of one of the female captives and no weapons were found on them. The elements in Mr Yekatom's group took the women inside Cœur de Lion's house while Saint Cyr's interrogation continued outside, and from where they could hear what was happening outside. Elements in Mr Yekatom's group continued to interrogate Saint Cyr and beat him, despite him showing his identification card and insisting that he was a FACA member. Cœur de Lion, who was observing Saint Cyr's mistreatment, encouraged the assailants and ordered them to continue, saying, inter alia, that the victims were 'Muslims' and 'Seleka' and to 'do the job properly'. Elements in Mr Yekatom's group specifically beat Saint Cyr's legs, breaking them, and tied him up in 'arbatacher' manner, continuing to assault him. An element in Mr Yekatom's group, cut off Saint Cyr's toes, fingers, and an ear, being encouraged by Cœur de Lion's presence at the scene and his words, and feeling that there was no choice but to do it. P-1704, P-1705, and P-1716 were present when Mr Yekatom's elements interrogated and beat Saint Cyr and cut off his toes, fingers, and an ear. After Saint Cyr's beating and maiming, the elements of Mr Yekatom's group took him away. Saint Cyr then died. His relatives never saw him again and his dead body was never recovered.

The evidence shows that Cœur de Lion, who was present at the scene and observing Saint Cyr's mistreatment, encouraged the assailants and ordered them to continue, saying, inter alia, that the victims were 'Muslims' and 'Seleka' and to 'do the job properly'. According to P-1839, Cœur de Lion encouraged the elements, including her, saying that they were 'doing great' ('C'était bien ce que tu fais') and they should 'not regret' ('il faut pas regretter, c'est normal'), that the victims were 'Muslims' and 'Seleka', that they had come to spy on them and kill them, and that 'God had delivered them' ('Dieu les a livrés'). P-1716 said that when Cœur de Lion arrived, people had a lot of respect for him and were reporting everything that was happening to him and that he was the one in 'command' of the elements who were there. P-1716 stated that Cœur de Lion said to 'his men that were beating' Saint Cyr to 'do the job properly' and they continued to beat Saint Cyr. P-1716, when asked specifically if Cœur de Lion gave the order to cut Saint Cyr's ears, said that it was difficult to know who gave this order.

According to P-1839, Cœur de Lion encouraged the elements, including her, saying that they were 'doing great' ('C'était bien ce que tu fais') and they should 'not regret' ('il faut pas regretter, c'est normal'), that the victims were 'Muslims' and 'Seleka', that they had come to spy on them and kill them, and that 'God had delivered them' ('Dieu les a livrés'). P-1716 said that when Cœur de Lion arrived, people had a lot of respect for him and were reporting everything that was happening to him and that he was the one in 'command' of the elements who were there. P-1716 stated that Cœur de Lion said to 'his men that were beating' Saint Cyr to 'do the job properly' and they continued to beat Saint Cyr. P-1716, when asked specifically if Cœur de Lion gave the order to cut Saint Cyr's ears, said that it was difficult to know who gave this order.

The evidence shows that an element in Mr Yekatom's group cut off Saint Cyr's 'toes, the fingers, and the ear' ('les orteils, les doigts et l'oreille'), being encouraged by Cœur de Lion's presence at the scene and his words and feeling that there was no choice but to do it. P-1839 said that this element cut off these body-parts without specific orders from anybody, and also said that if one did not do it, one would not be trusted and so this element did it to gain the trust of the leaders. P-1839 clarified that some 'people' were encouraging them to do it ('poussent à le faire') and that this element felt that there was no choice but to do it.

paragraph_text_preview: From the evidence, the exact location of Saint Cyr's mistreatment is unclear, but it appears that it took place around Cœur de Lion's house that had a wide compound and was next to a mango tree. P-1839 said that it occurred on the veranda of Cœur de Lion's house when the women were inside. P-0967 said that, during this time, from inside the house, she could hear cries and realised that it was Saint Cyr who was being subjected to this beating. P-1705 and P-1716 seem to recall a slightly different location but still placed it close to Cœur de Lion's house: according to P-1705, it happened 'behind' Cœur de Lion's house, while P-1716 thought that the beating and the cutting of the ear happened 'near' a house where Saint Cyr was later taken, and that this was not on the school property.

paragraph_text_preview: The evidence shows that after his mistreatment and when the night fell, the elements of Mr Yekatom's group took Saint Cyr 'away'; he then died and his relatives never saw him again, nor was his dead body ever recovered. P-1705 recalled that, after being tied up and beaten, Saint Cyr was thrown onto the ground in front of the window of Cœur de Lion's house. P-1716 also said that they realised that it would be very unlikely that he would still be able to stay alive. The Chamber finds that, around the time that Saint Cyr was being beaten, elements in Mr Yekatom's group beat the remaining three men, P-1704, P-1705, and P-1716, and threatened them with death. P-1705 testified that he, together with P-1716 and P-1704, was taken behind the house and beaten by the Anti-Balaka. P-1716 stated that the three men were beaten with sticks and hands and it was everyone who beat them. The men were forced to go on their knees with their hands on their heads and the Anti-Balaka hit and beat them. P-1704 stated that he was hit everywhere, including his head and body, and that the men were beaten repeatedly in turns and told that they were going to get killed. Mr Yekatom was not present at the scene during the mistreatment of Saint Cyr, P-1704, P-1705, and P-1716. However, shortly after the fact, Mr Yekatom came to know about this incident, including the actions of the element that had cut off Saint Cyr's toes, fingers, and an ear. Later, Mr Yekatom told P-1839 that this element had done a 'good job' insofar. Mr Yekatom did not punish this element for these acts and, on the contrary, rewarded this element with posts of responsibility within his group, including as part of his security detail. Mr Yekatom considered Saint Cyr a 'traitor' and 'in cahoots with the Seleka' and that therefore, they could not 'keep him'. When asked about Saint Cyr's treatment, Mr Yekatom said in Sango 'eforolo tonga na papai' -- meaning that 'they peeled the papaya', 'they removed the skin like they would do to a papaya'.

Indeed, the Chamber cannot rely on P-0954 to establish conclusions on how the Yamwara Incident unfolded or how Saint Cyr died. However, P-0954's evidence is telling about where he placed Mr Yekatom in relation to the Yamwara Incident.

As set out below, P-0954's testimony demonstrates that details of the Yamwara Incident were indeed relayed to him. His evidence contains descriptions which have an inescapable similarity with the Yamwara Incident as described above and noticeably show that he was indeed talking about the Yamwara Incident and would have received this information from those who knew about it. For example, P-0954 stated that Mr Yekatom's elements 'attacked Djotodia's wife, as she travelled in a vehicle with her aide-de-camp \[when\] \[...\] \[t\]hey were in Boeing on their way to a funeral', that they then brought 'Djotodia's wife' to 'Yekatom's base' and she was released later, and that the killing of the aide-de-camp happened at the time when Mr Yekatom was still based at Yamwara, before Djotodia had left power.

While it is unclear which details about the incident he learnt from Mr Yekatom himself and which he was told by others, P-0954 is clear about having a direct exchange with Mr Yekatom on the death of someone he knows to be the 'aide de camp to Djotodia's wife', which the Chamber understands to be a reference to Saint Cyr.

When describing the phone call in court, P-0954 said that he came to know from Mr Yekatom and some other elements around him that Mr Yekatom's elements stopped the 'wife of Djotodia' and her 'aide-de-camp' who were on their way to bury someone in Boeing, which was under Mr Yekatom and Ngremangou at the time, identifying him as a 'Seleka' and subsequently 'this element was coldly killed before Yekatom' ('élément a été froidement abattu \[...\] devant Yekatom') . Upon receiving this information, P‑0954 checked that 'the element was indeed killed' ('l'élément a été tué') and was a 'FACA person', and said that 'Yekatom said this person was together with the Seleka' ('Yekatom a dit qu'il est en connivence avec la Séléka') and so he was 'a traitor' and 'therefore needs to be killed' ('donc, il faut pas le garder, \[...\] il faut le tuer') and that this is why he was killed ('le gars a été tué').

Based on this and having regard to the overall circumstances of their captivity and mistreatment endured until that point, the Chamber is convinced that Mr Yekatom's presence and words at this stage were not reassuring to the female captives, contrary to what is argued by the Yekatom Defence. The Chamber recalls that the female captives had been captured, mistreated, stolen from, forcibly undressed and searched, threatened with death, interrogated about their ethnic background, and kept captive under gunpoint. The Chamber also has regard to the fact that, at this stage, the female captives were still in the dark about Saint Cyr's state and that of the other men accompanying them. While they had heard Saint Cyr's cries and interrogation outside, they did not know what had happened to him and what would be their fate and that of the other male captives.

In the Chamber's view, regardless of Mr Yekatom's purported calmness as argued by the Yekatom Defence, his presence, words, and actions did not reassure the female captives of their safety or release. Having assessed Mr Yekatom's words that P-0967 and P-1811 both recalled, the evidence shows that the female captives had no indication about, or reason to believe, the genuineness of Mr Yekatom's composure or purported efforts to have them released, or the possibility that they would be released. Furthermore, the Chamber notes that the mistreatment of the captives did not stop following Mr Yekatom's meeting with the female captives.

Having regard to Mr Yekatom's interactions with the female captives on the night of 24 December 2013, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom knew that his elements had captured, mistreated, and kept them at gunpoint at Yamwara. The same evening of these events at Yamwara, P-1654, who was Saint Cyr's father, came to meet Mr Yekatom at Yamwara. Mr Yekatom, with Bojos and Cœur de Lion, questioned P‑1654 about his family for hours, including about his ethnicity, and threatened him and his family with death. They asked him why 'the Goula', in particular, Mamour's relative, had been invited to the funeral; they also asked about Saint Cyr's relation with him. Mr Yekatom did not inform P-1654, who was fearful for Saint Cyr, about the state and location of Saint Cyr or that of the other captives. After hearing the questioning from Mr Yekatom and his elements and upon P-1654's return from Yamwara to his house, the day after Saint Cyr and the others were captured, P-1654 and the rest of his family fled Boeing. Mr Yekatom was aware of Saint Cyr's presence and mistreatment at Yamwara, at the very latest during P-1654's encounter with him on the evening of 24 December 2013. Mr Yekatom knew that his elements had mistreated Saint Cyr, and that he subsequently died. Mr Yekatom knew that, at the time of his capture, Saint Cyr was escorting the three women, with whom he had familial relations, together with the other three men, to find transport to go home, in the context of a burial of a family relative. Mr Yekatom knew that Saint Cyr had family links with the 'Goula' and that he was unarmed at the time of his capture.

Saint Cyr was not amongst them.

According to P-0967, this 'leader' escorted the Five Captives as they walked from Yamwara during the night with the 'soldiers' forming columns, they walked slowly and she did not know how long they walked, as it was an area she was unfamiliar with. P‑0967 said that, along the way, they were told to stop and arrived at a place full of elements where there was a house, and they were told to stay near the house, then someone came over and asked her to stay calm and that they were going to take them to the Sangaris. P-0967 said that after this, they stopped three times on the way; the elements escorting them would gather together and then come back telling the Five Captives to keep walking.

P-1811 recalled being told that there were people around that wanted to hurt them and so the elements brought the Five Captives on foot to a deacon who was not far away. P‑1811 recalled being guarded by a FACA member, who she did not know before and whose name she did not recall, and that this person would follow them everywhere, even to the shower, because otherwise the others might hurt them. It is unclear whether it refers to any particular time but during their stay behind the airport, P-1811 recalled that the 'spokesperson' told them to stay where they were; there were 'Anti-Balaka' members who must have had a family link with Bozizé and was after P-1811 ('qui \[...\] m'en voulait') and wanted them to be killed ('Lui voulait qu'on soit tués'); while the others said that they could not hurt them. On the morning of 25 December 2013, Mr Yekatom met P-1704, P-1705, P-0967, P-1811 and one other captive at this location and introduced himself. On or about 27 December 2013, P-1704, P-1705, P‑0967, P-1811 and one other captive were released and handed over to Sangaris.

As per P-0884, he was directly involved in facilitating the release of what he called 'hostages', together with Ngremangou, and described it in quite some detail. P-0884's understanding of what unfolded at Yamwara is limited to what he was told by others. However, P-0884's account of the captives being held at Sylvestre Yagouzou's base in a house and their subsequent release contains some specific details.

P-0884 said that at one point, 'the wife of General Mamour, General Djotodia' and 'children' who were 'all Muslims' came across some of Mr Yekatom's elements who stopped them. P-0884 and Ngremangou were informed and decided to free the people who had been taken hostage as the situation could 'degenerate' and it would have been 'serious' if 'the men' had killed them. According to P-0884, Ngremangou and his elements left to meet Mr Yekatom, and after discussions they were able to get the hostages and 'they took them to Boy'. As there was a great deal of tension because these people were 'Muslims', P-0884 put them in a house and stood guard for two days to make sure that no one could come and assault them. The Chamber has considered P-0884's evidence in light of the Yekatom Defence's arguments with a view to assessing Mr Yekatom's group's coordination with other 'Anti-Balaka' groups, not with a view to assessing Mr Yekatom's responsibility regarding the Yamwara Incident, which is a related but separate matter.

In the Chamber's view, the Yekatom Defence's arguments that P-0884's testimony on these events is not credible does not have merit. Indeed, P-0884 cannot be relied upon for the purpose of evaluating the commission of crimes underlying the Yamwara Incident as he was not an eyewitness, and his account contains discrepancies that cannot be reconciled with what the Chamber knows from first-hand accounts of the incident. P‑0884 was also clear that he received parts of the information from the captives and that he himself did not visit Mr Yekatom's base to retrieve the hostages. Nonetheless, when P-0884's testimony is considered keeping in mind the source of his knowledge, it is quite telling when it comes to Mr Yekatom's role in the release of the captives. It appears that, in P-0884's mind, there was no question that Mr Yekatom had the authority to release hostages kept at Yamwara and would hand them over to the people sent by Ngremangou.

In any event, in concluding on Mr Yekatom's role in the Yamwara Incident, the Chamber has relied on his direct interactions with, and actions described by, the Five Witnesses, P-1839, P-1654 and P-0954.

The Chamber notes that the Yamwara Incident impacted several individuals. The Chamber has assessed them in detail below. The Anti-Balaka's advance through and takeover of villages along the PK9-Mbaïki Axis The departure of Mr Yekatom's group from Yamwara and its advance on the axis Starting on 10 January 2014, Mr Yekatom and elements under his control left Yamwara and advanced from Bangui on the road towards Mbaïki, taking over a number of villages in the Lobaye prefecture, located in the south-west part of the country, including Sekia, Ndangala, Bimon, Kapou, Bossongo and Pissa. They did not meet with resistance as they passed from PK9 to Sekia and Pissa, since the Seleka had fled these areas after learning that the Anti-Balaka were approaching. At the time of the group's presence on the Mbaïki road, Mr Yekatom, Cœur de Lion and Alkanto instructed the elements to kill all the Muslims in their area.
Following Michel Djotodia's resignation on 10 January 2014, Mr Yekatom and elements under his control left Yamwara and headed towards the Mbaïki road.

The Chamber notes that the Yekatom Defence refers to P-1839's allegations that she never heard Mr Yekatom issuing orders to attack unarmed Muslim civilians and that the order was to defend themselves if the enemy, the Seleka, attacked, to dispute the evidence that Mr Yekatom issued orders to kill Muslims. Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili stated that Mr Yekatom's instructions for the 'troops' were that they were going to 'fight the enemy and not the civilians'. Vivien Beina testified that at a certain point in time, Mr Yekatom made clear that Muslims could continue their activities on the PK9-Mbaïki axis without any problems.

The Chamber notes that from its above conclusions, it follows that chasing out the Seleka from the PK9-Mbaïki axis and freeing up the road necessarily implied chasing out the Muslims as well, as the Anti-Balaka considered them to be the same. The Chamber further notes that the allegations in the preceding paragraph contrast with abundant evidence indicating that the freedom of movement of Muslims on the PK9-Mbaïki was limited at the time. The Chamber will discuss this evidence further below.

From the above, the Chamber is unable to conclude by which degree Mr Yekatom might have inflated the number of his elements along the PK9-Mbaïki axis when preparing lists of elements for the disarmament process, or when speaking to journalists or NGOs -- if he did so at all. Indeed, taking Mr Yekatom's affirmation on his own group's size together with the fact that Vivien Beina was unable to provide any estimate of the group's size, merely stating that it was 'less than' 3,000, is insufficient to lead the Chamber to any conclusion in this regard. Rather, and bearing in mind the other evidence before it, set out above, including from individuals who were in a position to make informed estimates, the Chamber concludes that Mr Yekatom's group along the PK9-Mbaïki axis comprised at least 1,000 elements.

Furthermore, the Chamber notes that when asked whether after Djotodia's resignation there were elements who said that they were Anti-Balaka but were not part of Mr Yekatom's group in Lobaye, Vivien Beina agreed and indicated that 'there were subgroups, armed groups that were non-identified who came from the bush or from the forest to carry out exactions', and that it was 'very frequent'. The Chamber, however, notes that it reached its above conclusion taking into account the evidence mostly provided by Anti-Balaka elements, including members close to Mr Yekatom and his group, whom it would expect to be able to discern between members of their own movement and unidentified armed groups coming from the bush or the forest to commit exactions. The Chamber, therefore, does not consider that this circumstance has any bearing on its conclusion regarding the number of elements in Mr Yekatom's group along the PK9-Mbaïki axis.

The above is illustrated by an incident in which Mr Yekatom killed two of his aides-de-camp and shot at another element of his group. In particular, Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili indicated that on 24 April 2014, at PK9, he witnessed a disagreement between other elements from his group and a former FACA captain regarding the theft of his goats, and decided to intervene to calm things down. Mr Yekatom approached the group with some of his men; he carried an AK47 in firing position and shot at them. Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili was hit in the upper thigh and fell to the ground. Mr Yekatom ordered his men to take him to the hospital. Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili was hospitalised for two to three weeks. The other two elements, Seda and Fadal, were also brought to the hospital. Seda, a soldier dressed in military uniform, died two or three days later, while Fadal, who wore civilian clothing, was already dead by the time he was taken to the hospital. The witness explained that after this incident, he was no longer involved with the Anti-Balaka. Mr Yekatom never apologised to him and avoided him since then. The witness did not complain to the gendarmerie because he was afraid that Mr Yekatom would 'finish \[him\] off' as he knew that Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili had witnessed the killing of Seda and Fadal.The Chamber notes the Yekatom Defence's submission that according to both Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili and Vivien Beina, 'the single alleged "Seda incident"' concerned an attempt by Habib Beina to return farm animals looted by 'RFACPP members', which resulted in these members threatening Mr Yekatom and thereafter having a 'duel' with him. The Yekatom Defence thus portrays this incident as a 'duel' between two equal parties where misbehaved elements provoked Mr Yekatom and got injured. The Chamber is of the view that regardless of the misbehaviour of the elements, the incident's relevance lies in that it neatly reflects that as the leader of his group, Mr Yekatom had authority to sanction the elements under his command, and did so by injuring or even killing those who dared to disobey or otherwise challenge him. In the Chamber's view, incidents such as this one served Mr Yekatom to assert his power within the group and send a message to the rest of the elements.

paragraph_text_preview: The evidence indicates that Freddy Ouandjio aka Cœur de Lion was Mr Yekatom's deputy on the PK9-Mbaïki road. Indeed, numerous witnesses described Cœur de Lion as Mr Yekatom's deputy, including elements of Mr Yekatom's group and members of the Anti-Balaka movement and coordination, as well as individuals who personally interacted with both of them when the group arrived in Mbaïki. Some of these witnesses, including P-1839 and P-1962, specifically indicated that Cœur de Lion gave the orders to the elements on the Mbaïki road and was the person in charge when Mr Yekatom was not there. Likewise, P-2353 stated that when Mr Yekatom was not in Mbaïki, Cœur de Lion was 'in charge'.

Accordingly, and in light of the evidence above, the Chamber rejects the Yekatom Defence's submissions that even if it accepted that Ouandjio was assigned the title of 'deputy', there is no probative evidence that this resulted in a de facto hierarchical relationship between Mr Yekatom and Ouandjio.

Moreover, the Chamber notes that the Yekatom Defence seems to make contradictory arguments when asserting that Mr Yekatom could not be the leader of any group or movement because of his FACA title, which he used to publicly introduce himself, while at the same time suggesting that Cœur de Lion's title as 'deputy' -- and the fact that those around him perceived him as such -- cannot even be considered as an indication of the role he performed. Following this argumentation would mean for the Chamber to rely on a formal title and rank to assess someone's role without looking at the factual circumstances, but not to rely on a, even if less, formal title while looking at the factual circumstances. In the view of the Chamber, in its factual analysis one cannot be divided from the other. Contrarily to the Yekatom Defence's position, the Chamber considers highly relevant that the elements of Mr Yekatom's group consistently testified to Cœur de Lion being the 'deputy'. This is regardless of the purported formality of the title 'deputy' or whether military and non-military members understood it differently. In both formal and informal sense, military or civilian, it conveys the same and unambiguous directional flow of authority.

In relation to the Yekatom Defence's submissions concerning P-1786, the Chamber notes that P-1786 stated that despite the fact that Cœur de Lion was Mr Yekatom's deputy, they did not always get along; Cœur de Lion kept his distance from Mr Yekatom, he did not like that Mr Yekatom did not fight in the front lines with them and thought that he kept money from the Seleka. P-1786 also stated that Mr Yekatom was close to Momokama and Habib Beina. The Chamber is of the view that the fact that Mr Yekatom had a smoother or close personal relationship with other elements of his group does not detract from the fact that Cœur de Lion was under Mr Yekatom's command.

P-1839 specified that the base was located behind a church that was situated a few metres to the left of a customs checkpoint when approaching it from Bangui. The Chamber further notes that Gérard Ouambou recorded in a video footage, as he himself explained, Mr Yekatom's elements based in Sekia.

In addition to the base, Mr Yekatom's group took over the checkpoints in Sekia. P-1839 explained that the group set up two roadblocks to check the vehicles passing through and ensure the security of the Anti-Balaka base. P-1839 also referred to another roadblock, under control of the state and then occupied by the Seleka, to which 'the chiefs of each section \[went\] to collect money'. Witnesses P-0954, P-1858 and P-1974 similarly testified that the Anti-Balaka controlled the checkpoints in Sekia.

The Chamber notes that D29-5016 indicated that there was no Anti-Balaka group in Bossongo and that they were in 'C\[entrapalm\]'. The Chamber notes that Roger Okoa-Penguia confirmed, when asked, that Centrapalm, a company that processed palm oil, was located in Bossongo. It also recalls that Roger Okoa-Penguia confirmed that there were two checkpoints in Bossongo. The witness explained that before 2013, armed gendarmes were deployed at a checkpoint located 'in front of the road that leads to the Centrapalm \[...\]' to protect Centrapalm from thefts. Asked about a second checkpoint inside Bossongo, Roger Okoa-Penguia stated there were mobile checkpoints organised at specific times of the year. He also confirmed that a gendarmerie brigade in Bossongo provided security to Centrapalm. The Chamber also recalls that the witness confirmed that the Anti-Balaka took over these checkpoints. In a similar vein, P-1786 and Brice Emotion Namsio indicated that Mr Yekatom had elements at Centrapalm. Raymond Mongbandi also mentioned that Mr Yekatom had been stationed at Centrapalm before the Seleka left Mbaïki. Likewise, Brice Emotion Namsio testified that at some point in time Mr Yekatom 'went to base himself' in Centrapalm, controlling 'all that area'. In light of the evidence above, which indicates that Mr Yekatom's elements controlled Bossongo and its checkpoints, the Chamber disregards this part of D29-5016's evidence.

The Chamber finds that these arguments, addressed below in detail, are without merit. Rather, in the face of overwhelming evidence, also discussed below, the Chamber is of the view that Mr Yekatom and his group took over the checkpoints on the PK9-Mbaïki axis with the aims of identifying Muslims and financing the group and its needs.

Secondly, it notes that while the above evidence indicates that Mr Yekatom allowed the gendarmerie and the national staff to go back to their stations in the PK9 and Sekia checkpoints, that same evidence shows that Mr Yekatom did not give them back any effective power. In the words of the former general director of the gendarmerie in the context of the encounter at the PK9 bridge, whatever happened after crossing the PK9 barrier was under the Anti-Balaka's competence. It further notes that while these authorities were allowed to go back to the PK9 and Sekia checkpoints, they did so alongside Anti-Balaka elements posted there, who were mostly armed FACA members dressed in military uniform. The Chamber considers that there is a nuanced but relevant difference between allowing the authorities to be physically present in their duty stations and handing them over effective responsibility for the checkpoints, as argued by the Yekatom Defence. It is also the Chamber's view that this does not equate to the Anti-Balaka leaving all checkpoints, as Roger Okoa-Penguia described.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that the Yekatom Defence disputes P-1823's account, which it considers 'manifestly unreliable', in particular as regards the timing of the incident and his alleged recognition of the individuals involved. However, for the reasons detailed below, the Chamber is unconvinced by its arguments.

As regards the timing, the Chamber notes that P-1823 stated that after the Bangui Attack, he went to Petevo in the 6^th^ arrondissement and stayed in Bangui 'for almost a month' because it was not safe to travel at the time. During his testimony, he explained that he returned to Mbaïki after Michel Djotodia's resignation because before, 'Mbaïki had been taken over by the Seleka, and these are not people you can collaborate with'. He further explained that after Michel Djotodia's resignation, he could not stay in Bangui 'doing nothing', so he 'got up \[his\] courage and took the risk of returning, but taking a lot of precautions at the same time'. P-1823 also confirmed having attended a reconciliation meeting in Petevo during which an imam was attacked, and which the Yekatom Defence counsel suggested took place on 13 December 2013. P-1823 indicated that after the incident in Petevo, he left Bangui 'after a few days' as he could not have spent 'the new year' in Bangui, he had to leave to join his family.

Regarding the specific barrier at which P-1823 was stopped and Mr Yekatom's presence thereat, the Chamber notes that P-1823 confirmed that '\[t\]he barrier was before crossing the bridge'. He also indicated that people at the barrier wore 'things around their neck and on their arms', and confirmed that the gris-gris shown to him in a video footage was 'the same get-up that they were wearing'. P-1823 also confirmed, when asked twice, that Mr Yekatom was 'omnipresent', moving around, giving instructions, at 'the main base', PK9. Lastly, P-1823 indicated that Mr Yekatom was in his 'get-up' but had no gris-gris as such. The Chamber considers that while the witness indicated that he was stopped at a barrier before crossing the bridge (which the Yekatom Defence qualifies as P-0954's barrier), every other detail he provided about the incident actually points to the barrier taken over by Mr Yekatom's elements at the other side of the PK9 bridge. Accordingly, the Chamber is of the view that P-1823 erred when describing the exact location of the barrier but otherwise considers P-1823's account of the incident credible and reliable.

P-0954 described it as follows: 'To pass these checkpoints, God had to be with you, really. Otherwise, you could be killed. So you had to be really careful. They were there to check the vehicles, to control the motorbikes, the people, and also to find out what equipment there was in the various vehicles, and whether it was a vehicle of the Muslims or the positions of the Muslims or whether the Muslims were passing through or finding out who was passing through in order to aid their position, to betray their position. These were all the points that checkpoints were looking for'. The Chamber notes that the Yekatom Defence challenges this part of P-0954's evidence, amongst others, but considers that this witness's unique position at the time, together with his closeness to Mr Yekatom's group and knowledge of the area, makes his evidence particularly relevant. In the Chamber's view, the fact that he used strong language to describe that situation in particular does not make this part of his evidence less reliable or credible. The Chamber also notes that in any event, his description accords with the other evidence outlined above.

Moreover, the evidence also shows that the Anti-Balaka used the checkpoints on the PK9-Mbaïki axis to raise money to finance the group and its needs.

In this context, the Chamber notes P-1839's description of the role and activities of the treasurer of Mr Yekatom's group during this time. In particular, P-1839 testified that the day after their arrival in Sekia, an element was assigned as treasurer and, as such, Mr Yekatom ordered this element 'to collect the money from the roadblocks'. In the beginning, Mr Yekatom drove the treasurer to the roadblocks with his car, then the treasurer went by public transport; initially, it was every day and later every other day. The treasurer collected money at the roadblocks of PK9, Sekia and Bimon gathered from the people crossing the road, and also vehicles, motorbikes and large trucks. Mr Yekatom used this money if he needed to buy something and would sometimes direct to whom the treasurer had to give the collected money to. According to P-1839, the treasurer saved the rest of the money in a bag, which she kept with her when sleeping. When asked whether Mr Yekatom checked how the treasurer collected the money and what was done with it, P-1839 said that Mr Yekatom 'checked everything'. She confirmed that the treasurer was with Mr Yekatom most of the time when the money was collected at checkpoints.

This particular information is relevant only for the purposes of the general context. At the same time, this information is also relevant in relation to Muslim civilians fleeing from Mbaïki to Chad and other locations in the CAR. The evidence below reflects what witnesses described in this general context.

P-2419 further explained that on the evening of the Saturday following Michel Djotodia's resignation, the local youths of the village rose against the Seleka and after hearing a young Christian saying that '\[a\]ll Arabs are the same', he decided to hide. From his hiding place, he saw how the local youth set alight the mosque, and looted and destroyed houses of Muslims. P-2419 then hid in the house of his brother-in-law, a Christian; on the following morning, he saw through a window how Mr Yekatom arrived in Bimon with 'his men' and parked their vehicles in P-2419's brother-in-law's courtyard, and thereafter left, leaving some of the men that had come in the vehicles behind. On the night of Mr Yekatom's arrival, P-2419 fled to the bush near the village of États-Unis, where he met the 29 Fulata who had returned to Bimon. He described that life was difficult in the bush, they slept outdoors, there was not enough to eat, and he did not have any news about his family. While in the bush, P-2419 heard that the Anti-Balaka in Bimon searched the houses one by one looking for Muslims as well as people's mobile phones looking for Muslims' phone numbers. After two weeks in the bush, he walked to Bangui with one of the Fulata, accompanied by a local Christian from Bimon, pushing a 'pousse-pousse' with firewood as disguise, since this work is not usually done by Muslims. On the way to Bangui, they passed Anti-Balaka barricades at Ndangala, Yamboro, Sekia Ngyabourou and Samba, with their cart being searched at each barricade and them being asked to pay 100 francs at the Sekia barrier. P-2419 thought they arrived at the Central Mosque in PK5 on 27 January 2014. Once there, one of the local Christians told him that the Anti-Balaka had been informed of the place where the Fulata had been hiding in the bush but that 'Rambo' had stopped them from killing the Fulata because some of them were his 'cousins'.

paragraph_text_preview: Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo stated that following an incident in Mbata around the time of Djotodia's resignation in which the Seleka killed six people, 'the local militia' killed a Muslim and some houses were burnt and destroyed, Seleka colonel Anour helped the Muslims in Mbata move to Mbaïki. He explained that the Muslims feared an Anti-Balaka attack after the Bangui Attack; they noticed that after 5 December 2013, the Anti-Balaka movement was gaining momentum as more people joined their ranks. He also explained that Muslims felt 'unprotected' because there were no Seleka in Mbata at the time, so they followed colonel Anour's suggestion to join other Muslims in Mbaïki, 'where they would be protected by the Seleka'. While Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo did not specify a timeframe for the departure of Muslims from Mbata to Mbaïki, the Chamber considers that the details of his account regarding the Seleka's intervention, similar to those of P-2354, allow it to reasonably conclude that it occurred at the time when, and because, Mr Yekatom's group advanced along the axis.

paragraph_text_preview: In relation to P-2353, the Chamber notes that while he initially stated that he first made a trip to Bagandou to take Muslims to Mbaïki on 29 December 2013, he later testified that the last trip he made was to Bagandou and that it took place on the evening that the Seleka left Mbaïki -- which, according to the Chamber's finding below, occurred on 29 January 2014. Therefore, according to his testimony, P-2353 would have made the trip to Bagandou on 29 January 2014, when indeed the Seleka were still in Mbaïki. Further, P-2353 indicated that at the time, all the Muslims left Bagandou except for some farmers and an imam who was killed by 'young people acting \[...\] as Anti-Balaka'. The Chamber notes that this timeframe is consistent with P-2041's evidence according to which Imam Matar of Bagandou was killed by 'the youth of B\[agandou\]' on 25 January 2014, when the Anti-Balaka had not yet arrived in the village.

First, the Chamber indeed notes that the killing of two men in Bangui-Bouchia in October 2013 occurred months before Mr Yekatom's group advanced along the PK9-Mbaïki axis.

Second, the Chamber notes that even if some witnesses relate the movement of Muslims from along the axis also to the events in Bangui-Bouchia, their evidence includes further details which allow to date such movement more specifically. P-1666, for instance, testified that people from the various communes began to travel to Mbaïki after the events concerning 'Aba Zakaria and Mahamat' (referring to the Bangui-Bouchia incident), over the course of seven to 10 days, but at the same time indicated that Muslims began moving, going to Mbaïki, after Michel Djotodia resigned. Bearing in mind that placing this movement generally 'after' the Bangui-Bouchia incident does not indicate that it was immediately thereafter, the Chamber considers of import the witness's specification as to when Muslims moving from the communes began arriving to Mbaïki.

Fourth, regarding the Yekatom Defence's suggestion that two interrelated factors, notably the withdrawal of the Seleka and 'the outbreak of mass anti-Muslim violence', exclusively explain the Muslims' departure from the axis, the Chamber considers that the fact that some Muslim inhabitants along the axis could have fled due to these factors does not detract from the fact that other Muslim inhabitants fled due to the advance of Mr Yekatom's group along the axis. In fact, considering the evidence outlined above, the Chamber is of the view that a significant proportion of the Muslim civilian population along the axis fled to Mbaïki due to this advance.

Accordingly, and in light of the above conclusion, the Chamber considers that the Yekatom Defence's further submission that the 'RFACPP's advance was not a factor in the departure of Muslims from towns and villages along the axis' is without merit. Regarding its related submission that evidence indicating the contrary 'arose from an objectively unfounded belief that the RFACPP would target Muslims that remained', the Chamber recalls P-1839's evidence that at the time of the group's presence on the Mbaïki road, Mr Yekatom, Cœur de Lion and Alkanto instructed the elements to kill all the Muslims in the area. The Chamber further recalls its discussion of the way in which Anti-Balaka groups, including that of Mr Yekatom, pursued and implemented its core objective of removing Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power, which equated the Muslim civilian population in general, especially in western CAR, with the Seleka and thus perceived this population as their enemy. The Chamber also refers to its findings on the acts perpetrated by Mr Yekatom's elements in Mbaïki, including the harassing and threats made to the Muslim civilian population and Djido Saleh's killing. Likewise, in relation to the Yekatom Defence's submission that 'Muslims' fear of the RFACPP appears to have been rooted in their mistaken belief that the RFACPP and the "anti-balaka" \[...\] were one and the same', the Chamber recalls its findings concerning the relation of Mr Yekatom's group with the Anti-Balaka movement.

paragraph_text_preview: Raymond Mongbandi stated that Muslims fleeing to Mbaïki 'were numerous running into thousands' and 'might have doubled the number of Muslims \[already living\] in Mbaïki'. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo indicated that he believed there was anything between 500 to thousands of Muslims from other areas which were added to the population of Muslims already residing in Mbaïki at the time. P-2389 stated that at least 500 Muslims moved to Mbaïki at that time. P-2041 estimated that around 2,000 Muslims fled from the neighbouring villages to Mbaïki. D29-5013 testified that at least 3,000 Muslims fled to Mbaïki to find refuge. Guerrino Perin testified that 'over a thousand' Muslims fled to Mbaïki. P-2354 stated that while he did not know the number of refugees in Mbaïki, 'there were many, more than a thousand'. P-1666 provided a number far beyond these estimations, indicating that he estimated that 15,000 or 16,000 Muslims from Mbaïki's commune fled to Mbaïki over the course of seven to 10 days.

Several witnesses described the living conditions of the Muslim community in Mbaïki as being very difficult at the time.

According to P-2353, Muslims arrived in Mbaïki with 'nothing on them'. In this context, the Chamber recalls that Muslims had to flee leaving their possessions behind. Muslims arriving to Mbaïki mainly stayed in the neighborhoods of Yerima and Baguirmi, which were predominantly Muslim. Witnesses indicated that within these neighborhoods, some Muslims were hosted by Muslim family or friends, while others had to sleep on house porches, under trees or at the Baguirmi mosque. Raymond Mongbandi reported that Muslims coming from 'the B\[oda\] area' went to the MISCA base, located at the coffee cooperative behind the prefect's office in Mbaïki.

According to Raymond Mongbandi, there was 'little food' in Mbaïki. P-2389 stated that '\[a\]s the number of Muslims in Mbaïki started to increase it became more difficult to get food'. P-2353 indicated that they could 'barely eat' in Mbaïki. Diakité Aboubakar provided the following detailed account: When the evacuees arrived in M\[baïki\], prices of everything went high. There was not enough meat for the people. There was a general shortage of food including vegetables like coco, aubergines, peanuts, manioc etc. Some of the evacuees had brought food but that was all finished. The reserve in the city was all depleted. By the time they left the city, there was nothing left. Life was very difficult. They must have remained in M\[baïki\] for about two weeks before the trucks came and took them. Several witnesses described the atmosphere in Mbaïki as one of hunger and fear. In particular, Raymond Mongbandi reported that '\[t\]he refugees were constantly worried, fearing an Anti-Balaka attack with them as the target for retribution and they were unhappy as they felt they were being forced out and into Chad'. In the same vein, P-2353 testified that 'it was hunger and the death threat that weighed on the populations. When you are hungry, when you've got nothing to eat and you've got the death threats as well, life becomes terrible'. Arrival of Mr Yekatom's group to Mbaïki Mr Yekatom and elements under his control entered Mbaïki on 30 January 2014. That day, a meeting was held at the St Jeanne d'Arc Church in Mbaïki, with Mr Yekatom and members of his group, representatives of the Mbaïki civilian and religious authorities, international organisations and NGOs, as well as the Sangaris. At the meeting, the removal of the Muslim civilian population from Mbaïki, which was a foregone conclusion at that point, was decided. After the meeting finished, Mr Yekatom addressed the crowds outside of the meeting location and subsequently at Mbaïki's bus station, where he delivered 'peace messages' similar to those he had expressed at the meeting. The presence of the Sangaris and other international actors in Mbaïki at that time compelled Mr Yekatom to bring this 'peace message' to Mbaïki and prevented attacks of his group against the Muslim civilian population. After the meeting, the prefect and other individuals contacted the authorities to arrange the convoy that would transport the Muslim civilian population out of Mbaïki.

The Chamber does not consider the above evidence to be mutually exclusive. The evidence by Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo and Antareze-De-Neve Madongagba is clear on their meeting with Mr Yekatom in Pissa to arrange a meeting with the Seleka still present in Mbaïki. That D29-5013 similarly reached out with a view to organising such a meeting which then included further international stakeholders does not distract from this evidence. Importantly, and as further discussed below, a meeting at the St Jeanne d'Arc Church in Mbaïki did take place, albeit not involving the Seleka.

The Chamber notes in this regard that (i) P-1813 testified that one night the Seleka called him to say that they were leaving and moving to another place following their superior's instructions; (ii) Guerrino Perin testified that Colonel Anour called his deputy 'Abbot Antarese' and informed him that the Seleka were leaving; and (iii) Antareze-De-Neve Madongagba testified that they learned the Seleka left one night because two or three Central African Seleka elements who refused to leave sought refuge at the cathedral the same night. The Chamber does not consider that Antareze-De-Neve Madongagba not mentioning being called by Colonel Anour discredits, as such, the evidence of Guerrino Perin or, in turn, the reliability of the testimony of Antareze-De-Neve Madongagba. The fact remains that the Seleka left Mbaïki on the night of 29 January 2014. The Chamber further notes the evidence of P-2353, who, while stating that the Seleka left 'shortly' after Michel Djotodia had resigned, also said that the Seleka left at night, without warning, and that the Anti-Balaka arrived the next morning (*see* P-2353 Statement, CAR-OTP-2100-0226-R03, at 0234, para. 47). P-1666 similarly testified that the Seleka left 'one day or two days' before the Anti-Balaka arrived in Mbaïki (*see* P-1666: T-230, p. 58, line 21 -- p. 59, line 2).

The Yekatom Defence submits that Mr Yekatom's negotiations with Seleka colonel Anour led to the peaceful withdrawal of the latter's forces from Mbaïki by the end of January 2014. The Chamber considers that the evidence pointed to in this regard is inapt to reach this conclusion. While Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo described hearing from Seleka elements that Mr Yekatom had reached out to them and told them to leave Mbaïki, as discussed above, and Guerrino Perin suggested that there was good will between 'the Seleka, Adam' and Mr Yekatom to avoid inter-communal violence, the evidence available does not indicate that the Seleka in Mbaïki left because of any exchanges with Mr Yekatom. Guerrino Perin himself said as much when indicating that while the Seleka had agreed to have a meeting, they received orders 'from elsewhere' to depart and regroup in the north, as did Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo.

Notably, P-1839 confirmed that less than a hundred Anti-Balaka elements went to Mbaïki together with Mr Yekatom on that first day. Raymond Mongbandi stated that Mr Yekatom arrived in Mbaïki accompanied by many Anti-Balaka elements, including Cœur de Lion, 'to install his about 50 to 100 elements in Mbaïki'. P-2041 estimated that on 30 January 2014, at least 2,000 Anti-Balaka entered Mbaïki. P-1666 testified that on the first day, about 100 to 200 Anti-Balaka elements entered Mbaïki, that this number 'slowly but surely' grew in the following days, and that by the time he left Mbaïki, he estimated that they amounted to almost 1,000 elements, including 'the young people from the locality who joined their ranks'. Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili stated that when he became deputy ComZone of Mbaïki, he and the ComZone had around 80 to 90 people under their command. He later testified that he and the ComZone Sete had about 40 elements under their control in Mbaïki. Antareze-De-Neve Madongagba estimated that there were between 25 and 30 Anti-Balaka elements in Mbaïki on the day of the meeting; and further indicated that it is possible that 'other people came to join Mr Yekatom's elements' but that he did not believe there had been 1,000 elements present in Mbaïki at any time.

The Chamber heard the testimony of eight individuals who participated in the meeting: Raymond Mongbandi, Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo, P-2041, Diakité Aboubakar, P-1666, Guerrino Perin, D29-5013 and Antareze-De-Neve Madongagba. Based on their evidence, as well as the notes taken during the meeting by P-2041 (the 'Notes'), the Chamber concludes that it unfolded as described below.

Second, and regardless of how Mr Yekatom publicly introduced himself in certain settings, the Chamber recalls that witnesses unambiguously identified him as the leader of the Anti-Balaka group on the PK9-Mbaïki axis. Third, and specifically with regard to the Mbaïki meeting, it notes that witnesses indicated that they had contact with him prior to and for the purposes of preparing the meeting in his role as leader of the Anti-Balaka in the area. Fourth, the Chamber notes that regardless of how he introduced himself that day, Mr Yekatom's statements at the meeting, which are subsequently discussed, could have only been made by a leader and a representative of the Anti-Balaka with the sufficient authority to speak and make commitments on its behalf.

In this regard, the Chamber notes that several witnesses indicated that the removal of Muslims from Mbaïki was decided at the meeting. Their evidence, as well as the evidence outlined further below, shows that at this point, their removal from Mbaïki was a foregone conclusion. Notably, Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo stated that one of the issues they discussed at the meeting was 'the movement of the Chadian Muslim community'. He later clearly indicated that the decision to take them out of Mbaïki 'was taken and discussed during the meeting in St Jeanne d'Arc' and on that occasion only. Roger Okoa-Penguia stated that '\[a\] decision was taken to have the Muslims leave for their security, to avoid a blood bath, to avoid the Muslims being killed by the Anti-Balaka'. Diakité Aboubakar confirmed that the departure of Muslims to Chad was discussed at the meeting and that he specifically recalled the prefect and Imam Langaba talking about it. D29-5013 further indicated that part of 'their' request during the meeting was that when the convoy moved on, everybody guaranteed their safety until they left the Lobaye zone. She also indicated the 'conclusion' of the meeting was that 'the Muslim communities would be able to leave the place without any acts of violence or abuse'. Further, the Notes include a reference to 'notre sorti de \[Mbaïki\] pour \[aller\] au Tchad le 06/02/2014'.

The evidence also indicates that while the decision to remove the Muslim community from Mbaïki was taken at the meeting, informal enquiries and discussions on the dislocation took place beforehand. In particular, Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo stated that the Chadian Muslim community in Mbaïki felt threatened and prior to the Anti-Balaka's arrival in Mbaïki spoke with the Chadian authorities 'to see if there was a way they could be evacuated'. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo also stated that prior to the Mbaïki meeting, the representatives of the Malian Muslim community also told him that they would leave with the Chadian Muslims if the latter were being 'evacuated'. Moreover, a witness testified that in the context of the preparations of the meeting, an individual involved in these preparations went to see Mr Yekatom 'to negotiate' and ask him whether he could agree 'to some kind of solution for the Muslims in Mbaïki', further indicating that this individual was successful in their mission, namely, 'to ensure the release of the Muslims'. In the Chamber's view, this shows that D29-5013 discussed with Mr Yekatom the possibility of moving Muslims out of Mbaïki before the meeting. This would explain D29-5013's indication, when asked whether the decision to 'evacuate' Muslims had been taken before the meeting, that that was her understanding because when 'they' spoke to 'them', 'they' all said that it was preferable and necessary for their security to leave.

The evidence shows that after the meeting, the prefect and other individuals contacted the authorities to arrange the convoy that would transport the Muslim community out of Mbaïki. Indeed, Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo testified that he, the bishop and the DRC and HCR representatives were given the mission of contacting 'the highest authorities in Bangui' so that some of the vehicles that had come from Chad could be sent 'to get the Muslims out of Mbaïki, the Muslims who were being threatened'. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo mentioned that the delegate of the Chadian Muslim community was responsible for contacting the ambassador or the representative of the Chadian state who was in Bangui with the same purpose. Raymond Mongbandi stated that the prefect and the bishop travelled to Bangui to inform the head of state, who then informed the Chadian head of state, who then made arrangements to 'evacuate' the Muslims from Mbaïki.

The Chamber observes that Raymond Mongbandi's evidence is consistent with the overall evidence on this subject. Raymond Mongbandi stated that the decision to 'evacuate' Muslims from Mbaïki was made after the meeting, but also that the decision to 'evacuate' was 'basically the fruit of this meeting'. He also referred to a meeting in which the Muslims learnt about the decision to 'evacuate', when '\[t\]he Seleka were still present in Mbaïki', and which was 'an open invitation for the Anti-Balaka to attend and agree not to harm Muslims'. In the Chamber's view, the witness seemed to be referring to the 30 January 2014 meeting in Mbaïki despite confusing some details. Further, when asked during his testimony, Raymond Mongbandi referred to one meeting in which 'the Anti-Balaka' were present 'that had to do with cohabitation between the two communities in Mbaïki' -- which the Chamber considers makes reference to the meeting held in Mbaïki on 30 January 2014 --; and another one related to the 'evacuation' of Muslims to Chad, held in a 'discreet way', which concerned the local authorities and the administration' and which 'the Anti-Balaka did not attend'. In the Chamber's view, the description of this second 'meeting' corresponds to the arrangements made by the authorities after the meeting held in Mbaïki on 30 January 2014 to secure the convoy.

paragraph_text_preview: According to D29-5013, Mr Yekatom told the young people who were waiting outside that they were too young, that their place was either in the fields with their parents or in school, and that he needed professionals.

The impression of some of those who witnessed the scene was that the youth was disappointed with Mr Yekatom's words. In fact, several witnesses shared the view that the only reason why Mr Yekatom and his group did not attack the Muslim population in Mbaïki was because of the presence of the Sangaris and other international forces.

P-1666, while feeling reassured by Mr Yekatom's words, also indicated that if the Anti‑Balaka did not attack, it was because their leader had instructed them in this regard, because 'he' made a commitment during the meeting, and because the FOMAC and the Sangaris forces were present, all of which ensured that no attack occurred.

P-2389 felt that Mr Yekatom and the Anti-Balaka could not attack them 'only because of the presence of the S\[angaris\]' and opined that if the Sangaris had not been in Mbaïki, the Anti-Balaka would have attacked and killed Muslims in Mbaïki.

Relatedly, one of Mr Yekatom's former elements, Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili, stated that when the group arrived in Mbaïki, '\[t\]he only obstacle to take the town was the French Army' and that 'the French Army' instructed Mr Yekatom's group 'not to harass people and not to pillage or to create disorder'.
P-1666 testified that Eric from the Sangaris asked 'the Anti-Balaka leader' not to walk around Mbaïki town with weapons, after which the Anti-Balaka retreated with their weapons to the abattoir.

The Chamber further recalls P-2041's detailed explanation of how the Sangaris asked Mr Yekatom to order the youngsters surrounding the church on the day of the meeting to stop harassing the Muslim delegation that wanted to leave the place.

The evidence outlined above shows that the presence of Sangaris forces and other international actors in Mbaïki at that time compelled Mr Yekatom to bring a peace message to Mbaïki and prevented his group from attacking the Muslim population. The role played by the Sangaris forces in Mbaïki was not limited to being physically present in the town, but also included the concrete orders and interventions described above, such as instructing Mr Yekatom and his group not to harass people and not to walk around with weapons. While the Sangaris forces later left Mbaïki to intervene in Boda, as already discussed above, the decision to remove the Muslim civilians inhabiting Mbaïki had already been decided at the St Jeanne d'Arc Church meeting. Indeed, at the time at which Mr Yekatom pledged securing order in Mbaïki and not harming its Muslim inhabitants, he was aware that these same inhabitants would leave not long thereafter.

It notes that Raymond Mongbandi elaborated on this point further during his testimony: '\[...\] this decision was taken because there was a total breach of trust. In this regard, the Chamber recalls P-1839's evidence that at the time of the group's presence on the Mbaïki road, Mr Yekatom instructed the elements to kill all the Muslims in the area. P-1666 testified about a first encounter with Cœur de Lion in which certain individuals from the Mbaïki Muslim community handed over to Cœur de Lion the money collected among the Muslim traders. Cœur de Lion told these individuals that 'after Rambo he was the boss and was in control', gave them his telephone number and told them to call him if 'any uncontrolled element' threatened or abused civilians so that he could intervene. Because 'the boss' was not there when the first collection took place, a second collection was carried out when Mr Yekatom arrived and the abovementioned individuals handed him over 100,000 CFA. Mr Yekatom gave them 'reassurances', explained to them why he had taken up arms and that he carried out patrols between Bangui, Pissa and PK9, and that they should cooperate with his deputy in the field if there were any problems.

The Chamber notes that while witnesses do not seem to agree on the number and location of the bases, it can conclude that Mr Yekatom's group settled in at least one base in Mbaïki.

The Chamber notes that D29-5013 also indicated that she was not based in Mbaïki, and went back 'two or three times' between the time of the meeting and the Muslims' departure from Mbaïki. The Anti-Balaka also attacked a gendarme patrol in Mbaïki which was there to protect the population, taking the patrol's weapons and the service car that they were using.

The Chamber heard numerous witnesses who described the threats made to the Muslims in Mbaïki, and the harassment they were subjected to, following the arrival of Mr Yekatom's group in the town.

Some of these witnesses claimed that those who threatened and harassed Muslims were mostly the local youngsters of Mbaïki, who saw in the Anti-Balaka an opportunity to take revenge for the abuses committed by the Seleka, considered the 'protectors' of Muslims. These witnesses seemed to draw a clear line between the Anti-Balaka elements that arrived in Mbaïki and the local youngsters who were not officially part of the group, and who outnumbered the Anti-Balaka elements, according to their evidence.

This is the case of Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo, who explained that after the abuses committed by the Seleka, deemed 'the protectors of the Muslims', and following their departure from Mbaïki and the arrival of the Anti-Balaka, the 'indigenous population' were up in arms against the Chadian community. They assumed that the Anti-Balaka would enable them 'to wreak revenge upon the Muslim population because their protectors were no longer there'. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo explained that 'independently of the Anti-Balaka', many individuals 'amongst the indigenous population' wanted to attack the Muslims and loot their possessions. The witness stated that 'a lot of young people were interested in this, \[...\] they invented themselves as Anti-Balaka', and got close to the Anti-Balaka 'to come to an agreement and to harm the Muslim community'. He also testified that the Anti-Balaka in Mbaïki were FACA and 'young people who had set themselves up as Balakas and had integrated that group of Balakas against the Muslims'.

Further, the Chamber notes that other witnesses pointed out that elements of Mr Yekatom's group, as well as local youngsters, threatened local Muslims.

Specifically, P-1839 described the threats made by an Anti-Balaka element belonging to Mr Yekatom's group, in Mr Yekatom's presence, on the day of their arrival in Mbaïki. P-1839 explained that after the meeting at the St Jeanne d'Arc Church, while Mr Yekatom, herself and another element, 'Cube Maggi', were driving around Mbaïki, she saw how Cube Maggi threatened the Muslims who were on the roadside and sitting on their terraces. 'Cube Maggi' threatened them with a hand gesture, waving his finger back and forth, while saying something along the lines of '\[w\]e'll finish with you' with his window open. P-1839 also indicated that Mr Yekatom did not say anything to 'Cube Maggi', did not tell him off for doing so.

paragraph_text_preview: Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo indicated that Mr Yekatom would meet with MISCA/MINUSCA in Mbaïki to discuss reported incidents of 'misbehaviour of the Anti-Balaka', both before and some time after the death of Djido Saleh. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo testified that some of the elements who committed abuses such as threats, 'verbal attacks', 'acts of violence' and pillaging were 'among the accused's group in different places', but that there were also young people 'who were passing themselves off as elements of the accused, while they were not'. The witness recalled that at least on one occasion, Mr Yekatom brought to the MISCA compound individuals who had reportedly conducted acts of violence in a given locality and who, according to the witness, were acting on their own and not on behalf of Mr Yekatom. He also confirmed recalling an incident described in a document, stating that Mr Yekatom brought a number of people and weapons back from a mission and to the residency of the prefect. The document suggests that, 'according to Alfred Rombo', the aim of this mission was to disarm 'these fake militia that disturb the rural population', and assist MISCA to ensure free circulation of people and goods in the Lobaye and Ombella-M'Poko prefectures. The Chamber notes in this regard that Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo stated that the population that was being disturbed was not Muslim as in the peripheral locations, only members of the 'indigenous population' were present.

Raymond Mongbandi categorically denied the question of whether Mr Yekatom worked with MISCA to ensure safety in Lobaye. He acknowledged, however, that Mr Yekatom attended meetings which MISCA also attended. When asked, Raymond Mongbandi also denied hearing that MISCA asked Mr Yekatom to patrol the regions to re-establish public order, indicating that they only saw each other once in St Jeanne d'Arc to talk about restoring peace. When asked about a handwritten note, the witness indicated that the authorities 'wanted the Anti-Balaka to stop their hostilities and contribute to the restoration of peace in the country and in the town', which is why the Anti-Balaka laid down their weapons. However, the witness did not recall the incident described in the note nor having participated in a ceremony of handing over weapons. When shown a document related to the discharge of the weapons by MISCA to the gendarmerie as mentioned in the note, Raymond Mongbandi indicated that while it certainly showed 'a certain degree of collaboration', what he saw happening in the field was different.

paragraph_text_preview: At the same time, however, the Chamber is mindful that the efforts and measures described above took place after the removal of the Muslim civilian population from Mbaïki had been decided and/or carried out. The evidence outlined above can only be assessed considering this context. This is the case of the identification and disarming of 'fake Anti-Balaka'. Indeed, the Chamber observes that the event in which Mr Yekatom disarmed 'fake Anti-Balaka' took place in April 2014, that is, more than one month after the Muslims were removed from Mbaïki. Also the other evidence discussed above suggests that events such as the handing over of weapons, or Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili being tasked with identifying 'fake Anti-Balaka' in Mbaïki, took place after the Muslim civilian population was removed from Mbaïki. In relation to Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili's task, the Chamber in any event notes that it did not hear any concrete evidence on specific measures taken by the witness in Mbaïki to fulfill his duty to identify 'fake Anti-Balaka'.

Moreover, the Chamber notes that despite the meetings Mr Yekatom attended, Raymond Mongbandi indicated that Mr Yekatom did not cooperate with MISCA/MINUSCA to ensure security in Mbaïki. In this regard, the Chamber recalls Raymond Mongbandi's unique and relevant position at the time as mayor of Mbaïki.

Further, the Chamber notes that Mr Yekatom and Cœur de Lion offered their phone numbers in the context of receiving payment by the Muslim traders who, according to P‑2354, asked to be treated favourably in return.

In this context, the Chamber also notes P-0974's evidence, according to which he went to Mbaïki when other Anti-Balaka were already there, and while there, a French captain asked to meet with the Anti-Balaka leader to ensure nothing would happen to the Muslims and to allow the Chadians to 'evacuate' them. P-0974 went to the meeting with Cœur de Lion where they were told by the French captain that he did not want weapons in town and not to harm the Muslims, which, according to P-0974, was a warning to them.

In any event, the Chamber considers that the alleged efforts or measures displayed by Mr Yekatom were clearly insufficient because members of his group continued to threaten and harass the Muslim civilian population, irrespective of whether members of the local population also issued threats. The violence the Anti-Balaka exerted on Muslim civilians did not end as a consequence of the measures Mr Yekatom implemented but because the Muslims were removed from Mbaïki and transported elsewhere.

Dislocation of Muslims from Mbaïki On 6 February 2014, Chadian forces transported a first group of Muslim civilians from Mbaïki to Chad and other locations in the CAR. These Muslim civilians had to leave their belongings behind. They left Mbaïki in fear of the Anti-Balaka and, in particular, due to the arrival of Mr Yekatom's group to Mbaïki. The total number of Muslims removed from Mbaïki at the time amounted to at least 3,000. As a result of this dislocation, very few Muslim civilians remained in Mbaïki. The living conditions in the refugee camps in Chad were extremely difficult.

The trucks arrived in Mbaïki early in the morning and left the town once Muslims had boarded the trucks, that same morning. The dislocation was therefore completed within the day.

P-2389 stated that he saw 20 big military green trucks arriving to Mbaïki that morning, and that he estimated that each truck could take around 80 people. Roger Okoa-Penguia stated that 61 trucks were needed to get out 'thousands of Muslims' from Mbaïki. Diakité Aboubakar stated that there must have been about 30 big trucks to 'evacuate' 'the Chadians'. P-2041 mentioned ten wheeled military trucks, and estimated that more than a hundred people were loaded on each truck. He also testified that 2,000 Muslims left the town of Mbaïki that day. P-2354 referred in his statement to a 'convoy of 8 trucks' that went from Mbaïki to Bangui, while he indicated later that a total of 16 trucks were used to 'evacuate' everyone. D29-5013 indicated that there were 17 large trucks and more than 3,000 people who wanted to leave Mbaïki.

The Chamber recalls that at that time, the Muslim inhabitants of the town of Mbaïki amounted to at least 2,000. It further recalls its conclusion that at least 1,000 Muslims had fled to Mbaïki from surrounding towns and villages. Accordingly, the Chamber concludes that at least 3,000 Muslims were removed from Mbaïki that day. The Chamber considers that this number is coherent with and supported by most of the evidence provided in this respect, set out above. It is also consistent with the evidence indicating that as a result of the removal of Muslim civilians from Mbaïki, very few Muslims remained in Mbaïki.

P-1666 described how he felt that day: When I left Mbaïki it was extremely difficult. I had tears in my eyes. The Christians came, they took our hands. They cried, we cried. It was very moving. We didn't expect this departure. We didn't think that one day we would leave from this town. You must remember, we invested a lot. We built a lot up and all of a sudden we had to abandon everything and leave. It was really with great sadness because we were forced to abandon everything which we had shared as we grew up, so there was a lot of sadness. It was difficult. It was very hard to bear.

The evidence indicates that in addition to the trucks of the Chadian forces, the convoy that left Mbaïki that day also included private vehicles. Diakité Aboubakar and D29-5013 indicated that some Muslims of Chadian origin provided their vehicles to transport people. P-2353 stated that he carried people, as well as the family luggage and possessions, in his three vehicles and followed the Chadian truck on which his family had left for Bangui. According to P-2353, he used one of the vehicles to transport 40 people, as well as his family luggage and possessions. He also stated that he followed the Chadian convoy with his vehicles while his family travelled in one of the Chadian trucks. Similarly, P-1666 testified that he and his 'brothers and sisters' used their own vehicles to drive to Kilometre 5 with the Chadian convoy. P-2354 also indicated that he joined the convoy in his pickup with his wives and children.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber also notes that some witnesses mentioned that mosques in Mbaïki were attacked and/or damaged after the Muslims' departure from Mbaïki. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo specifically stated that one mosque was attacked by thieves from Bangui and surrounding areas, and that the metal sheets of the roof of another mosque had been stripped off, and that he did not think it was done by the Anti-Balaka. P-0475 testified that all mosques were destroyed. Diakité Aboubakar stated that following the 'evacuation' of the Muslims of Chadian origin from Mbaïki, the Anti-Balaka destroyed all the mosques. He further indicated that one month before giving his statement in March 2019, he had been in Mbaïki with Guerrino Perin and had taken pictures of the destroyed mosque. Antareze-De-Neve Madongagba testified that after the Muslims left Mbaïki, the two mosques 'were not destroyed' but windows and doors were removed and the mosques 'were not in very good condition'. D29-5013 asserted that no mosque in Mbaïki was destroyed, but did not explain how she knew this. On the basis of the above, the Chamber considers that the mosques in Mbaïki were in the least damaged, but it is unable to conclude by whom.

The Chamber, however, considers that there is overwhelming evidence, set out above, which demonstrates that Muslims fled Mbaïki because they were afraid of the Anti-Balaka. These fears were not unfounded or based on the mere presence of the Anti-Balaka in the town. In this regard, the Chamber recalls its findings above that elements belonging to Mr Yekatom's group, as well as local youngsters, threatened and harassed the Muslim civilian population of Mbaïki -- the former as soon as they arrived in the town. From that moment onwards, Muslims in Mbaïki were not able to move around freely and their living conditions worsened by the day. As described by various witnesses, Muslims felt that they had no choice but to leave Mbaïki as they believed that the Anti-Balaka would kill them if they stayed any longer.

Accordingly, the Chamber puts no weight on the claims that Muslims left Mbaïki because an 'evacuation' had been arranged in advance, or because Muslims 'wanted' to leave regardless of the Anti-Balaka. The Chamber reiterates that even if Muslims agreed or requested to be removed from Mbaïki, they did so because they felt that their lives were in danger as long as they stayed in Mbaïki. In the Chamber's view, this reflects that there was a genuine lack of choice on their part. Thereafter, the Congolese MISCA transported a second group of Muslims out of Mbaïki to Bangui and other locations.

Several witnesses indicated that after the Chadian forces transported the first group of Muslims out of Mbaïki, the Congolese MISCA arrived in Mbaïki and transported a second group of Muslims out of the town.

P-2041 testified, when asked, that while the Muslims who had come to Mbaïki from the neighbouring area to seek refuge were 'evacuated' on the same day, a smaller number of Muslims were 'evacuated' by the MINUSCA.

P-1666 confirmed, when asked, that after the 'evacuation' of the first group of Muslims from Mbaïki, 'the Malian community' remained in the town until they were 'evacuated', after which '\[t\]he only person who remained was the mayor and his family'.

Diakité Aboubakar provided further details. In particular, he explained that the Chadian forces left 'the Muslim West Africans' behind because he had not been informed on time about the 'evacuation' of 'the Chadians' and they were therefore not ready to move. He stated that he was caught by surprise when he saw 'a Chadian vehicle with a big gun arriving in the city', and later confirmed with a Chadian merchant delegate that they would be 'evacuated' that day. He also testified that 'the Central African Muslims' and 'the West Africans' stayed in Mbaïki town for a week more. During this time, they cohabited with the Anti-Balaka, and while the Anti-Balaka did not attack or kill any Muslims, there were threats. In this respect, the Chamber recalls the incident Diakité Aboubakar mentioned, which happened during his period, in which some Anti-Balaka elements surrounded the mosque in which he was praying alone and told him to leave.
