P-2353 said during his interview in 2019 that he wanted to return to his village in Mbaïki when the situation permitted, but did not see that happening any time soon. During his testimony, P-2353 expanded as follows: I sought refuge in a foreign country and everything happened during my absence. My house, my shop, all my property was pillaged and destroyed. Even my coffee machine was taken away. \[...\] ever since I got here, I'm scared to go back to Mbaïki. I'm stuck in Bangui. I'm scared. I was born in a city and I really strive to contribute to the city. I ran a business and everything was annihilated and it is extremely sad. And this is why I don't even have the courage to go to Mbaïki and this is why I stayed on in Bangui. If you have your own house and you're driven out of your house and someone takes all your possessions, what can you do? You can only be sad. Once we got to Chad, we got there because it was war. There was a war going on in our country. Once we got there, our children lived under the trees. But those children were not born under the trees. We spent three months there. And three months later, it was very difficult there, so we had to leave that place and move onward. It's a very painful impact and on several levels. I was a shopkeeper and I had employees. And today I've lost everything, just about everything. I've got nothing. All the fruit of my investment is gone. \[...\] my wives are just about managing to meet their needs. My children are all scattered and it's very difficult to meet their needs. \[...\] But after these events, I've lost everything. I've lost everything. The little ones with me, I manage to send them to school, but the children who are slightly elder in age have left school, have dropped out. I don't know how they're going to fend for themselves tomorrow. The second problem is I do not have a home. \[...\] Sometimes I have problems in paying my rent. \[...\] I've got financial problems, and I really am struggling to meet the needs of my family.

paragraph_text_preview: Following the removal of Muslims from Mbaïki, Djido Saleh (hereinafter: 'Saleh'), the second deputy mayor of Mbaïki, and his family, were among the very few remaining Muslims in Mbaïki.
Various witnesses indicated that despite expressing their concerns to Saleh for his and his family's safety, he refused to leave Mbaïki when the Muslim population was removed from the town.

Raymond Mongbandi testified that Saleh believed that his mayor's badge would protect him against violence and that this is why he decided to stay. According to the witness, members of the community, including religious authorities, asked Saleh to get into one of the vehicles transporting Muslims out of Mbaïki, but he refused.

According to the witness, members of the community, including religious authorities, asked Saleh to get into one of the vehicles transporting Muslims out of Mbaïki, but he refused.

P-2041 similarly testified that as he was in a vehicle that had joined the convoy to leave Mbaïki, he saw Saleh and had a brief conversation with him in which Saleh told him that he was not going to 'budge' and that nothing was going to happen.
Likewise, Diakité Aboubakar stated that he 'pleaded' with Saleh on several occasions to leave Mbaïki and warned him that he would otherwise get killed.

Raymond Mongbandi also stated that the MISCA, the prefect, the deputy prefect and himself worried about Saleh's situation and feared for his safety at the hands of the Anti-Balaka. The witness indicated that about three days before Saleh was killed, he and the first deputy mayor went to see Saleh and offered to take him to the MINUSCA site, but he refused. According to the witness, the Anti-Balaka occupied a house close to Saleh's house to surveil his activities, and both the witness and the MISCA colonel told Saleh that he was in danger and that he should leave his house, but Saleh refused to do so, arguing that he 'feared nothing' and that there was 'no risk weighing on him'.

footnote_content: P-1838 Statement, CAR-OTP-2100-0252-R05, at 0268, para. 90; P-1838: T-215, p. 30, lines 14-18. The Chamber notes that witnesses often seem to refer to the acronyms of international forces operating in the CAR across the relevant period interchangeably and irrespective of which force may in fact have been active at any particular time. It appears that the '*Mission internationale de soutien à la Centrafrique sous conduite africaine*' (MISCA) started replacing the previously deployed assistance in July 2013, whereas the '*Mission multidimensionnelle intégrée de stabilisation des Nations unies un République centrafricaine*' (MINUSCA) started operating in September 2014 (*see* Resolution S/RES/2149 (2014), CAR-OTP-2001-1043, at 1049-50, paras 18-20; UN SG Report, CAR-OTP-2001-1057, at 1057, para. 1; Press article, CAR-D29-0002-0690, at 0692-93). Given the deployment of various international or internationalised forces in the CAR over prolonged periods, the Chamber considers this confusion of terms to be understandable and will refer to the acronyms as they were used in witnesses' testimonies, with the understanding that this may not necessarily accurately refer to the force in fact operating at the respective time.

In addition, besides witnesses expressing concern for Saleh's and his family's safety, as set out above, Raymond Mongbandi provided a detailed account of an incident involving Mr Yekatom's elements and Saleh which occurred prior to his killing. According to Raymond Mongbandi, shortly after the Anti-Balaka arrived in Mbaïki, Cœur de Lion summoned Saleh to a meeting, where Saleh was interrogated. After hearing about an argument between Saleh and the Anti-Balaka, the witness rushed to his office in the town hall, which the Anti-Balaka had occupied, and introduced himself to Cœur de Lion as the mayor of Mbaïki, told him to address him instead of Saleh, and told Saleh to go home. According to Raymond Mongbandi, the Anti-Balaka 'were making life difficult' for Saleh. He described Saleh's interrogation as 'rather rough' and 'a kind of intimidation' which he attributed to the fact that Saleh was the only Muslim left in Mbaïki. Raymond Mongbandi confirmed, when asked, that at the meeting he had the impression that the Anti-Balaka wanted to kill Saleh.

The Chamber notes that Raymond Mongbandi testified that at the time of Saleh's interrogation, 'there were no longer any Muslims in Mbaïki', '\[t\]he trucks had extracted all the Muslims from Mbaïki', '\[t\]here was only one \[Muslim\] left' (*see* P-1838: T-215, p. 19, lines 3‑4). At the same time, it notes that P-2041 and P-1666 indicated that Cœur de Lion was killed in Boda, that they saw his body when it was brought to Mbaïki and that this happened before their evacuation from Mbaïki (*see* P‑2041 Statement, CAR-OTP-2104-0003-R02, at 0014, para. 62; P-1666: T-232, p. 6, lines 14-22). The Chamber also notes the Yekatom Defence's argument that 'P-1838's uncorroborated claim that Ouandjio had previously "interrogated" Saleh in a "threatening" manner, "because at the time there were no more Muslims in Mbaïki"' should be disregarded, *inter alia*, 'given that Ouandjio had died [prior]{.underline} to the evacuation of the Mbaïki Muslims, thus rendering the very basis of the supposed threat logically and chronologically incoherent' (*see* [Yekatom Defence Closing Brief](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/hoq9zogj/), ICC-01/14-01/18-2737-Corr-Red, para. 541, footnotes omitted). However, the Chamber notes that Raymond Mongbandi also indicated that the interrogation took place '\[s\]hortly after the Anti-Balaka arrived \[to Mbaïki\]', on the first day he met Cœur de Lion (*see* P-1838 Statement, CAR-OTP-2100-0252-R05, at 0268, para. 91; P-1838: T-215, p. 18, lines 6-22, p. 19, lines 7-14), which occurred before Cœur de Lion left Mbaïki for Boda. Thus, considering this and his overall account, the Chamber considers that Raymond Mongbandi erred when mentioning that there were no longer Muslims in Mbaïki at the time of the interrogation, and finds his account otherwise reliable and credible.

The Chamber further recalls that around this time, shortly after the departure of Muslims from Mbaïki, Catherine Samba-Panza visited Mbaïki together with the French minister of defence Le Drian, holding a speech in which she called on the Anti-Balaka in general to stop the violence. On 28 February 2014, a group of individuals attacked Djido Saleh's house while he and his family were inside. Djido Saleh's family fled. As Djido Saleh tried to flee, the group of individuals pursued him and threw stones at him. Djido Saleh tried to defend himself with a bow and at least one arrow. The group of individuals, which included at least three elements of Mr Yekatom's group, one of them being Honorine Gbafalo, killed him as he tried to reach the gendarmerie. Honorine Gbafalo cut off his genitals. Other individuals beat him and cut parts of his body, including one of his ears and his neck, partly severing his head. These individuals targeted Djido Saleh on the basis that he was a Muslim. Following the death of Djido Saleh, Mr Yekatom told Raymond Mongbandi that the killing was 'an accident' and that he would pay for the burial, which he never did. As a direct consequence of the killing, MISCA ordered Mr Yekatom and his elements to leave Mbaïki, which they immediately did.

paragraph_text_preview: P-1339 testified that Honorine Mbafolo spoke to him about Saleh's killing and confessed her involvement. In particular, P-1339 explained that after neighbours had pointed out that a Muslim called 'Dido' was hiding in a house, and when this person went out for prayer, 'Mbafolo Honorine', on her own accord, took two elements with her, they went to the house, and beat and killed the man. Honorine Mbafolo then cut off 'Dido''s sex. When P-1339 spoke with Honorine Mbafolo, who was positioned at a checkpoint to raise money for sustenance, and who still had blood on her hands when returning, he asked her why she had done it and she responded that the Seleka had taken her 'moto', computer, and what she had put in her mind to do, what she had decided on doing, could not be erased. P-1339 further explained that after Honorine removed Saleh's sex, which she was 'very delighted to do', the MINUSCA was forced to 'react and shoot at them'. MINUSCA started shooting at the fleeing elements, and also those based at Socatel, including P-1339, were shot at, so they fled. MINUSCA also dismantled the checkpoints, and when P-1339 asked an element called Ngombé and another whose name he could not recall why they left without asking their opinion leading to MINUSCA shooting at them, they made clear to him that the only person they had to answer to was their chief. According to the explanations P-1339 was given, the three of them -- Honorine Mbafolo, chief Ngombé and a third element -- were involved in killing Saleh. P-1339 confirmed that Honorine Mbafolo was a member of 'the group' at the time of Saleh's killing and indicated that she was one of the women who joined 'them' in the bush. Ngombé was a military, chief of section 4, and P-1339 did not ask him any questions for fear of him getting angry with P-1339, who was just a civilian, and he also said to P-1339 that it was not P-1339 who commanded him.

paragraph_text_preview: Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili testified that there was a 'misunderstanding' between Saleh and 'one of our people', and that after hearing noises, he went 'there' and saw the body. The witness further explained that after Saleh's killing, he discussed with Sete the information he received from people, and it was up to Sete to report to Mr Yekatom.

P-1786 explained that he was in Mbaïki when he heard that Saleh had started attacking some people close to his house, after which the population of Mbaïki got upset and lapidated him with pebbles and stones. He indicated that Saleh was not attacked with sticks or machetes and that it was not the Anti-Balaka who killed him but 'the youth of Mbaïki'. Upon hearing about it, the witness asked his soldiers not to get close to the place of the incident 'so that the Anti-Balaka \[were\] not accused of being the perpetrators of this murder'. P-1786 indicated that the 'youth of Mbaïki' told him about the killing. He confirmed knowing Honorine Gbafolo and her nickname 'Mama Tia Godobe', and that she was in Mbaïki at the time, but that he did not know whether she was involved in Saleh's killing.

Indeed, Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo, commenting on this note, testified that he heard that 'when the group of Anti-Balaka, young people' arrived at Saleh's house, he threatened to attack them, but Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo did not receive any details as to Saleh having a weapon or wounding any of the people (*see* P-1813: T-182, p. 64, line 1 -- p. 65, line 3). Another suggestion that Saleh would have been attacked 'by his own neighbours' (*see* Special Advisor Statement, CAR-OTP-2001-0446, at 0446) or by a 'mob' (*see* Press Article, CAR-D29-0002-0686) does not, in the Chamber's view, in and of itself exclude the participation in the killing of individuals affiliated with Mr Yekatom's group. *See also* paragraphs 3660-3669 below.

The Chamber notes that the three insider witnesses who provided evidence about Saleh's killing differ in their accounts of who committed the killing. The Chamber finds P-1786's account the least reliable one. First, according to P-1786, he heard that Saleh started attacking some people close to his house before he was attacked. Yet none of the other witnesses mentioned this. On the contrary, and as set out above, the evidence indicates that Saleh was in his house with his family when he was suddenly attacked by a number of individuals, at which point he tried to defend himself. Second, P-1786 expressly indicated that Saleh was not attacked with sticks or machetes, which contradicts the video footage showing individuals beating Saleh with axes, machetes, sticks and knives. Third, P-1786 was not present during this incident and heard about it from others.

As for the accounts of Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili and P-1339, the Chamber notes that both witnesses involved at least one Anti-Balaka element in Saleh's killing, Honorine Gbafolo. Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili seemed to indicate that those who initiated the attack and killed Saleh were civilians of Mbaïki, with the element 'Mama Tia Godobe' taking part in the killing. P-1339 indicated that an Anti-Balaka chief and two elements killed Saleh, and that Honorine Gbafolo herself explained to him what she had done and why. The Chamber considers that both accounts are reliable and not necessarily contradictory with each other. In light of this evidence, the Chamber disregards P-1786's evidence stating that it was 'the youth of Mbaïki' and not the Anti-Balaka who killed Saleh, also bearing in mind that he subsequently stated not knowing whether 'Mama Tia Godobe' had been involved in the killing.

Specifically with regard to Honorine Gbafolo, the Chamber notes that the video footage of the mistreatment of Saleh's body shows, as described above, an individual approaching the body, cutting off Saleh's genitals with a knife and quickly running away from the scene while other individuals cheered. This individual, whose face in that particular scene is not visible, appears again later in the video, and is clearly a woman. Some individuals in the video footage itself mention that a woman cut off the genitals of the body lying on the ground. This same individual can also be seen in the video footage as one of the persons dragging Saleh's body, as well as putting her foot on Saleh's head, which was partly severed.

Furthermore, it was generally known that elements of Mr Yekatom's group wore a mixture of civilian and military clothing; indeed Mr Yekatom himself appears in many footage in civilian clothing, rather than in his official military attire. On this basis, and in light of the evidence outlined above, the Chamber considers that the mere fact of individuals involved in the killing of Saleh wearing civilian clothing does not mean that Saleh was killed by a 'mob' composed exclusively of Mbaïki local inhabitants.

Taking into account all of the above, the Chamber concludes that Saleh was killed by a group of individuals which included at least three elements from Mr Yekatom's group, one of them being Honorine Gbafolo. The Chamber has further considered in this context the evidence indicating that Saleh had already received threats by the Anti-Balaka before his death and, in particular, Raymond Mongbandi's account according to which Mr Yekatom's elements, including his deputy Cœur de Lion, interrogated Saleh prior to his death -- an interrogation which Raymond Mongbandi considered 'rather rough' and 'a kind of intimidation' which made the witness think that the Anti-Balaka wanted to kill Saleh.

Raymond Mongbandi stated that Saleh's family -- his wife and child -- could not attend Saleh's burial, which he organised 'because the situation was very risky' considering the wife was Muslim and '\[i\]f the Anti-Balaka took note of her presence, she could have been executed'. Raymond Mongbandi testified that after his killing, Saleh's body was put at the funeral site; he then managed to find a Muslim who could administer the funeral rites in accordance with Muslim tradition, after which Red Cross officials brought a bag and the body was buried -- all this without the participation of Saleh's family. The witness mentioned that in addition to the Red Cross, the accountant and the secretary-general of the town hall provided assistance, as well 'the Mbaïki youth', who under the supervision of the MISCA dug up a grave, and the MISCA itself, which escorted them to the cemetery, 'this really allow\[ing\] Djido's burial'.

The Chamber further notes that when asked about the impact that Saleh's death had on him, Raymond Mongbandi indicated that '\[w\]hat really caused an impact on \[him\] was the fact that a human being was decapitated', which he described as 'a horrible act'.

Furthermore, Raymond Mongbandi explained how Mr Yekatom came to see him the day after the killing and told him that it had been 'an accident'. According to Raymond Mongbandi, Mr Yekatom did not give any explanation for the death, offered to assist with the expenses of Saleh's burial and told him after receiving a phone call that he had to go to see the MISCA colonel at the crossroads. The witness also explained that he saw 'them' (referring to Mr Yekatom and the MISCA colonel) discussing and that the MISCA colonel ordered Mr Yekatom and all his men to leave Mbaïki, after which they all left immediately for Pissa. In the aftermath of the killing and as a direct consequence of it, MISCA requested Mr Yekatom and his elements to leave Mbaïki.

Specifically, when Raymond Mongbandi discussed with Mr Yekatom as outlined above, the witness explained that the MISCA colonel instructed Mr Yekatom and his elements to leave Mbaïki immediately, which they did, with the exception of the elements who were originally from Mbaïki, who 'probably' stayed in Mbaïki. Raymond Mongbandi specified that when Mr Yekatom met the MISCA colonel, they were a bit away from him but he could see them, and that Mr Yekatom was told that there could not be 'two captains' in Mbaïki, that the town had to be governed by the MISCA, and they ordered him to leave. According to the witness, Mr Yekatom left after this conversation and went back to his base in Pissa.

paragraph_text_preview: Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo stated that after the Anti-Balaka group in Mbaïki killed Saleh, the head of MISCA in the area went to the witness's house and told him that they had chased away the Anti-Balaka. The witness saw Mr Yekatom again when he came to Mbaïki, but they did not speak about the killing. He also did not recall, when asked during his interview, what he and Mr Yekatom discussed on the phone conversations that, according to CDR, they had on 28 February and 1 March 2014. He knew that MISCA and the gendarmerie were supposed to conduct an investigation on the incident, but did not know what happened to the people responsible for the killing. Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo believed that MISCA or Mr Yekatom's elements contacted Mr Yekatom to inform him about the killing. The witness also stated that at some point in time, MISCA was asked to arrest Mr Yekatom but instead of doing so, they contacted him and asked to speak to him. Having been read information according to which he would have participated in a meeting with MISCA, gendarmerie and Mr Yekatom on 2 March 2014 at which Mr Yekatom would have said that he knew the person responsible for Djido Saleh's killing and having sanctioned him, the witness stated not recalling such occasion. While he did not recall precisely this meeting, he testified that they met on several occasions, including MINUSCA, municipality, defence and security forces, and Mr Yekatom, 'for him to be able to catch the attention of some of his elements who had conducted acts of violence at a number of locations in the locality'.

The Yekatom Defence argues that Raymond Mongbandi made an 'unfounded and conclusory link' between MISCA taking control of the Mbaïki roundabout after Saleh's killing, and the 'expulsion' of Mr Yekatom. The Chamber does not share this reading of Raymond Mongbandi's evidence. Rather, it is clear from the information he provided that the encounter between Mr Yekatom and MISCA took place shortly after Saleh's killing. Further, the Chamber recalls the evidence provided by P-1339 and Alexandre Kouroupe-Awo according to which MISCA, in the immediate context of Saleh's killing, chased away not only the individuals in the direct vicinity of the location at which Saleh was killed and his body mistreated, but also elements of Mr Yekatom's group based at Socatel at that time. Even if the encounter between Mr Yekatom and MISCA coincided with MISCA taking full control of the town, as suggested by the Yekatom Defence, this does not negate the Chamber's conclusion that MISCA asked Mr Yekatom and his elements to leave Mbaïki as a direct consequence of Saleh's killing. Mr Yekatom is charged with conscription and/or enlistment of children under the age of 15 in his group at various locations, including Boeing, Sekia, Pissa, and Batalimo, and the assignment of various tasks to them, such as participating in hostilities, including during the Bangui Attack, between 'at least December 2013 and August 2014'.

The Prosecution submits that children under the age of 15 years were present in Mr Yekatom's group from at least December 2013 through August 2014 and were recruited 'in line with the Anti-Balaka's widespread and well documented practice'. It relies, inter alia, on P-2476's alleged experience in Mr Yekatom's group as a former 'child soldier' and on witnesses who claimed to have seen other children at Yamwara and along the PK9-Mbaïki axis during the relevant period. Further, it relies, inter alia, on Mr Yekatom's interactions with the alleged 'child soldiers', his attendance in the ESF ceremony in August 2014, and on meetings with P-2018 to establish his intent.

P-1839 did not know Bougie Noire's functions, and had heard from other elements that he had already killed someone and had already cut a young man's head. Importantly, P-1839 did not know his true age, but he was certainly not 'of age', meaning that he was not yet 18 years old. P-1839, who was 17 or 18 at the time, thought that she was a lot older than Bougie Noire. P-1839 estimated that Bougie Noire was 11 or 12 years old, noting that he was the 'smallest' of the two 'children' who were with Rombhot. P-1339 also spoke of an element called Bougie Noire but did not provide any estimates as to his age. The Chamber has also received Bougie Noire's identity card, indicating that he was born in 1996, and therefore, would have been over 16 years at the time.

Having regard to the above, the Chamber concludes that there may have been children generally present at checkpoints and roadblocks along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, including some under the age of 15 years. However, based on what is before it, the Chamber cannot conclude that these were indeed children under the age of 15 that had been enlisted or conscripted as members of Mr Yekatom's group or were otherwise directly associated with that group's activities. All witnesses discussed above provided their own impressions about the ages of these children. These estimates were not sufficient for the Chamber to conclude beyond reasonable doubt that these children were indeed children under the ages of 15 years. In addition to this, there was further no reliable indication that these children were members of, or otherwise had a role in, Mr Yekatom's group.
The Chamber now turns to P-2476's evidence about his experience in Mr Yekatom's group in Mbaïki.

Having regard to its conclusions concerning P-2476's credibility, the Chamber by majority, Judge Chung dissenting, cannot conclude that P-2476 was enlisted in Mr Yekatom's group in Mbaïki. On this basis, the Chamber by majority, Judge Chung dissenting, cannot conclude that there were any children under the age of 15 in Mr Yekatom's group in Mbaïki.

The Chamber recalls Judge Chung's appreciation of the Yekatom Defence's challenges to P-2476's credibility. In particular, Judge Chung considers that P-2476's account was credible when the latter described his recruitment into Mr Yekatom's group at Mbaïki by Cœur de Lion, spending at least one week there.

On this basis, Judge Chung considers that a combined reading of the evidence provided by P-2476, P-2018 and P-1974 satisfies the standard required to find beyond reasonable doubt that there was at least one child under the age of 15 years in Mr Yekatom's group in Mbaïki.

Judge Chung, having regard to P-2476's evidence, considers that P-2476 was assigned several tasks at the Mbaïki base, including guarding the base, buying provisions, and cooking for the elements, not leaving the base. P-2476 said that they stayed behind at the base when Cœur de Lion left for combat. P-2476, asked who gave them the instructions to guard the base, testified that it was those that were stationed at the Mbaïki base; he did not know their names but could identify them. P-2476 said that he never took part in fighting himself, he did not have to carry anything for the elements or work at any of the barriers. P-2476 said that he was not given a firearm; he had a large kitchen knife to defend himself and the base. P-2476 said that he and the other children took the knives that were at the base after Anti-Balaka left to Sekia. P-2476 said that if they saw neighbours or inhabitants of the village come near the base to see what was happening, they would ask them to leave; there was absolutely nothing in the base to be seen; they would not hurt them. Judge Chung notes that P-2018 recalled P-2476 as a 'small child' in the group. Judge Chung further notes that P-2018 was forthcoming in that he did not recall P-2476's role within Mr Yekatom's group. P-2018, reminded that he had stated in his statement that 'Kevin Mbomassa' had been allocated the role of a 'commissionaire' to run errands for the group, said that he had lost the verification sheets that contained the different roles that these children played. P-2018 said that it was the children themselves who stated what role they played in the group, which enabled them to include them.

Judge Chung finds P-2476 credible when he described the mistreatment of children at the Mbaïki base. P-2476 described a visit by Mr Yekatom to the Mbaïki base when the latter used violent words and behaviour towards the children there. P-2476 recalled one incident, when Mr Yekatom was not there, in which the other children, named Gere Kondo and Tchoutchou were punished and 'badly beaten' for having stolen an item on the instructions of one of the chiefs at the Mbaïki base, whose name he did not know. P-2476 recalled one other incident in which Gere Kondo was beaten by a chief, whose name he did not remember, for having stolen his money. Accordingly, Judge Chung finds that Mr Yekatom directly verbally abused the children at the Mbaïki base and his subordinates physically assaulted them.Judge Chung considers P-2476 credible when he said that 'they' would give them ('us') cigarettes and marijuana to smoke but he refused to do so; they did not force him to do it, while the other two children smoked marijuana.

Participation in the ESF programme

The Chamber now turns to the ESF programme that was launched in 2014 for children in armed groups in various locations, including in Mbaïki, by ESF under the aegis of the CAR government Ministry of Social Affairs.

The Prosecution relies on Mr Yekatom's attendance at the ESF ceremony to show that 'several of the 153' children that Mr Yekatom demobilised as part of the ESF programme were below 15 years of age and part of his group.

The Chamber finds that the ambit of the ESF programme extended to children under 18 years and included children that were not members of Mr Yekatom's group. This was observable by those not part of ESF and who attended the ESF ceremony on 4 August 2013. It was a public event and open to all to attend. Having regard to the above, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom's participation in the ESF ceremony on 4 August 2013 does not demonstrate that he knew of, or otherwise accepted, the presence of children under the age of 15 years in his group.

As regards Mr Yekatom's signing of the Declaration, the Chamber notes that it does not mention the ages of the children that he was purportedly releasing. While there is reference to the UNSC resolution 1612, this was insufficient to conclude that Mr Yekatom knew that the Declaration concerned children under 15 years. Indeed, this resolution is not limited to children under 15 years old. Further, the Chamber notes that the Declaration also does not reference any list that may have been prepared as part of this programme, let alone the ESF List prepared by P-2018.

On this basis, the Chamber by majority finds, Judge Chung dissenting, that there is reasonable doubt that Mr Yekatom knew or accepted the contents of the Declaration as true, specifically in respect of the children referred to therein.

In Judge Chung's view, at least one of the '153 children' mentioned in the Declaration included P-2476, whom he finds credible despite the latter's participation in the ESF programme. Judge Chung further notes that P-2476 recalled Mr Yekatom having visited the Mbaïki base at least once and verbally abused the children present there. Accordingly, Judge Chung considers that Mr Yekatom knew of the presence of children within his group at the Mbaïki base.

Based on the above, the Chamber, by majority, Judge Chung dissenting, finds there to be no evidence on the basis of which findings as to the presence of children under the age of 15, and Mr Yekatom's potential responsibility therefore can be entered. paragraph_text_preview: When evaluating the intensity of the conflict to determine its 'protracted' character, chambers consider factors such as: (i) the seriousness and frequency of attacks and armed clashes; (ii) the spread of clashes over territory and the group's ability to control territory over a period of time; (iii) whether any ceasefire orders had been issued or agreed to; (iv) the type and number of armed forces deployed, including any involvement of the government; (v) the type of weapons used; (vi) whether the situation had attracted the attention of the UN Security Council, or involvement of other international organisations; (vii) whether those fighting considered themselves bound by international humanitarian law; and (viii) the effects of the violence on the civilian population, including the extent to which civilians left the relevant area, the extent of destruction, and the number of persons killed. Exercise of control over a part of the territory is not required, though the importance of this factor increases in the absence of active hostilities. It is also not required that the violence be continuous and uninterrupted -- the Chamber need only find that the violence goes beyond isolated or sporadic acts.

paragraph_text_preview: When evaluating whether an entity qualifies as an 'organised armed group', chambers consider factors such as: (i) the existence of a command structure, the existence of headquarters, the issuing of political statements, and the use of official spokespersons; (ii) the military (operational) capacity of the armed group, which may be shown by, for example, the ability to define a unified military strategy, the use of military tactics, the ability to carry out (large scale or coordinated) operations, the control of territory, and having a territorial division into zones of responsibility; (iii) the logistical capacity of the armed group, indicated, among others, by the existence of a supply chain for military equipment, as well as by the group's ability to move troops around and to recruit and train personnel; (iv) the existence of an internal disciplinary system and the ability to implement international humanitarian law; and (v) the group's ability to speak with one voice, indicated, for example, by the capacity of the leadership to act on behalf of its members in political negotiations and to conclude agreements, such as cease-fire or peace agreements. Crimes against humanity

The chapeau of Article 7(1) of the Statute, which sets out the contextual elements of crimes against humanity, reads: '\[f\]or the purpose of this Statute, "crime against humanity" means any of the following acts when committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population, with knowledge of the attack'. The provision is complemented by Article 7(2)(a) of the Statute which stipulates: '"\[a\]ttack directed against any civilian population" means a course of conduct involving the multiple commission of acts referred to in paragraph 1 against any civilian population, pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or organizational policy to commit such attack'.

An 'attack' in this context means a 'course of conduct involving the multiple commission of acts referred to in \[Article 7(1)\]'. The requirement that the acts form part of a 'course of conduct' indicates that Article 7 is meant to cover a series or overall flow of events, as opposed to a mere aggregate of random or isolated acts. As clarified by the Appeals Chamber, 'this does not mean that a trial chamber must have regard to the totality of the activities and military operations of a state or organisation' to establish whether there was a 'course of conduct' or that the attack 'targeted a civilian population'. The 'multiple commission of acts' sets a quantitative threshold involving a certain number of acts falling within the course of conduct.

paragraph_text_preview: The 'course of conduct involving the multiple commission of acts' must take place 'pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or organizational policy to commit such attack' within the meaning of Article 7(2)(a) of the Statute. The Elements of Crimes specify that the '"policy to commit such attack" requires that the \[...\] organization actively promote\[s\] or encourage\[s\] such an attack against a civilian population'. For purposes of this judgment, only the 'organisational policy' prong is relevant.

As regards the 'organisation' pursuing the policy, the Chamber adheres to the definition established by Trial Chamber II: In the Chamber's view, the connection of the term "organisation" to the very existence of the attack and not to its systematic or widespread nature presupposes that the organisation has sufficient resources, means and capacity to bring about the course of conduct or the operation involving the multiple commission of acts referred to in article 7(2)(a) of the Statute. It therefore suffices that the organisation \[has\] a set of structures or mechanisms, whatever those may be, that are sufficiently efficient to ensure the coordination necessary to carry out an attack directed against a civilian population.

paragraph_text_preview: As the terms 'pursuant to or in furtherance of' imply, the policy requirement ensures that the multiple acts forming the course of conduct are linked. It ensures that acts which are unrelated or perpetrated by individuals acting randomly on their own are excluded.

paragraph_text_preview: A policy may consist of a pre-established design or plan, but it may also crystallise and develop only as actions are undertaken by the perpetrators. The 'policy' may be inferred from a variety of factors, such as: (i) a recurrent pattern of violence; (ii) the existence of preparations or collective mobilisation orchestrated and coordinated by the organisation; (iii) the use of public or private resources to further the policy; (iv) the involvement of organisational forces in the commission of crimes; (v) statements, instructions or documentation attributable to the organisation condoning or encouraging the commission of crimes; and (vi) an underlying motivation. In principle, a state or organisation committing a systematic attack against a civilian population will satisfy the policy requirement.

paragraph_text_preview: The war crimes charged in the present case require, as their contextual elements, that the relevant conduct took place in the context of and was associated with an armed conflict not of an international character. The perpetrator's conduct need not take place as part of hostilities, meaning that the nexus requirement could still be satisfied for crimes temporally or geographically remote from the actual fighting. What is required is a sufficiently close link to the hostilities -- the Chamber may take into account, amongst other factors, the status of the perpetrator and the victim, whether the act may be said to serve the ultimate goal of a military campaign, and whether the crime is committed as part of, or in the context of, the perpetrator's official duties.

These nexus requirements find their subjective equivalent in the requisite knowledge or awareness of the perpetrator.
In the case of a war crime, the perpetrator must have been aware of factual circumstances that established the existence of an armed conflict.

paragraph_text_preview: In the case of a crime against humanity, the perpetrator must know that the conduct was part of or intended the conduct to be part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population. However, it is not necessary that the perpetrator be aware of the precise details of the plan or policy of the State or organisation.

These nexus and awareness requirements must be met in order to prove any crime against humanity or war crime. All crimes set forth in the next sub-section must have been committed with the required nexus and awareness of the perpetrator. Specific elements

In the following, the Chamber will set forth the relevant applicable law of the individual crimes with which Alfred Yekatom and Patrice-Edouard Ngaïssona are charged. The crimes are embedded in the context that gives them their international character and differentiates them from ordinary crimes.

No particular harm to civilians need be caused; the crime is directing the attack as such.

Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute proscribes '\[o\]rdering the displacement of the civilian population for reasons related to the conflict, unless the security of the civilians involved or imperative military reasons so demand'.
In order for the war crime of displacement to be committed, the following material elements need to be fulfilled: <!-- -->

The perpetrator ordered a displacement of a civilian population.Such order was not justified by the security of the civilians involved or by military necessity.The perpetrator was in a position to effect such displacement by giving such order.In accordance with the Elements of Crimes, an order to displace is required, and the perpetrator must have been in a position to effect such displacement by giving such order. Such order does not necessarily have to be in writing and may be issued in a variety of means, to be determined on a case-by-case basis.

The jurisprudence of the Court is not settled as to when the 'attack' must have occurred. Trial Chamber VIII indicated that the first material element of Article 8(2)(e)(iv) of the Statute encompasses 'any acts of violence against protected objects', without making any distinction as to whether the act was carried out in the conduct of hostilities or after the object had fallen under the control of an armed group. Other chambers -- notably, Trial Chamber VI and Trial Chamber X -- have considered that this war crime did require the attack to take place during the actual conduct of the hostilities.

paragraph_text_preview: For torture as a crime against humanity, Article 7(2)(e) of the Statute further requires that '\[s\]uch person or persons were in the custody or under the control of the perpetrator'. Torture as a crime against humanity also requires that the pain or suffering did not arise only from, and was not inherent or incidental to, lawful sanctions.

In contrast, for torture as a war crime, the custody/control element is not required. Instead, for the war crime of torture there is an additional mental element specified below. The war crime must also be committed against persons taking no active part in the hostilities, including members of armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat.

In addition to the mental elements specified in Article 30 of the Statute, the war crime of torture further requires that: The perpetrator inflicted the pain or suffering for such purposes as: obtaining information or a confession, punishment, intimidation or coercion or for any reason based on discrimination of any kind.

The crime of other inhumane acts is committed, either by act or omission, when the following two material elements are fulfilled: <!-- -->

The perpetrator inflicted great suffering, or serious injury to body or to mental or physical health, by means of an inhumane act. Such act was of a character similar to any other act referred to in article 7, paragraph 1, of the Statute. The category of 'other inhumane acts' serves as 'residual category' of crimes against humanity, designed to criminalise an act that does not specifically qualify as any of the other crimes under Article 7(1) of the Statute, based on the understanding that an exhaustive enumeration of inhumane acts is impossible.

paragraph_text_preview: For the crime of imprisonment or other severe deprivation of physical liberty to be committed, the gravity of the conduct must have been 'such that it was in violation of fundamental rules of international law', for example in case there is no legal basis to detain a person or the person is denied any procedural rights.

As is clear from the Elements of Crimes, it is sufficient for purposes of the provision that one person be detained. The duration or brevity of detention does not, as such, determine whether a deprivation of physical liberty is severe. Rather, whether a deprivation of physical liberty is severe will have to be determined on a case-by-case basis.
Finally, the perpetrator must have been aware of the factual circumstances that established the gravity of the conduct. Persecution (Article 7(1)(h)) ######

footnote_content: Article 7(3) of the Statute stipulates: 'For the purpose of this Statute, it is understood that the term "gender" refers to the two sexes, male and female, within the context of society. The term "gender" does not indicate any meaning different from the above'.
paragraph_text_preview: Material elements (actus reus) Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute defines persecution as conduct against any identifiable group or collectivity on political, racial, national, ethnic, cultural, religious, gender as defined in paragraph 3, or other grounds that are universally recognised as impermissible under international law, in connection with any act referred to in this paragraph or any crime within the jurisdiction of the Court.

Article 7(2)(g) of the Statute stipulates that '"\[p\]ersecution" means the intentional and severe deprivation of fundamental rights contrary to international law by reason of the identity of the group or collectivity'.
The crime is committed when the four material elements are fulfilled.

footnote_content: The Chamber heeds to footnote 21 of the Elements of Crimes which stipulates: 'This requirement is without prejudice to paragraph 6 of the General Introduction to the Elements of Crimes'. Para. 6 of the General Introduction reads: 'The requirement of \'unlawfulness" found in the Statute or in other parts of international law, in particular international humanitarian law, is generally not specified in the elements of crimes'.
paragraph_text_preview: The first of these elements is that the perpetrator severely deprived, contrary to international law, one or more persons of fundamental rights. Not every infringement of human rights is relevant but only a 'severe deprivation' of a person's 'fundamental rights contrary to international law' (emphasis added). This may include a variety of rights, such as the right to life, the right to personal liberty, the right not to be held in slavery or servitude, the right not to be subjected to torture or cruel treatment, inhuman or degrading treatment, and the right to private property.

The second and third elements of the crime of persecution are that the perpetrator targeted such person or persons by reason of the identity of a group or collectivity or targeted the group or collectivity as such, and that such targeting was based on political, racial, national, ethnic, cultural religious, gender as defined in article 7, paragraph 3, of the Statute, or other grounds that are universally recognised as impermissible under international law.

paragraph_text_preview: The targeted group can be defined both in a positive or a negative manner, meaning that it may be the case that the perpetrator targeted only members of a certain group or collectivity or that the perpetrator targeted individuals for not belonging to a certain group or collectivity.

paragraph_text_preview: In evaluating the alleged status as a protected group, the particular political, social, and cultural context are relevant, as are, in addition to the objective factors relevant to the discriminatory ground alleged, the subjective perception of belonging of both the perpetrator and the victim. It is noted, however, that while it must be demonstrated that the perpetrator targeted certain persons, a group, or a collectivity, based on one of the prohibited grounds, it is not required that all victims of the crime of persecution be members, sympathisers, allies of, or in any other way related to, the protected group.

Conscription, enlistment and use of children under the age of fifteen years to participate actively in hostilities (Article 8(2)(e)(vii))

footnote_content: [*Ongwen* Trial Judgment](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/kv27ul/), ICC-02/04-01/15-1762-Red, para. 2768; [[*Ntaganda* Trial Judgment](http://www.legal-tools.org/doc/80578a/)](http://www.legal-tools.org/doc/80578a/), ICC-01/04-02/06-2359, para. 1104.
paragraph_text_preview: Article 8(2)(e)(vii) of the Statute concerns the crime of conscripting, enlisting and using children under the age of 15 years in hostilities. Conscription or enlistment alone are sufficient and it is therefore not required that a child under 15 years of age who has been conscripted or enlisted also be 'used' to participate actively in hostilities. The crime is committed when the following two material elements are fulfilled: <!-- -->

footnote_content: [*Ongwen* Trial Judgment](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/kv27ul/), ICC-02/04-01/15-1762-Red, para. 2769; [[[*Lubanga* Appeals Judgment](http://www.legal-tools.org/doc/585c75/)](http://www.legal-tools.org/doc/585c75/)](http://www.legal-tools.org/doc/585c75/), ICC-01/04-01/06-3121-Red, paras 278, 311-312; [[*Ntaganda* Trial Judgment](http://www.legal-tools.org/doc/80578a/)](http://www.legal-tools.org/doc/80578a/), ICC-01/04-02/06-2359, para. 1107 (noting that '\[i\]t may be difficult to distinguish between voluntary and forced recruitment in the case of children under the age of 15, particularly since such individuals may be unable to give genuine and informed consent when enlisting in an armed force or group.').
paragraph_text_preview: The perpetrator conscripted or enlisted one or more persons into an armed force or group or used one or more persons to participate actively in hostilities. Such person or persons were under the age of 15 years. 'Conscripting' has been defined as the coercive and 'enlisting' as the voluntary integration of children under the age of 15 years into an armed force or group. The element of compulsion distinguishes both forms of integration and is established by taking into account 'whether the force, threat of force or psychological pressure applied was of such a degree and so pervasive, that individuals can be said to have been forced to join the armed force or group'. This compulsion must be determined on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances of the child and the way they were recruited.

paragraph_text_preview: As concerns the use of such children, to 'participate actively in hostilities' ranges from direct participation in hostilities to other supporting combat-related activities. Conversely, activities unrelated to hostilities fall outside of Article 8(2)(e)(vii) of the Statute. Patrice-Edouard Ngaïssona is charged with the crime of destroying property of an adversary as a war crime, within the meaning of Article 8(2)(e)(xii) of the Statute. This provision also governs 'seizing' such property, but only destruction of property is relevant in this case.

paragraph_text_preview: Third, such property must have been protected from that destruction under the international law of armed conflict. The property is protected under international law when it does not constitute 'military objectives', namely 'objects which by their nature, location, purpose or use make an effective contribution to military action and whose total or partial destruction, capture or neutralization, in the circumstances ruling at the time, offers a definite military advantage'. Whether or not the action offered a 'military advantage' must be evaluated from the attacker's perspective for each targeted object and 'such advantage must be definite and cannot in any way be indeterminate or potential'. As a result, objects of the adversary lose their protection under international law of armed conflict if and for such time as they are 'military objects'.

Pillaging (Article 8(2)(e)(v))
The first material element of pillaging is that the perpetrator appropriated certain property.

The pillaging of a town or place comprises all forms of appropriation of property, including appropriation committed by individuals in their own interest and acts of organised or systematic appropriation.

The second material element of pillaging is that the appropriation was without the consent of the owner.

paragraph_text_preview: When the property owner has fled, such appropriations must be assumed to have been without the owner's consent absent any contrary indication. This could occur, for example, when items are appropriated from an empty house whose residents have fled. The concept of private property and the right to property must be understood as encompassing not only the property of individuals, but also the communal property of the communities. It must also take into consideration the customary law of the community (i.e. practices on possession, titles and registration).

paragraph_text_preview: Appropriations justified by military necessity cannot constitute the crime of pillaging. Military necessity requires that the appropriation's use be directed to further the war effort and thus be used for military purposes. This is in contrast to appropriations for private or personal use. The perpetrator must have specifically intended to deprive the owner of the property and to appropriate it for private or personal use. If combatants appropriate property essential to their survival, such as food, this alone does not make the appropriation one of military necessity. Rape (Article 7(1)(g) and Article 8(2)(e)(vi))

paragraph_text_preview: The perpetrator invaded the body of a person by conduct resulting in penetration, however slight, of any part of the body of the victim or of the perpetrator with a sexual organ, or of the anal or genital opening of the victim with any object or any other part of the body.The invasion was committed by force, or by threat of force or coercion, such as that caused by fear of violence, duress, detention, psychological oppression or abuse of power, against such person or another person, or by taking advantage of a coercive environment, or the invasion was committed against a person incapable of giving genuine consent.The establishment of one of the coercive circumstances or conditions set out in the second element is sufficient for penetration to amount to rape. It is not necessary to prove the victim's lack of consent and there is no requirement of resistance on the part of the victim.

paragraph_text_preview: An indirect perpetrator controls the person or persons who execute the material elements of the crime by subjugating their will. This subjugation of the will is what distinguishes indirect perpetration from ordering, where a lesser degree of influence is required. The crucial element is the perpetrator's control of the action of another person or persons to such a degree that the will of that person becomes irrelevant, such that their action must be attributed to the perpetrator as if it were his or her own. Whether the controlled person is also criminally responsible for the crime is irrelevant.

The use of an organisation is one such way, but this is a factual consideration and not a requirement for establishing this mode of liability. In such a case, while the potential physical perpetrators are interchangeable within the organisation, the criterion of control means that the indirect perpetrator used 'at least part of the apparatus of power subordinate to him or her, so as to steer it intentionally towards the commission of the crime, without leaving one of the subordinates at liberty to decide whether the crime is to be executed.'

The execution of the material elements of the crime by the co-perpetrators may take place through yet another person or persons, including, as just stated above, through the use of an organisation to control such persons. This mode of liability has been referred to, in the jurisprudence of the Court, as 'indirect co-perpetration'.

paragraph_text_preview: Indirect co-perpetration requires the following objective elements: (i) the existence of an agreement or common plan, between the accused and one or more other persons, to commit the crimes or to engage in conduct which, in the ordinary course of events, would result in the commission of the crimes; and (ii) the control of the members of the common plan over a person or persons who execute the material elements of the crimes by subjugating the will of the direct perpetrators. paragraph_text_preview: Indirect co-perpetration requires the following objective elements: (i) the existence of an agreement or common plan, between the accused and one or more other persons, to commit the crimes or to engage in conduct which, in the ordinary course of events, would result in the commission of the crimes; and (ii) the control of the members of the common plan over a person or persons who execute the material elements of the crimes by subjugating the will of the direct perpetrators. While such concerted action may be a relevant consideration, it is not, in the absence of direct evidence of the agreement, the only basis on which a chamber may infer the existence of a common plan. Indeed, '\[t\]here is no legal impediment to inferring the common plan from the wider circumstances, including the events on the ground'. In case a common plan is executed through persons who function as a tool of the co-perpetrators, the conduct such persons may be a relevant consideration to determine the existence of an alleged common plan.

[]{#_Toc204094649 .anchor}IntroductionAfter establishing, on the basis of the analysis of the relevant evidence, the facts of the case, the Chamber proceeds to the subsumption of the factual findings within the legal characterisation proposed in the corresponding charges, meaning to the application of the law, as laid out above, to the factual findings and the analysis of each element of each of the crimes charged, including the constituent elements of the accused's criminal responsibility.

The Chamber addresses first the two sets of contextual elements, crimes against humanity and war crimes, of the crimes charged. Thereafter, the Chamber addresses the charges as presented the individual 'set' of facts they respectively relate to: (i) the attack in Bangui, including Boeing and Cattin, on 5 December 2013; (ii) the attack in Bossangoa on 5 December 2013; (iii) the events at Yamwara between on or around 24 December 2013 and on or around 27 December 2013; and (iv) the events along the PK9-Mbaïki axis between on or around 10 January 2014 and on or around 6 February 2014, and on or around 28 February 2014. In each of the sub-sections, the Chamber proceeds again in two steps, addressing first the specific objective elements of each charged crime, and second the individual criminal responsibility of the two accused, as applicable, including the mental elements of the crimes.

The Chamber recalls that the modes of liability for both accused are presented in the alternative. As further explained below, the Chamber accepts the primary alternative stated in the charge for each of the accused, which is responsibility under Article 25(3)(a) of the Statute as indirect perpetrator, or direct or indirect co-perpetrator, as the case may be, in relation to Mr Yekatom, and under Article 25(3)(c) of the Statute for aiding, abetting or otherwise assisting in relation to Mr Ngaïssona. The primary alternative being established, the Chamber does not proceed to consider the further subsidiary modes of liability, Article 25(3)(b) and (d) of the Statute, respectively.

Concurrence of crimes, also referred to as cumulative conviction, is a situation where the same facts satisfy the legal definition of multiple crimes. In this regard, the Chamber notes that there is no provision in the Statute explicitly requiring it to exclude some legal qualifications of facts on the ground that they are in impermissible concurrence with other legal qualifications of the same facts; also, the provisions on sentencing may be considered in themselves adequate to address, in the context of the determination of the sentence to be imposed, those instances in which a person is convicted of more than one crime on the basis of the same conduct. Nonetheless, the Chamber agrees with the consistent stance of Trial Chambers of the Court that there are certain limitations on the permissibility of concurrence of crimes and consequential cumulative convictions. In particular, it has consistently been held that convictions may be entered cumulatively if the conduct in question violates two distinct provisions of the Statute, each having a 'materially distinct' element not contained in the other, i.e. an element which requires proof of a fact not required by the other. ### Contextual elementsContextual elements of war crimes

At the outset, the Chamber notes that none of the parties dispute the existence of an armed conflict between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka beginning in at least September 2013. The Prosecution submits that by September 2013, the Anti-Balaka had become an organised armed group engaged in a sustained and intense armed conflict against the Seleka in western CAR. While the Ngaïssona Defence argues that the Anti-Balaka was a 'myriad of self-defence groups' growing spontaneously in response to the Seleka violence, it submits that 'the Anti-Balaka', as an entity, was engaged in an armed conflict with the Seleka during the events in Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 and carried out a lawful attack there, consistent with IHL. Similarly, while the Yekatom Defence disputes that Mr Yekatom's group was part of the Anti-Balaka, it submits, inter alia, that Mr Yekatom took up arms to defend the population from 'enemy forces' with 'full commitment to his military training and respect for IHL principles', and was carrying out a legitimate military operation against the Seleka in Bangui on 5 December 2013.

Bearing in mind the above, the Chamber considered apposite to first address the contextual elements of war crimes, followed by those of crimes against humanity, so as to have regard to the circumstances surrounding the armed conflict which existed alongside an organisational policy, discussed below, within the entire context in which the Anti-Balaka emerged and how such policy developed, in light of the Defence's arguments. Violence between organised armed groups

In its assessment, the Chamber has first noted the events leading to the emergence of both the Seleka and the Anti-Balaka and their respective positioning before the start of armed clashes between them.

The Chamber considered how the Seleka came to take over Bangui in March 2013. The Chamber found that around August 2012, a coalition of armed groups opposing then-President François Bozizé emerged in the CAR under the name of the 'Seleka', led by CAR citizens and including elements from Chad and Sudan. Michel Djotodia became the leader of the Seleka. The Chamber found that starting in late 2012, the Seleka advanced towards Bangui. The Libreville agreement, concluded in January 2013, presented an attempt to end the crisis, leading to a government including representatives of various factions, with François Bozizé remaining president and Nicolas Tiangaye as prime minister, Michel Djotodia as deputy prime minister and minister of defence, and Mr Ngaïssona as minister of youth, sports, arts and culture. The Chamber found that, at the same time, the widely reported advance of the Seleka, and violent acts and abuses committed in this context, including against civilians, sparked reactions within the civilian and political sphere: COCORA and COAC were two organisations which were active in mobilising support for François Bozizé in light of the Seleka advance. They erected checkpoints or roadblocks at which passers-by and vehicles were checked, with the objective of identifying Seleka infiltrators and people deemed to be associated with or in support of them, including Muslims. The individuals manning these checkpoints were armed with bladed weapons and, in some cases, with AK-47s. The Chamber found that the Seleka took control of Bangui on 24 March 2013 and Michel Djotodia proclaimed himself President of the CAR.

The Chamber noted the violence attributed to the Seleka after the takeover. The Chamber found that after the Seleka took control of Bangui on 24 March 2013, they committed violence and abuses in various localities across the CAR, in particular against individuals considered to be associated with François Bozizé, his Gbaya ethnic group, his government's security forces, and non-Muslims. Mr Ngaïssona's properties in Bangui were looted. However, the Muslim civilian population was not entirely spared from this violence.

The Chamber has considered the composition and strength of the Seleka over the course of the year 2013. The Chamber found that the Seleka included fighters in particular from Chad and Sudan. It was led by Central African Muslims. The Chamber found that the number of Seleka elements varied greatly in the course of 2013. While counting several thousand elements at the time of the take-over in March 2013, their numbers grew significantly until the end of that year.

The Chamber considered how the Anti-Balaka emerged as an armed group following the Seleka takeover. The Chamber found that self-defence groups in various localities across the CAR formed or re-activated from previous existence very quickly following the take-over of power by the Seleka in March 2013 and individuals within those groups also obtained amulets or gris-gris. The Chamber found that these self-defence groups that initially formed in the provinces aimed at defending against the abuses and violence committed by the Seleka, within which framework some considered necessary to remove Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power. The Chamber found that while initially having formed separately, these groups started out with a common enemy and increasingly coordinated their activities, thereby essentially forming one movement. It was this movement that came to be known as the Anti-Balaka. The Chamber found that due to the religious and ethnic commonalities between the Muslims in the CAR and the Seleka, the Anti-Balaka perceived the former as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka. On this basis, as the Anti-Balaka emerged and coalesced in pursuit of its core objective, its elements targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, killing and dislocating them. The Chamber found that Mr Yekatom briefly went to Zongo in 2013 and then started forming a group, over which he assumed control, with Freddy Ouandjio, also known as Cœur de Lion, and Habib Beina, with a view to planning a response to the Seleka violence and removing Michel Djotodia and the Seleka from power.

The Chamber further noted how the Anti-Balaka began structuring further aimed towards armed action and the kinds of weapons that were usually employed by them. The Chamber found that certain individuals and local groups converged onto and joined together in Gobere, north-east of Bossangoa. In Gobere, civilians and former members of the FACA and PG gathered, and (i) organised into various sub-groups with a leader each; (ii) set up or maintained contacts with groups and individuals in other locations, including Maxime Mokom in Zongo, who was considered to be a coordinator of operations; (iii) organised trainings in weapon handling and combat by FACA members; and (iv) made further plans with a view to descending onto Bangui and removing the Seleka and Michel Djotodia from power. At the same time, former members of the FACA and PG also in other localities created new or joined pre-existing self-defence groups, organising themselves into military-like structures and assuming or sharing command over them. The Chamber found that the armed groups forming at the time were armed mainly with makeshift and bladed weapons, hunting rifles, service weapons retained by members of the FACA, and weapons they seized from the members of the Seleka after engaging them in hostilities. The Chamber found that, in the months leading up to the Bangui Attack, Mr Yekatom and his group armed and trained in the bush.

Having regard to these conclusions, the Chamber finds that the Anti-Balaka were organised for purposes of its determinations under Article 8 of the Statute and had all the relevant bearings to constitute one armed group. This is also shown by the clashes in which the Anti-Balaka were involved, as discussed below, that further demonstrate the Anti-Balaka's operational capacity and the ability to carry out large scale and coordinated attacks in specific locations at specific times. 'Protracted' character of the violence

The Chamber noted how, where, and how often, the various Anti-Balaka groups in the provinces clashed with the Seleka during their advance to Bangui beginning in September 2013. The Chamber found that during their advance towards Bangui, various Anti-Balaka groups started engaging in attacks against the Seleka from September 2013 onwards. Such attacks were not limited to Seleka forces, but included attacking localities with Muslim civilians. The Chamber found that Anti-Balaka attacks were launched around Bossangoa and in Bouca (Ouham prefecture), in Ndjo, Bossembélé, Boali and Gaga (Ombella-M'Poko prefecture), as well as in Bouar (Nana-Mambéré prefecture). As part of these attacks, Anti-Balaka elements attacked Bossangoa on 17 September 2013. The Chamber found that throughout the advance and during these attacks, Anti-Balaka groups targeted Muslim civilians.

The Chamber has considered the involvement of Mr Yekatom's group that shows that he was assigned a specific territorial target and a zone of responsibility. The Chamber found that Mr Yekatom's group coordinated with other Anti-Balaka groups to participate in the Bangui Attack. The Chamber found that in the early morning of 5 December 2013, Mr Yekatom launched an attack on Boeing, attacking the Boeing Market, the Boeing Mosque, before proceeding to attacking Cattin. The Chamber found that Mr Yekatom's instructions to his elements concerning the attack in Bangui on 5 December 2013 were to fight the Seleka and included targeting sectors where 'Muslims' were to be found. The Chamber found that after setting up in Yamwara in Bangui for some time, Mr Yekatom's group moved down the PK9-Mbaïki axis following Michel Djotodia's resignation.

The Chamber considered the aftermath of the coordinated attacks on Bangui and Bossangoa and whether the situation attracted the attention of the regional and international community in an attempt to cease hostilities. The Chamber found that on 10 January 2014, Michel Djotodia resigned, leading to the end of his government, following which the Seleka forces started to withdraw from Bangui, in particular towards the north and north-east of the CAR. For purposes of its determination of whether the contextual elements of the crimes against humanity charged in this case are fulfilled, the Chamber considered a number of factors. Recalling of factual findings

The Chamber recalls the background that gave rise to the Anti-Balaka looking at events from August 2012 onwards. The Chamber found that around August 2012, a coalition of armed groups opposing then-President François Bozizé emerged in the CAR under the name of the 'Seleka', led by CAR citizens and including elements from Chad and Sudan, with Michel Djotodia as its leader. The Chamber found that on 24 March 2013, the Seleka took control of Bangui and Michel Djotodia proclaimed himself President of the CAR. The Chamber found that after the Seleka took control of Bangui on 24 March 2013, they committed violence and abuses in various localities across the CAR, in particular against individuals considered to be associated with François Bozizé, his Gbaya ethnic group, his government's security forces, and non-Muslims. However, the Muslim civilian population was not entirely spared from this violence. Mr Ngaïssona's properties in Bangui were also looted. The Chamber found that the Seleka included fighters in particular from Chad and Sudan and was led by Central African Muslims. Due to the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and in light of its perceived composition, tensions in particular between Muslim and non-Muslim communities in CAR increased.

The Chamber considered how the various groups forming the Anti-Balaka subsequently emerged. The Chamber found that self-defence groups in various localities across the CAR formed or re-activated from previous existence very quickly following the take-over of power by the Seleka in March 2013 and individuals within those groups also obtained amulets or gris-gris. The Chamber further considered how the Anti-Balaka's perceptions evolved during this time. The Chamber found that due to the religious and ethnic commonalities between the Muslims in the CAR and the Seleka, the Anti-Balaka perceived the former as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka. paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that the Defence takes issue with the nature of the Anti-Balaka as an organisation. The Ngaïssona Defence argues that the Anti-Balaka were not a 'top-down organisation' but a 'myriad of self-defence groups that spontaneously rose out of the Seleka's heinous and continuous crimes against the civilian population following the 24 March coup'. It further argues that the emergence of the Anti-Balaka was sporadic and by its very nature, 'this movement was diffuse\[d\]' and 'often indistinguishable from the general population, and fundamentally elusive due to its constantly fluctuating expansion and evolution'. The Ngaïssona Defence argues that it is a 'fundamentally flawed narrative' to consider that the Anti-Balaka was 'a homogenous group' that would have 'shared a common objective to violently target "the Muslim civilian population in western CAR"' resulting in the commission of the charged crimes 'throughout the entire period of the charges and across the country'. It argues that there was a lack of specificity regarding the 'inner circle' and insufficient level of coordination within 'each alleged geographical group'. Similarly, the Yekatom Defence argues that the 'Anti-Balaka' is a nebulous term, and that, in any event, Mr Yekatom's group was not Anti-Balaka.

The Chamber notes that the legal framework and the jurisprudence do not provide the contours which an 'organisation' must fulfil for purposes of finding an 'organisational policy'. The Chamber recalls that for the purpose of assessing 'organisational policy', it 'suffices that the organisation has a set of structures or mechanisms, whatever those may be, that are sufficiently efficient to ensure the coordination necessary to carry out an attack directed against a civilian population'. Accordingly, the Chamber considers that there is no requirement, as a matter of law, that an organisation for the purposes of Article 7 of the Statute be homogenous, or otherwise a strictly hierarchical, top-down organisation, as such. Indeed, it may well include a variety of groups, as long as those groups have 'mechanisms' sufficiently efficient to ensure 'coordination' necessary to carry out the attack within the meaning of the framework.

The Chamber considers that the evolution of the Anti-Balaka clearly shows how some individuals and the local self-defence groups, including Mr Yekatom's group, began organising and developed structures and mechanisms over time and came to be known as the Anti-Balaka. Markers of these structures and mechanisms appeared in (i) having common organisational forces underlying all Anti-Balaka attacks in the form of common leaders, who coordinated their actions and instructed the various Anti-Balaka groups; (ii) the various Anti-Balaka groups communicating with each other during their advance towards Bangui; (iii) the existence of a plan to mount highly coordinated attacks on Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 and the preparations undertaken in advance of these attacks; (iv) successfully carrying out coordinated attacks on two separate locations on the same day with the shared goal; and (v) the Anti-Balaka groups continuing to engage in hostilities in early 2014, at least, following the same pattern of conduct underlying the discussed Anti-Balaka attacks in 2013. In this instance, how the various Anti-Balaka organised internally on a granular level, including whether they were strictly hierarchical or homogenous, is immaterial. In the view of the Chamber, the Anti-Balaka had sufficient bearings of an organisation for the purposes of finding an organisational policy within the meaning of Article 7 of the Statute.

The Ngaïssona Defence argues that it was the context of the Seleka violence that 'gave rise to the Anti-Balaka movement' and that it had 'no connection whatsoever to an alleged organizational policy that would have been implemented' by Bozizé's 'alleged inner circle, including Mr N\[gaïssona\]'. The Chamber notes the Ngaïssona Defence argument that as the 'groups evolved', the 'official position of the Anti-Balaka was circulated and was clearly to target the Seleka with the aim of ousting D\[jotodia\] only'. It further argues that the Anti-Balaka shared 'one legitimate objective: ousting the criminal Seleka regime and liberating the CAR population from its oppression, not to attack the Muslim civilian population', and that the 'Anti-Balaka groups acted pursuant to legitimate and lawful goals and did not agree to target the Muslim civilian population'. It further argues that Bozizé's return was an 'option', rather than an 'objective'. paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber recalls that an organisational policy may crystallise and develop also as actions are undertaken by the perpetrators. In the present case, the Chamber considered that, in order to determine whether the Anti-Balaka carried out an attack, as alleged, it was necessary to have regard to the overall flow of events, beginning well before the Anti-Balaka came to be known as a 'movement', including the evolution of the roles of the various actors, including both the accused.

In the view of the Chamber, while the initial impetus for the self-defence groups to emerge may have been in response to the Seleka violence, over time, the various Anti-Balaka groups joined and coalesced around the objective to oust the Seleka and inflict retributive violence on Muslim civilians. In this respect, the objective -- as argued by the Ngaïssona Defence, meaning the ousting the Seleka and liberating the CAR population from its oppression -- did not exclude attacking the Muslim civilian population. The Chamber considers immaterial for purposes of its determination the question of whether the aim to remove Michel Djotodia and oust the Seleka from the CAR was legitimate and lawful. What was of significance, and indeed material, was that during their advance to Bangui, various Anti-Balaka groups engaged in attacks against the Seleka from September 2013 onwards and that such attacks included targeting Muslim civilians.

To the extent that the Defence challenge that the organisational policy did not target Muslim civilians, the Chamber notes that, when assessing the Anti-Balaka actions towards Muslim civilians, a clear and distinct pattern of violence is discernible when comparing the various attacks that the Anti-Balaka groups launched in the provinces in September 2013 with the attacks on 5 December 2013 in Bangui and Bossangoa. This pattern is also seen in the advance of Mr Yekatom's group on the PK9-Mbaïki axis, as well as the attacks that took place in 2014, after Mr Ngaïssona became general coordinator of the Anti-Balaka. Further, based on the temporal and geographic extent of the attack, the Chamber finds that it was widespread within the meaning of Article 7(1) of the Statute. In addition, considering that throughout the period of the charges the Anti-Balaka attacked Muslim civilians whom they perceived as associated with the Seleka and it followed a similar pattern, the Chamber finds that these attacks were also systematic.
