Considering that the Anti-Balaka perceived Muslims as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka, and thus targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, the attacks in Bangui and Bossangoa, as well as the actions at Yamwara and along the PK9-Mbaïki axis form part of the attack against the civilian population within the meaning of Article 7 of the Statute as defined in this section. The Chamber recalls, at the outset, that a civilian population need not be the sole and exclusive target of an attack. Within the meaning of this crime, members of armed forces and any other legitimate combatant may be present in a civilian population. The presence within the civilian population of individuals who do not fit within the definition of civilians does not deprive the entire population of its civilian character. For this reason, even if the Yekatom Defence's arguments are to be believed on the fact that there were Seleka bases 'in, and along the road to Cattin' or that the alleged victims were armed Seleka combatants, this did not deprive the civilian population of Boeing and Cattin of its civilian character as such.

In the view of the Chamber, Mr Yekatom's conduct, including his presence in the group that attacked Boeing and Cattin, together with his instructions before the attack, clearly show that his group's attack meant to target the Muslim civilian population of Boeing and Cattin. In the view of the Chamber, it was clear to his elements that the primary aim of the attack was not a military target or persons actively participating in hostilities. Further, and in light of this, the Chamber need not engage with the abstract argument that even an indiscriminate attack, in violation of the principle of proportionality, does not constitute an attack against the civilian population.

Having regard to these conclusions, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom and his elements directed an intentional attack against the civilian population, as such, in Boeing and Cattin. Mr Yekatom's participation and execution of the attack was such that, by its nature, it could only have been undertaken intentionally. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the first, second, and third element of the war crime of attacking civilians, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, namely that the perpetrator directed an intentional attack against a civilian population as such or individual civilians not taking direct part in hostilities, are met. ######

Murder as a crime against humanity and as a war crime (Counts 2 and 3)Under Counts 2 and 3, Mr Yekatom and Mr Ngaïssona are charged with murder as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Statute, and murder as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute of five to 13 persons, including Hassan Mahamat, at the Boeing market, four Muslim persons in Cattin, and Nina Pascal at the Boeing market, in the context of the attack on Bangui, including Boeing and Cattin, on 5 December 2013. Recalling of factual findings

The Chamber found that elements in Mr Yekatom's group killed Hassan Mahamat in the morning of 5 December 2013 during the attack on the Boeing Market. Hassan personally interacted with certain Seleka officials prior to 5 December 2013 in his role as delegate of the male Muslim traders at the Boeing Market. Hassan had at least one weapon in his shop with which he fired in self-defence during the attack of 5 December 2013 carried out by Mr Yekatom's elements. Further, Mr Yekatom's elements killed two unnamed Muslim traders at the Boeing Market during this attack. Boeing Market traders and the Seleka personally interacted with each other at the Boeing Market and were seen by others as associating with each other. There is no indication that any of the two unnamed Muslim traders were armed during the attack or otherwise engaged in combat at the time of their death. During the attack on Cattin, elements of Mr Yekatom's group killed at least one Muslim man, who was not armed, nor engaged in combat, at the time of his death. The elements targeted this Muslim man on the basis that he was an 'Arab' and the victim eventually succumbed to the injuries inflicted on him.Killing of one or more persons

The Chamber now turns to the status of the victims at the relevant time. The Chamber recalls the Yekatom Defence's arguments concerning the status of the victims at the Boeing Market. The Yekatom Defence argues that the evidence raises reasonable doubt that the alleged victims were armed Seleka combatants and/or civilians actively participating in the hostilities. The Yekatom Defence argues that the alleged victims did not benefit from the protection under Article 8(2)(e)(i) and were legitimate military targets. The Yekatom Defence submits that the traders at the Boeing Market were armed and actively participating in hostilities and had joined the Seleka in March 2013, instead of being merely civilians who had picked up arms in self-defence, and that they were 'fully embedded within the enemy force' by December 2013. As regards the unnamed Muslim man in Cattin, the Yekatom Defence argues that his civilian status cannot be presumed given the context in which the alleged killings took place, and it must be established that the victim was a civilian taking no active part in the hostilities. In determining whether these victims were taking an active part in hostilities before their death, the Chamber must have regard to the relevant facts and specific situation of the victims at the relevant time, including the location of the killings, whether the victims were carrying weapons, and the clothing, age and gender. As regards Hassan, one of the named Muslim traders at the Boeing Market, the Chamber finds that he was a civilian at the time of his death and therefore had a protected status under international humanitarian law, which he did not lose during the attack on the Boeing Market. The Chamber recalls that in order for a civilian to lose such protection, it is required that their acts have a belligerent nexus, meaning they were specifically designed to directly cause the required threshold of harm in support of a party to an armed conflict and to the detriment of another. In the view of the Chamber, having regard to its findings above, Hassan retained his protected civilian status when Mr Yekatom's elements attacked the Boeing Market, including when he fired at them in self-defence, by using necessary and proportionate force. In assessing whether Hassan used necessary and proportionate force in self-defence, the Chamber recalls that Mr Yekatom launched the attack on Boeing by firing an automatic pistol in the air when his group reached the Boeing Market, following which the armed elements continued and advanced. No matter how many elements Mr Yekatom's group was composed of at the time, the Chamber considers that Hassan's firing, faced with a sizeable group of attackers, was well within the parameters of a proportionate self-defence. Accordingly, in respect of the distinct elements of murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, that the person be either hors de combat, or a civilian, medical personnel, or religious personnel taking no active part in the hostilities, and that perpetrator was aware of the factual circumstances that established this status, the Chamber finds that this requirement is met in respect of each victim.Forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity and displacement as a war crime (Counts 4 and 5)Under Counts 4 and 5, Mr Yekatom and Mr Ngaïssona are charged with forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, and displacement as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute, for the dislocation of nearly all Muslim persons residing in Boeing and Cattin to PK5, a predominantly Muslim neighbourhood in Bangui, other parts of the CAR or neighbouring countries, starting from 5 December 2013 in the context of the attack on Bangui, including Boeing and Cattin, on 5 December 2013. The Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom's launching of the attack on Boeing and Cattin and how his elements carried out the attack, leading to the attack on the Boeing Mosque and the killing of Muslim civilians in Boeing and Cattin, created an environment where it was physically, materially, and psychologically unsafe for Muslim persons there, forcing them to leave and flee Boeing and Cattin. The Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom's launching of the attack on Boeing and Cattin, the establishment of his base in Yamwara, and the continued presence of the Anti-Balaka in Bangui meant that these Muslims from Boeing and Cattin, who were in PK5 at the time, could not return to their homes.

As regards the requirement that the crime must take place 'by expulsion or other coercive acts', the Chamber recalls that forcible transfer and deportation are 'open-conduct' crimes in that the perpetrator may commit several different acts that may qualify. In assessing this element in respect of both forcible transfer and deportation in the present case, the Chamber recalls that the term 'forcibly' is not restricted to physical force, but may include inter alia threat of force or coercion, such as that caused by fear of violence. The Chamber finds that both forcible transfer and deportation, as noted above, took place as a result of the fear of violence that was set in motion by Mr Yekatom's launching of an attack on Boeing and Cattin and the crimes committed there by his elements. In the view of the Chamber, the Muslim persons fleeing Boeing and Cattin had no genuine choice in leaving to PK5, other parts of the CAR, or to the neighbouring countries. The Chamber recalls in this regard that there must be a genuine lack of choice on the part of the person or persons forcibly transferred, and that the prevailing situation and atmosphere, and other relevant circumstances, including in particular the victims' vulnerability, has to be taken into account when assessing whether the individuals transferred indeed had a genuine choice. In the view of the Chamber, Muslim persons in Boeing and Cattin would not have wished to flee, absent the attack by Mr Yekatom's group and their presence there, as part of the larger Bangui Attack. The Chamber considers that even if other factors contributed to the fear of violence, the existence of such factors added to the context, but are inapt by and of themselves to impact the Chamber's conclusion that Muslim persons in Boeing and Cattin would not have fled absent the attack by Mr Yekatom's group and their presence.

The Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom's acts amounted to 'coercive acts' pursuant to the first element of deportation or forcible transfer as a crime against humanity. The Chamber has considered not necessary to engage with the Yekatom Defence's argument that the Prosecution did not establish that Mr Yekatom took advantage of a coercive environment.

Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the requirement of forcible transfer is met in respect of the movement of a majority of Muslim persons fleeing Boeing and Cattin from 5 December 2013 onwards to PK5 and other parts of the CAR, in the context of the attack by Mr Yekatom's elements on 5 December 2013 on Boeing and Cattin. The Chamber finds that the requirement of deportation is met in respect of the movement of these Muslim persons, who further fled from PK5 to neighbouring countries. Thus, the Chamber finds that the first requirement of forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, namely that the perpetrator forcibly transferred or deported, without grounds permitted under international law, one or more persons to another State or location, by expulsion or other coercive acts, is met. Lawful presence

The Chamber has further considered that there is no evidence on the record, nor any arguments advanced by the parties, indicating that the Muslims living in Boeing and Cattin at the time were not lawfully present there. Accordingly, and recalling that Muslim persons were present and living in Boeing and Cattin at the time of the Bangui Attack, the Chamber finds that the second requirement of element of forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, namely that such person or persons were lawfully present in the area from which they were so deported or transferred, is met. In addition to the factual findings above, the Chamber recalls that Mr Yekatom's group attacked Boeing and Cattin with the express instructions to target sectors where 'Muslims' were to be found. The Chamber thus finds that these requirements for forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, as well as for displacement as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute, are also met. Order to displace

The Chamber now turns to the distinct requirements of displacement as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute, namely that the perpetrator ordered a displacement of a civilian population.

The Yekatom Defence refers to the Ntaganda jurisprudence and argues that the military operations undertaken on 5 December 2013 were 'legitimate in that they were directed against military targets and complied with the principles of distinction and proportionality' and that its objective 'also served to protect the civilian population from the continued atrocities committed by the Seleka forces'. The Yekatom Defence argues that neither aspect of the Ntaganda jurisprudence is fulfilled in the present case. As regards the first aspect requiring an express order, the Yekatom Defence argues that Mr Yekatom did not issue any orders to displace the civilian population in relation to the attack on 5 December 2013. It further argues that the use of the term 'ordered' in the first element of displacement as a war crime was deliberate and its objective was to implicate the individual giving the order of displacement and not someone who simply carries out the displacement. It submits that the Ntaganda jurisprudence should be read keeping in mind the charges in the present case as framed against Mr Yekatom, which include ordering as a mode of liability pursuant to Article 25(3)(b) of the Statute. Reading the charges in the present case together with the Ntaganda jurisprudence, it argues that an order based on an act or omission as a result of which displacement would occur would be 'rendered meaningless' as it 'effectively creates a Russian doll effect'. It asserts that 'only \[...\] orders to displace a civilian population' are 'the correct application' of this element of the crime. As regards the second aspect concerning 'an act or omission as a result of which such displacement would occur', the Yekatom Defence argues that it must still be established that the order had a direct effect on the commission of the crime and that Mr Yekatom was aware of this 'i.e. the occurrence would be virtually certain'.

As regards the requirement of an 'order', the Chamber considers that conduct alone can constitute an order. This is consistent with the Ntaganda jurisprudence that states that an order within the meaning of this crime itself needs only to instruct another person in any form to (i) displace a civilian population; or (ii) perform an act or omission as a result of which such displacement would occur.

In light of this, the Chamber finds that, in the present instance, Mr Yekatom's act of firing an automatic pistol in the air thereby launching an attack on Boeing and instructing his elements, prior to the Bangui Attack, to target all sectors where Muslims are to be found is sufficient to constitute an 'order' within the meaning of the first element of displacement as a war crime. It was a combination of these two acts that directly led to the commission of this crime. The Chamber considers that by attacking Boeing and Cattin under these premises, Mr Yekatom's elements were ordered to perform an act as a result of which the displacement of the Muslim civilian population from those areas would necessarily occur. In the Chamber's view, Mr Yekatom's conduct constituted an 'order' within the ordinary sense of the word, in that it required an imperative action to follow, namely an attack creating the conditions in which the displacement of the civilian population would inevitably take place. The Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom need not have given a formal order, written or otherwise, to his elements or to the Muslim civilian population spelling out expressly that the displacement must occur.

The Chamber also considers that while modes of liability are a lens through which to assess the conduct of an accused, they offer limited support on what meaning to give to the elements of a crime. In any event, the requirements of an 'order' both as an element of this war crime and as a mode of liability can be fulfilled by conduct not including an express order, as such. The Chamber recalls that, in the present case, the charges against Mr Yekatom include liability for commission under Article 25(3)(a) of the Statute or, in the alternative, by ordering the commission under Article 25(3)(b) of the Statute. In the view of the Chamber, the charges in the present case, as framed, provide no normative guidance on how the material elements of the war crime of displacement must be interpreted. In this respect, the Chamber is not assisted by the Yekatom Defence's arguments and cannot determine the theoretical implications of a 'Russian doll effect' in the abstract.

Further, the Chamber is satisfied that there is a direct link between Mr Yekatom's act of launching an attack on Boeing in the context of the present case and the displacement of the Muslim civilian population from Boeing and Cattin. The Chamber further considers that, in the present case, Mr Yekatom's conduct need not have been the sole reason why the Muslim civilian population fled. This is because the Chamber is otherwise satisfied that had it not been for the attack launched by Mr Yekatom and his group at Boeing and Cattin, the concerned Muslim civilian population would not have displaced. As noted in its evidentiary analysis as well as in its conclusions on Count 4, while there may have been other factors that compounded or added to the reasons for displacement, they did not sever the link between Mr Yekatom's acts and the displacement.

The Chamber is of the view that Mr Yekatom's specific and express instructions before the Bangui Attack of targeting sectors where 'Muslims' were to be found, seen together with the Chamber's findings on the attack on Boeing and Cattin, during which Mr Yekatom's elements targeted Muslim civilians drawing no distinction between them and the Seleka, establish conclusively the existence of an 'order' within the meaning of this crime. The Chamber considers that by attacking Boeing and Cattin under these premises, Mr Yekatom's elements were ordered to perform an act as a result of which the displacement of the Muslim civilian population from these locations would necessarily occur. paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber recalls that, as a matter of law, the elements of the war crime of an attack against a building dedicated to religion do not require any damage or destruction to the object in question, meaning there is no outcome requirement. For the purpose of this war crime, it was sufficient that Mr Yekatom's elements 'directed an attack'. Subsequent taking apart or otherwise 'dismant\[ling\]' of the Boeing Mosque, as argued by the Yekatom Defence, is immaterial to the Chamber's legal conclusions on the charged crime. This is also supported by the Ntaganda Trial Judgment which noted that the elements of this war crime only require the perpetrator to have 'launched an attack against a protected object and it need not be established that the attack caused any damage or destruction to the object in question'.
Accordingly, the Chamber considers that firing a rocket at the mosque during the conduct of hostilities is sufficient to constitute 'directing an attack' at the protected object.

On this basis, the Chamber finds that the first element of the war crime of attacking protected objects, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(iv) of the Statute, namely that the perpetrator directed an attack, is met. Protected object

Further, at the time of the events, Boeing Mosque was serving the Muslim communities of Boeing and Cattin and served no military objective at the time of the attack. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the second element of the war crime of attacking protected objects, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(iv) of the Statute, namely that the object of the attack was one or more buildings dedicated to religion, which were not military objectives, is met. ######

Recalling of factual findings

Specifically, the Chamber considers that Hassan Mahamat, two unnamed Muslim traders at the Boeing Market, and one unnamed Muslim man in Cattin were deprived of their right to life. Further, Muslim persons in Boeing and Cattin had to flee following the attack by Mr Yekatom's elements and were deprived of their right to liberty and security of person, right to liberty of movement, right against arbitrary or unlawful interference with their family, and home, right to property. Individual criminal responsibility ######

Mr YekatomThe Chamber now turns to Mr Yekatom's responsibility under Counts 1 to 6 and 8. Mr Yekatom is alleged to have committed the aforementioned crimes 'jointly with' or 'through' others under Article 25(3)(a) of the Statute. Control over the crimes or control of person(s) who execute the material elements of the crime

The Chamber recalls that the crimes charged under Counts 1 to 6 and 8 were committed by Mr Yekatom and his elements during their attack on Boeing and Cattin, as part of a coordinated attack on Bangui on 5 December 2013.

The Chamber recalls that, in 2013, Mr Yekatom formed a group, including Cœur de Lion and Habib Beina, over which he assumed control with a view to planning a response to the Seleka violence and removing Djotodia and the Seleka from power.

On 5 December 2013, Mr Yekatom's group coordinated with other Anti-Balaka groups to participate in the Bangui Attack. The movement of Mr Yekatom's group in the bush, when superimposed onto those from other groups who proceeded towards Bangui along the same time frame, shows that this coordination had begun well before November 2013. In the months leading up to this attack, Mr Yekatom and his group armed and trained in the bush. In the afternoon of 4 December 2013, Mr Yekatom chose some of his elements and instructed them to move towards Bangui. Mr Yekatom's instructions to his elements concerning the attack on 5 December 2013 were to fight the Seleka and included targeting sectors where Muslims are to be found. Mr Yekatom's instructions were understood by the elements to accept that Muslim civilians would be killed as a result of the fighting based on his elements not having been trained or instructed to apply the principle of distinction during combat and bearing strong anti-Muslim sentiment and feelings of vengeance against the Seleka. On the night of 4 December 2013, Mr Yekatom and some of his elements conducted reconnaissance and visited the Boeing Market to assess its precise geographical location and conduct reconnaissance. The same night, Mr Yekatom instructed his elements to target Seleka positions along the Boeing-Cattin-PK5 direction and this included attacking the Muslims traders at the Boeing Market before moving along the route to PK5. On 5 December 2013, Mr Yekatom was himself present in the group that arrived at the Boeing Market and launched the attack on Boeing by firing his automatic pistol in the air. It was on his instructions that his elements carried out the attack on the Boeing Market and the Boeing Mosque during their advance towards PK5.

The Chamber found that Mr Yekatom's group was seen as and understood to be part of the Anti-Balaka. Accordingly, the Chamber considers that the Anti-Balaka could rely on him to execute the Anti-Balaka policy to target Muslim civilians.

The Chamber further considers that his role as the founder and chief of his group, as well as the one providing instructions and himself participating in the Bangui Attack, and that Mr Yekatom had control over the crimes committed by the elements in his group. On the basis of the factual conclusions recalled above, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom was aware of how his elements would interpret his instructions to 'target those sectors where Muslims were to be found' and not restrict their attack to the Seleka. Mr Yekatom was aware that his instructions would be understood as also targeting Muslim civilians.

In relation to Counts 1, 4, 5 and 8, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom's responsibility underlying these counts is best captured as a direct perpetrator for having founded his group and himself launching and carrying out the attack, as a chief of his group and an armed participant in it. In arriving at this conclusion, the Chamber has considered that parts of the attack launched by Mr Yekatom were not committed directly by him but indirectly through other elements in his group. This included Alkanto who shot the 'rocket' at the Boeing Mosque and Cœur de Lion and Habib Beina, who shot at the Muslim traders at the Boeing Market, and unnamed elements who killed the Muslim man in Cattin. However, in the view of the Chamber, the mode of responsibility of indirectly committing through others does not fully or meaningfully capture the entirety of Mr Yekatom's conduct underlying these counts. Particularly, in respect of Counts 4 and 5, the Chamber considers that it was the entirety of Mr Yekatom's conduct, as discussed above, that created the conditions, including an environment of fear of violence, as a result of which the Muslims in Boeing and Cattin fled. Mental elements

As regards Mr Yekatom's mens rea, the Chamber first recalls its factual findings above.The Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom's conduct in the context of the Bangui Attack was such that it can only have been intentional. Further, and on this basis, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom (i) intended to carry out an attack against the Muslim civilian population of Boeing and Cattin; (ii) intended his elements to murder Muslim traders at the Boeing Market, including Hassan Mahamat and two unnamed Muslim traders; (iii) knew that his elements would kill Muslim civilians in Cattin; (iv) knew that his elements would attack the Boeing Mosque; and (v) knew that the launching of his attack and the instructions to his elements would cause the Muslims from Boeing and Cattin to flee.

As regards Mr Yekatom's mens rea, the Chamber first recalls its factual findings above.The Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom's conduct in the context of the Bangui Attack was such that it can only have been intentional. Further, and on this basis, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom (i) intended to carry out an attack against the Muslim civilian population of Boeing and Cattin; (ii) intended his elements to murder Muslim traders at the Boeing Market, including Hassan Mahamat and two unnamed Muslim traders; (iii) knew that his elements would kill Muslim civilians in Cattin; (iv) knew that his elements would attack the Boeing Mosque; and (v) knew that the launching of his attack and the instructions to his elements would cause the Muslims from Boeing and Cattin to flee.

The Chamber further considered that Mr Yekatom knew that his act of launching an attack on Boeing, his own participation in the attack, his instructions to target 'all sectors' where Muslims are to be found, and his instructions to his elements on the eve of the Bangui Attack would create the conditions forcing a majority of Muslims in Boeing and Cattin to leave. The Chamber finds no merit in the Yekatom Defence's argument that the Prosecution did not 'lead any evidence which would depict Mr Yekatom undertaking acts which threaten or intimidate the Muslim population in a manner calculated to force the population to leave Boeing or Cattin'. Having to show that the accused's acts were 'calculated to force the population to leave' introduces an additional mental requirement that does not exist in the elements of the crime. In the view of the Chamber, it is sufficient that Mr Yekatom knew his act to cause the Muslim persons to flee.

Turning to the specific knowledge requirements concerning the charged crimes, the Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom and his elements knew that Muslim traders would be present on the morning of 5 December 2013 given the reconnaissance that Mr Yekatom and his elements conducted on the night of 4 December 2013. Mr Yekatom, as a FACA member, knew that unarmed Muslim traders at the Boeing Market enjoyed civilian protection. Mr Yekatom's elements, including P-1339, knew that Hassan Mahamat, a Muslim trader bearing a weapon at the time of the attack, was firing in self-defence. Mr Yekatom and his elements must have known that Hassan was employing necessary and proportionate force in self-defence.The perpetrator need only be aware of the factual circumstances that established the victim's status. In this context, the Chamber recalls that international humanitarian law explicitly provides for situations where there is doubt as to a person's civilian status: in case of doubt whether a person is a civilian, that person shall be considered to be civilian. Mr Yekatom and his elements must have been aware that they should operate on this basis. Even if entertaining the possibility that Mr Yekatom and his elements may have held the suspicion or an inaccurate assumption that all or some Muslim traders at the Boeing Market were Seleka, such a possibility, suspicion or assumption of the perpetrator does not change the status of the victims at the time of the attack, nor the applicable law. As regards the unnamed Muslim man in Cattin, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom and his elements must have known that Muslims were living in Cattin before and at the time of the Bangui Attack. Mr Yekatom knew that his elements would target Muslim civilians during the attack on Bangui, given his instructions to his elements prior thereto. Mr Yekatom knew that, just before attacking Cattin, his elements had targeted Muslim civilians and a building dedicated to Muslim religion. In light of the above, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom and his elements were aware of the factual circumstances that established the civilian status of all the four Muslim men that Mr Yekatom's elements killed. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the third element of murder as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute is met.Second, the Chambers considers that Mr Yekatom and his elements must have known that Muslims were living in Boeing and Cattin before and at the time of the Bangui Attack and when he launched the attack on 5 December 2013, and that their presence was lawful. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom and his elements were aware of the factual circumstances that established the lawfulness of the presence of Muslims in Boeing and Cattin.

Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the third element of deportation or forcible transfer as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, namely that perpetrator was aware of the factual circumstances that established the lawfulness of such presence, is met.

Third, the Chamber recalls Mr Yekatom's instructions concerning the attack on 5 December 2013 included targeting sectors where 'Muslims' were to be found. Mr Yekatom's elements were aware that they were attacking a religious building and that it did not serve any military objective. Taking these two facts together, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom's elements intended Boeing Mosque to be the object of the attack. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the requirement is met in respect of the third element of the war crime of attacking protected objects, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(iv) of the Statute, namely that the perpetrator intended such building dedicated to religion to be the object of the attack.

In addition to the above, the Chamber recalls its findings that Mr Yekatom knew that his elements perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis. On this basis, the Chamber concludes that Mr Yekatom meant for the Muslim civilian population in Boeing and Cattin to be severely deprived of its rights on the basis of their religious and ethnic commonalities with the Seleka. Accordingly, the specific intent requirement applicable to the crime against humanity of persecution, pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute, is also met. Conclusion

On the basis of the above, for Counts 1, 4, 5 and 8, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom committed jointly with others, within the meaning of Article 25(3)(a) of the Statute: (i) an attack against the civilian population of Boeing and Cattin as such as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(i) of the Statute (Count 1); (ii) forcible transport and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, of a majority of Muslim persons in Boeing and Cattin (Count 4); (iii) displacement as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute, of the Muslim civilian population in Boeing and Cattin (Count 5); and (iv) persecution as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute (Count 8).

For Counts 2 and 3, the Chamber finds that, based on the same conduct outlined above, Mr Yekatom committed through others, within the meaning of Article 25(3)(a) of the Statute, the crimes of murder as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Statute (Count 2), and murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute (Count 3). As regards Count 6, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom committed through others, within the meaning of Article 25(3)(a) of the Statute, the war crime of attacking a building dedicated to religion, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(iv) of the Statute (Count 6). ######

Consistent with the jurisprudence of the court, and contrary to the Ngaïssona Defence arguments, the Chamber need not require a causal link between Mr Ngaïssona's aid and assistance to the Anti-Balaka and the crimes committed by them. Similarly, the Chamber recalls that no minimum threshold of such assistance was necessary, as a matter of law, and therefore, the Chamber considers the Ngaïssona Defence's arguments concerning the limited nature of his support immaterial to its determination. It was further not required, as argued, that Mr Ngaïssona's assistance must have been made to specific persons or a specific group. In this regard, financial or psychological assistance generally to the Anti-Balaka, without identifying any specific element or group, was sufficient. Mr Ngaïssona need not have been personally in contact with Mr Yekatom or his group, or indeed with any of the Anti-Balaka elements on the ground, to have assisted the commission of the crimes by them. Further, Mr Ngaïssona need not have known all the details of the crimes, simply that the Anti-Balaka will commit the crimes in the ordinary course of events. In this respect, the Chamber is satisfied when looking at such crimes on a macro-level and not the specific details of these crimes, of which Mr Ngaïssona would have had knowledge of.

The Chamber considers that also financial assistance provided for purposes other than purchase of weapons or ammunition, or other matters not directly linked to specific hostile acts, can amount to a form of assistance through which liability under the Statute can be incurred, as long as the required elements under the Statute are fulfilled. Indeed, the Chamber considers that also financial contributions which aim at sustaining an armed group, such as to provide for its food or other sustenance, can amount to such assistance. This is because, in the view of the Chamber, such financial assistance contributes to maintaining such armed group in existence and operation.

In the view of the Chamber, regardless of what Mr Ngaïssona's concerns and motives may have been at the time, it is clear, on the facts, that Mr Ngaïssona provided financial, organisational and psychological support to the Anti-Balaka with the knowledge of the crimes that the Anti-Balaka were committing during their advance towards Bangui. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the only reasonable conclusion in these circumstances is that Mr Ngaïssona was not only aware that the Anti-Balaka would commit these crimes in the ordinary course of events, but intended for them to commit these crimes in Bangui during the Bangui Attack and lent his assistance with the aim of facilitating such crimes.

Turning to the specific knowledge requirements concerning a number of the charged crimes, the Chamber recalls its finding that Mr Yekatom's instructions to his elements included targeting sectors where 'Muslims' were to be found. Mr Yekatom's instructions were understood by the elements to accept that Muslim civilians would be killed as a result of the fighting based on his elements not having been trained or instructed to apply the principle of distinction during combat and bearing strong anti-Muslim sentiment and feelings of vengeance against the Seleka. Mr Yekatom also instructed his elements to target Seleka positions along the Boeing-Cattin-PK5 direction and these instructions encompassed attacking the Muslim traders at the Boeing Market before moving along the route to PK5. The Chamber further found that Mr Ngaïssona knew and was informed of the advance of the groups towards Bangui as well as of the hostilities during this advance, including the killings and dislocation of Muslim civilians from the locations mentioned.

Turning to the specific intent requirements concerning a number of charged crimes, the Chamber recalls the same findings as above, as well as its finding that Mr Ngaïssona knew that the Anti-Balaka perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis.

Conclusion

On the basis of the above, the Chamber therefore finds that, within the context of the attack on Bangui, including Boeing and Cattin, carried out by the Anti-Balaka including Mr Yekatom's group on 5 December 2013, Mr Ngaïssona aided, abetted or otherwise assisted, within the meaning of Article 25(3)(c) of the Statute, the commission of the following crimes: (i) attack against the civilian population as such as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(i) of the Statute (Count 1); (ii) murder as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Statute (Count 2); (iii) murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute (Count 3); (iv) forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute (Count 4); (v) displacement as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute (Count 5); (vi) directing an attack against a building dedicated to religion, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(iv) of the Statute (Count 6); and (vii) persecution as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute (Count 8). Attack against the civilian population as such as a war crime (Count 30)Under Count 30, Mr Ngaïssona is charged with the war crime of directing an attack against the civilian population as such, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(i) of the Statute, in Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, on the basis of the conduct pertaining to Counts 31 to 33, 35, 37 and 39 to 42. Recalling of factual findings

The Chamber found that on 5 December 2013, in coordination with the Anti-Balaka attack on Bangui on the same day, Anti-Balaka elements, divided into two groups led by Florent Kema and Théophile Ndangba, respectively, carried out an attack on the town of Bossangoa which started at approximately 13:00 and lasted until the late afternoon or early evening. The Chamber also found that during the attack, the Anti-Balaka targeted residential areas, including the Boro neighbourhood, generally known as the Muslim neighbourhood in Bossangoa, with the intention of showing that the Anti-Balaka were attacking not only Bangui but also in the provinces, and to 'free' the town from Seleka and all Muslims, thereby targeting Muslim civilians and drawing no distinction between them and the Seleka. The Chamber found that during the attack, the Anti-Balaka was well armed, with some AK-47s and RPGs, as well as hunting weapons. The Chamber further found that during the attack, several individuals were injured, an Anti-Balaka element forced P-2462 into sexual intercourse, and at least 18 persons were killed. The Chamber also found that during the attack, the Muslim civilian population of Bossangoa fled the attacked neighbourhoods to seek shelter at the École de la Liberté, where their numbers rose into several thousands. The Chamber found that the Muslim civilians that had sought refuge at the École de la Liberté remained confined to the school premises for fear of threats by the Anti-Balaka, staying there in cramped and generally dire conditions. The Ngaïssona Defence also submits that the attack was proportionate.

On the facts, the Chamber recalls its discussion in relation thereto above, in which it concluded that the great majority of Muslims in Bossangoa did not join the Seleka and were not otherwise armed at the time of the attack. On the law, the Chamber recalls that a civilian population need not be the sole and exclusive target of an attack. The presence within the civilian population of individuals who do not fit within the definition of civilians does not deprive the entire population of its civilian character. Therefore, even if the Ngaïssona Defence's arguments are to be believed that the Anti-Balaka targeted legitimate military objectives, this did not deprive the civilian population in Bossangoa of its civilian character as such.

Murder as a crime against humanity and as a war crime (Counts 31 and 32)Under Counts 31 and 32, Mr Ngaïssona is charged with murder as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Statute, and murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, on 5 December 2013 in Bossangoa. Killing of one or more persons

The Chamber found that in the course of the attack on Bossangoa, the Anti-Balaka killed at least 18 persons. Thus, the Chamber finds that the first legal element of both murder as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Statute, and murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, namely that the perpetrator killed one or more persons, is met.

The Ngaïssona Defence argues that the identity and mens rea of the perpetrator(s) are not established as 'it is impossible to discount the possibility that the alleged victims might have been unfortunately killed in cross or friendly fire'.

In this regard, the Chamber recalls its finding, on the basis of its analysis of the evidence before it, that it was indeed the Anti-Balaka who killed the individuals. Status of the persons killed

The Ngaïssona Defence further argues that the Chamber 'cannot reasonably exclude the possibility that the alleged victims might have been actively participating in hostilities at the time of their death'.

The Chamber recalls in this regard its finding, on the basis of its analysis of the evidence before it, that the persons found to have been killed by the Anti-Balaka were not armed or taking part in hostilities. Specifically, the Chamber considered the evidence before it indicating that these individuals were not members of the Seleka, not armed at the time of their death, and not otherwise engaged in fighting against the Anti-Balaka at the time of their death on 5 December 2013. The argument of the Ngaïssona Defence that it cannot be 'excluded' that the victims 'might' have actively participated in hostilities is, without more, speculative and therefore inapt to impact the Chamber's conclusion. The Chamber finds that there are no indications in the evidence to suggest that the individuals found to have been killed by the Anti-Balaka during the attack in Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 had lost their protected status as civilians at the time of their death.

On the basis of the above, the Chamber therefore finds that the second element of murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, namely that the person or persons killed were either hors de combat, or were civilians, medical personnel, or religious personnel taking no active part in the hostilities, is also met. ######

Destruction of the adversary's property as a war crime (Count 33)Under Count 33, Mr Ngaïssona is charged with destruction of property as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(xii) of the Statute, on 5 December 2013 and in the days thereafter in Bossangoa. Destruction of certain property

The Chamber found that at some point between 5 and 8 December 2013, the Anti-Balaka burned and destroyed residential structures, lived in by Muslims at the time of the attack, in the immediate vicinity of the imam's residence. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the first element of the war crime of destruction of property, namely that the perpetrator destroyed certain property, is met. Property of an adversary

The property in question belonged to the individuals living in the residences in the immediate vicinity of the imam's property, which the Chamber found to have been Muslims. The Chamber reiterates its finding that the Anti-Balaka elements perceived Muslims as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka, and targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, accordingly. Accordingly, the second element of the war crime of destruction of property, that the property was property of an adversary, is also met. Protection from destruction under international law of armed conflict

Considering that the objects destroyed were residential structures, and recalling its conclusion that there were no Seleka bases in the area in question and further that no clashes between the Anti-Balaka and the Seleka took place in the area around the imam's residence, the Chamber also finds that no circumstances are indicated on facts which could mean that the objects constituted military objects. The Chamber thus finds that the property destroyed was protected from that destruction under the international law of armed conflict. There is also no indication on facts that the destruction was required by military necessary. The third and fifth elements of the war crime of destruction of property, namely that, respectively, the property was protected from destruction under the international law of armed conflict and the destruction was not required by military necessity, are therefore established. ######

Forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity and displacement as a war crime (Counts 37 and 38)Under Counts 37 and 38, Mr Ngaïssona is charged with forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute and displacement as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute, for the dislocation of Bossangoa's Muslim population to the École de la Liberté, before being evacuated to other locations, in the context of the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 and in the days following the attack. Recalling of factual findings

The Chamber found that during the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, the Muslim civilian population of Bossangoa fled the attacked neighbourhoods to seek shelter at the École de la Liberté, where their numbers rose into several thousands. The Chamber found that Muslim civilians that had sought refuge at the École de la Liberté remained confined to the school premises for fear of threats by the Anti-Balaka, staying there in cramped and generally dire conditions. The Chamber found that the Muslim civilians at the École de la Liberté were dependent on the protection of international forces for their safety and could not leave the school premises venturing into Bossangoa without risk to their person. The Chamber further found that eventually, in light of the prevailing insecurity as well as the dire and cramped living conditions at the École de la Liberté, all Muslims staying at the school were transported away from Bossangoa to Chad in two separate convoys, leaving in February and April 2014, respectively, following which Bossangoa was emptied of its Muslim population. Perpetrator deported or forcibly transferred one or more persons to another State or location, by expulsion or other coercive acts

The Ngaïssona Defence argues that Muslim civilians left their homes as result of a lawful attack and for their own security, and that their displacement to the École de la Liberté was 'not only allowed under IHL, but arguably required by it'.

The Chamber recalls, on the facts, its conclusion that the Anti-Balaka, in launching its attack on Bossangoa, specifically targeted residential areas, including the Boro neighbourhood which was generally known as the Muslim neighbourhood in Bossangoa, drawing no distinction between Seleka and Muslim civilians. The Chamber further recalls, on the law, that the 'forcible' nature of a displacement need not be physical force, but may include threat of force or coercion, such as that caused by fear of violence, duress, detention, psychological oppression or abuse of power, or by taking advantage of a coercive environment.

The Chamber is of the view that the attack on Bossangoa in general, and the specific targeting of Muslim residential areas and the Muslim civilian population therein created conditions which made it physically, materially and psychologically unsafe for Muslim civilians there, forcing them to leave and flee to the École de la Liberté. The Chamber further considers that in light of the prevailing conditions around the École de la Liberté following the attack, these Muslims could not return to their homes. The Chamber also finds that the conditions at the École de la Liberté following the attack were such that these Muslims could not only not return to their homes, but saw themselves being forced to leave Bossangoa altogether. The Chamber considers that the fear of threats by the Anti-Balaka, combined with the deplorable conditions at the École de la Liberté, amounted to 'coercive acts'.

In this context, the Chamber also notes the Ngaïssona Defence's argument that the departure of Muslim civilians for Chad was 'entirely voluntary' and not attributable to the Anti-Balaka. The Chamber recalls in this regard that there must be a genuine lack of choice on the part of the person or persons forcibly transferred, and that the prevailing situation and atmosphere, and other relevant circumstances, including in particular the victims' vulnerability, has to be taken into account when assessing whether the individuals transferred indeed had a genuine choice.

The Chamber recalls that the Muslim civilians of Bossangoa fled to the École de la Liberté due to the Anti-Balaka attack on the town on 5 December, and that they remained confined at the school for fear of threats by the Anti-Balaka, staying in cramped and generally dire conditions, with these conditions as well as the prevailing insecurity leading to the transfer of all Muslim staying at the school to Chad. In the Chamber's view, the circumstances under which the Muslim civilians reached the École de la Liberté, combined with those under which these Muslim civilians remained at the École de la Liberté, make clear that these individuals had no genuine choice but to flee their homes for the school, as well as agreeing to be transported away from the school thereafter. Any 'reconciliation efforts', as mentioned by the Ngaïssona Defence, did not lead to the creation of conditions which would have allowed Muslims confined to the École de la Liberté to return to their homes as they remained dependent on the protection of international forces for their safety and could not leave the school without risk to their person. The Chamber considers that an agreement, or even a wish expressed, to be transported, does not mean that such transfer was 'entirely voluntary', as argued by the Ngaïssona Defence. On the contrary, the Chamber considers that it is clear on the facts that the conditions leading to their fleeing to the École de la Liberté and circumstances thereat were such that the Muslim civilians that fled to and stayed at the École de la Liberté did not have a genuine choice to stay in Bossangoa and return to their homes.

The Chamber recalls that the Muslim civilians of Bossangoa fled to the École de la Liberté due to the Anti-Balaka attack on the town on 5 December, and that they remained confined at the school for fear of threats by the Anti-Balaka, staying in cramped and generally dire conditions, with these conditions as well as the prevailing insecurity leading to the transfer of all Muslim staying at the school to Chad. The Chamber further considers that the circumstances mentioned were created by the Anti-Balaka. This is based on its finding that the Anti-Balaka attacked Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, and within this attack specifically targeted residential areas, as well as on the finding that Muslims who had fled to the École de la Liberté had to stay there for fear of threats by the Anti-Balaka, and despite the deplorable conditions there. This is irrespective of whether the Anti-Balaka were in full control of Bossangoa following its attack on the town. The Chamber is of the view that but for the Anti-Balaka attack on Bossangoa and its continued presence there, maintaining the prevailing insecurity, the Muslims that had fled to the École de la Liberté would not have stayed there and would not have been transported to Chad subsequently.

On the basis of the above, the Chamber thus finds that the requirement for forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, namely that the perpetrator forcibly transferred or deported, without grounds permitted under international law, one or more persons to another State or location, by expulsion or other coercive acts, is met. Lawful presence

In relation to the question of the Muslims' lawful presence in the area, the Chamber considers that there is no indication on the facts that the Muslims residing in Bossangoa were not lawfully present there. The Chamber recalls in this regard that the perpetrator need not make any legal evaluation as to the lawfulness of presence in an area, but need only be aware of the factual circumstances establishing the 'lawful presence'. Recalling its finding that the Anti-Balaka targeted residential areas of Bossangoa, including Boro which was known as the Muslim neighbourhood of the town, with the stated aim of 'freeing' the town not only from the Seleka, but from all Muslims, the Chamber considers that the Anti-Balaka were, on the facts, aware, that the Muslims in Bossangoa were lawfully present in their areas. 'Without grounds' and 'not justified'

Specifically as regards the requirement, under Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, that the transfer or deportation took place 'without grounds permitted under international law', and the requirement under Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute that the displacement was 'not justified by the security of the civilians involved or by military necessity', the Chamber recalls that the Anti-Balaka attacked Bossangoa with the stated aim of 'freeing' the town from Seleka and all Muslims. The Chamber further recalls its conclusion that in attacking residential areas, including those generally known as Muslim neighbourhoods, the Anti-Balaka drew no distinction between the Seleka and all Muslims in Bossangoa.

Specifically as regards the requirement, under Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, that the transfer or deportation took place 'without grounds permitted under international law', and the requirement under Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute that the displacement was 'not justified by the security of the civilians involved or by military necessity', the Chamber recalls that the Anti-Balaka attacked Bossangoa with the stated aim of 'freeing' the town from Seleka and all Muslims. The Chamber further recalls its conclusion that in attacking residential areas, including those generally known as Muslim neighbourhoods, the Anti-Balaka drew no distinction between the Seleka and all Muslims in Bossangoa.

In light of the above, and absent any contrary indication on the facts, the Chamber does not consider that the transfer and displacement of Muslim civilians to the École de la Liberté, and Chad thereafter, had grounds permitted under international law, or otherwise was justified by the security of these civilians or military necessity. The Chamber thus finds that these requirements for forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, as well as for displacement as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute, are also met. Order to displace

The Chamber now turns to the distinct requirement of displacement as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute that the perpetrator 'ordered' the displacement of a civilian population and was in a position to effect such displacement by giving such order.

The Ngaïssona Defence argues that there was no such order to displace or otherwise to perform an act or omission as the result of which such displacement would occur, by either Mr Ngaïssona or someone under his authority, who was 'in a position to effect such displacement by giving such order'.

The Chamber recalls its finding that the Anti-Balaka attacked Bossangoa with the stated aim of showing that the Anti-Balaka were attacking not only Bangui but also in the provinces, and to 'free' the town from the Seleka and all Muslims, as well as its finding that the Anti-Balaka perceived the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and therefore targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR.

Similarly, the Chamber considers on this basis also that the Anti-Balaka groups attacking Bossangoa were in a position to effect such displacement. The Chamber found that the Anti-Balaka during its attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013 targeted residential areas, including the Boro neighbourhood, generally known as the Muslim neighbourhood in Bossangoa, to 'free' the town from Seleka and all Muslims, thereby targeting Muslim civilians. The Chamber further found that during the attack, the Anti-Balaka forced into sexual intercourse one woman, and killed at least 18 individuals. It also found that during the attack, the Muslim civilian population of Bossangoa fled the attacked neighbourhoods to seek shelter at the École de la Liberté, where their numbers rose into several thousands. The Ngaïssona Defence argues that there is 'no credible evidence that Anti-Balaka elements severely restricted the physical liberty of Muslim civilians by forcing them to remain' at the École de la Liberté, since (i) Muslim civilians were not detained as they had the possibility to leave the school premises, and (ii) there is no evidence that Anti-Balaka elements were the reason why they remained in the school. The Ngaïssona Defence submits that the 'crucial element of control' of the perpetrators over the location at which Muslims were kept is missing.The Chamber considers that had it not been for the fear of threats by the Anti-Balaka, the Muslims confined to the École de la Liberté would not have chosen to remain there in the mentioned deplorable conditions. Indeed, as found, the Muslims at the school were dependent on the protection of international forces and could not leave the school without risk to their person. That some Muslims may have ventured out of the school at their own risk does not mean that such risk did not exist. The Ngaïssona Defence further submits that even if the Chamber were satisfied that the Anti-Balaka elements committed part of the underlying crimes, the required discriminatory intent remains unproven, since the 'very low number of alleged civilian casualties, compared to the large amount of people who were safely evacuated away from the hostilities is probative of an attack that did not target civilians based on their ethnicity, religion or political affiliations', and that neither general behaviour of alleged perpetrators nor circumstances surrounding the commission of alleged crimes allow to infer a discriminatory intent.

The Chamber disagrees with the Ngaïssona Defence's suggestion that discriminatory intent cannot be inferred, and proven, in light of a 'low number' of civilian casualties, when compared to those who were 'safely evacuated'. The Chamber understands this to argue that a certain minimum proportion of any group would have to be targeted for a Chamber to be able to infer and conclude on the discriminatory intent required by the crime of persecution. No such requirement exists under the law.

Indeed, the law is clear in requiring that the perpetrator severely deprived, contrary to international law, 'one or more persons' of fundamental rights. Thus, even one individual may be subject to such severe deprivation of fundamental rights. This is combined with the elements further requiring that the perpetrator targeted 'such person or persons' by reason of the identity of a group or collectivity, or targeted the group or collectivity as such, and that such targeting was based on political, racial, national, ethnic, cultural religious, gender as defined in Article 7(3) of the Statute, or other grounds universally recognised as impermissible under international law. Determinative is therefore not the number of casualties within a group or collectivity when compared to those within the same group of collectivity that did not. Determinative is, rather, that 'one or more persons' were severely deprived of fundamental rights, and 'such person or persons' were targeted because of the identity of the group or collectivity, based on the grounds mentioned. The Chamber is of the view that this can be established through a variety of factors and need not rely on inferring the requisite intent on the basis of whatever may be considered a 'high' number of casualties in the circumstances.

paragraph_text_preview: In the view of the Chamber, the knowledge of an abstract 'risk' of certain types of crimes being committed is insufficient for it to find Mr Ngaïssona's individual criminal responsibility in relation to Counts 40 and 41. Article 30(3) of the Statute specifies that knowledge means 'awareness that a circumstance exists or a consequence will occur in the ordinary course of events'. The phrase 'will occur in the ordinary course of events' in Article 30(2)(b) and (3) of the Statute requires 'virtual certainty' that the consequence in question would occur. The Chamber agrees with prior jurisprudence that this implies that 'the consequence will follow, barring an unforeseen or unexpected intervention that prevent this occurrence'.

The Chamber is indeed satisfied that Mr Ngaïssona had 'virtual certainty' that killings, injuries, dislocation, and destruction of property would occur in the ordinary course of events during the attack on Bossangoa on the basis outlined above. However, the Chamber is not convinced that his knowledge on the basis of 'virtual certainty' extended to rape occurring in the ordinary course of events.

The Chamber emphasises in this regard that, according to its evaluation of the evidence, it is convinced, beyond reasonable doubt, that an Anti-Balaka element raped P-2462 during the attack on Bossangoa on 5 December 2013. The Chamber further emphasises that it is not of the view that sexual violence in general is an 'exceptional' occurrence in the context of armed conflicts. On the contrary.

At the same time, the Chamber underscores that it must base its conclusions on the specific evidence and charges as presented and confirmed before it, and in relation to the individual criminal responsibility of a specific accused. It is within this specific, and limited, context that the Chamber is unable to conclude, on the basis of the evidence before it, that Mr Ngaïssona had 'virtual certainty' that rape would occur in the ordinary course of the Anti-Balaka attack in Bossangoa. The Chamber recalls in this regard that it found a clear pattern of criminal conduct relating to the targeting of Muslim civilians with killings, injuries, dislocation, destruction of property and attacks against buildings dedicated to religion in the context of the Anti-Balaka attacks during its advance towards Bangui from September 2013, during the coordinated attacks on Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, in relation to the events at Yamwara at the end of December 2013, as regards the events along the PK9-Mbaïki axis following Michel Djotodia's resignation, as well as in relation to the Anti-Balaka attacks in western CAR in early 2014. All this led the Chamber to conclude that Mr Ngaïssona was aware that such criminal conduct would occur in the ordinary course of events and, indeed, that he performed his own conduct for purposes of facilitating the commission of such crimes. However, the Chamber cannot conclude the same as regards the cases of rape that occurred in Bossangoa, one of which Mr Ngaïssona is charged with. Conclusion

On the basis of the above, the Chamber therefore finds that, within the context of the attack on Bossangoa, carried out by the Anti-Balaka on 5 December 2013, Mr Ngaïssona aided, abetted or otherwise assisted, within the meaning of Article 25(3)(c) of the Statute, the commission of the following crimes: (i) attack against the civilian population as such as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(i) of the Statute (Count 30); (ii) murder as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Statute (Count 31); (iii) murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute (Count 32); (iv) destruction of the adversary's property as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(xii) of the Statute (Count 33); (v) forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute (Count 37); (vi) displacement as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute (Count 38); (vii) imprisonment and other forms of severe deprivation of physical liberty as a crime against humanity (Count 39); and (viii) persecution as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute (Count 42). At the outset, the Chamber was not assisted by the Yekatom Defence's arguments challenging the relative gravity of the charged conduct in other cases. Further, the Chamber could draw no conclusions on the Yekatom Defence's theoretical argument that the drafters of the Statute intended to exclude cruel treatment from being considered a crime against humanity. The Chamber further grants that a variety of judicial bodies have applied the definition of 'other inhumane acts' restrictively, and that not every conduct is grave enough to fulfil the gravity requirement. The Chamber also considers both gravity and the notion of 'an inhumane act' require a value judgment and a subjective assessment of the circumstances against situations where the gravity requirements were not fulfilled.
As set out below, the treatment of the six persons in the present case, when considered as a whole, squarely fulfilled the gravity requirement.

In respect of the three female captives, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom's elements subjected them to mental suffering by threatening them with death, using the phrase 'peeling the papaya' at the checkpoint, threatening them with death during their captivity at Yamwara in Cœur de Lion's house, as well as during their captivity at the second location in Yamwara, without Saint Cyr. Mr Yekatom's elements subjected them to physical suffering by searching them at Yamwara, forcing them to undress to their underwear, and keeping them in captivity at gunpoint in both the locations where they were kept at Yamwara. Having regard to the circumstances and the manner in which the group was apprehended, searched and threatened with death at the checkpoint and during their transfer to Yamwara, the Chamber finds that they bore no resemblance whatsoever to any 'investigative' act legally carried out. It did not have any of the characteristics of a lawful action, regardless of whether it would have been, otherwise, lawfully sanctioned. If anything, what was clear throughout the events was that none of the members of the group, including Saint Cyr, was armed or posed a threat to the security of elements at Yamwara. In this context, the Chamber considers that the recovery of a SIM card in the trousers of one of the women at Yamwara by one of Mr Yekatom's elements or finding a Seleka card on Saint Cyr did not mean that the group, including Saint Cyr, were suddenly rendered without protection as civilians under the legal framework. It also did not render lawful retrospectively the manner in which the group, including Saint Cyr, was apprehended. The Chamber is convinced that elements in Mr Yekatom's group had no reason to entertain suspicions against the group, including Saint Cyr, let alone consider, as argued, that these suspicions were 'reasonable'.

In arriving at this conclusion, the Chamber considered irrelevant the Yekatom Defence's arguments pointing to the circumstances of the search of the vehicle in which some of the members of the group were travelling with the corpse of Saint Cyr's brother. The Chamber considers that this search of the vehicle was also neither 'routine' nor lawful, noting that Mr Yekatom's group had no legal basis to set up a checkpoint or to grant themselves the authority to carry out searches of the vehicles and individuals in and around Yamwara.

In respect of the third element of torture as a crime against humanity under Article 7(1)(f) of the Statute, namely that the pain or suffering inflicted did not arise only from, and was not inherent in or incidental to, lawful sanction, the Chamber finds that there was no nexus between the actions of Mr Yekatom and his elements and any lawful sanction. Neither Mr Yekatom nor his elements had any lawful authority or basis to set up a checkpoint where Saint Cyr was apprehended. They equally did not have the legal authority or basis to stop and search Saint Cyr there, to bring him to Yamwara, or to keep him there. Neither Mr Yekatom, Alkanto at the checkpoint, nor Cœur de Lion at Yamwara, had any legal authority or basis to require elements in Mr Yekatom's group to beat, interrogate, threaten, or maim Saint Cyr. Turning to the distinct element of torture as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, that the person be either hors de combat, or a civilian, the Chamber has considered the circumstances of Saint Cyr's abduction and custody at Yamwara and his status during this time. The Chamber finds that Saint Cyr was a civilian at the time of his abduction. The Chamber recalls that he, along with the other men in this group, was escorting the women, with whom he had familial relations, to find transport to go home. Saint Cyr was not armed at any stage of the events, as shown by the fact that no arms were recovered from the group during the two searches, one at the checkpoint and one at Yamwara. Saint Cyr was not carrying out any activities that would have altered his civilian status at the time of his abduction. This conclusion is not affected by Saint Cyr holding a rank within the FACA at the time, or the discovery of the purported 'Seleka card' on him, following a search by Mr Yekatom's element. The Chamber thus concludes that the distinct element of torture was a war crime under Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, namely that the person be hors de combat or a civilian, is met. ######

As set out in its factual findings and its conclusions below, without having recourse to the legal discussion above, the Chamber was satisfied that the severity requirement was met for each of the six persons when their individual circumstances were assessed holistically.

In respect of the three female captives, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom's elements subjected them to mental suffering by threatening them with death, using the phrase 'peeling the papaya' at the checkpoint, threatening them with death during their captivity at Yamwara in Cœur de Lion's house, as well as during their captivity at the second location in Yamwara, without Saint Cyr. Mr Yekatom's elements subjected them to physical suffering by searching them at Yamwara, forcing them to undress to their underwear, and keeping them in captivity at gunpoint in both the locations where they were kept at Yamwara. Mr Yekatom's elements further subjected them to mental suffering by keeping them around the location where their family member, Saint Cyr, was beaten, his legs were broken, he was tied up in 'arbatacher' manner and several of his body parts were cut off within hearing distance from them. Mr Yekatom's elements subjected them to physical suffering by making them walk overnight to another location close to the M'Poko airport, in the context of an armed conflict, where they were kept in captivity in circumstances that to P-0967 and P-1811 were frightening.

The Chamber emphasises that there is no minimum requirement of duration that a deprivation of liberty must fulfil under Article 7(1)(e) of the Statute, and therefore, it need not be for a prolonged period of time, as also noted in the Burundi Decision. In this respect, the Pre-Trial Chamber III considered duration together with the overall circumstances of detention when assessing the severity of the physical deprivation of liberty. The fact that the Burundi Decision itself concerned longer durations of detention has no bearing whatsoever on how the express requirements of Article 7(1)(e) of the Statute must be read.

Indeed, it would be artificial when assessing deprivation of liberty to only look at duration, divorcing it from the surrounding circumstances. In this respect, the Chamber has regard to the case-law under international human rights instruments concerning captivity for a duration comparable to the present case, cited in the Burundi Decision in support of its finding that 'brevity of detention alone cannot be brought forward as an argument to deny the severity of the deprivation of physical liberty'. In all of these cited cases, duration of detention was only one of the factors that the concerned court or committee considered to assess arbitrariness of detention.

Turning now to the second element of imprisonment and other forms of severe deprivation of physical liberty as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(e) of the Statute, namely that the gravity of the conduct was such that it was in violation of fundamental rules of international law, the Chamber finds that this requirement is met by Mr Yekatom's elements apprehending the seven persons without any legal basis and providing none of them with access to any procedural rights for the entire duration of their captivity.

In assessing whether there was a violation of fundamental rules of international law, the Chamber has considered two factors: whether Mr Yekatom had the legal basis to apprehend and keep in captivity the seven persons and whether Mr Yekatom granted to the seven persons any procedural safeguards required under international law.

As regards the first factor, and despite some interaction with national authorities, the Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom and his elements had no legal basis to arbitrarily apprehend persons on the basis of suspicions at checkpoints. Mr Yekatom and his elements had no legal authority, prescribed by law or otherwise, to keep the seven persons in captivity. Even if such legal basis existed, Mr Yekatom had further no legal authority to subject the seven persons to the mistreatment that accompanied their captivity. As regards the second factor, the Chamber considers that there was no indication that Mr Yekatom's elements granted any of the seven persons access to any procedural rights that accompany such deprivation of liberty, for example, the right to be informed of the grounds of why they were being apprehended and held captive, the right to legal assistance, and the right of independent and impartial review of the necessity of captivity.

First, on the facts, with no arms being found on any of them, none of the seven in the group posed any threat to the security of Mr Yekatom, or his elements based at Yamwara. This conclusion is not affected by the recovery of a SIM card hidden in the trousers of one of the women, as there is no indication of why this SIM card was hidden, on whom exactly it was found, and whether Mr Yekatom's elements made any inquiry with the captives concerning this SIM card. Their interrogation by Mr Yekatom's elements appeared to have been restricted to the captives' family links and ethnicities, rather than genuine inquiries about determining their protected status as civilians.

Second, none of the seven captives were members of the Seleka forces nor spies. The Chamber recalls that Mr Yekatom's elements continued to interrogate Saint Cyr and beat him, despite him showing his identification card and insisting that he was a FACA member. This conclusion is not affected by the recovery of the purported 'Seleka card' on him, following a search by Mr Yekatom's element. Further, apart from some of the women captives having family relations with Mamour, who was the minister of defence in the Seleka government, there was no indication that any of the seven were indeed themselves Seleka members.

As regards Saint Cyr's status at the relevant time, the Chamber has considered the circumstances of Saint Cyr's abduction and custody at Yamwara and his status during that time. The Chamber finds that Saint Cyr was a civilian at the time of his abduction. The Chamber recalls that he, along with the other men in this group, was escorting the women, with whom he had familial relations, to find transport to go home. Saint Cyr was not armed at any stage of the events, as shown by no arms being recovered from the group during the two searches, one at the checkpoint and one at Yamwara. Saint Cyr was not carrying out any activities that would have altered his civilian status at the time of his abduction.
