The Chamber considered the circumstances showing why Mr Yekatom's elements stopped the seven persons at the checkpoint. The Chamber found that when elements from Mr Yekatom's group apprehended these seven persons at a checkpoint led by Alkanto close to the Lapo N'Gomat family house and Yamwara, Alkanto pointed to the women as belonging to the family of Mamour and Michel Djotodia in the presence of the elements in his group. In respect of the third element of persecution as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute, namely that such targeting was based on political, racial, national, ethnic, cultural, religious, gender as defined in article 7, paragraph 3, of the Statute, or other grounds that are universally recognised as impermissible under international law, the Chamber finds that this requirement is met, by virtue of such targeting being based on religious grounds. Committed in connection with any act referred to in Article 7(1) of the Statute or any crime within the jurisdiction of the Court

In respect of the fourth element of persecution as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute, namely that the conduct was committed in connection with any act referred to in Article 7, paragraph 1 of the Statute or any crime within the jurisdiction of the Court, the Chamber finds that this requirement is met in respect of all the seven persons. The conduct of Mr Yekatom's elements, wherein they severely deprived the seven persons of physical liberty and subjected them to great suffering, or serious injury to body or to mental or physical health, including torture and murder, amounted to acts referred to in article 7, paragraph 1 of the Statute and were linked to the targeting. [Article 30]{.underline}The Chamber now turns to Mr Yekatom's mens rea underlying Counts 11 to 17 pursuant to Article 30 of the Statute requiring intent and knowledge of the crimes.

The Chamber has regard to Mr Yekatom's knowledge of the incident, his presence at Yamwara later in the evening of 24 December 2013, and his direct interactions with Saint Cyr's father and the three women captives. In particular, Mr Yekatom also knew that the female captives were Muslim. Mr Yekatom knew that his elements had mistreated Saint Cyr, and that he subsequently died. When asked about Saint Cyr's treatment, Mr Yekatom said in Sango 'eforolo tonga na papai' -- meaning that 'they peeled the papaya', 'they removed the skin like they would do to a papaya'. Mr Yekatom considered they could not 'keep' Saint Cyr as he was a 'traitor' and 'in cahoots with the Seleka'. Indeed, when Mr Yekatom paid a visit to the three women and the two men at the Anti-Balaka base close to the airport in the following day(s), Saint Cyr was notably not amongst them.

As set out below, Mr Yekatom and his elements inflicted pain and suffering on Saint Cyr for the purpose of punishment, intimidation, and discrimination based on religion.

At the outset, the Chamber recalls that the element in question cut off Saint Cyr's toes, fingers, and an ear, being encouraged by Cœur de Lion's presence at the scene and his words and feeling that there was 'no choice'. In light of this, the suggestion that this element, as a direct perpetrator, may have also had other motivations for executing the crime, namely, to 'prove her worth', is irrelevant for a finding of Mr Yekatom's responsibility. In the view of the Chamber, other purported motivation held by this element do not negate her acts and intention to inflict pain and suffering on Saint Cyr for the purpose of punishment, intimidation, and discrimination based on religion.

The Chamber finds that the words and actions of Mr Yekatom's elements show that Saint Cyr's mistreatment was for the purpose of discrimination based on religion. Mr Yekatom's elements perceived Saint Cyr as being part of a group that was being considered 'all Muslim' at the time of its capture at the checkpoint. In Cœur de Lion's presence, elements in Mr Yekatom's group, including Bojos, interrogated Saint Cyr on his identity, ethnicity, and reasons for being there with the women, also demanding he speak in the dialect associated with his ethnicity. Saint Cyr and another captive, who were Boffi from their father's side and Goula from their mother's side, gave their ethnicity but neither could speak their dialect. Saint Cyr said that he was 'Boffi' but could not speak in this language. When Saint Cyr was unable to do so, elements in Mr Yekatom's group accused him of being 'Goula', and therefore associated with Djotodia. Elements in Mr Yekatom's group continued to interrogate Saint Cyr and beat him, despite him showing his identification card and insisting that he was a FACA member. During Saint Cyr's beating, Cœur de Lion was using terms like 'Muslims' and 'Seleka'.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes the Yekatom Defence's argument that Alkanto had 'personal vendetta' towards P-1811 and that his 'vigilance was further heightened by his personal grievances' against her and her husband. The Chamber finds that these personal motives did not have any relevance for establishing the elements of the crime. There is nothing in the legal framework of the Court requiring proof of motive of the direct perpetrator of a crime underlying crimes against humanity to establish the mental elements of such crimes. The Chamber also considers that merely because personal motivations can be identified, it does not necessarily follow that the required nexus with the widespread or systematic attack is inevitably lacking.

The Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom knew that neither he nor his elements had any legal authority to capture the seven persons at the checkpoint and keep them at Yamwara. Mr Yekatom, as a FACA member, was aware of the applicable regime under international humanitarian law as well as the CAR domestic regime. Mr Yekatom must have known that the seven persons should have been granted the basic procedural rights during their captivity. Mr Yekatom knew that, regardless of the purported suspicions entertained by his elements, his elements had no legal authority or basis to subject the seven persons to the mistreatment during their captivity.

The Chamber found that Mr Yekatom knew that, at the time of his capture, Saint Cyr was escorting the three women, with whom he had familial relations, to find transport to go home, in the context of a burial of a family relative. Mr Yekatom must have known that the other male captives, namely, P-1704, P-1705, and P-1716, were similarly accompanying the women and for the same reason. In respect of P-1716, who was released the following morning after his father paid a ransom to Cœur de Lion and Mr Yekatom, Mr Yekatom knew that P-1716 was being kept at Yamwara, at the very latest on the morning of 25 December 2013 when P-1716's father paid a ransom to Cœur de Lion and Mr Yekatom. Mr Yekatom must have known that P-1716 was part of the seven persons that had been apprehended at the checkpoint and had been assimilated in the group. In respect of Saint Cyr, the Chamber finds that Mr Yekatom knew that Saint Cyr was being targeted because of his association with the women in the group and considered him a 'traitor' and 'in cahoots with the Seleka'. In respect of P-0967, P-1811, and another captive, the Chamber found that Mr Yekatom knew that his elements had captured and kept them at gunpoint at Yamwara. Further, on the morning of 25 December 2013, Mr Yekatom met the five captives, namely, P-0967, P-1811, P-1704, P-1705, and another captive, at the Anti-Balaka base and introduced himself. Mr Yekatom was aware that Sylvestre Yagouzou had kept the five in this location close to the M'Poko airport surrounded by Anti-Balaka elements.

Mr NgaïssonaThe Chamber now turns to Mr Ngaïssona's responsibility under Counts 11 to 17. Mr Ngaïssona is alleged to have committed the aforementioned crimes by facilitating the commission of the crimes as set out in the confirmed charges by aiding, abetting or otherwise assisting in their commission under Article 25(3)(c) of the Statute. Recalling of factual findings
The Chamber refers to the factual findings as recalled above.

In addition, the Chamber found that between the coordinated attacks on Bangui and Bossangoa of 5 December 2013 and until his return to Bangui on 14 January 2014, Mr Ngaïssona remained informed of the continued activities related to the Anti-Balaka, and continued liaising with various individuals in this regard. Aiding, abetting or otherwise assisting

In light of this, the Chamber finds that Mr Ngaïssona, by funding and supporting the Anti-Balaka prior to the attacks on Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013, and subsequently, aided, abetted, or otherwise assisted in the commission of the crimes underlying Counts 11, 13 (in respect of the six persons), 14 and 17 forming part of the Yamwara Incident by Mr Yekatom's elements. For the same reasons, the Chamber, by majority, Judge Kovács dissenting, finds that Mr Ngaïssona aided, abetted, or otherwise assisted in the commission of crimes underlying Counts 12, 13, 15 and 16 concerning Saint Cyr's torture and murder. As discussed in further detail below, Judge Kovács considers that the mental element, namely, that Mr Ngaïssona was aware that this crime would take place in the ordinary course of events, was not satisfied in respect of Saint Cyr's torture and murder. Mental elements

As regards Mr Ngaïssona's mens rea, the Chamber recalls its finding that Mr Ngaïssona made his contributions fully aware that the Anti-Balaka would violently target the Muslim civilian population in the west of the CAR, committing the widespread attack that ultimately took place from September 2013 through February 2014, including the seminal coordinated Anti-Balaka attacks of Bangui and Bossangoa on 5 December 2013. Mr Ngaïssona knew and was informed of the advance of the groups towards Bangui as well as of the hostilities during this advance, including the killings of Muslim civilians from these locations. Mr Ngaïssona knew that the Anti-Balaka perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis. The Chamber further considered that Mr Ngaïssona provided his financial aid, organisational assistance and psychological support to the Anti-Balaka in the context of anti-foreign sentiments and inflammatory rhetoric openly expressed by François Bozizé and others, which incited vigilance against those perceived to support the Seleka, in particular Muslim civilians.

The Chamber, by majority, Judge Kovács dissenting, finds that Mr Ngaïssona knew that the Anti-Balaka would also torture and kill Muslim civilians within the context of the Yamwara Incident, within the meaning of Article 30(3) of the Statute which requires that 'a circumstance exists or a consequence will occur in the ordinary course of events'.

Judge Kovács has considered the particularity of the conduct concerning Saint Cyr's torture involving an element in Mr Yekatom's group cutting off his toes, fingers, and an ear for reasons, inter alia, that this element may gain the trust of the chiefs in Mr Yekatom's group. Judge Kovács also notes, in this context, the particular circumstances of Alkanto bearing negative feelings centred around a desire for revenge against the women, accompanied by Saint Cyr. Judge Kovács further notes that the Chamber did not find any instances of torture, similar to that faced by Saint Cyr, in any of the crimes that the Anti-Balaka committed in their advance to Bangui prior to 5 December 2013. Further, he considers that the charges, as confirmed, indeed do not contain any comparable incidents. In this respect, he draws a distinction between the incident concerning Djido Saleh in which his body parts were cut off when he was already dead, and not before, as was the case with Saint Cyr.

In this respect, he draws a distinction between the incident concerning Djido Saleh in which his body parts were cut off when he was already dead, and not before, as was the case with Saint Cyr.

Accordingly, Judge Kovács considers that these facts taken together show that the particular cruelty involved in the crime of torture, namely the cutting off of Saint Cyr's toes, fingers, and ear did not take place in the ordinary course of events within the meaning attributed to it in the jurisprudence as outlined above. In his view, the personal and specific nature of the motives of Mr Yekatom's elements that contributed to the commission of this crime created a break in what one could consider 'the ordinary course', as required by Article 30(3) of the Statute, and therefore considers that this test is not satisfied in this specific instance in respect of Mr Ngaïssona. Further, Judge Kovács is of the view that it was Saint Cyr's torture that resulted in his death, and therefore, similar considerations also apply to Saint Cyr's murder. To conclude on this aspect, Judge Kovács considers that Mr Ngaïssona was not aware that Muslim civilians would be subjected to the particular cruelty resulting in their death, as was the case with Saint Cyr, in these circumstances.

Judge Kovács considers it appropriate to clarify that these considerations do not apply to the cruel treatment of the six persons nor of the killings of Muslim civilians generally as outlined in other contexts. Based on the factual findings recalled above, Judge Kovács agrees with the majority that Mr Ngaïssona was aware that the Anti-Balaka would mistreat Muslim civilians.

The majority has noted Judge Kovács' views and considers that the Chamber's assessment of torture was not limited to the cutting off of Saint Cyr's body parts and extended to the entire circumstances concerning his mistreatment. Further, the Chamber found that Mr Ngaïssona was aware that the Anti-Balaka would inflict great suffering, or serious injury to body or to mental or physical health on Muslim civilians. The Chamber also found that Mr Ngaïssona was aware that the Anti-Balaka would kill Muslim civilians. In the view of the majority, this awareness of mistreating and killing Muslim civilians included within its ambit, cutting off of body parts, regardless of whether such specific incidents of comparable nature would have taken place, prior to the Yamwara Incident, in the context of the crimes committed in the Anti-Balaka's advance to Bangui before 5 December 2013.

Further, the majority's considerations apply regardless of whether Saint Cyr's death resulted from his torture. In the view of the majority, the fact that Judge Kovács differentiates between cutting off of body parts of Saint Cyr when alive and Djido Saleh when dead does not affect the majority's conclusion.
Turning to the special intent requirement that Mr Ngaïssona's assistance was made with the aim of facilitating the commission of the charged crimes, the Chamber recalls its considerations above.

Having regard to the above, the Chamber finds that Mr Ngaïssona provided his financial contributions and support to the Anti-Balaka for the purpose of facilitating the crimes against the Muslim civilian population, including killings of Muslims. In particular, the Chamber notes that Mr Ngaïssona knew and was informed of the hostilities committed by the Anti-Balaka during their advance towards Bangui. Mr Ngaïssona also remained informed of their continued activities until his return to Bangui on 14 January 2014.

Accordingly, the Chamber, by majority, Judge Kovács dissenting in respect of Saint Cyr's torture and murder, finds that the only reasonable conclusion in these circumstances is that Mr Ngaïssona was not only aware that the Anti-Balaka would commit these crimes in the ordinary course of events, but intended for them to commit these crimes forming part of the Yamwara Incident and lent his assistance with the aim of facilitating such crimes.

Having regard to his views above, Judge Kovács considers that Mr Ngaïssona could not have lent his assistance with the aim of facilitating Saint Cyr's torture and murder. At the same time, Judge Kovács considers appropriate to clarify that he agrees with the majority that Mr Ngaïssona lent his assistance with the aim of facilitating the crimes, including the cruel treatment of the six persons and the killing of Muslim civilians generally as outlined in other contexts.

The majority has noted Judge Kovács' views and recalls that in order to satisfy the special intent requirement that Mr Ngaïssona's assistance was made with the aim of facilitating the commission of the charged crimes, it was not necessary to have been aware of the specific details of each of the crimes. In the present instance, in the view of the majority, it was sufficient that Mr Ngaïssona was aware that the Anti-Balaka would target Muslim civilians in the ordinary course of events.

On this basis of the same factual findings recalled above, the Chamber finds that the following specific knowledge requirements are met: (i) that the perpetrator was aware of the victims being either hors de combat, or civilians, medical personnel or religious personnel taking no active part in hostilities, applicable to murder, torture, and cruel treatment as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute; (ii) that the perpetrator was aware of the factual circumstances establishing the nature and gravity of the inhumane act inflicting great suffering, or serious injury to body or to mental or physical health, pursuant to Article 7(1)(k) of the Statute; and (iii) that the perpetrator was aware of the factual circumstances establishing the gravity of conduct, applicable to imprisonment and other forms of severe deprivation of physical liberty, pursuant to Article 7(1)(e) of the Statute.

Turning to the specific intent requirements concerning a number of charged crimes, the Chamber recalls the same findings as above, as well as its finding that Mr Ngaïssona knew that the Anti-Balaka perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis.

On this basis, the Chamber concludes that Mr Ngaïssona intended the Muslim civilian population to be discriminated against on the basis of their religious and ethnic commonalities with the Seleka. Accordingly, the specific intent requirement applicable to the crime against humanity of persecution, pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute, is also met. Conclusion

On the basis of the above, the Chamber therefore finds that, within the context of the captivity of seven individuals at Yamwara by Mr Yekatom's elements on 24 December 2013 and the subsequent transfer and captivity of five of them until their release on or around 27 December 2013, Mr Ngaïssona aided, abetted or otherwise assisted, within the meaning of Article 25(3)(c) of the Statute, the commission of the following crimes: (i)  other inhumane acts as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(k) of the Statute (Count 11); (ii) cruel treatment as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, for six persons (Count 13); (iii) imprisonment and other forms of severe deprivation of physical liberty as a crime against humanity, pursuant to by Article 7(1)(e) of the Statute (Count 14); (v) and (iv) persecution as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute (Count 17).

Further, the Chamber, by majority, Judge Kovács dissenting, finds that Mr Ngaïssona aided, abetted, or otherwise assisted in the commission of crimes of (i) torture as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(f) of the Statute (Count 12); (ii) torture as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute, for Saint Cyr, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute (Count 13); (iii) murder as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Statute (Count 15); and (iv) murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute (Count 16). Judge Kovács would have acquitted Mr Ngaïssona on Counts 12, 13, 15 and 16 in respect of Saint Cyr's torture and killing. Accordingly, Judge Kovács has not considered Saint Cyr's torture and murder for the purposes of assessing Mr Ngaïssona's liability for persecution as a crime against humanity (Count 17), but agrees with the majority on the outcome for this count. As regards forcible transfer and deportation, the Yekatom Defence challenges the causal link between the movement of Mr Yekatom's group along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and 'the displacement and evacuation of the Muslim population'. It argues that the coercive environment was created by 'a convergence of adverse events, all of which was unconnected to Mr Yekatom's conduct'. As part of these adverse events, the Yekatom Defence points to the Muslim population becoming more vulnerable following the resignation of Michel Djotodia and the withdrawal of Seleka forces and the 'increase in the intensity of hostilities between local communities' with retaliation against Muslims being undertaken by local civilians and self-defence groups who had taken up arms prior to the arrival of Mr Yekatom's group along the axis. It further submits that the Muslim population fled their localities towards Mbaïki 'at times upon the advice or instruction of the Seleka', having lost protection from the Seleka forces. It submits that the Muslim population was mistaken in its understanding as to who the perpetrators of crimes were that led to their forced expulsion, and was also mistaken that the arrival of Mr Yekatom's group would result in conflict. The Yekatom Defence submits that the victims' decision 'to leave the localities prior to the commission of crimes or threatening acts due to a fear of violence commonly associated with armed conflict, or a general fear or distrust of the particular authority in question does not allow for the conclusive determination' on the causal link. It argues that the first element of Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute is not met where the individual voluntarily leaves the area before any coercive circumstances arise and where the conduct following their departure was not aimed at creating conditions to hamper their return.

As regards the war crime of displacement, in addition to its submission that the movement of Mr Yekatom's group was legitimate, the Yekatom Defence submits that Mr Yekatom issued no specific order for it to occur, nor has the Prosecution established that Mr Yekatom's instructions had a direct effect on the commission of the crime and he would have been virtually certain that his instructions would result in the commission of the crime in the ordinary course of events.

As regards the requirement that the crime must take place 'by expulsion or other coercive acts', the Chamber recalls that forcible transfer and deportation are 'open-conduct' crimes in that the perpetrator may commit several different acts that may qualify. In assessing this element in respect of both forcible transfer and deportation in the present case, the Chamber recalls that the term 'forcibly' is not restricted to physical force, but may include inter alia threat of force or coercion, such as that caused by fear of violence.

The Chamber has considered the existence of coercive acts concerning three sets of persons that were dislocated within the relevant timeframe: first, those that were dislocated from locations along the PK9-Mbaïki axis as soon as Mr Yekatom's group began advancing on 10 January 2014; second, those that were dislocated as Mr Yekatom's group advanced along the axis, took over villages, and took over checkpoints; and third, those that were dislocated from Mbaïki during the period that Mr Yekatom's group was present there.

As regards the first set, the Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom leaving Yamwara with his elements and advancing towards Mbaïki starting on 10 January 2014 was sufficient, in itself, to create the coercive circumstances due to which the Muslims along the axis dislocated. In the Chamber's view, the subsequent takeover of villages, taking over of checkpoints, and continued armed presence of Mr Yekatom's group along this axis hampered the return of these Muslims to their homes during this time and thereafter.

As regards the second set, the Chamber considers that the dislocation took place as a result of the fear of violence that was set in motion by Mr Yekatom's advance, taking over of a number of villages in the Lobaye prefecture, and taking over of checkpoints during this advance towards Mbaïki. The Chamber recalls that it found that by the time that Mr Yekatom's group arrived Mbaïki on 30 January 2014 and met the relevant authorities there, the removal of the civilian population from Mbaïki was a foregone conclusion.

As regards the third set, the Chamber considers that the dislocation of these Muslims from Mbaïki occurred because of Mr Yekatom's actions mentioned above combined with living in conditions of overcrowding, hunger, and fear of death from the Anti-Balaka.

As regards all three sets mentioned above, the Chamber finds that both forcible transfer and deportation took place as a result of the fear of violence that was set in motion by Mr Yekatom's acts. In the view of the Chamber, the Muslim persons, in all three sets, fleeing along the PK9-Mbaïki axis had no genuine choice in leaving their homes to other parts of the CAR, or to the neighbouring countries. The Chamber recalls in this regard that there must be a genuine lack of choice on the part of the person or persons forcibly transferred, and that the prevailing situation and atmosphere, and other relevant circumstances, including in particular the victims' vulnerability, has to be taken into account when assessing whether the individuals transferred indeed had a genuine choice. In the view of the Chamber, Muslims along the PK9-Mbaïki axis would not have wished to flee, absent the circumstances created by Mr Yekatom's group in that area, including, in particular, their advance towards Mbaïki, their armed presence in the Lobaye prefecture, their takeover of villages, and taking over and setting up of checkpoints in several locations.

The Chamber considers that even if other factors contributed to the fear of violence, the existence of such factors added to the context, but are inapt by and of themselves to impact the Chamber's conclusion above. In the view of the Chamber, the purported loss of the Seleka presence only reaffirms the Chamber's conclusion that these Muslims left as a result of Mr Yekatom's acts and not as a result of a fear of violence commonly associated with armed conflict, as argued by the Yekatom Defence. The Chamber could draw no conclusion on the Yekatom Defence's argument that these Muslims were being protected by the Seleka presence there and dislocated for loss of that protection. In any event, as noted above and below, the Chamber considers that while there may have been other factors that compounded or added to the reasons for displacement, they did not sever the link between Mr Yekatom's acts and the dislocation of Muslims.

Having regard to this, the Chamber finds that the acts of Mr Yekatom and his group amounted to 'coercive acts' pursuant to the first element of deportation or forcible transfer as a crime against humanity.

Before turning to the remaining requirements of forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, the Chamber recalls that Muslims in Mbaïki at the time were composed of three groups: (i) Mbaïki inhabitants; (ii) Muslims who fled from localities along the PK9-Mbaïki axis; and (iii) Muslims who fled from other locations in the Lobaye prefecture.

The Chamber finds that the requirement of forcible transfer is met in respect of the movement of all three categories of Muslim persons mentioned above, who were dislocated to other parts of the CAR, in the context of Mr Yekatom's advance from Bangui to Mbaïki. The Chamber finds that the requirement of deportation is met in respect of the movement of these Muslim persons, who further fled from Mbaïki to Chad and other locations. Thus, the Chamber finds that the first requirement of forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, namely that the perpetrator forcibly transferred or deported, without grounds permitted under international law, one or more persons to another State or location, by expulsion or other coercive acts, is met. paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber now turns to the second requirement of forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, namely that such person or persons were lawfully present in the area from which they were so deported or transferred, is met. The Chamber considered that there is no evidence on the record, nor any arguments advanced by the parties, indicating that these Muslims living along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and those living in Mbaïki at the time were not lawfully present there. This applied also to those Muslim persons who had been dislocated to Mbaïki from localities not along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and who found themselves dislocated from their homes to Mbaïki during this time. The Chamber recalls in this regard also that 'lawful presence' does not mean that the victim must have had legal residence in the area. The protection under this provision extends to individuals, who, for whatever reason, have come to live in a community, including internally displaced persons, who have established temporary homes after being uprooted from their original communities. In light of this, the Chamber finds that, in the present instance, Mr Yekatom's group's advance towards Mbaïki, takeover of villages, taking over of checkpoints, armed presence along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and Mr Yekatom's instruction to his elements to kill all the Muslims in their area is sufficient to constitute an 'order' within the meaning of the first element of displacement as a war crime. It was a combination of these actions that directly led to the commission of this crime. As the Chamber has found that (i) Mr Yekatom was a participant to the agreement with Cœur de Lion and Alkanto pursuant to which Mr Yekatom's group advanced along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and engaged in conduct including the commission of crimes, and (ii) the conduct of Mr Yekatom's group's elements, who executed the material elements of the crimes must be attributed to Mr Yekatom, Cœur de Lion and Alkanto as their own, the Chamber will now assess the involvement of Mr Yekatom in those crimes to determine whether he had control over the crime by virtue of his essential contribution to it and the resulting power to frustrate its commission.

The Yekatom Defence submits that Mr Yekatom did not control the direct perpetrators by subjugating anyone's will or by making an essential contribution to any crime, since (i) his group was far smaller and less organised than argued by the Prosecution, with Mr Yekatom not presenting himself as leader of the group; (ii) members of Mr Yekatom's group joined voluntarily to protect the civilian population and could leave the group at will and without sanction, and Mr Yekatom not being in a position to subjugate the will of his group's members; (iii) Mr Yekatom and Cœur de Lion operated two units with independent functionality across material aspects throughout the charged period; and (iv) committing crimes was antithetical to the purpose of Mr Yekatom's group as understood by him.

The Chamber reiterates its findings that at the time of the advance along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, Mr Yekatom's group numbered at least 1,000 elements, that Mr Yekatom was the undisputed leader of this group, and that Mr Yekatom, with Cœur de Lion and Alkanto, gave instruction to their elements to kill the Muslims in their area. Aiding, abetting or otherwise assisting

In light of the above, the Chamber finds that Mr Ngaïssona, by funding and supporting the Anti-Balaka in 2013 and continuing to do so in 2014, in addition to taking steps to further formalise the Anti-Balaka's structure, aided, abetted or otherwise assisted in the commission of the aforementioned crimes in the context of the Anti-Balaka's advance through and takeover of villages along the PK9-Mbaïki axis. On this basis, the Chamber finds that the following specific knowledge requirements are met: (i) that the perpetrator was aware of the factual circumstances establishing the lawfulness of presence in the area, applicable to forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute; and (ii) that the perpetrator was aware of the victims being either hors de combat, or civilians, medical personnel or religious personnel taking no active part in hostilities, applicable to murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute.

Further, the Chamber recalls its finding that Mr Ngaïssona knew that the Anti-Balaka perceived, and himself perceived, the Muslims in the CAR as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka and that the Anti-Balaka targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR, on this basis.

On this basis, the Chamber concludes that Mr Ngaïssona intended for the Muslim civilian population to be discriminated against on the basis of their religious commonalities with the Seleka. Accordingly, the specific intent requirement applicable to the crime against humanity of persecution, pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute, is also met. Conclusion

On the basis of the above, the Chamber therefore finds that, within the context of the Anti-Balaka's advance through and takeover of villages along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, Mr Ngaïssona aided, abetted or otherwise assisted, within the meaning of Article 25(3)(c) of the Statute, the commission of the following crimes: (i) forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute (Count 24); (ii) displacement as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute (Count 25); (iii) murder as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(a) of the Statute (Count 26); (iv) murder as a war crime, pursuant to Article 8(2)(c)(i) of the Statute (Count 27); and (v) persecution as a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 7(1)(h) of the Statute (Count 28). Recruitment of children under the age of 15 into the Anti-Balaka and their use (Count 29)

Under Count 29, Mr Yekatom is charged with conscription, enlistment and use of children under the age of fifteen years to participate actively in hostilities as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(vii) of the Statute, for the conscription and/or enlistment of children into his group at various locations, including Boeing, Sekia and Pissa along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and in Batalimo along the Pissa-Mongoumba axis, and the assignment of a variety of tasks to them, such as, inter alia, participating in hostilities, including the Bangui Attack, between at least December 2013 and August 2014. Mr Yekatom is alleged to have committed the aforementioned crimes 'jointly with' or 'through' others under Article 25(3)(a) of the Statute.
The Chamber recalls that, considering the evidence before it, the Chamber, by majority, Judge Chung dissenting, was unable to conclude on the age or presence of children in Mr Yekatom's group.

Judge Chung would have concluded on Mr Yekatom's responsibility for the enlistment, conscription and use of children under the age of 15 in his group based on P-2476's account. Judge Chung is of the view that Mr Yekatom, through Cœur de Lion, enlisted P-2476, who was under 15 years at the relevant time, in his group in February 2014 for a period of one week. Judge Chung considers that Mr Yekatom, through his elements, used P-2476 for activities such as guarding the Mbaïki base, buying provisions, and cooking for the elements. Accordingly, Judge Chung would have found that Mr Yekatom committed through others, within the meaning of Article 25(3)(a) of the Statute, the enlistment and use of children under the age of fifteen years to participate actively in hostilities as a war crime pursuant to Article 8(2)(e)(vii) of the Statute (Count 29). Therefore, in accordance with Article 78(1) of the Statute, the Chamber must identify and assess 'such factors as the gravity of the crime and the individual circumstances of the convicted person'. Rule 145(1)(c) of the Rules further mandates the Chamber to consider, inter alia, the extent of the damage caused, in particular the harm caused to the victims and their families, the nature of the unlawful behaviour and the means employed to execute the crime, the degree of participation of the convicted person, the degree of intent, the circumstances of manner, time and location, and the age, education, social and economic condition of the convicted person. Rule 145(2) of the Rules further stipulates that the Chamber shall also take into account any mitigating and aggravating circumstances, as appropriate. Gravity

Second, if the person is convicted of multiple crimes, the Chamber must pronounce 'a joint sentence specifying the total period of imprisonment' pursuant to Article 78(3) of the Statute. This joint sentence 'shall be no less than the highest individual sentence pronounced'.

Third, and finally, Article 78(2) of the Statute requires the Chamber to deduct from the sentence any time that the convicted person spent in detention upon an order of the Court. Factors and circumstances applicable to both accused

paragraph_text_preview: As stated above, the Statute requires the Chamber to determine, for each accused, an individual sentence for each crime before determining a joint sentence. However, certain factors and circumstances relate to the convicted person as such and are thus applicable to several, or even all crimes, and the individual sentences to be determined for an accused. In this respect, the Chamber recalls that in accordance with Article 78(1) of the Statute, it shall take into account, inter alia, the 'individual circumstances of the convicted person'. Similarly, Rule 145(1)(b) of the Rules mandates the Court to 'balance all the relevant factors, including any mitigating and aggravating factors' and to consider the 'circumstances \[...\] of the convicted person'. Subparagraph (c) further mandates it to take into consideration, inter alia, the 'age, education, social and economic condition of the convicted person'.
Moreover, the Chamber notes that in the context of a multi-accused case, there may be factors and circumstances which are of relevance to all the accused.

Accordingly, and in light of the relevant submissions by the participants, the Chamber first addresses factors and circumstances applicable to both accused before turning to those specific to either Mr Yekatom or Mr Ngaïssona. The Chamber clarifies that the conclusions in the following section have been drawn at this juncture merely for the clarity of written reasoning and efficiency. Nonetheless, the Chamber, in accordance with the applicable law set out above, recalls and duly considers them in the context of determining each individual sentence for the crimes of which Mr Yekatom or Mr Ngaïssona, respectively, are found guilty. Aggravating factors Commission of the crimes for any motive involving discrimination

The Chamber notes that Rule 145(2)(b)(v) of the Rules provides that the '\[c\]ommission of the crime for any motive involving discrimination on any of the grounds referred to in article 21, paragraph 3' constitutes an aggravating factor. The latter explicitly lists 'religion or belief', 'political or other opinion', and 'ethnic \[...\] origin'.

To the extent that the Defence argue that the accused did not act with discriminatory intent, the Chamber recalls that the evidence establishes the contrary. First, it recalls its finding that the Anti-Balaka perceived Muslims in the CAR, due to religious and ethnic commonalities, as collectively responsible for, complicit in, or supportive of the violence and abuses committed by the Seleka, and on this basis violently targeted the Muslim civilian population, specifically in the west of the CAR. In that context, the crimes the accused are convicted of were all committed for discriminatory motives, in that the Muslim civilian population was targeted because of its perceived religious and ethnic commonalities with the Seleka.

The Chamber further recalls that it established that Mr Yekatom and Mr Ngaïssona themselves intended the Muslim civilian population to be targeted in relation to the crimes that took place in the context of all charged incidents.

paragraph_text_preview: Finally, in relation to the alleged absence of serving culturally appropriate food, the Chamber recalls that this matter falls exclusively within the purview of the Registrar and is subject to the Presidency's judicial review and has been addressed by them. paragraph_text_preview: Specifically regarding Mr Yekatom's purported efforts along the PK9-Mbaïki axis -- which are at the core of the Yekatom Defence's submissions -- the Chamber notes that they were motivated by ulterior motives, as well as undermined by Mr Yekatom's conduct and that of his elements during this period. Notably, it recalls that it was the presence of the Sangaris and other international actors in Mbaïki at the time which compelled Mr Yekatom to bring his 'peace message' to Mbaïki and prevent attacks of his group against the Muslim civilian population. Moreover, Mr Yekatom delivered his 'peace message' only once he arrived to Mbaïki and attended the meeting at the St Jeanne d'Arc Church, in which the removal of the Muslim population from Mbaïki, which was a foregone conclusion at that point, was decided. The Chamber also notes that Raymond Mongbandi, the mayor of Mbaïki at the time, did not confirm that Mr Yekatom cooperated with the MISCA/MINUSCA to ensure security in Mbaïki. paragraph_text_preview: Efforts to minimise harm The Yekatom Defence submits that Mr Yekatom concretely and genuinely sought to minimise the harm caused to the victims. According to the Yekatom Defence, the evidence establishes that Mr Yekatom (i) personally undertook measures to ensure that the principle of distinction was respected; (ii) issued directives making clear that the Muslim population was not to be targeted; (iii) undertook enquiries and instigated appropriate measures when violations against the Muslim population or their property occurred, or attempted to prevent further violations; (iv) undertook efforts to restore the security apparatus across the Lobaye prefecture and collaborated with local actors to prevent harm to the Muslim population; and (v) implemented measures to alleviate fear amongst the civilian population in relation to the RFACPP's activities, including conducting military training exercises without firing live ammunition or blanks, and taking particular routes so as 'not to unnecessarily frighten the civilian population'.

paragraph_text_preview: Efforts to minimise harm The Yekatom Defence submits that Mr Yekatom concretely and genuinely sought to minimise the harm caused to the victims. According to the Yekatom Defence, the evidence establishes that Mr Yekatom (i) personally undertook measures to ensure that the principle of distinction was respected; (ii) issued directives making clear that the Muslim population was not to be targeted; (iii) undertook enquiries and instigated appropriate measures when violations against the Muslim population or their property occurred, or attempted to prevent further violations; (iv) undertook efforts to restore the security apparatus across the Lobaye prefecture and collaborated with local actors to prevent harm to the Muslim population; and (v) implemented measures to alleviate fear amongst the civilian population in relation to the RFACPP's activities, including conducting military training exercises without firing live ammunition or blanks, and taking particular routes so as 'not to unnecessarily frighten the civilian population'.

With respect to points (i) and (ii), the Chamber recalls that the evidence establishes the opposite. Concretely, the Chamber found that Mr Yekatom expressly instructed the elements under his command to attack Muslim civilians, in the context of events relating to crimes as charged in this case and himself did not draw an appropriate distinction between Seleka members and Muslim civilians when giving instructions to his elements.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that in support of its point (iii), the Yekatom Defence presents two arguments. It refers, on the one hand, to Mr Yekatom's intervention during a disagreement between elements from Stéphane Chrisostome Dawili's group and a former FACA captain regarding the theft of his goats on 24 April 2014 at PK9. In this regard, the Chamber recalls that Mr Yekatom's intervention during this incident consisted of shooting at the involved elements, leading to the death of two of them and injuring the other, who was hospitalised for two to three weeks. At the outset, the Chamber recalls that the facts underlying the crimes of which Mr Yekatom is convicted overlap to a certain degree. Accordingly, they need to be taken into consideration for more than one crime. The Chamber clarifies that this does not constitute 'double-counting'. In this respect, it notes the Appeals Chamber's jurisprudence that '\[t\]he calculation of an individual sentence necessarily entails an assessment of all the circumstances relevant to a particular crime', including those circumstances that may be relevant to the determination of more than one individual sentence. Indeed, 'if the circumstances relevant to more than one individual sentence were to be excluded from the calculation of any of those individual sentences, the true culpability of a convicted person for a particular crime would be unclear'. However, as stated above, any relevant factual overlap is accounted for in the context of determining a joint sentence, to ensure reflecting the proper culpability of an accused. With regard to the discriminatory dimension of all crimes, the Chamber additionally recalls its findings above.

In the present section, the Chamber addresses crime-specific considerations in relation to each of the 20 crimes of which Mr Yekatom is convicted. The analysis is grouped by the following incidents, which feature the same or at least connected underlying facts: (a) the crimes committed in the context of the attack on Bangui, including Boeing and Cattin -- the Bangui Attack (Counts 1 to 6 and 8); (b) the crimes committed in the context of the events at Yamwara on and around 24 December 2013 -- the Yamwara Incident (Counts 11 to 17); and (c) the crimes committed in the context of the Anti-Balaka's advance through and takeover of villages along the PK9-Mbaïki axis (Counts 24 to 28). paragraph_text_preview: Attack against the civilian population as such as a war crime (Count 1)The war crime of attack against the civilian population as such violates the principle of distinction, which is at the core of international humanitarian law. The purpose of this principle, and of the incrimination of intentional attacks on civilians in the Statute, is to protect lives and to avoid the suffering of individuals not taking a direct part in hostilities during an armed conflict.

footnote_content: *See* paragraph 3788 above. *See also* [*Ongwen* Sentencing Judgment](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/vj1y8k/), ICC-02/04-01/15-1819-Red, para. 149; [*Ntaganda* Sentencing Appeals Judgment](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/94hzsf/), ICC-01/04-02/06-2667-Red, para. 101; [*Ntaganda* Sentencing Judgment](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/yyw2ef/), ICC-01/04-02/06-2442, para. 53.
paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that the war crime of attacking the civilian population as such is a conduct crime which, for its commission, does not require a result in terms of infliction of an actual harm or death on civilians. The Chamber considers that generally, conduct crimes are in abstracto less serious than result crimes which do require an infliction of harm on the victim. Nonetheless, considering the protected interests at stake, the Chamber deems this crime to be of high gravity in abstracto.

The Chamber recalls, however, that it may consider harm arising as a consequence of a crime in the context of sentencing. In the present case, as set out in detail in the sections below, extensive harm was inflicted on the civilian population as a result of the attack on Boeing and Cattin. In the view of the Chamber, this heightens the gravity in concreto of Count 1. The Chamber recognises that these consequences constitute the relevant facts underlying the other crimes Mr Yekatom is convicted of in the context of the Bangui Attack. While all relevant circumstances must be considered in the context of the individual sentence under this count, these factual overlaps are duly taken into account in the determination of the joint sentence.

On the basis of the concrete circumstances, the Chamber considers the gravity of the crime to be high in concreto. In addition to the considerations in relation to the extent of the harm caused, the Chamber considers the nature of the unlawful behaviour to be of particular relevance to the assessment of the gravity of the crime. It recalls the nature of the targets comprising the attack -- a market, a mosque and unarmed civilians --, and that these were not legitimate military targets. Specifically, upon Mr Yekatom's instructions, Mr Yekatom's group attacked the Boeing Market where the Muslim traders were shot at. Mr Yekatom's group also attacked the main mosque serving both the communities of Boeing and Cattin, as well as an unarmed man in Cattin. Further, the Chamber notes that while it is unclear to what extent Mr Yekatom's group was armed during the attack, what is clear is that they possessed and used some firearms, as well as a rocket. It also recalls that in the Boeing Market specifically, Mr Yekatom's elements shot in all directions.

paragraph_text_preview: \[a\]fter the death of my husband, I know that once he's dead, everything is over. I cannot stop thinking about him, reminiscing about our life, his generosity, especially towards my family, because I came from a poor family and we were lucky to have him as part of our family. Everything we asked him to do, he would do. So today, even when I am with the others, I might forget for a while, but if I'm alone, I think about him. When I lack something, I think about what he would do if he had been present, and so this drives me into a situation where I become practically sick. The Chamber recalls that while P-2682 moved to PK5 a few days before the events at the Boeing Market, her continued stay in PK5 is inevitably linked to the death of her husband and the threats to her life that she received from an unidentified speaker speaking from Hassan's phone. During her stay in PK5, she mourned her husband in an environment with uninhabitable living conditions, which aggravated her loss. As a result of the conditions in PK5, she fled to Chad, fearing for her safety. The Chamber recalls that in her testimony, P-2682 described how this displacement affected her, notably that it made her 'scared' and sad and that in Chad she 'was really suffering' because of the death of her husband.

paragraph_text_preview: Forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity and displacement as a war crime (Counts 4 and 5)The prohibition of forcible transfer of population and deportation is intended to protect the right of individuals to remain in their homes and communities and not to be deprived of their property by being forcibly displaced to another location. In this respect, it guards against the wholesale destruction of communities. It constitutes a serious crime due to the fact that people are illegally moved against their will or without having a genuine choice in the matter, from the area in which they are lawfully present, leading to their exclusion from and potential destruction of the economic and social life of their communities. Accordingly, the Chamber deems this crime to be of high gravity in abstracto.

paragraph_text_preview: Forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity and displacement as a war crime (Counts 4 and 5)The prohibition of forcible transfer of population and deportation is intended to protect the right of individuals to remain in their homes and communities and not to be deprived of their property by being forcibly displaced to another location. In this respect, it guards against the wholesale destruction of communities. It constitutes a serious crime due to the fact that people are illegally moved against their will or without having a genuine choice in the matter, from the area in which they are lawfully present, leading to their exclusion from and potential destruction of the economic and social life of their communities. Accordingly, the Chamber deems this crime to be of high gravity in abstracto.

Ordering the displacement of a civilian population as a war crime is also intended to protect the right of individuals to remain in their homes and communities and not to be displaced without justification during a non-international armed conflict. However, noting that ordering displacement does not require for displacement as such to actually occur, the Chamber considers the crime under Article 8(2)(e)(viii) of the Statute to be in abstracto less serious compared to forcible transfer of population or deportation under Article 7(1)(d) of the Statute, which requires the actual infliction of harm on the victims. Accordingly, the Chamber deems this crime to be of substantial gravity in abstracto.
Turning to the assessment of the facts in concreto, the Chamber considers the gravity of Counts 4 and 5 to be high.

At the outset, the Chamber highlights the significant number of persons affected by the crimes underlying Counts 4 and 5. It recalls that, from 5 December 2013 onwards, the majority of Muslims of Boeing and Cattin fled to PK5, while some others fled to other parts of the CAR, in the context of the attack by Mr Yekatom's group on Boeing and Cattin. The Chamber further highlights that some Muslims endured forced displacement multiple times. It recalls that with the influx of Muslims fleeing the Bangui Attack, PK5 became overcrowded, uninhabitable, and unsafe. As a result, some Muslims fled to neighbouring countries, fearing for their safety.

In this regard, the Chamber recalls the scale of the movement of Muslims outside of the CAR and emphasises that they had to leave their homes and were removed from their known surroundings. The Chamber notably received evidence from Anti-Balaka witnesses that Muslims were sent to Chad, Cameroon and Congo with the assistance of the international and MISCA forces.

In relation to the war crime of displacement specifically, the Chamber recalls that this crime does not require for displacement as such to actually occur. Considering this, the Chamber finds the fact that Muslim inhabitants were effectively displaced as a direct consequence of the actions of Mr Yekatom's group to heighten the gravity of the crime under Count 5. The Chamber considers that this displacement was objectively foreseeable to Mr Yekatom, given that he knew that the launching of his attack and the instructions to his elements would cause the Muslims from Boeing and Cattin to flee.

It notes that they endured the loss of their family members, loss of their home, loss of their belongings, and sense of material and non-material unsafety for prolonged periods. Notably, Muslims who fled to PK5 continued to feel threatened by the Anti-Balaka's presence in and around PK5 and Bangui. This climate of fear contributed to the lack of freedom of movement within and outside of PK5. It made it almost impossible to leave PK5 safely. This is illustrated by P-2472 who explained that after the Bangui Attack, there were 'continuous attacks by the Anti-Balaka against the Muslim population in \[Bangui\] for approximately three months. The Muslims who were living in PK5 were encircled and could not go out. We spent many months unable to sleep and being in constant fear of being attacked'.

Compounding this was the fact that at PK5 the living conditions were difficult and dire -- with a lack of food, medicines, basic sanitary conditions and rest, making the environment practically uninhabitable, in addition to being overcrowded and unsafe. Catherine Samba-Panza explained that the enclaves such as the one at PK5, were 'really not fit for \[...\] human life'.

Victims notably experienced physical and emotional suffering, considering in particular the difficult conditions at the time of their displacement or at the locations they were displaced to, particularly in PK5 which the Chamber found was practically uninhabitable. paragraph_text_preview: To the contrary, the CLRV2 submit, inter alia, that (i) the majority of victims are still unable, more than 10 years later, to return; (ii) returning to one's country of origin without being able to effectively return to one's own home with the same means as before cannot reasonably reduce the gravity of the crimes; and (iii) the people who returned experienced major difficulties in re-establishing themselves and finding employment, notably as their homes were occupied during their absence and/or looted or destroyed, and they lost everything when they left.

The Chamber notes that the majority of the evidence cited by the Yekatom Defence relates to the return of peace to Mbaïki or the Lobaye prefecture, rather than the return of previously displaced Muslim civilians from Boeing or Cattin. While some Muslim inhabitants who fled in the context of the attack by Mr Yekatom's group on Boeing and Cattin may have eventually returned to their own homes after the period relevant to the charges, it is also clear to the Chamber that many others could not and some were not even able to return to the CAR.

In this regard, the Chamber does not consider that the harm deriving from displacement necessarily ended by virtue of either (i) an eventual return to the CAR from abroad; or (ii) for those displaced within the CAR, settling elsewhere. The Chamber recalls that victims had to leave their houses and for some, their belongings behind, and thus emphasises that their return to the CAR or their place of origin does not mean that they were able to reach the same standards of living or live in the same conditions as before, and does not reduce the gravity of the crimes as such.

Turning to the arguments as to the necessity of a 'cut-off point', the Chamber recalls that it may consider any consequences arising from the crimes in the context of sentencing, as long as they were objectively foreseeable to the accused. In this regard, the Chamber considers that the harm described above, including beyond the initial displacement of victims, is inherent to the nature of the crimes, derives from, and is sufficiently linked to them. It thus considers of limited relevance to its present assessment the fact that other factors may have played a role in some victims not returning to their places of origin following the events.

paragraph_text_preview: Persecution as a crime against humanity (Count 8)In relation to the crime against humanity of persecution, it is noted that persecution is essentially a crime against equality of all persons regardless of their political, racial, national, ethnic, cultural, religious or gender affiliation or identity, and regardless of any other ground of discrimination universally recognised as impermissible under international law. The blameworthiness of the crime lies in the deprivation of fundamental rights underlying it, and additionally -- and crucially -- in the discrimination by the perpetrator in selecting the target(s). Therefore, the Chamber considers that persecution is a particularly serious crime in abstracto.

Turning to the assessment of the facts in concreto, the Chamber considers the gravity of Count 8 to be high. In this regard, the Chamber highlights that Mr Yekatom's elements targeted a substantial number of Muslim persons on religious grounds, and violated numerous fundamental rights, namely, the right to liberty and security of person, right to liberty of movement, right against arbitrary or unlawful interference with their family, and home, right to property, right to freedom of religion, right not to be denied the right to practice their own religion in community with other members of their group, and in the case of four Muslim men, going as far as denying them their right to life. Mr Yekatom specifically meant for the Muslim civilian population in Boeing and Cattin to be targeted because of their religious and ethnic commonalities with the Seleka.

However, the Chamber considers that multiple other circumstances significantly heighten Mr Yekatom's degree of participation and show that he acted with a high degree of intent. First, the Chamber recalls that at Yamwara, Mr Yekatom was considered the chief, had unlimited control over his elements' activities, and the elements involved in the Yamwara Incident reported to him. As stated above, and specifically with regard to the Yamwara Incident, the Chamber finds that from the moment of the capture of the seven persons and at least until their respective death or release, Mr Yekatom retained full control over the actions of his elements and of their will. Second, Mr Yekatom was not only aware that his elements committed crimes against the seven persons, but was present at Yamwara during the evening of 24 December 2013; and interacted with the Five Captives, Saint Cyr's father and P-1839. Third, he not only failed to discipline or sanction his elements' criminal behaviour, but even approved of it. His approval, participation in, and power over the execution of the crimes can further be deduced from his use of the phrase 'eforolo tonga na papai' after the events, meaning that they 'peeled the papaya', a term equally used by his elements at Yamwara on multiple occasions during this incident. In light of his supreme role at Yamwara, the Chamber considers that Mr Yekatom's aforementioned behaviour endorsed his elements' criminal conduct and encouraged them to continue in the commission of crimes.

The Chamber is mindful that certain factual findings on Mr Yekatom's acts only pertain to specific crimes committed at Yamwara. Where this is the case, they are discussed in the context of the relevant crimes below. Nonetheless, these differences do not lead to different conclusions regarding Mr Yekatom's degree of participation and intent for the individual crimes committed. On the contrary, taking all of the above as well as the below crime-specific considerations into account, the Chamber considers Mr Yekatom's degree of participation to be significant and his intent high for each of the crimes underlying Counts 11 to 17.

Another feature common to all crimes committed at Yamwara is their commission for motives involving discrimination. In this regard, the Chamber recalls that the seven persons were targeted by Mr Yekatom's group on the basis that they were perceived to be Muslims, as well as Mr Yekatom's intent in that regard. Alkanto, who led the checkpoint at which the seven persons were apprehended, and over whom Mr Yekatom had undisputed authority, identified the female captives as being related to Michel Djotodia and Mamour as well as being Muslims, and ordered their transfer to Yamwara. This identification marked the beginning of various death threats expressed by his group against all seven persons. Mr Yekatom's and his elements' discriminatory approach is further demonstrated by virtue of their interrogating of the six persons, as well as P-1654, about their ethnicity and demanding the male captives to speak in the dialect associated therewith. As indicated above, the Chamber considers this circumstance to be an aggravating factor within the meaning of Rule 145(2)(b)(v) of the Rules for the crimes underlying Counts 11 to 17.

Lastly, the Chamber considers that the following circumstances should be taken into account in assessing Counts 11 to 17, as they concern the nature of the unlawful behaviour and the means employed, as well as the impact of the crimes.

First, the Chamber finds that the environment set up by the Anti-Balaka at Yamwara was deliberately vicious and chosen to increase the suffering of the seven persons. Notably, it recalls that Yamwara was a base with approximately 1,000 Anti-Balaka elements present and that the captives were brought there only a few weeks after the Bangui Attack, during which Mr Yekatom's elements had killed Muslim civilians. The Chamber also considers it relevant that some of Mr Yekatom's elements, who kept the seven persons captive, were armed and continuously demonstrated their willingness to use their weapons against the captives. For instance, when the three women were being kept inside Cœur de Lion's house, an element at the main entrance had a weapon pointed in their direction. Further, Mr Yekatom's elements holding the women captive inside the second house were also armed, with at least a machete and a firearm. P-1811 recalled that an element grazed the wall with a machete, surprising P-0967 by raising it towards her and calling her a 'chicken'.

The Chamber also considers it relevant that some of Mr Yekatom's elements, who kept the seven persons captive, were armed and continuously demonstrated their willingness to use their weapons against the captives. For instance, when the three women were being kept inside Cœur de Lion's house, an element at the main entrance had a weapon pointed in their direction. Further, Mr Yekatom's elements holding the women captive inside the second house were also armed, with at least a machete and a firearm. P-1811 recalled that an element grazed the wall with a machete, surprising P-0967 by raising it towards her and calling her a 'chicken'.

Furthermore, the captives were continuously threatened to be killed by Mr Yekatom's elements and treated as 'traitors'. From the moment they were apprehended at the checkpoint until being brought to the location behind the airport, or in Saint Cyr's case until his death, they were confronted with graphic death threats such as to be 'skinned like a papaya'. In particular, at the checkpoint, they were told that 'today we are going to sow some seeds', which P-1811 understood to mean that 'since the soil is wet, it would open and they would bury them there'. P-0967 explained that when hearing such language '\[i\]t was quite clear to \[them\] that it meant that \[they\] would be buried that day'.

The Chamber considers that all of these harms were objectively foreseeable to Mr Yekatom. In this respect, it recalls that Mr Yekatom, fully aware of the Anti-Balaka's objectives and policy, set up a base at Yamwara together with his group, as well as checkpoints along its perimeter to monitor the passage of vehicles and people. He was aware that FACA members of his group, who also trained civilian elements, bore strong anti-Muslim sentiments and feelings of vengeance against the Seleka and that his elements would not distinguish between Seleka and Muslim civilians during combat. Moreover, the resulting harms caused to the surviving captives of the Yamwara Incident by virtue of their mistreatment, as well as the impact on Saint Cyr's family and friends as a result of his torture and murder, were inherent to the nature of the crimes committed during the Yamwara Incident. ######

Turning to the assessment of the facts in concreto, the Chamber considers the gravity of Count 14 to be high. It recalls its findings above regarding the circumstances of and the means employed to execute all crimes committed at Yamwara, in particular the enormous brutality exercised. Notably, the female captives were put in a situation where they had no choice but to listen and guess about his fate, the men witnessed his mistreatment first-hand.

paragraph_text_preview: Finally, the Chamber is not persuaded by the Yekatom Defence's argument that Count 14 is of reduced gravity as the 'duration of the alleged imprisonment of the Lapo family members amounted to a single evening'. First, this is not supported by the evidence for all captives: amongst the six persons, five were held from 24 until on or about 27 December 2013, and only P-1716's detention lasted one night. As regards Saint Cyr, the Chamber notes that his captivity was cut short by no other reason than his murder by Mr Yekatom's elements. Second, the Chamber is, in any event, of the view that the duration of the six persons' captivity cannot be considered in isolation. Rather, it must be considered jointly with the other circumstances surrounding the events, as set out above and below.

Accordingly, it addresses these counts jointly in this section.

The crime of other inhumane acts pursuant to Article 7(1)(k) of the Statute is particularly serious as it is directed against a person and requires the perpetrator to intentionally inflict great suffering, or serious injury to body or to mental or physical health. Irrespective of the crime's residual nature, 'inhumane acts' are considered to be 'serious violations of international customary law and the basic rights pertaining to human beings, drawn from the norms of international human rights law, which are of a similar nature and gravity to the acts referred to in \[A\]rticle 7(1) of the Statute'.

The right not to be subjected to torture is a non-derogable right recognised in customary and conventional international law and as a norm of ius cogens. The gravity of this crime, both as a war crime and as a crime against humanity, must therefore be considered very high in abstracto.

Turning to the assessment of the facts in concreto, the Chamber considers the gravity of the crimes underlying Counts 12 and 13 (torture of Saint Cyr) as particularly high. In this respect, the Chamber highlights the circumstances of and the means employed to execute these crimes. While the crimes only concern one individual, Saint Cyr, the manner in which he was mistreated was particularly depraved and violent. Notably, he was unarmed and beaten by multiple perpetrators for a considerable amount of time. The assailants knocked Saint Cyr to the ground, used a stick to force him down on his knees and specifically beat his legs, breaking them. His hands and feet were tied together in the back in the 'arbatacher'-style and despite his inability to defend himself, the assailants continued assaulting him. Eventually an element in Mr Yekatom's group went as far as to cut off his toes, fingers and an ear.

Turning to the assessment of the facts in concreto, the Chamber considers the gravity of Count 17 to be high. In this regard, the Chamber highlights that Mr Yekatom's elements targeted a total of seven individuals at Yamwara on religious grounds, and violated numerous fundamental rights of the captives, namely, the right to liberty and security of person, right against arbitrary arrest and detention and related procedural guarantees, right not to be subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and right of all persons deprived of their liberty to be treated with humanity and with respect for their inherent dignity and, in Saint Cyr's case, going as far as denying him his right to life. Mr Yekatom intended his elements to persecute the seven persons on the basis that they were perceived to be Muslims.

The Chamber considers that multiple circumstances significantly heighten Mr Yekatom's degree of participation and show that he acted with a high degree of intent. First, Mr Yekatom was the undisputed leader of the Anti-Balaka group along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, comprising at least 1,000 elements, and he had full control over his elements during the advance along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and subsequent events in Mbaïki. Second, at the time of the advance along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, an agreement existed between Mr Yekatom, Cœur de Lion and Alkanto to establish control over the area as well as to remove all Muslims therefrom, including by killing them. Third, Mr Yekatom, along with Cœur de Lion and Alkanto, gave instructions to elements of the group to kill all the Muslims in the area. Fourth, Mr Yekatom instructed his elements to advance along the axis, and during this advance he and the elements under his command took over villages, occupied checkpoints and set up bases, including in Mbaïki. Fifth, Mr Yekatom took part in the meeting at the St Jeanne d'Arc Church in Mbaïki, at which the removal of the Muslim civilian population from Mbaïki -- which was a foregone conclusion at that point -- was decided. Sixth, Mr Yekatom knew that elements of his group committed acts of violence in Mbaïki. Efforts and measures to prevent these acts were taken only after the removal of the Muslim civilian population from Mbaïki had been decided and/or carried out.

Forcible transfer and deportation as a crime against humanity and displacement as a war crime (Counts 24 and 25)The Chamber refers to its considerations above as to the gravity in abstracto of the crimes of forcible transfer and deportation, and of displacement.

Turning to the assessment of the facts in concreto, the Chamber considers the gravity of Counts 24 and 25 to be high. In this respect, the Chamber recalls that, due to and in fear of the advance of Mr Yekatom's group along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, a significant proportion of the Muslim civilian population fled their towns and villages along the axis, with at least 1,000 Muslim civilians fleeing from locations along the PK9-Mbaïki axis and in the Lobaye prefecture to Mbaïki. At least 3,000 Muslim civilians were later removed from Mbaïki, with very few Muslim civilians remaining in the town as a result. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the number of persons affected by the crimes underlying Counts 24 and 25 was significant and considers particularly noteworthy that they constituted a large part of the Muslim civilian population present along the PK9-Mbaïki axis.

In relation to the war crime of displacement specifically, the Chamber recalls that this crime does not require for displacement as such to actually occur. Considering this, the Chamber finds the fact that Muslim inhabitants were effectively displaced as a direct consequence of the actions of Mr Yekatom's group to heighten the gravity of the crime under Count 25. The Chamber considers that this displacement was objectively foreseeable to Mr Yekatom, recalling that, inter alia, the instructions of Mr Yekatom, Cœur de Lion and Alkanto and consequent actions of the elements in Mr Yekatom's group would necessarily result in Muslim civilians seeking shelter elsewhere and leaving their homes, and that Mr Yekatom intended for Muslim civilians to be dislocated.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber notes that the majority of the evidence cited by the Yekatom Defence relates to the return of peace to Mbaïki or the Lobaye prefecture, rather than the return of previously dislocated Muslim civilians along the PK9-Mbaïki axis. Regarding the latter, while some Muslim civilians may have eventually returned to the villages and towns along the PK9-Mbaïki axis after the period relevant to the charges, the evidence on the record in this respect is scarce, mostly refers to an eventual return several years after the initial displacement, and, in any event, does not establish that all, or even a majority, were able to return to their villages or towns, or even to the CAR.

In this regard, the Chamber does not consider that the harm deriving from displacement necessarily ended by virtue of either (i) an eventual return to the CAR from abroad; or (ii) for those displaced within the CAR, settling elsewhere. The Chamber recalls that victims had to leave their houses and their belongings behind, and thus emphasises that their return to the CAR or their place of origin does not mean that they were able to reach the same standards of living or live in the same conditions as before, and does not reduce the gravity of the crimes as such.

Turning to the arguments as to the necessity of a 'cut-off point', the Chamber recalls that it may consider any consequences arising from the crimes in the context of sentencing, as long as they were objectively foreseeable to the accused. In this regard, the Chamber considers that the harm described above, including beyond the initial displacement of victims, is inherent to the nature of the crimes, derives from, and is sufficiently linked to them. It thus considers of limited relevance to its present assessment the fact that other factors may have played a role in some victims not returning to their places of origin following the events.

Further considering the nature of Mr Yekatom's role in the context of his group's advance along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, as well as his essential contributions and participation in an agreement that entailed removing all Muslims from the area, the Chamber is satisfied that the harm and consequences described above were objectively foreseeable to Mr Yekatom. In this context, regarding the Yekatom Defence's submission that Mr Yekatom took concrete steps to assist victims, the Chamber refers to its above findings.

paragraph_text_preview: Turning to the assessment of the facts in concreto, the Chamber considers the gravity of Counts 26 and 27 to be particularly high. The Chamber finds the circumstances of and the means employed to execute Saleh's murder particularly cruel and brutal, which significantly heightens the crimes' gravity. It recalls that a group of individuals -- which included at least three elements of Mr Yekatom's group --, attacked Saleh's house while he and his family were inside, pursued Saleh and threw stones at him as he tried to flee, and killed him near the gendarmerie of Mbaïki. Further, the vicious cutting off of parts of Saleh's body shortly after his death, in combination with the cruel and humiliating behaviour and utterances displayed and spoken concurrently, were particularly heinous and demonstrate an utter disregard for physical integrity and human dignity. Notably, the Chamber recalls that upon his killing, the attackers dragged Saleh's body along the ground, partly undressed him, cut off his genitals, one of his ears and his neck, partly severing his head, and beat his body. They also put their feet on different parts of Saleh's body and pretended to further harm him with their weapons. While the scene took place, the attackers insulted and made fun of Saleh, discussed eating his flesh and burning his body, and boasted about their actions. The mistreatment of Saleh's body was filmed and some individuals repeatedly asked that pictures of the body and of themselves be taken.
