The Chamber considers the mistreatment of Saleh's body to be directly linked to the crimes of murder and inherent to their nature, particularly noting the context in which they occurred, as well as objectively foreseeable to Mr Yekatom. It recalls that Mr Yekatom, Cœur de Lion and Alkanto instructed the elements to kill all the Muslims in the area, that elements under Mr Yekatom's command threatened and harassed Muslim civilians in Mbaïki -- which Mr Yekatom was aware of --, and further threatened Saleh as one of the very few remaining Muslims in town, and that Saleh was targeted and his body mistreated because he was a Muslim. It also recalls that Mr Yekatom's elements bore strong anti-Muslim sentiment and feelings of vengeance against the Seleka, which Mr Yekatom was aware of. In the circumstances, the Chamber considers that it was foreseeable for Mr Yekatom that in some instances his elements' attacks on Muslims would escalate and lead to such kind of mistreatment.

Turning to the assessment of the facts in concreto, the Chamber considers the gravity of Count 28 to be high. In this regard, the Chamber highlights that Mr Yekatom's elements targeted a substantial number of Muslim civilians on religious grounds, and violated numerous fundamental rights, namely, regarding displaced Muslims, the right to liberty and security of person, right to liberty of movement, right against arbitrary or unlawful interference with their family and home, and right to property, and, in Saleh's case, denying him his right to life. Mr Yekatom specifically meant for the Muslim civilian population along the PK9-Mbaïki axis to be targeted because of its religious commonalities with the Seleka.

Determination of joint sentence

Having determined the individual sentences for each crime of which Mr Yekatom is convicted, the Chamber now turns to its determination of the joint sentence for all crimes, which must reflect Mr Yekatom's total culpability. According to Article 78(3) of the Statute, the total term of imprisonment shall be no less than the highest individual sentence pronounced. In Mr Yekatom's case, the minimum joint sentence is thus 14 years. The maximum sentence shall not exceed 30 years of imprisonment or a sentence of life imprisonment in conformity with Article 77(1)(b) of the Statute.

In determining the joint sentence, the Chamber is called to pronounce a sentence in line with the Court's primary purposes of punishment -- retribution and deterrence. It is conscious that the sentence imposed on the accused should also be suitable to give effect to the strong condemnation of the crimes at stake in this case by the international community.

In this context, the Chamber also acknowledges the victims' desire for justice, to be re-empowered and for an adequate punishment to be imposed upon both accused. It also accepts the CLRV2's submission that deterrence, both of the accused and others, plays a crucial role in this case 'in light of the still prevailing situation of relative conflict, insecurity and impunity of the CAR'. Conversely, the Chamber finds it entirely inappropriate to consider the fact that previous proceedings before the Court in the 'CAR Situation' ended with acquittal and non-confirmation of charges, noting that neither Mr Yekatom nor Mr Ngaïssona had any involvement in these cases.

paragraph_text_preview: First, the Chamber notes that a factual overlap exists between crimes which concurrently constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity and are thus only distinguished by their different contextual elements. Notably, this concerns the crimes of murder (Counts 2 and 3, 15 and 16, as well as 26 and 27, respectively) and, to a certain extent, torture (Counts 12 and 13).

Second, there is a partial overlap in the conduct underlying the crimes respectively committed within the context of (i) the Bangui Attack; (ii) the Yamwara Incident; and (iii) the Anti-Balaka's advance through and takeover of villages along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, as well as in the respective harm and consequences deriving from these crimes.

paragraph_text_preview: Specifically, with respect to the crimes committed within the context of the Bangui Attack, the Chamber notes that the conduct underlying Counts 1 to 6 and 8 broadly overlaps. It also observes that the harm and consequences deriving from the crime of forcible transfer and deportation, and the crime of displacement (Counts 4 and 5) overlap. Additionally, it observes that the crime of directing an attack against the civilian population as such (Count 1) was committed by way of conduct, and resulted in harm, which in turn constituted facts underlying separate crimes committed in the context of this attack. With respect to the crime of persecution (Count 8), the Chamber observes an overlap insofar as the crime was committed through acts constituting also the crimes under Counts 1 to 6. Furthermore, the discriminatory dimension underlying the crime of persecution was also considered as an aggravating factor in relation to Counts 1 to 6.

footnote_content: *See also* [Yekatom Defence Sentencing Brief](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/x6fp6zvp/), ICC-01/14-01/18-2746-Red, para. 13 ii).
paragraph_text_preview: With respect to the crimes committed during the Yamwara Incident, the Chamber notes that the conduct underlying Counts 11 to 17 partly overlaps. It also observes the factual overlaps between the consequences, in particular the harm on the surviving captives, of the crimes of imprisonment and other forms of severe deprivation of physical liberty (Count 14), other inhumane acts (Count 11) and cruel treatment (Count 13), as well as between the consequences of the crimes of torture (Counts 12 and 13) and murder (Counts 15 and 16), in particular with regard to the emotional and psychological harm on Saint Cyr's family and friends. In addition, it notes that the crime of persecution (Count 17) was committed through acts also constituting the crimes under Counts 11 to 16 and that the discriminatory dimension underlying the crime of persecution was further considered as an aggravating factor in relation to Counts 11 to 16, with the exception of the war crime of torture under Count 13.

footnote_content: *See also* [Yekatom Defence Sentencing Brief](https://www.legal-tools.org/doc/x6fp6zvp/), ICC-01/14-01/18-2746-Red, para. 13 iii).
paragraph_text_preview: With respect to the crimes committed in the context of the Anti-Balaka's advance along the PK9-Mbaïki axis, the Chamber notes that the conduct underlying Counts 24 to 28 partly overlaps. Moreover, it observes the overlap between the harm and consequences deriving from the crime of forcible transfer and deportation, and the crime of displacement (Counts 24 and 25). Additionally, it recalls that the crime of persecution (Count 28) was committed through acts also constituting the crimes under Counts 24 to 27 and that the discriminatory dimension has also been considered an aggravating factor in relation to Counts 24 to 27.

Having duly considered the above, the Chamber does not consider the timeframe or these overlaps to have a significant bearing on its determination of Mr Yekatom's joint sentence. In this respect, it notes that Mr Yekatom is convicted of 20 crimes, which were committed in the context of three separate incidents, spanning over different geographical areas. Furthermore, Mr Yekatom committed these crimes in the context of an organised armed group and as part of a wider policy, in which he voluntarily participated. Moreover, Mr Yekatom was fully aware of all of these crimes and played a key role in their commission.

Most importantly, the Chamber notes that -- with the exception of the abovementioned overlaps -- the crimes committed by Mr Yekatom were wholly distinct and violated a wide array of fundamental protected interests. Notably, these protected interests included the right to life; the right not to be subjected to torture, and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; the right to liberty and security of person; the right to liberty of movement; the right to freedom of religion and to not be denied the right to practice their own religion in community with other members of their group; the right to property; the right against arbitrary arrest and detention and related procedural guarantees; the right against arbitrary or unlawful interference with their family and home; and the right of all persons deprived of their liberty to be treated with humanity and respect for their inherent dignity.

For the same reasons, the Chamber also considers that a joint sentence corresponding to the highest individual sentence pronounced is incapable of reflecting Mr Yekatom's total culpability. Accordingly, the Chamber finds it appropriate to set Mr Yekatom's joint sentence slightly higher than 14 years.

In determining his joint sentence, the Chamber further considered the Yekatom Defence's submissions regarding Mr Yekatom's rehabilitation and reintegration prospects. Specifically, the Yekatom Defence submits that the Chamber must consider whether any sentence imposed against Mr Yekatom would adequately allow for his reintegration and contribute to the maintenance of peace and reconciliation in the CAR. In its submission, it argues that Mr Yekatom 'qualifies on all counts to be reintegrated into society', taking into account his individual and mitigating circumstances, including the fact that he is now 50 years old and that his military and political career 'are behind him'.

The Chamber acknowledges that reintegration and rehabilitation may constitute relevant considerations in determining an appropriate sentence. However, it also recalls the Court's consistent jurisprudence that it should not be given undue weight. Noting the specifics of Mr Yekatom's case and the conclusions drawn above, the Chamber does not consider his prospects of reintegration and rehabilitation to be exceptional. Accordingly, it affords this factor only limited weight in determining the appropriate joint sentence.
In light of the above considerations, the Chamber sentences Mr Yekatom to a joint sentence of 15 years.
This sentence is pronounced unanimously. While Judge Chung would have convicted Mr Yekatom of Count 29, he does not consider his dissent in this respect to have any impact on the joint sentence.

The Chamber is of the view that this term is proportionate to Mr Yekatom's specific individual circumstances, conforms with the purposes of punishment under the Court's legal framework, and adequately acknowledges the victims' suffering and harm, whilst safeguarding Mr Yekatom's prospects of rehabilitation and reintegration into society. Consequently, the Chamber considers imprisonment to constitute a sufficient penalty for Mr Yekatom and therefore does not impose any fine in addition thereto. Deduction of time spent in detention

The Chamber recalls that, in accordance with Article 78(2) of the Statute, '\[i\]n imposing a sentence of imprisonment, the Court shall deduct the time, if any, previously spent in detention in accordance with an order of the Court'.

Efforts to promote peace, reconciliation and social cohesionThe Ngaïssona Defence submits that Mr Ngaïssona's concrete and genuine efforts to promote peace and reconciliation between Muslims and non-Muslims of the CAR should be given significant weight. In particular, the Ngaïssona Defence lists eight concrete actions which it submits contributed to peace and to protect the Muslim population. Furthermore, it argues that Mr Ngaïssona never personally gained from these actions, referring to the many obstacles he faced as Anti-Balaka national coordinator, and that they demonstrate Mr Ngaïssona's genuine will as a political leader to use his influence to calm the intercommunal violence. It also submits that several of the measures proposed by Mr Ngaïssona were adopted by the transitional government and the international community, which confirms that they were genuine and concrete. It adds that the limited success of these initiatives should not bear any weight and that several witnesses, including Catherine Samba-Panza, testified that the situation in the CAR would have been worse without Mr Ngaïssona.

The Chamber further notes that within the first months of becoming general coordinator, Mr Ngaïssona provided the transitional government with a plan for the billeting and inclusion of Anti-Balaka elements in a DDR programme. While a DDR programme was eventually set up some years later, the Chamber is not persuaded by the argument that Mr Ngaïssona's involvement in the DDR proposals can be construed as a genuine peace effort. Instead, it considers that Mr Ngaïssona was primarily motivated by ulterior motives, including financial and political reasons.

First, in terms of Mr Ngaïssona's financial motivations, it recalls the testimony of Jo-Brice Ouabiro Dana who stated that Mr Ngaïssona said during a meeting that taking care of the Anti-Balaka should not only be his responsibility, but that they should start a process with the government to take care of them. Second, in terms of Mr Ngaïssona's political motivations, it is clear from the evidence that Mr Ngaïssona and the Anti-Balaka as a whole wanted to be taken into account within the transition process, including for personal interests, and that the DDR proposals were utilised for this purpose. For example, the Chamber received evidence that Mr Ngaïssona sought a post as DDR coordinator within the new transition government. Third, and most importantly, the Chamber notes that it has received evidence which suggests that the proposals were not genuine. For example, the Chamber considers of note in this regard the testimony of Catherine Samba-Panza, who said that Mr Ngaïssona's statement of being ready to put down weapons was a 'political spin' ('effets d'annonce'). Accordingly, Mr Ngaïssona's actions in relation to the DDR programme have not been taken into consideration for the purpose of the present assessment.

paragraph_text_preview: The Chamber also notes that it received evidence that Mr Ngaïssona made some efforts to stop and deter the Anti-Balaka from committing crimes both during and after the period relevant to the charges, including by giving elements money for their needs. At the outset, it notes that it does not consider such financial assistance mitigating on the basis that this would run counter to the Chamber's finding that financial contributions which aim at sustaining an armed group, such as to provide for its food or other sustenance, can amount to a form of assistance through which liability under the Statute can be incurred. The Chamber also does not consider the setting up of a 'military police' by the general coordination under Mr Ngaïssona's lead as mitigating. It considers that at no point did Mr Ngaïssona systematically or genuinely seek to prevent the Anti-Balaka from committing crimes. In this regard, the Chamber recalls its discussion on the concept of 'fake Anti-Balaka' and its conclusion that Mr Ngaïssona used this concept to suggest that the violence and abuses attributed to the Anti-Balaka were committed by individuals not linked to the Anti-Balaka. The Chamber further recalls that in an interview in July 2014, when asked about violent acts committed by the Anti-Balaka, Mr Ngaïssona sought to portray them as isolated acts by specifically identified individuals, which, at that time, Mr Ngaïssona knew not to be correct. In the present section, the Chamber addresses crime-specific considerations in relation to each of the 28 crimes of which Mr Ngaïssona is convicted. Each section contains general considerations applying to all crimes of the relevant incident. This has been done merely for clarity and avoidance of duplication. paragraph_text_preview: Destruction of the adversary's property as a war crime (Count 33)The war crime of destruction of an adversary's property is a crime against the right to property, which is in principle of lesser gravity than crimes against life, physical integrity, and personal liberty and dignity. Considering the protected interests at stake, the Chamber deems this crime to be of substantial gravity in abstracto.

In this respect, the Chamber notes that the actual gravity of this crime is variable, taking into account factors such as the economic consequences for the victims and the number of victims. Further, in addition to the deprivation of the right of property of the owner, the crime's gravity may increase depending on the de facto function of the property destroyed, particularly if it included people's homes. Indeed, in such cases, the perpetrators do not merely destroy structures, but also destroy people's homes -- a place where the victims ought to have been able to feel shielded and safe, depriving them of a private place, a shelter and a sense of security.

In this respect, the Chamber recalls that the Bossangoa Attack, and the specific targeting of Muslim residential areas and the Muslim civilian population therein, forced Muslim civilians to flee and seek shelter at the École de la Liberté, where their numbers rose into several thousands. Nonetheless, this consideration must be assessed alongside the fact that Mr Ngaïssona is convicted of 28 crimes, which were committed in the context of four separate incidents, spanning over different geographical areas. Furthermore, he committed these crimes in the context of an organised armed group and as part of a wider policy, in which he voluntarily participated.

Importantly, the crimes resulted in the violation of numerous fundamental protected interests, including the right to life; the right to physical integrity; the right not to be subjected to torture, and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; the right to liberty and security of person; the right to liberty of movement; the right to freedom of religion and to not be denied the right to practice their own religion in community with other members of their group; the right to property; the right against arbitrary arrest and detention and related procedural guarantees; the right against arbitrary or unlawful interference with their family and home; and the right of all persons deprived of their liberty to be treated with humanity and respect for their inherent dignity.

Considering the above, the Chamber finds that a joint sentence corresponding to the highest individual sentence pronounced is incapable of reflecting Mr Ngaïssona's total culpability. Accordingly, the Chamber considers it appropriate to set the joint sentence for Mr Ngaïssona slightly higher than 11 years.

On the contrary, given Mr Ngaïssona's high profile in the CAR, inter alia, due to his past roles in the FIFA, the CAR politics and as general coordinator of the Anti-Balaka, as well as the resulting heightened public awareness of his trial, the Chamber considers it crucial to set a sentence which has a deterrent effect not only on Mr Ngaïssona, but which also effectively deters others. The Ngaïssona Defence's related arguments concerning the particular context in which Mr Ngaïssona committed these crimes, notably as a reaction to the alleged Seleka crimes, have however been taken into account above.

paragraph_text_preview: Lastly, the Chamber takes note of the Ngaïssona Defence's suggestion to consider 'non-carceral sentences'. It considers this proposal to be incompatible with the Court's legal framework and thus does not consider this submission further.
In light of the above considerations, the Chamber sentences Mr Ngaïssona to a joint sentence of 12 years.

This sentence is pronounced unanimously. While Judge Kovács would have acquitted Mr Ngaïssona of Counts 12, 13, 15 and 16 concerning Saint Cyr's torture and murder, he does not consider his dissent in this respect to have any impact on the joint sentence.

The Chamber is of the view that this term is proportionate to Mr Ngaïssona's specific individual circumstances, conforms with the purposes of punishment under the Court's legal framework, and adequately acknowledges the victims' suffering and harm, whilst safeguarding Mr Ngaïssona's prospects of rehabilitation and reintegration into society. Consequently, the Chamber considers imprisonment to constitute a sufficient penalty for Mr Ngaïssona and therefore does not impose any fine in addition thereto. Deduction of time spent in detention
